📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're all about Meta's Muse AI, you might want to grab your Wear OS watch. The company unveiled that its cute AI assistant is rolling out.

On X this week, the Muse account confirmed that the AI is now available on Google and Apple wearables. The post states, "Works around the clock, and now on your wrist." Meta's AI now supports Wear OS and the Apple Watch. Users will find the cute, cuddly-looking creature that Meta revealed in a previous Muse AI announcement.

Sources indicate that we can infer much of Muse AI's capabilities through this short post on X. The AI will almost certainly help consumers with daily tasks and queries, while also bringing certain capabilities to apps, messages, and the like.

It has been revealed that funnily enough, this seems like another expansion for Meta's Muse AI. If you remember, this cute creation debuted with the "Muse Charm" in September. The Muse Charm looks like a Tamagotchi, and the creation only adds to that comparison. Meta noted the charm was designed to keep users connected with Muse via 5G. The Muse Charm features a 2-inch OLED touchscreen, a camera, a microphone, and speakers.

In a recent development, during its reveal, Meta's CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, mentioned, "We’ve packed a lot of technology with this little guy. So, if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what’s going on around you." What's more, the included camera gives the Muse Charm some real-world practicality. Customers can ask it about what they see, such as a sign in another language.

The Muse Charm was also stated to encroach on smartwatch pricing (which sounds a little weird following this Wear OS announcement).

The Muse Charm, or rather Muse AI in general, is a part of Meta's ambitions for a "people first" era.

Industry observers note that meta revealed Muse Spark earlier this year as its newest LLM, marking a newly introduced direction. The company notes the AI is "small and fast by design, yet capable enough to reason through complex questions." Muse Spark uses multiple AI agents to tackle tasks accurately and swiftly. For health-related queries, Meta says Muse leverages its knowledge base, built from training data provided by over 1,000 physicians.

#201. Cornelis Unveils CN6000: What 800G Networking Means for AI and Supercomputers

Cornelis Unveils CN6000: What 800G Networking Means for AI and Supercomputers

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cornelis has introduced CN6000, an 800-gigabit networking family designed to reduce the time AI accelerators and supercomputers spend waiting for data.
  • The November 12 announcement introduces both Omni-Path and Ethernet adapters, alongside an Omni-Path switch.
  • Sources indicate that the commercial goal is straightforward: expensive processors produce more useful work when the network can keep up with them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cornelis has introduced CN6000, an 800-gigabit networking family designed to reduce the time AI accelerators and supercomputers spend waiting for data. Its headline claim is striking: up to 1.6 billion messages per second on its Omni-Path SuperNIC. Understanding what that means, however, requires separating three different measures of network performance: bandwidth, message rate, and latency.

The November 12 announcement introduces both Omni-Path and Ethernet adapters, alongside an Omni-Path switch. Cornelis says hardware is available for evaluation and early deployments, with partner systems expected in the first quarter of 2027.

Sources indicate that the commercial goal is straightforward: expensive processors produce more useful work when the network can keep up with them. A faster GPU does little to shorten a distributed job while it is waiting for another machine to send a result.

Sources indicate that an AI cluster is a group of connected computers working together. The network carries everything from large blocks of model data to small coordination messages. Its performance has several dimensions:.

800G means 800 gigabits per second. Dividing by eight gives a nominal 100 gigabytes per second, before protocol overhead and other practical limits. It describes data-carrying capacity, not how promptly a chatbot generates words.

Message rate measures a different bottleneck. Sending many tiny pieces of information requires the adapter to process many separate operations, even when they do not fill the link’s bandwidth. Cornelis’s Omni-Path product brief specifies its 1.6-billion-message rate as bidirectional. It is an aggregate capability, not a claim that one application completes that many sequential requests every second.

Latency matters when the next calculation must wait for a message. In Cornelis’s internal 8-byte Intel MPI ping-pong test, the reported latency was 0.95 microseconds for CN6000 versus 1.2 microseconds for NVIDIA InfiniBand XDR at 800G, approximately 21% lower. MPI, or Message Passing Interface, is a standard way for parallel scientific programs to communicate.

That test measures a particular small-message exchange. It does not establish that a training run, simulation, or inference service will finish 21% faster. The outcome depends on how often the application communicates, the sizes of its transfers, congestion, and the rest of the system.

Recent findings suggest that A network interface card, or NIC, connects a server to the network. “SuperNIC” is Cornelis’s product terminology for its specialized high-performance adapters. A switch connects those server links and forwards data between them. The complete arrangement of adapters, switches, links, and communication software is commonly called a fabric.

The distinction is important when buying a cluster. Installing a capable adapter does not automatically upgrade every switch, cable, or software path that its traffic will encounter.

CN6000 offers two fabric choices. Omni-Path is Cornelis’s purpose-built interconnect for parallel computing. Ethernet is the widely used networking foundation familiar to data center operators. The Ethernet adapter targets customers seeking high-performance communication while retaining compatible Ethernet switching infrastructure. InfiniBand, the technology in the benchmark comparison, is another specialized computing fabric; its switches are not interchangeable with Omni-Path switches.

The CN6000 platform therefore represents a family of components and deployment options, rather than a guarantee that any combination of network equipment produces the same result.

The Ethernet SuperNIC implements RoCEv2: Remote Direct Memory Access over Converged Ethernet, version two. The underlying idea, RDMA, lets network hardware move data between authorized memory regions on different machines without making the host CPU copy every payload through the conventional networking path.

According to recent reports, think of it as arranging a direct delivery between two approved locations, instead of asking an intermediary to repeatedly receive and copy the contents. The CPU still has work to do in establishing and managing communication; the benefit is reducing its involvement in the data movement itself.

In a recent development, NVIDIA’s RoCE documentation explains that version two carries RDMA traffic using IP and UDP headers, allowing it to traverse routed IP networks. Efficient deployment still depends on network configuration and congestion behavior, not merely the presence of an Ethernet connector.

It has been revealed that cornelis’s Ethernet product brief describes hardware offload, support for large numbers of simultaneous operations, and Priority Flow Control. That flow-control mechanism can pause selected traffic classes to help avoid packet loss. The announcement places Ultra Ethernet support on a software-patch path; buyers should distinguish that planned capability from the initial RoCEv2 offering.

According to recent reports, AI inference is the process of using a trained model to produce an answer. For a language model, it includes prefill, which processes the prompt, and decode, which generates the response one token at a time.

Some serving systems run those stages on separate groups of processors so each group can be sized for its job. This is called disaggregated inference. The separation introduces a handoff: information calculated while reading the prompt must reach the processors generating the answer.

Sources indicate that that information includes the key-value cache, usually shortened to KV cache. It stores intermediate attention data so the model can reuse previous work. It is neither the model’s entire set of weights nor simply a saved text transcript.

In a recent development, NVIDIA’s Dynamo documentation describes the sequence: process the prompt, transfer its KV cache, then generate tokens on the decode worker. Faster transfers can make that separation more practical. But moving the cache adds work of its own, so disaggregation is useful when the scheduling and hardware benefits outweigh the handoff cost.

On Omni-Path, CN6000 uses credit-based flow control: a sender transmits according to the receiving side’s available capacity. Adaptive routing can distribute traffic over available paths, while multiple network planes provide separate paths through the fabric.

In a recent development, the Omni-Path brief describes two independent 400G data paths that together provide 800G aggregate bandwidth. If one plane needs service, the other can remain available, though losing part of the network does not preserve its original full capacity.

Industry observers note that the platform also includes a hardware root of trust, secure boot, and device attestation. These help establish that firmware and device identity are trustworthy. Its use of post-quantum digital signatures concerns authentication and integrity; it should not be read as a blanket claim that every network payload is encrypted.

CN6000 follows Cornelis’s earlier scale-out networking work, including the expanded AMD collaboration for scientific computing. Its appeal is the combination of high-performance interconnects with a wider choice of processors and network environments.

For buyers, the useful comparison is the time and cost required to complete their own workload. A simulation that repeatedly exchanges small updates may benefit from lower latency and higher message rates. A service moving large caches may care more about sustained transfer speed and congestion. Both need an appropriate fabric, functioning software support, and qualified server configurations.

CN6000’s announcement adds another option for building those systems. Its peak figures identify capabilities worth testing; the practical win is keeping more compute productive while real applications run.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that google has never said which apps work with Gemini task automation, but Android Authority found a hidden Android 17 target list with at least 134 of them.
  • Sources indicate that most of us are probably familiar with generative AI.
  • When Google first introduced Gemini task automation, they never specified which apps will work with it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that google has never said which apps work with Gemini task automation, but Android Authority found a hidden Android 17 target list with at least 134 of them. It spans food, travel, shopping, and ride apps plus Microsoft Office and Slack, though being on the list doesn’t guarantee Gemini can do a given task in that app.

Sources indicate that most of us are probably familiar with generative AI. It’s what models like Claude and ChatGPT are basically about. You enter a prompt, and the AI responds. It’s more reactive and less proactive. However, agentic AI is becoming the next trend in the space, and it looks like Google’s Gemini task automation covers quite a number of apps on Android.

When Google first introduced Gemini task automation, they never specified which apps will work with it. Instead, Google’s support page only mentions “select apps.” They also say that it supports “everyday tasks,” which includes booking flights and accommodations, buying tickets, and buying and selling products. Not particularly helpful.

However, thanks to Android Authority, they found a hidden server-side target app list on Android 17 that suggests that there are at least 134 apps that can take advantage of Gemini task automation.

This includes apps that are region-specific. For instance, there are apps specific to Australia and Canada that made the list. This includes McDonald’s, KFC, Starbucks, Best Buy, Burger King, and 7-Eleven. It also appears that the target app list goes beyond the categories Google previously mentioned.

It covers productivity apps too, like Microsoft Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams, OneNote, Slack, and Evernote. However, it’s worth noting that an app being on the list doesn’t automatically mean support for task automations. As Android Authority notes, apps need to be on the target list, but at the same time, Gemini needs to support the task you’re asking for.

All of this is to suggest that Google is laying down the groundwork for future updates to Gemini’s capabilities.

InfoQ Homepage Podcasts Doing The Right Thing: Accountability In The Age Of AI Coding Summary.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Shane Hastie: Good day, folks. This is Shane Hastie for the InfoQ Engineering Culture Podcast. Today I'm sitting down with Hugo Venturini. Hugo, welcome. Thank you for taking the time to talk to us.

Hugo Venturini: Thank you, Shane, for having me.

Shane Hastie: Now, we are sitting in opposite sides of the world. I'm in Upcoming Zealand and you are somewhere in Europe.

Hugo Venturini: Yes, right now I'm in Spain, in Valencia.

Shane Hastie: Nice. You've got a beautiful warm summer. I'm sitting in a pretty cold winter, but we'll get past that. My normal starting point with these conversations is, who's Hugo?

Industry observers note that hugo Venturini: So I'm a software engineer. I defended my PhD on the debugging of optimized code in 2008. And after that, I joined the industry as a software engineer and I climbed the ladder one step after the other. Senior then manager. I was a manager at Meta, Facebook at the time. I was accountable for the type checker and the compiler of the hack language. Eventually I decided to try to create my own organization, grew it, then joined another organization, was the CTO of Qwant, the search engine, 90 people in the organization from network engineers to AI researchers. And right now, I work in a software company, startup company that deals with tooling for AI, to help AI do the right thing, so to speak.

Shane Hastie: The right thing. What do we mean when we say, "The right thing", today?

Recent findings suggest that hugo Venturini: Somebody's making a decision about what should be provided as a product to users. Somebody's about to write the code. Somebody will test it. Somebody will make the decision to release this to prod and somebody will use it. It can be all different people or it can be the same person at every step. Doing the right thing, to me, is solving the problem to a user. And then at every step, you got doing the right thing of that step. And for a code generation, it is generating the proper code to some extent.

Shane Hastie: Now, somebody made a decision, but all too often today we are seeing the addiction of, "Yeah, but the agent did this. The code generator did this".

Hugo Venturini: I think humans are in charge and humans should be accountable and are, most of the time, at least to what I can see, and that's the right thing. I'm not minimizing what it does, but AI is just another tool. It's a very powerful tool. And don't get me wrong, I still got these wow moments several times, not a day, but at least a week. And yet if it fails, the one conducting this great tool is accountable, is in charge and should answer what goes wrong. Doing the proper thing is doing what the human asks it to do. And when you want to generate code, code has to be to the colon, to the semi-colon, to the character. And if it does not, many times, the proper tooling can actually tell the AI how to loop and give the right feedback. So when it comes back to the human, a great deal of what could be automated has been automated.

Shane Hastie: One of the things that we are seeing, and various studies are pointing to this, the size of pull requests are getting bigger and bigger. I've heard stories of the 2000 lines, a senior engineer who's got a backlog of over 300 pull requests, each of which is hundreds of lines long waiting to be reviewed.

In a recent development, hugo Venturini: First, the size of pull request is a problem which does not rise with AI. It was already existing before. And the first thing is asking yourself, "Should I review everything?" Sometimes you got all that boilerplate. We could already, before AI, automate the verification. Let me do this. If it compiles, that's already a good thing. If it passes all the tests you've created, if it behaves the way you wanted it, do you really need to review the code? That was already not the case before.

Second thing is, already before as well, and I've lived in an organization that was working like this, you don't have to go for a signature of a diff for every single diff you do. Eventually people are good enough, senior enough or do trust each other that claims, "I can totally merge this diff without having anybody reviewed it. And if it goes wrong, I'm accountable for fixing it. That'd be okay, but I'm totally sure and people trust me to merge it already". And sometimes you've got the heart of the product which you want to create and you need to be able to review for two reasons. First, for quality. Second, for sharing the knowledge, of course. And sometimes it's really just boilerplate that you can totally merge it.

In a recent development, with AI, big reviews always, and you can still, I believe, not go for who's got the biggest review, but who's handy enough to get your AI to create the proper diff and the proper stack of diff. So you get only one to review what the heart of the product is. I think with AI, because of the wow effect, some people are playing this game of the wow effect with, "Look, I have rewritten this entire big product in only one diff", which is just for the show. Let's face it, nobody does this. And before, at the group of engineers, if anybody were doing this, we were all telling him or her, "Please, help us review your code". That's one thing. And after that, you got the number of diffs and that's another problem.

According to recent reports, how do you review for number of diffs? I don't have any good answer and I'm really eager to have anybody telling me, "How do you do this?" Right now, what we've decided in my team is we don't review everything. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Cloud expanded its AI agent monitoring and evaluation tools on November 13, 2026, adding customer-controlled logging, dashboards, privacy safeguards and spending limits across BigQuery and Looker for managed data agents and custom agents built with Agent Development Kit (ADK) or LangGraph.
  • The system uses a common telemetry path for first-party and custom agents.
  • It has been revealed that several core monitoring features are generally available (GA).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Cloud expanded its AI agent monitoring and evaluation tools on November 13, 2026, adding customer-controlled logging, dashboards, privacy safeguards and spending limits across BigQuery and Looker for managed data agents and custom agents built with Agent Development Kit (ADK) or LangGraph.

The system uses a common telemetry path for first-party and custom agents. Managed Conversational Analytics agents emit telemetry automatically, while custom ADK or LangGraph agents can send structured telemetry with single-line SDK instrumentation. The data lands in BigQuery tables owned by the customer for analysis in Google Cloud’s developer and administrator tools.

It has been revealed that several core monitoring features are generally available (GA). BigQuery Studio’s prebuilt dashboards track usage, active sessions, top knowledge sources and latency. Looker System Activity dashboards for Conversational Analytics are also GA in Looker (Google Cloud core) and Looker (original), covering engagement and token usage. User ratings and query review in the Responses & feedback tab remain in preview.

Industry observers note that google Cloud separates operational telemetry from conversation content so administrators and agent owners can govern the two layers independently. Cloud Monitoring supplies aggregate metrics for request volume, latency and token usage, while Cloud Trace provides step-by-step spans for each request. Cloud Trace observability scopes can consolidate telemetry across multiple agent projects.

Industry observers note that those operational metrics and sanitized first-party trace spans exclude customer core content, including user prompts, model responses, internal thoughts and generated SQL. This allows platform teams to monitor activity without automatically giving operational tools access to the substance of each interaction.

For deeper auditing, agent owners and editors can opt into conversation logging for individual agents. A Google-managed service agent then streams prompts, responses and turn-level telemetry through the BigQuery Storage Write API into a customer-owned agent_events table. The table inherits the dataset’s identity and access management permissions, customer-managed encryption keys and VPC Service Controls.

Privacy guardrails check each turn before logging and skip logging for that turn when a knowledge source uses row-level security, column-level policy tags or dynamic data masking. If a logging error occurs, the user’s chat session continues uninterrupted. The design therefore distinguishes broad operational visibility from narrower, explicitly enabled access to full interactions.

It has been revealed that google Cloud claims custom agents can retain more diagnostic detail through the open-source ADK plugin, which can stream full tool-invocation trees, time-series telemetry and multimodal payloads into BigQuery. First-party conversation logging deliberately strips low-level tool arguments and internal SQL.

In a recent development, the logs also provide a basis for cost management. Each BigQuery conversation turn records input, output, thought, cached and total token counts alongside total turn latency. Looker System Activity separately reports estimated input and output tokens across business-intelligence workloads.

According to recent reports, per-query caps on BigQuery bytes scanned use dry-run estimates to block oversized queries without incurring on-demand scan charges. Separately, daily input and output token quotas for BigQuery and the Conversational Analytics API are in preview. Those quotas can be applied per project, user or agent through the Google Cloud console or gcloud CLI.

The combination pairs consumption reporting with active limits. Byte-scan caps address query spending before execution, while the preview token quotas extend enforcement to agent consumption across projects, people and individual agents.

Google Cloud’s open-source Prism tool tests Conversational Analytics agents grounded in BigQuery tables or Looker Explores. It supports reusable test suites, regular-expression assertions and multi-region agent discovery, with evaluations focused on SQL accuracy and answer quality before prompt, model or schema changes reach users.

Recent findings suggest that prism can write completed evaluation runs to BigQuery tables partitioned by day, placing benchmark results alongside production agent_events records for analysis in BigQuery and Looker. Native first-party BigQuery agent evaluations are separately available in preview through an API and a guided Colab notebook.

Industry observers note that the announcement makes customer-owned BigQuery telemetry the common layer for monitoring, cost controls and evaluation, tying agent oversight to existing warehouse permissions and security controls. Managed conversation logging and the main dashboards are GA, while token quotas, native evaluations and some Looker feedback features remain in preview. For production teams, deployment design therefore includes both the boundary between operational traces and full conversations and the differing availability of each control.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that “Out here at Fort Knox, we’re looking at how autonomous mobility technology can be paired with payloads to enable new warfighter capabilities,” explained Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA.
  • According to recent reports, during the demo an operator received a tip about a simulated threat alongside some satellite imagery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Pentagon has been testing packs of autonomous ground vehicles (UGVs) in simulated combat situations. In mid-October, at Fort Knox’s St. Vith Range in Kentucky, four UGVs “worked as a team, negotiating and surveilling the rolling landscape in search of enemy forces,” recalls a DARPA blog post. These UGVs are highly modular and can be kitted out with a wide range of tactical add-ons, but target engagement was controlled by a human operator. This latest exercise was prompted by the request of European allies.

It has been revealed that “Out here at Fort Knox, we’re looking at how autonomous mobility technology can be paired with payloads to enable new warfighter capabilities,” explained Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA. The blog notes that this location was also chosen as it represents a similar landscape to the European theater.

According to recent reports, during the demo an operator received a tip about a simulated threat alongside some satellite imagery. They then sent the pack of UGVs to the area to surveil the landscape and identify targets. Smartly, a sole UGV went ahead of the pack to scout, with the three others waiting behind. The scout UGV was equipped with a flying drone. In a real-world scenario this could have been flown for better visuals or to strike the targets from the sky. “Soldiers can mount anything and everything onto – 240 Bravos, drones, rockets,” said a technician attending the demo, as they are “super modular platforms.” The blog indicates three of the four UGVs in the exercise had drones.

After the designated area was scouted by the leading autonomous ground vehicle, other UGVs followed on “to provide cover and support.” A simulated rocket was fired at a target identified about 300 yards from the robot pack. Finally, the last robot came out of cover, higher up over a ridge, to assess the field of conflict.

Sources indicate that it was emphasized that during the exercise, a human operator was controlling any kinetic engagement. “All the mobility, all the movement, all the detections, all of that is autonomous,” explained Gregory. “But they don’t pull the trigger until a human states pull the trigger.”.

This exercise was part of DARPA’s Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency, or RACER program. Expertise required for RACER’s success includes vehicle design, algorithm technologies, super intelligence, and secure communications.

According to recent reports, after five years of work, these UGVs can now be instructed to complete tasks on the battlefield, instead of being manually driven, notes Gregory. They roam off-road as fast as any human driver could manage, at a minimum.

In a recent development, testers reckon the UGV packs are ready for deployment and use in “a host of other missions, including food, ammunition and supply logistics and more,” according to the DARPA blog. More UGV pack hunting tests are scheduled for December, with a group of serving soldiers involved.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has officially entered the "Hey Gemini" era with the launch of its first Android XR smart glasses yesterday.

Google has slowly been integrating Gemini into pretty much every aspect of its apps and services. You can now find Gemini everywhere, from the best Android phones to Google services like Sheets, Gmail, and pretty much everything in between.

And with the organization retiring Google Assistant last year, Google has been gradually switching everything over to Gemini. The launch of its first Android XR "Intelligent Eyewear" smart glasses yesterday is yet another example of that shift.

When Google revealed its Android XR-powered smart glasses yesterday, the organization revealed that users will be able to access Gemini not by saying "Hey Google," as we at the moment do on Android phones and smart home devices, but by using the upcoming "Hey Gemini" hotword instead.

Saying "Hey Gemini" on these smart glasses will trigger the same Gemini-powered AI assistant we've been using for quite some time now. However, this is the first time Google has introduced a different hotword for Gemini, moving away from the familiar "Hey Google" phrase and signaling a clear shift in how the firm wants consumers to interact with its AI assistant.

In a recent development, for now, the "Hey Gemini" hotword doesn't work on other devices like Android phones or smart home devices, which still rely on "Hey Google" to activate the assistant. However, it's pretty clear that Google is moving toward making Gemini the face of its AI-powered experiences, and the upcoming hotword could eventually make its way to other devices as well.

Of course, Google hasn't confirmed whether or when it plans to replace "Hey Google" across its other products. But with "Hey Gemini" now making its debut on Android XR smart glasses, it'll be interesting to see how long the familiar Google Assistant hotword sticks around.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20.

In a recent development, intelligent Eyewear is meant to be worn all day rather than the sunglasses-heavy approach taken by others. The frames are 40-44 grams with the weight balanced evenly.

There are two open-ear speakers for balanced audio and clear vocals. Control is done by a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes, or via voice commands, with Google debuting a latest “Hey Gemini” hotword.

Another way to control Intelligent Eyewear is through your Pixel Watch or Galaxy Watch, with Fitbit Air support coming next year:.

According to recent reports, each pair features a physical on/off switch so you can “wear them as regular glasses only.” On the privacy front, there is a white indicator light when you take a photo or video that gets saved to your gallery. If the light is covered or maliciously disabled, the glasses will stop recording, with Google running a hardware check when they are charging. Recording also stops when you take off the glasses.

Notably, Gemini commands that invoke the camera — like visual search or translation — will not save images or videos to your Gemini History. These visuals won’t be used to train AI models or for ad targeting. Additionally, the glasses will “automatically redact bystanders’ faces from these visuals before Gemini processes them.”.

Sources indicate that battery life (245mAh) is rated at nine hours on a single charge, with a fully topped-up charging case (Gentle Monster’s shown below) offering seven full charges. Power is transferred via contact pins located on the underside of the nose bridge.

Android XR runs on the Qualcomm Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 with 2GB of RAM and 64GB of storage. Other specifications include Bluetooth 5.4, Wi-Fi 6E, and IPX4 water resistance. Samsung is responsible for engineering the hardware, while there are two eyewear brands at launch.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three styles and a total of 14 variations. Alden, Reid, and Wren are inspired by the brand’s “most beloved silhouettes.” Pricing starts at $395 for optical and sun styles in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black.

The Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear collection features six frames in bold colors like dark red, pink, gray, and yellow, with 16 total variations. They can be paired with tinted, clear, blue, or brown lenses, with prescription options available for most designs. Pricing starts at $449 and will be available in the US and South Korea.

Intelligent Eyewear can be used for contextual visual searches, asking Gemini about your day, and having it accomplish tasks.

Google Maps offers turn-by-turn directions, while there’s real-time Google Translate in over 70 languages.

Like on phones, Gemini Guided Vision “offers conversational audio descriptions to people with vision impairments.” This can be used to read fine print, identify color differences, find items, and explore unfamiliar places.

According to recent reports, these glasses also serve as always-available headphones with support for YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, and Audible. The Glasses companion app supports:.

Pre-orders for Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear start today with retail availability on December 10.

Industry News: Google Rolls Out Fix for Missing Vitals and Fitness Data in Health Platform

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google has released a fix for Google Health that restores missing health metrics and fitness data for affected iOS people.
  • Google Health is supposed to be the place where your health and fitness data is consolidated.
  • According to Android Authority, Google has confirmed to the publication that it is rolling out a fix for the Google Health app that will address missing vitals and data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has released a fix for Google Health that restores missing health metrics and fitness data for affected iOS people. The enhancement, version 5.12.2, addresses missing readings, including heart rate variability, blood oxygen, and skin temperature.

Google Health is supposed to be the place where your health and fitness data is consolidated. It’s like a dashboard for all things health-related, so we can imagine how some people are annoyed that certain vitals and data were missing. Thankfully, Google has pushed out a Health fix.

According to Android Authority, Google has confirmed to the publication that it is rolling out a fix for the Google Health app that will address missing vitals and data. This comes on the heels of the release of version 5.12 last week.

The trouble started after version 5.12 landed last week. Fitbit users reported missing heart rate variability, blood oxygen, and skin temperature readings. Resting heart rate and breathing rate vanished for some people too. One support thread opened on November 9 said vitals had been missing for two to three days. Google states no data was lost. Version 5.12 also added blood pressure logging for Fitbit Air users.

Recent findings suggest that in a statement shared with Android Authority, a Google spokesperson mentioned, “We are rolling out a fix for the issue where a small number of iOS owners were missing metrics like vitals and daily totals for steps, distance, and energy burned. Updating to app version 5.12.2 will fix the issue. No user data was lost.”.

Sources indicate that that being stated, if your vitals are still missing, here’s what you can do. For affected iPhone people, they can check the App Store for version 5.12.2. You can also try signing out of Google Health and back in again. Some users say this brought the readings back. Some users also said switching to the weekly or monthly view helped.

It’s worth mentioning that Google only mentioned iOS in its statement. So it’s unclear whether Android customers saw the same bug. Most Android users are still on version 5.11 anyway, so they might be safe. Either way, it won’t hurt to double-check. If you do notice any missing vitals, you should probably report it to Google ASAP so they can work on a fix.

#192. Presentation: The Influence Toolkit

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 36m • 📚 Deep Dive (7103 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

Presentation: The Influence Toolkit

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 36 min read (7103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~36 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage Presentations The Influence Toolkit.
  • Henry Wilson shares actionable tools from the BBC Sounds re-architecture to help senior engineering leaders drive technical strategy.
  • Henry Wilson is Senior Architect in the BBC’s Product Group, responsible for backend audio teams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Presentations The Influence Toolkit.

Henry Wilson shares actionable tools from the BBC Sounds re-architecture to help senior engineering leaders drive technical strategy. He discusses building buy-in, navigating active resistors, using RFCs and ADRs, and balancing tradeoffs - showing that effective software architecture is fundamentally about communication, relationship-building, and organizational influence.

Henry Wilson is Senior Architect in the BBC’s Product Group, responsible for backend audio teams. Having worked as a Principal Engineer and Senior Architect at the BBC, he focuses on technical leadership, organizational influence, and senior IC career pathways while guiding complex backend systems and engineering teams.

Software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Henry Wilson: I want to start today with a thought exercise. I want you to think about what single skill makes you excel in your current job. I'm sure some of you are thinking about your technical skills, your ability to design architectures, to write code or to solve problems. Maybe some of you are thinking about your research skills, your ability to draw together information from different sources and synthesize it into a plan of action. I'm sure there are many other possible answers that you could have thought of. My view is that if, like me, you're a senior individual contributor at a large organization, the single skill which contributes most to your effectiveness in your role is influence. I would wager that's also true for any of you that hold senior engineering management roles. Let's talk about influence.

I'm a senior architect responsible for the teams in the BBC's audio backend. Just to give a flavor of what those teams do, they deliver the backend functionality for the BBC's audio offering. On BBC Sounds, the BBC's flagship audio experience where they serve an audience of 4.8 million weekly active owners. On third party platforms like Apple and Spotify, where the BBC's RSS platform is responsible for 85 million content downloads a month.

I'm sure some of you are thinking, why influence? There are many facets to a senior individual contributor role. Why do I want to talk to you about this one? I want to talk to you today about influence, because I've spent a lot of time in the last few years thinking about it. My career at the BBC has seen me move between different roles and different teams, from engineer to senior engineer, then principal engineer, and now architect. In those different roles, I've seen firsthand the power that good influence can have, and what can happen when influence is used in the wrong way. I've also found myself frustrated when I haven't been able to influence a decision in the way that I want to. Why couldn't I persuade that individual or group to adopt the approach I'm suggesting? What could I have done differently that might have led to a different outcome?

Recent findings suggest that another reason that I want to talk about influence is that it's about communication. Communication really fascinates me. Language is so powerful, so versatile, but also so full of nuance. I love exploring it and understanding how I can make better use of the potential power of my words. The English language leaves an awful lot of room for ambiguity, for accidental implication or for misunderstanding. Ultimately, while senior IC roles are very technical, they're also all about communication. The phrase individual contributor might imply that you sit in a corner on your own being awesome and smashing out contributions, but the reality in large organizations is that you spend far more of your time communicating than you do writing code or creating designs. Even the code that we do write and the designs and documents we create are forms of communication. Ultimately, we're all expressing and communicating ideas all the time in different ways.

It has been revealed that finally, I want to talk about influence because it feels particularly significant for architects. Now, not all organizations have architecture as a separate role from engineering. Some will use senior principal or other staff-plus roles to fulfill a lot of the same duties around technical strategy and technical leadership. At the BBC, architecture sits as a distinct discipline from engineering, which can lead to teams lacking understanding of what architecture's role is and being unsure as to how they should respond if their architect is telling them something they don't understand or is giving them direction that might not match the direction that their colleagues in engineering are giving them. The man in the picture here is the man none of us want to be and none of us want to work with. The architect in the ivory tower handing down their perfect designs, but devoid of context about how those designs will be implemented and become a practical reality.

They might have influence, but if they do, they're using it in the wrong way. The difference between the ivory tower architect, someone who is likely to be isolated, might be disliked and definitely won't be effective, and the friendly neighborhood architect who the team want to work with and who helps them solve problems is all about communication and all about influence.

It has been revealed that what do we really mean when we talk about influence in the context of senior IC roles? Let's start with this dictionary definition. There are some useful aspects to this, in particular around our ability to have an effect on someone or something, and focusing on the character, development, or behavior of that personal thing. As senior individual contributors, we're often trying to influence behaviors of people or teams, when we want to influence process or ways of working, or we're trying to influence the character and development of the software being built by leading teams to make good technical decisions. Influence is so key to these roles. Without it, it's really hard to be effective in the space. There are likely to be many different targets that you might be trying to influence in different situations. The teams that you have technical responsibility for, the senior leadership in your area, and other disciplines you work with, like product, UX, and architecture or engineering.

In a recent development, influence for these roles is not the same as managerial authority. Managers still need the ability to influence their staff beyond just saying, I'm your boss, please do as I ask. Nonetheless, there is a reasonable expectation that if your boss asks you to do something, you'll probably do it. Senior IC roles can't rely on that. They need to build reputation with the individuals and teams they're trying to influence. That generally revolves around building relationships. One analogy which I sometimes find useful to consider when we talk about influence is to think of it as a catalyst. We can build our influence by nurturing our relationships, proving ourselves useful to the teams and individuals we work with, being measured in our steer and our interventions. This influence gives us power when significant decisions need to be made and can be used to push technical decision-making forward at key inflection points.

I hope if you give me the benefit of your time today, you'll be able to take a few things away from this talk. Specifically, I intend to give you some tools or techniques you can use to influence the teams and stakeholders you interact with. I'm going to cover my experiences using these tools in different situations. I hope you'll see some parallels with your own teams and projects. You'll ultimately be able to leverage something from this talk to be more effective in your own role.

The project I'm going to focus on for this talk is a large-scale re-architecture within BBC Sounds, which was started around a year ago. This is part of wider org changes to move to the product operating model and start to embrace platform engineering. Why is this project important? Because the BBC needs to evolve its digital offering to stay relevant. The BBC's audio offering is a key part of the digital estate and we need to ensure that it's in a fit state to serve the audience. First, I want to cover the project context and the organizational changes at the heart of it. The previous team structure was organized around a product vertical for BBC Sounds. Within that vertical, a catalog team provided core metadata for available audio content. A business-led team consumed that metadata and defined the business logic which powers the BBC Sounds experience. That business logic was used to serve the audience-facing experience across clients on web, mobile, TV devices, and smart speakers.

With the move to platform engineering, this structure needed to change. Under the newly introduced structure, the catalog team would sit in platform and the previous business-led team would be split into two halves, one half providing platform APIs. The remaining part of that team would sit within the experiences area of the org, and the audience-facing client teams would also sit within experiences. What would that mean for the split of responsibilities for those new teams? The platform team would own core and personalized metadata with responsibility for creating APIs that describe the catalog of on-demand content, including podcasts, previously aired radio programs, and audiobooks, and live content, the BBC's stable of local and national radio stations. The experience team would own personalization and user experience concerns, building personalized responses based on user context, and owning the logic around experience-specific concerns, such as what content rails are presented in clients, and experience variants, such as the international mode which consumers are presented with when using the app on holiday.

Given that high-level context, I'm now going to drill into some of the complexities around this project and the challenges and opportunities they present when looking at them through the lens of influence. On the technical front, there were various complexities in the BBC Sounds backend landscape to contend with. The technical estate was complex, consisting of over 40 separate microservices with varying degrees of team knowledge and documentation. This is a very zoomed-out view of the estate, just to give you a little flavor of the number of connections and the number of dependencies between different microservices. Some of these key services lacked separation of concerns, mixing personalization, in particular details of user activity, with core API responses. This included the program metadata service, which I'll come back to a little bit more later on. Let's think about those system characteristics, complexity and choices about separation of concerns. We saw in the dictionary definition earlier that influence is about our ability to have an effect on the character of people or things.

In a recent development, persuading teams to revisit design decisions requires influence. The original estate design prioritized performant responses rather than service decoupling. Additionally, inter-service communication was handled via an RPC implementation using Thrift, built using Finatra and Finagle, which are no longer actively maintained. There was also a desire among platform engineering leadership to move away from the tech stack currently used in the estate. Existing services were built using Scala and there was a strong desire to move towards this tech stack that was more commonly used at the BBC due to challenges with recruitment, retention, and knowledge sharing. Through our influence lens, this second complexity is about behavior. If we're seeking to change the day-to-day behaviors of a team who are used to using a given set of tools and ask them to learn and use something different, understandably there could be some reluctance to make that change, and this is where our ability to influence becomes key.

The project also had social complexities. The team had previously operated using a monolithic team structure. There were three engineering teams consisting of 20-plus engineers across dev and test but they'd operated as one large team for over 5 years. There was also an inconsistency around buy-in levels within the team. Attempts to split the team had been attempted before and resisted, and not all members of the existing team were in favor of a split either from a technical point of view or an organizational point of view. Both factors ultimately pointed to a need to try and increase buy-in in order to help with morale and ensure progress on the project. Most social complexities are ultimately about our ability to influence behaviors, and from experience these situations can be really tricky. People problems are almost always harder than technical problems. Finally, there were complexities on the operational front that we needed to consider.

Most significantly this is a high traffic system powering a key audience-facing experience, so there was a need to ensure that the audience experience was not adversely impacted by any of the re-architecture work. On the out-of-hours support front, previously all services had been managed using a single on-call rota leaving a need to consider how to move to clear our ownership boundaries and separate on-call responsibilities across the platform and experience divide but without impacting our operational response. Looked at through our influence lens, again there's a desire to have an effect on system characteristics. We want the system to change but we don't want that to impact the audience, and there is a desire to have an effect on the team's behavior without degrading the operational outcomes.

Given that context, what was my approach? The first steps involved selling the vision to the team. The initial work was to sell the benefits of the change to the team and help them understand why we were doing this. The first key benefit was around increasing the speed of delivery. I'm firmly of the belief that smaller teams with more manageable technical estates can more easily reason about those technical estates and feel confident that they understand everything they're responsible for. This leads to engineers having less fear and greater confidence to evolve the software that they own. Additionally, this change will begin to unlock cross-functional audience experiences which weren't previously possible within the BBC digital estate, such as cross-experience recommendations. Many of you may be fans of "The Traitors," and may also be aware of the companion podcast, "The Traitors: Uncloaked." At present it's not possible to recommend the companion podcast to viewers of the show on iPlayer, and the move towards a platform engineering stance where generic capabilities are exposed to a variety of teams is a key part of breaking down those silos and enabling these richer audience experiences.

Recent findings suggest that I also needed to set expectation with the teams that this change wasn't optional. There was a clear strategy being set by senior leadership and a need to align around that strategy. This kind of project presents key tensions for anyone in an IC role, and that's because those roles rely on building and maintaining strong positive relationships with the teams and individuals you interact with. Operational strategy can't be ignored but the way that you implement that strategy can have a huge impact on your relationships within an organization. This is where we come to the first couple of tools in the influence toolkit. In order to sell the vision, I land on two things. Spoken communication either in person or via video calls is a huge part of the way that we influence people. That spoken communication can be one-to-one or in groups sometimes aided by presenting from slides or talking about documents.

It's absolutely essential to communicate the vision and build rapport across all levels and disciplines, whether that's engineering, delivery, product, architecture, UX, whatever disciplines you might happen to have in your organization. When I'm speaking to people and trying to sell a vision, I try and make space to allow time for questions and challenges, and to engage honestly with the doubts and fears that individuals might have about what's being proposed. Spoken communication is valuable but it doesn't always scale. If you're trying to influence a group of 30 or even 100, that's an awful lot of one-to-one interactions. This is where context documentation comes in. I led on the creation of context documentation that could be used to disseminate the vision to the wider team, and I collaborated closely with key engineers to outline the problem, the challenges, the rationale, and the planned next steps.

In a recent development, inevitably, during this vision setting period, there were some areas of pushback from some members of the team and I had to address those. One of the most significant areas of pushback was the view that we didn't have enough idea of future vision or future requirements to inform our approach for changing the technical estate. To address this, I liaised closely with colleagues in product and established that there were no concrete or hypothetical requirements that would be impeded by the proposed approach. Another really significant area of pushback was the view that doing this properly would take three years and anything else would be a bodge. Ultimately, my response to that was quite simple. We don't have the luxury of indulging in 3-year re-architecture projects which don't deliver audience-facing value. Tradeoffs would be required but this change represents an acceptable first step in the evolution of the estate.

When we're thinking about pushback, it can be useful to think about individuals and teams in the matrix of support and resistance. In the top right you've got active supporters. These people are thoroughly bought into whatever you're proposing and whatever you're trying to achieve. They're already cheerleading what you're doing so you shouldn't need to spend any time influencing them, and they should help in your ability to influence others because they're actively supporting your efforts. In the top left you've got passive supporters. They're not so vocal in their support either because they don't care enough or because they're not comfortable evangelizing to a wider team. You shouldn't need to spend that much time influencing here either but you're unlikely to get active help. In the bottom left you'll find passive resistors. They're opposed to your idea or your initiative, but they're not doing anything to really try and prevent things from happening.

Passive resistance can have an impact on morale because it can lead to grumbling. It's worth identifying anyone in this camp and spending some time trying to influence them, but they're definitely not the key group. Down in the bottom right you've got the active resistors. They're opposed to the idea or the plan and they're trying to head in another direction. This can manifest in a few different ways. Active resistance can involve arguing or dissenting in group discussions or in discussions one-to-one, but it can also present in a less obvious way where people say nothing but quietly keep on doing something that doesn't align with the strategy. The active resistors are the group that you should spend most of your time trying to influence, and they will often represent a disproportionately small number of people or teams within your overall sphere of responsibility. If you can influence these individuals to move to passive support or even active support, your ability to drive change will be hugely improved.

Sources indicate that back to the re-architecture. With the team aligned around the vision, the next step was to break down the problem into manageable chunks and identify the key areas that the teams would need to agree approaches for. I collaborated with stakeholders and discipline leads to identify the areas where significant changes would be required and where agreement would need to be reached. That included ways of working, how the teams would interact as they split apart, and how we would approach the work for the re-architecture. How the teams would approach AWS account management given that up until that point all infrastructure resources had been deployed to a single set of accounts. Agreeing ownership of the services in the existing estate between the newly introduced teams. Agreeing an approach to common libraries and whether there would be a need to adopt an InnerSource model. Looking at a strategy for contract testing to validate the new boundary between platform and experience teams.

Lastly, thinking about how to split functionality in the services at the heart of the estate which needed to change to support the re-architecture. When it comes to achieving consensus, I'm a huge fan of the combined process of RFCs and ADRs, which the teams I was working with in this instance were already familiar with. RFCs, that's request for comment documents, are a powerful starting point for decision-making. I led the creation of an RFC for each significant problem area. The process around RFCs allows for collaboration with key players, and then once you have consensus in a tight group you can widen the group you're seeking input from. This process really empowers good analysis, letting you tease out ideas, gain input, come to consensus, and push decision-making forward. Once each of these RFCs had come to a conclusion, decisions were documented using ADRs. That stands for architecture decision record.

If anybody isn't familiar with the idea of ADRs I really encourage you to look up this blog post by Michael Nygard. It's an excellent rundown of the concept behind that particular kind of documentation. ADRs provide a perfect format to ensure that key decisions are documented tersely for future reference. Documentation is really powerful but it's not enough on its own. It's also necessary to have regular check-ins with your stakeholders. These can be used to identify any remaining points of contention, have any debates that are still necessary. They provide an opportunity to really push for progress, to ask the group to find the compromise, ask if things are really a problem, and agree an approach so that you can move forward and not get bogged down.

In a recent development, A massive part of selling this vision was in helping the teams to understand the long-term strategy but also sending the message that this wasn't the end state, rather a useful stepping stone to allow further evolution of the estate as we evolve the audio offering in line with wider BBC digital aims. Viewing things through that lens, a number of tradeoffs and compromises were accepted. Initially, work on the platform side would create an API on a parity basis, so a newly owned API which provides the same functionality and a very similar API surface to the existing core service. This is probably not the API shape that we would choose if we were designing the API from scratch, and it will undoubtedly require further evolution. Attempting to redesign the API while also splitting the technical estate would have been too complicated and would have introduced unacceptable delays. A greater degree of coupling between platform and experience services than is ultimately desirable will persist for some time after the initial re-architecture work is complete.

Industry observers note that I consider this an acceptable tradeoff to reach a point of separate autonomous teams that are then empowered to further change their technical estates and continue to evolve the system's architecture towards newly introduced goals and requirements. A transitionary approach would be required around operational support. Out-of-hours rotas and the handling of business-as-usual maintenance tasks would not be able to immediately match the desired team structures, and this would be necessary to ensure that operational stability wasn't impacted by the re-architecture work.

I can't cover every facet of a project this large, so I'm going to zoom in on some areas where I feel my influence was particularly useful, starting with some decisions around the tech stack used by the platform API team. The team had taken a decision to use Node.js, moving away from Scala. I identified this as an opportunity to leverage the existing approach used in sister teams, such as the catalog team, and I leaned on my experience in those teams where I'd previously laid the foundations of a monorepo approach using CDK for infrastructure and CI/CD. I shared lots of prior art with the new platform team, including code samples and documentation. I conducted targeted knowledge sharing sessions with the team lead and the principal engineer in that space to ensure that they understood the rationale and advantages inherent in the approaches that I was sharing with them.

It has been revealed that I was also influential in guiding the team towards a managed service approach, an opportunity to move away from the maintenance burden associated with running services on EC2, which was heavily used in the previous estate. I suggested that the team should make more use of managed services, such as Lambda and ECS Fargate, and pushed the team to consider the tradeoffs and use the most managed solution wherever possible to keep overheads low, taking a serverless-first approach and only falling back to serverful options where compelling reasons existed. Back to the influence toolkit, these are the techniques that I lean on when I'm working on the ground with teams. Slack is such a valuable tool for collaboration, and it offers really unique opportunities to influence behavior and decision-making. Being present in team channels and observing day-to-day discussions provides valuable opportunities and allows you to spot technical problems or decision points where there might be an opportunity to share prior approaches or leverage existing organizational knowledge.

In a recent development, slack is so rich. You can link to other Slack conversations, GitHub examples, documentation, blog posts, anything you like. While Slack is a powerful tool, it's really important that you follow up on those discussions. Speak to the key players and make yourself available to answer questions and dig into the detail. Ultimately, the aim here is to empower the team to use tried and tested patterns as a springboard to deliver faster, but also to upgrade or evolve those approaches where newer libraries or tools might be more powerful.

Industry observers note that the second area I'd like to zoom in on is work around the core program metadata service, which I mentioned earlier on. Before the org change had been revealed, work had been planned to remove Thrift from the BBC Sounds estate in order to address security vulnerabilities in the underlying Finatra and Finagle libraries used in the implementation. Due to the complexity of the service implementation, this was many sprints of work for a large number of engineers. That work would ultimately be thrown away in less than a year due to replacement functionality being created in the platform space. Once I'd identified this risk, I raised the issue with senior leadership. There was pushback from the team around the security considerations and the difficulties associated with changing the team's roadmap at short notice. Ultimately, I secured agreement for a change of approach. Once we were further into the re-architecture project, discussions around how to split the core program metadata service began, and the engineers began to think about how far to go with the re-architecture work.

According to recent reports, some of the engineers were keen to look at a larger reimagination of how personalization might work across the estate. I identified this as a source of risk in terms of project timelines. A more complex reimagination could quickly grow arms and legs, leading to elongated project timelines and blocking any work which could deliver audience value. I pushed strongly for the team to distill options with a focus on simplicity and speed of delivery rather than notions of elegance or wider scope. Not a hack, but a pragmatic path forward.

Sources indicate that some of the discussions around the core program metadata service were difficult, with significant differences of opinion among stakeholders. Perhaps the most important part of the influence toolkit is how we use our influence to have those difficult discussions. Having allies is absolutely essential, whether that's your boss, your peers, or other key stakeholders on the projects that you're working on. That's because the best ideas and the strongest visions will still fail to gain traction if you don't have support, because change is hard. Finally, when approaching tricky discussions, radical candor can be hugely powerful. We need to be willing to have difficult conversations, approach them head-on, and be frank in the way that we address problems. It's important to ensure that we do the right thing, not the easy thing. I'm lifting a quote here from Kim Scott's book entitled, "Radical Candor," caring personally while challenging directly. Scott was talking about management, but I think the same principle applies to influence. If we build a reputation as a caring and empathetic co-worker, we build our influence. When we have good relationships with the people we're trying to influence, then we gain the ability to challenge directly and move discussions forward.

I want to touch on how to measure success. I want to bookend the re-architecture story by covering our progress so far. We're not finished, but we're on track. Agreement has been reached on all the major decision points, and those decisions have all been documented in ADRs for future reference. The platform team have already made a lot of great progress towards creating a latest API surface, and the building experiences to integrate with those new APIs is also underway. Now comes the trickier part, what could have gone better? At times, morale in the team has not felt as high as I might have liked. Change is hard, and there are many factors that affect how people feel, but ultimately this points to an area that I could have had more success. I'm not sure there's any such thing as perfect morale, but that doesn't mean we should ever stop trying to find it.

Some of my personal approaches weren't as successful as I'd hoped. Every individual is different, and it often takes time to establish the best way to interact with them. It can be hard to affect positive change when you don't have prior relationships to lean on, or if you're geographically at a distance from the person or team that you're trying to interact with. Sometimes my approach was wide of the mark, and I've tried to learn from those experiences. In terms of buy-in, I think my attempts at vision selling fell short with some members of the team. Now, 100% buy-in is probably unrealistic for a change of any significance, and I remain a big believer in the concept of disagree and commit. Nonetheless, there may have been ways that my vision selling could have been improved.

In a recent development, how do you measure success? How do you tell whether you're any good at influencing the individuals and teams around you? When you're looking to measure your influence around areas of technical complexity, you can track your success by the technical decisions the teams are making. What proportion of those decisions are roughly in line with your desired outcome? How much are those decisions deviating from what you might consider perfect? Reviewing these technical milestones frequently can help you get a feel for the success of your influence. Measuring influence on areas of social and operational complexity is potentially more difficult. You're looking to influence people's behaviors, but behavior can be hard to observe, and individuals won't always be honest about how they truly feel. Outcomes may be harder to track, but you can look for clues. Does morale feel higher? Are you having less difficult conversations? Are you able to classify any of the active resistors you've encountered as passive resistors or as supporters?

In a recent development, the best thing you can do is ask for feedback. Check in with your stakeholders and your teams. Ask them to give an honest assessment of how you're doing. If you feel brave, you can ask someone you often seem to disagree with to give you feedback. You might find something you can learn from and be able to incorporate into your practice, whether that's positive or negative.

The nature of feedback and the different ways we can receive it is something I want to touch on, because feedback comes in different forms, and these different signals can help us understand whether our influence is working in the way we want it to. When people think about feedback, they often mean direct feedback. Either you're actively asking someone to tell you how you're doing or to reflect on their interactions with you over the past six months, perhaps. Or someone has something they wish to address with you, and they provide direct feedback without request. Now, that kind of feedback is really useful, especially if you haven't had to ask for it. That means the person you're interacting with really wanted to tell you something, and that's something that you can always learn from, whether it's positive or negative. You can also get some really valuable insights from indirect feedback, and this is where relationships come in.

If you have friendly, positive relationships with the people around you, then the conversations you have can give you valuable indications of the success of your influence. To give an example, I bumped into one of the engineers in the platform API team a few months ago in the office, and I had a short conversation where I asked them how everything was going. They mentioned how positive they'd found the experience of moving into the new team structure and using the new tech stack, and how much more quickly the team were able to build things in this new world compared to their previous experience. These kinds of conversations could easily be dismissed as small talk, where nothing of value is likely to be learned, but in this case, I received an anecdotal indicator. The approach I'd proposed was working for the team. This kind of positive feedback loop, where we make helpful suggestions to teams, is how we build trust and ultimately grow our influence.

According to recent reports, let's recap the tools I've talked about in the influence toolkit. Spoken communication is so powerful. Find opportunities to talk to people, whether that's one-to-one, in groups, over a coffee, in workshops, whatever settings present themselves to you and feel right. Consider context documentation when you're trying to sell a vision to a substantial team, and use it to scale your influence beyond what can be achieved in one-to-one conversations. Leverage the power of the RFC and ADR process to build consensus and really drive decision-making. Make sure you review regularly with stakeholders around those decisions and keep key players in the loop. Spend time on the ground with your teams. Try and understand the challenges they face, and use tools like Slack to find opportunities to help and guide them. When you share thoughts with your teams in this way, make sure that you follow up. Make time to continue the discussions in the most appropriate way and drill into the detail. Build a network of allies so that your vision is nurtured and you have support when you need it for difficult conversations. Practice radical candor. Build your relationships and be prepared to challenge directly so that you can help your teams to make the right decisions.

It has been revealed that martell: You talked some about how we need to work to get our teams to buy into our vision. Sometimes you're in a place where the vision maybe isn't yours, and you need to get the team to buy into it. Maybe you're not 1,000% aligned. What does that look like? Other than disagree and commit, how do we do that?

Henry Wilson: That's really hard. Sometimes in senior leadership positions, we do get put in a position where the organizational strategy is moving in a certain direction, and it's not necessarily a direction we would have chosen. Ideally you would get some opportunity to feed into that technical direction. You would have the opportunity to talk to senior leadership and challenge, try and influence the direction that's moving in. I think if you aren't successful in that, if the organization is moving in a direction that you disagree with, you do have to disagree and commit. Either that or you have to find another job. That's a really hard position to be in. I think it asks a lot of people to positively sell a vision they don't truly believe in. I suppose you have to ask yourself how much you disagree with this. I think if you disagree with it too much, then maybe you do need to find another job.

Participant 1: What were the biggest challenges from the active resistors and how you tackled those?

Sources indicate that henry Wilson: I think the challenges in this case were, yes, I think there was a lot of pushback about whether this was something that we really wanted to do and whether it was being pursued for the right reasons. When you're dealing with technical teams that have been in place for a long time, regardless of what job title somebody might have or what seniority they technically hold, people who are long established in teams can have a lot of influence. I think that, yes, that presents challenges if key players are grumbling, and espousing a view that we shouldn't be doing this or that this is a waste of time or that it's doomed to failure in some way. There are no easy answers to those kinds of problems, unfortunately. You have to try and get people on side, try and explain the rationale for changes, explain why as an organization you're pursuing a given strategy, but yes, it can be difficult. Some people have very strong opinions and are very stuck in their ways.

Participant 2: How can you choose what hills to die on, if you know what I mean, and just like when you're butting heads with someone and you're like, do I let this go, do I drop it, or you're like, actually no, I really want to pursue this.

According to recent reports, henry Wilson: That's a really tricky judgment call. I think some of it has to be about how significant the change really is. I think you definitely have to try and identify as objectively as you can which areas are really significant, where there's some significant risk. Whether that's to do with timelines or to do with like ongoing maintenance, and you should try harder to persuade people, and where actually the direction they're heading in might not be the one that you would choose. It's more of a toss-up decision, at which point if you argue the toss over every one of those, then you're probably going to make yourself quite unpopular. I think the other thing to bear in mind is where there's an opportunity for learning. I think there's an element with these kind of IC roles where you can get into, trust me I'm a doctor mode.

Recent findings suggest that often, people will learn more from their own tried and tested experience of having gone down the wrong path and found out for themselves why it was the wrong path. I think there's a really interesting judgment call. Sometimes you can see that an approach is wrong, but it's still better to let the team learn that firsthand than to prescribe it or try and prohibit them from pursuing it. There's a really difficult judgment call there around, I suppose, effectively how much time is consumed in allowing an individual or a team to go down that path, and if it feels like a reasonable tradeoff of, ok, we'll lose a couple of weeks, but they'll learn something really valuable, then maybe you let them do it. If it feels like they're going to lose six months, then maybe you shouldn't.

Participant 3: I was just wondering if you've ever been in a situation where engaging somebody who you initially view as like an active resistor has led you to, I suppose, switch to their side or change your initial direction that you wanted to influence them in.

According to recent reports, henry Wilson: That isn't so relevant when you're talking about organizational strategy because you're not going to be terribly popular if you start off trying to sell a vision of organizational strategy and then start trying to undermine it. I think when it comes to slightly less totemic technical decisions, it's really crucial to try and approach those discussions with an open mind. Inevitably, I think all of us when we go into technical discussions, we're going to have some idea of what we think the best outcome to that discussion is, but we're not doing a great job if we're set in that view to the point where nothing that can happen in the discussion is going to influence it otherwise. I think we have to be open to the possibility that somebody could persuade us of a different point of view. Personally, I find that quite refreshing. If I've come in with an idea and then somebody succeeds in persuading me that a different approach would be better, then I've learned something that day and that's really valuable.

It has been revealed that yes, I think it's about trying to be as objective as possible when we consider these things, and trying to make sure that we're doing things on the merit of the technical approach, the actual objective reality as much as we can assess it of what the outcomes are going to be like, rather than notions of pet ideas or personal opinions about who might be voicing the idea. That makes it sound really easy. It's not. Like you walk into a discussion with some preconceived ideas and some biases, it's difficult sometimes to challenge your own assumptions, but yes, it's worth doing.
