#191. Breaking: Samsung S85H review: a great OLED TV for a lower price

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3277 w)

Breaking: Samsung S85H review: a great OLED TV for a lower price

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Samsung S85H is a mostly great budget OLED that delivers brilliant picture quality and is fantastic for gaming.
  • Excellent colors and contrast, with some minor concerns.
  • Great accuracy and some punch, but bass and soundstage lacking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Samsung S85H is a mostly great budget OLED that delivers brilliant picture quality and is fantastic for gaming. Its built-in sound is just average and there are some minor shortcomings, but overall, this is another superb affordable OLED that holds its own against rivals TVs like the LG B6 and TCL QM7L/C7L.

Fully stocked for movies, gaming and smart TV.

Excellent colors and contrast, with some minor concerns.

Great accuracy and some punch, but bass and soundstage lacking.

Razor-thin, lightweight: looks pricier than it is.

Tizen is mostly good, but doesn't beat webOS or Roku.

Every feature you need and fantastic performance.

Rival LG B6 is cheaper, but still offers superb bang-for-your-buck.

Sources indicate that why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.

The Samsung S85H is great entry-level OLED TV that can compete with the best TVs of 2026. It offers a near-full feature set, with brilliant performance at a competitive price. While its closest rival, the LG B6, is cheaper at the moment, and arguably the better buy — as I found when I compared it and the S85H side-by-side — this is still a very capable TV.

In a recent development, the S85H’s picture quality is excellent overall. It delivers punchy, vibrant colors, strong contrast, crisp, realistic textures and good motion handling. It does have a reflective screen, an issue the step-up Samsung S90H doesn’t suffer from, and there are sometimes black-crush problems in darker scenes, but the S85H’s picture is competitive with the best OLED TVs.

Recent findings suggest that sound quality in the S85H is a mixed bag. It has great accuracy, and at times punchy bass, but generally its limited two-channel speaker system can only do so much. Sound feels contained to the back of the screen, and while there is some extension beyond the TV’s frame, it doesn’t offer what one of the best soundbars could. It’s fine for day-to-day viewing, but you’ll want a soundbar if you’re after a more cinematic experience.

For gaming, the S85H is a fantastic budget-OLED option. It has a suite full of features up there with the best gaming TVs — 4K 120Hz, FreeSync and G-Sync, HDR10+ gaming and ALLM — as well as ultra-low input lag and four HDMI 2.1 ports. Its performance is responsive and smooth, and it serves as a superb gaming TV.

The S85H is good value for money. The 55-inch model I tested costs $999 / £999 / AU$1,999, putting it in the more affordable OLED bracket. While its nearest rival, the LG B6, is cheaper ($799 / £999 / AU$1,699 for the 55-inch), making it the better-value buy, the S85H still offers brilliant performance and features for the price, and that price is only going to get cheaper.

Sources indicate that the Samsung S85H is the entry-level model in Samsung’s 2026 OLED TV lineup, sitting below the mid-range S90H and flagship S95H/S99H. It’s available in sizes 48-83-inch, with the 55-inch model I tested launching for $1,499 / £1,399 / AU$2,499 in May-June 2026 (depending on region).

According to recent reports, since its release, the S85H’s prices have dropped across all sizes and in all regions. The 55-inch is now available (November 2026) for around $999 / £999 / AU$1,899, though you can find it for less at some retailers in some regions. The rival LG B6 55-inch is cheaper at the moment in the US and Australia, costing $799 / £999 / AU$1,699, but it’s likely that the ‘cheaper’ title will change hands a few times during these TV’s life cycles.

It has been revealed that closer to 100% is better. Taken using a colorimeter and test pattern generator.

A lower score is better. Taken using a colorimeter and test pattern generator.

Lower is better. Taken using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Video Signal Lag Tester.

It has been revealed that the S85H uses a WOLED panel, the same one as in the rival LG B6 and the same as the step-up S90H, though some sizes are reported to have QD-OLED. The S90H benefits from the upgraded NQ4 AI Gen 3 Processor, which allows for higher brightness and better color performance, while the S85H has the older NQ4 AI Gen 2 Processor built in. The Gen 2 is no slouch, though, and supports picture features such as 4K AI Upscaling and Real Depth Enhancer Pro.

The S85H supports HDR10+, including the new HDR10+ Advanced, HDR10 and HLG HDR formats, but as usual with Samsung TVs, there’s no support for Dolby Vision.

Industry observers note that for audio, the S85H has a 2-channel, 20W speaker system with support for Dolby Atmos. A number of AI sound features are included too, such as AI Sound Pro, as well as Object Tracking Sound (OTS) Lite. Q-Symphony, where the TV’s speakers can be used in conjunction with a supported Samsung soundbar, is also featured.

The S85H supports 4K 120Hz, full VRR including AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync, ALLM and HDR10+ gaming, which works across all of the S85H’s four HDMI 2.1 ports. There’s also a Game Hub, where cloud gaming apps are housed.

Tizen serves as the S85H’s smart TV platform, supporting all major streaming apps such as Netflix and Disney Plus. Tizen also features the Vision AI companion, which uses multiple AI agents to make content and even lifestyle recommendations you may ask such as recommended places for dinner.

As the S85H uses a standard WOLED panel, its brightness doesn’t match that of step-up OLEDs like the S90H or LG C6. In my testing it clocked a peak HDR brightness (on a 10% window pattern) of 833 nits and 854 nits in Filmmaker Mode and Standard respectively. Those scores put it in line with the rival LG B6E (which hit 808 nits and 727 nits in the same respective modes), but are much lower than those achieved by the step-up S90H, which measured 1,689 and 1677 in the same two modes.

Industry observers note that as for fullscreen brightness, the S85H hit just over 150 nits in both Filmmaker and Standard, which is about right for WOLED, but it’s still a significant drop compared to rival mini-LEDs such as the TCL QM7L/C7L, which hit over 600 nits. This means the S85H can struggle in bright rooms, and without an effective anti-glare coating, dark scenes can be hard to watch in brighter conditions, so this TV is best suited to viewing in ambient or dark conditions. Samsung’s step-up S90H OLED, on the other hand, easily handles bright rooms.

Starting with SDR content, the S85H does a good job of upscaling textures. Watching various programs on Samsung TV Plus, textures did look cleaner and sharpened than you’d get on some standard LED and mini-LED TVs, and with bolder colors. While the step-up S90H did a better job with upscaling, the S85H’s was still impressive nonetheless.

Switching to 4K HDR content, the S85H delivers excellent colors. Watching Elemental on Disney Plus in HDR10+, the bold oranges of the fire people and blues of the water people pop throughout the movie, even in the slightly dimmer Filmmaker Mode. Putting the S85H in Movie mode adds more brightness and a bit more color depth which works well for the animation. As Ember runs across multi-colored minerals, colors have a nice shine to them, showing the S85H’s punchy HDR highlights.

Watching a live-action movie, The Sound of Music, the S85H shows it can render realistic-looking colors too. The green fields and blue skies of Austria look wonderfully natural whenever they’re on screen, and the S85H shows true-to-life skin tones in the people as well.

In a recent development, measuring the S85H’s HDR color-gamut coverage, it registered 97.9% of the UHDA-P3 and 73.4% of the BT.2020 color spaces. These numbers are about right for a WOLED TV, but are starting to fall behind those of more premium OLEDs and RGB mini-LED TVs. Still the S85H’s colors were great overall.

The S85H also demonstrates strong contrast. In The Batman, which includes lots of scenes with lights cutting through the dark environments, such as in the Batcave and in aerial shots of Gotham, the S85H shows an excellent balance between these light and dark tones to create an authentic image. The same is true in Project Hail Mary, with both shots of space and scenes inside the ship showing the S85H’s powerful contrast and deep black levels.

Industry observers note that shadow detail is also great, with details and textures legible in challenging dark scenes, such as frames on the wall of Mayor Mitchell’s house in The Batman. I did notice during some particularly dark shots that the S85H was prone to some black crush, even in pitch-black viewing conditions. For the most part however, its contrast was impressive.

The S85H also demonstrated crisp textures in nearly every scene I watched, with people in particular looking true-to-life. This 3D-like level of detail was one of the S85H’s strengths over the LG B6E when I tested the two side-by-side, showcasing the effectiveness of the Real Depth Enhancer feature.

Finally, the S85H demonstrated very good motion for both sports and movies, although some setup is required. I found setting blur reduction to 3 and judder reduction between 3-5 (depending on the content and how fluid you want your picture) was the most effective. There were still some motion artefacts when watching a soccer match on Prime Video, with some blurring of textures in some shots, but the S85H was mostly effective.

The S85H’s two-channel, 20W speaker system isn’t strong enough to allow you to skimp on a soundbar if you want powerful and immersive sound for action-heavy movies and shows, and doesn’t match up to step-up TVs, but is mostly fine for day-to-day viewing and some movies.

Industry observers note that watching the Batmobile scene from The Batman, the S85H’s strength lay in the accuracy of sound, showing how effective the OTS Lite system was. As the Batmobile swerved through traffic, screeching tires and car horns were mapped with real accuracy between the sound and action on the screen.

Impacts also generated some nice punch. As the Batmobile clatters through a barricade, the sound of scraping metal had some weight to it, and as the Batmobile’s engine revved, there was some punchy bass. However, when I pushed the volume, the bass did seem to fizzle out, and high-end sound could be a little harsh.

While I did hear some extension of sound from the frame of the screen, particularly during the aforementioned swerving manoeuvres, the sound felt contained to the rear of the screen, making it feel like the viewing experience was lacking some depth. Speech was mostly clear throughout, but could get lost at times. Again, you want a cinematic experience, I’d hook up a soundbar.

It has been revealed that the most striking thing visually about the S85H is how thin it is compared to rival TVs in this price range. It has a sleek, metal frame and a razor-thin depth that suggest a more premium price. Even its rear panel is fairly trim, with only a small bump to accommodate the connection ports.

It has been revealed that for the 55-inch model I tested, two plastic feet were supplied which, while they felt a little cheap, were very easy to install. You can choose between two positions for the feet, narrow and wide, with the latter being very useful if you have a soundbar. The TV is also very light for a 55-inch model, but still felt sturdy when placed on a TV stand.

Recent findings suggest that the S85H comes with Samsung’s SolarCell remote, which offers solar and USB-C charging. Its small size means it could get lost quite easily, but it feels light in the hand, and offers all the usual options (streaming app shortcuts, settings, power and volume).

Samsung’s own Tizen serves as the smart TV platform for the S85H, and with it come a host of AI features via the Vision AI companion, which uses AI agents to help with content recommendation, lifestyle advice, and more general questions you might ask of a smart assistant (how long is a day on Jupiter was one of the example prompts). There are also a host of AI Picture and sound features via the AI Mode settings (found under the Advanced Features menu), such as AI Soccer Mode and Adaptive Sound Pro.

Industry observers note that tizen’s main three hubs on the main screen — For You, Live, and Game and Apps — host recommended content, live TV, gaming content and a general apps page respectively. These pages are generally laid out well, but do have banner ads that take up about a third of the page. I also found Samsung TV Plus autoplays on the For You page and can sometimes take over the page if left idle, which can be frustrating.

In a recent development, you can choose from a good number of picture settings, all housed in logical places within the settings menu. Some of these settings, such as Auto HDR Remastering for SDR content, can be effective. Sound settings are a bit more limited, and I’d have liked more than two sound mode options. Tizen is a solid interface overall, but doesn’t quite match up to LG’s webOS or Roku for ease-of-use.

According to recent reports, the S85H is an excellent choice for gaming. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, perfect for multiple consoles, and all of these support 4K 120Hz, full VRR including FreeSync and G-Sync, ALLM and HDR10+ gaming. The featured Game Hub is a useful home for all things gaming, and offers quick access to a connected console and cloud gaming apps.

The S85H’s input lag registered 9.2ms at 4K 60Hz and 4.5ms at 1080p 120Hz, the latter of which is one of the lowest scores I’ve seen. This translates into actual gaming too. Playing Battlefield V, motion felt incredibly smooth with razor-sharp response times — extremely useful when faced with tons of enemies.

Picture-wise, the S85H’s brilliant quality is great for gaming. The colors of autumnal trees during one mission really popped on screen, while textures were very crisp, and, during night-time missions, black tones were deep and contrast was strong.

The 55-inch S85H I tested presently costs $999 / £999 / AU$1,999, which is very good for a budget OLED. Considering the features and performance it delivers, it’s great value for money overall.

Industry observers note that right now, its major rival, the LG B6, is cheaper in most places. A 55-inch LG B6 (or in some cases LG B6E, which isn’t markedly different from the standard B6) costs around $799 / £999 / AU$1,699. The B6 offers near-identical features and performance, so right now it’s the better deal.

Recent findings suggest that the Samsung S90H is a notable step-up over the S85H, offering higher brightness, better picture quality and an anti-reflection screen for bright-room viewing. The 55-inch model costs $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,999, so if you’re in the UK and US and can stretch your budget, it’s worth the upgrade. Still, the S85H is good value overall, and I expect its prices will drop and fall more in line with those of the B6 as time goes on.

Read our TCL QM7L review and TCL C7L review.

I first started my testing of the Samsung S85H with casual viewing to assess which picture mode was best, landing on Filmmaker and Movie modes for movies and TV and Standard for sports and broadcast TV.

I then tested the S85H using reference 4K Blu-ray, analyzing its color, contrast, textures and detail and motion, while also using SDR sports and daytime TV to analyze its upscaling capabilities.

Once these tests were complete, I took measurements using a Murido Six G 8K test pattern generator, a Jeti Spectral 15VA spectroradiometer profiled with the a Klein K-10A colorimeter, and recorded the measurements using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software.

I tested the S85H's brightness, measuring on a white window pattern in sizes 1-100%, with a focus on 10% peak and 100% fullscreen brightness, in both SDR and HDR.

I then measured its color and grayscale accuracy in SDR using Delta-E averages (the margin for error between the test pattern signal and what's displayed on screen).

Next was HDR color gamut coverage, where I sued the UHDA-P3 (the color space used for 4K Blu-ray and digital cinema releases) and BT.2020 (becoming more commonly used) color spaces.

I also measured the S85H's HDR EOTF, using 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000 nits targets, which highlights the TV's accuracy between light and dark tones. I also measured its Spectral Power Distribution, which measures its color performance.

Finally, I measured its input lag in both 4K 60Hz and 1080p 120Hz using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Input Lag Tester.

Its “growth at all costs” mindset has actively poisoned people’s perception of the form factor. Under Meta’s watch, glasses have gained a creepy connotation before their utility has been fully realized.

Google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done. Every single aspect has been considered, and the result is worthy of being most people’s introduction to the form factor.

Officially, Android XR glasses are known as Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear. The branding is a mouthful, and I’m not quite sure “Intelligent Eyewear” will take off. Something more colloquial, like “Google glasses” — glasses.google is the landing page — or “Samsung glasses,” will probably stick in the public consciousness.

In a recent development, that critique aside, the name reflects how Google wants Intelligent Eyewear to actually replace your existing glasses. Unlike the Ray-Ban trap that I frankly think Meta did not consider, Google’s offerings are not situational or activity-based devices like sunglasses. These are a “smart” upgrade to the assistive device some people have to wear.

Industry observers note that as a wearable, smart glasses are a bit like smartwatches in that the platonic design is pretty well established and indistinguishable from traditional eyewear. Unlike watches, glasses are so visible on people’s faces that form overrides everything else.

Fortunately, the Samsung hardware I wore for an hour last week looks and feels like glasses, almost unremarkably so. I’d venture to say that audio-only glasses without a display are a solved design challenge. Google emphasized that, at 41 grams, this is the lightest pair of smart glasses on the market, and it worked to make sure the weight is distributed evenly.

The sides of the stems that face your head feature translucent plastic that lets you see the internal components. I liked that small design choice. You can control the glasses using voice commands, with Google debuting a latest “Hey Gemini” hotword for the form factor. While “Hey Google” and “OK Google” remain available, the new one is meant to reflect how big a role Gemini plays on smart glasses.

Sources indicate that there is also a touchpad on the right stem that accepts taps and swipes, while a button up top lets you take pictures and record video. Another way you’ll be able to control the glasses is with your Pixel Watch and Galaxy Watch. You can play/pause audio and enable Gemini using double-pinch and wrist gestures. Notably, gesture support is also coming to the Fitbit Air next year.

According to recent reports, from its internal testing, Google tells me that which input method people use is pretty situational and ends up being natural. At the beginning of my demo, I favored the touchpad, but by the end, I was leaning toward voice commands.

Sources indicate that when you’re capturing media that gets saved, there will always be a white blinking indicator light. There’s also another light in your field of vision that’s analogous to the camera and microphone privacy indicators in the top-right corner of Android phones. When I first put on the glasses, that light was distracting, but I rapidly forgot about it by the end of my demo.

It has been revealed that talking to Intelligent Eyewear uses Gemini Live. Some prompts, like take a picture or play a song, are one-shot “chat” commands in phone parlance, but for the most part, you’re using Gemini’s back-and-forth conversation mode. Google heavily customized the Gemini Live model for glasses to reduce latency, shorten responses, and tightly integrate the camera.

Recent findings suggest that even compared to my last demo in May, the latency of voice commands has come a long way. That said, I need more time to see if it’s really fast enough to use as a primary interaction method for most commands.

Google built a number of privacy protections into Intelligent Eyewear that are clearly in response to the current perception of smart glasses. There are some interesting ideas here, starting with how Gemini queries that involve a picture (like a visual search) won’t be saved to your Gemini History, used for model training, or ad targeting. For example, if you ask Gemini to find out what kind of plant you’re looking at, that image won’t be accessible anywhere else.

Similarly, Google will blur all faces and filter out bystander voices before it gets uploaded to Gemini in the cloud. This on-device processing occurs on your phone.

Recent findings suggest that since that visual media isn’t being saved, the external indicator light won’t be active when you’re talking to Gemini. The LED is only on when photos or videos are being saved and can be reviewed later.

That indicator light features anti-tamper detection that prevents recording. Algorithms detect whether the LED is covered by stickers or markers, with this process featuring hardware verification when the glasses are in their charging case.

Google’s “Glasses” companion app, with Samsung having a near-identical version for Galaxy phones, is pretty similar to the version for Pixel Watch. Unlike the bloated “Meta AI” app, it’s just for settings rather than the very definition of a growth hack with a full chatbot. The difference is staggering, and something Google deserves a bit of credit for in this age of throwing AI into every crevice of day-to-day smartphone usage.

It has been revealed that under the hood, the glasses are offloading a lot of processing to your phone. This includes HDR pipelines and video stabilization. The 12MP camera takes pictures in a 4:3 aspect ratio, while you can record up to 90 seconds of video. Images are transferred immediately to your phone over Wi-Fi, while videos wait until the glasses are charging to preserve battery life. I am so excited by point-of-view photography and the instantaneous capture the glasses offer, and early impressions of camera quality are positive.

Another thing I want to test is how Intelligent Eyewear fares as always-available headphones. There are two open-ear speakers and four microphones, and Google is clearly very proud of the noise-cancellation work in place.

It has been revealed that as someone who has been waiting for smart glasses since 2012, I cannot overstate my annoyance at how Meta allowed smart glasses to gain a scummy undertone, if not overtone. It should have been more proactive to societal problems. Meanwhile, Meta releasing glasses without a camera, thus removing the primary utility of real-world context, makes me deeply question its belief that this is the future.

Smart glasses that know what you’re interacting with in the world can be extremely useful. That always-available camera is a genuine physical advantage over smartphones. It unlocks newly introduced use cases and convenience that are just not possible with something that goes in your pocket.

Google took a long time to get back to glasses. From what I’ve used so far, the wait will be worth it. The hardware and designs are solid, while the software is chock-full of innovative, well-considered ideas.

Industry observers note that according to the slew of reports on Reddit, a number of basic health metrics have gone missing from the view in the mobile app on both Android and iOS, including overnight vitals such as resting heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and HRV. Google rolled out its 5.12 update last week, which appears to be the common link between user reports online.

Recent findings suggest that the bug isn't limited to just one device either — customers on the latest Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge models, the Fitbit Charge 6, and Fitbit Sense 2 are all experiencing this absence. These vitals are tracked daily to establish patterns and highlight changes in your health, so if they miss a day or two, it could have a huge impact on your readings.

According to recent reports, but despite these health metrics vanishing from thin air, it doesn't necessarily mean that your device has stopped tracking your data altogether. In some user cases, the device has continued monitoring health patterns, but the app has just failed to display them.

Still, it's not ideal, and users have been quick to jump on Google's case — but the company has issued some reassurance that it's looking into it.

Among the wave of reports on Reddit, one user went the extra mile and reached out to Google directly, sharing the email they received in response: 'it's a joke' they shared.

Other people turned to Google's support forum for answers, where one of Google's product experts stated they had escalated the issue.

Sierra released Personal Agent Protocol 1.0, known as Poppy, on November 13, 2026, with automatic support for every Shopify store and enablement across Meta’s Muse agent. Sierra remarked 60 additional companies are joining as design partners, bringing the total to more than 100.

Poppy defines how a personal agent acting for one user discovers a company and works through its APIs, website or company agent. The release follows five weeks of design partners testing drafts against real websites, APIs and agents. Its changes allow staged adoption, refine the use of existing standards, expand company guidance and agent feedback, and introduce extensions so industries can add capabilities without changing the core protocol.

According to recent reports, muse now automatically looks for Poppy first on every site it visits. Any company can implement the protocol independently, making it available when Muse visits its site. The newly introduced design partners include Cisco, Delta Air Lines, Intuit, Salesforce, Twilio and Zoom.

The draft specification requires a company to publish a poppy.json document at its domain’s /.well-known/poppy.json path over HTTPS. The document advertises available channels, capabilities and sign-in options, while the company chooses which channels and capabilities to offer.

A signed Session header identifies the personal agent and a pseudonymous user and connects activity across channels. Standard OAuth separately authorizes actions on a company account. Signed-out interactions can operate without an OAuth server, allowing a company to expose limited functionality before implementing account access.

User IDs remain stable at one firm but are opaque and different across companies, so businesses cannot use them to match customers with one another. Security rules require company content to be treated as data rather than instructions, addressing prompt-injection attempts to direct the model. Access tokens, refresh tokens, Session tokens, private keys, authorization codes and device codes must stay out of model context. Conversations also identify whether a person or AI wrote each message and support handoff to a person.

Every Shopify store now automatically publishes a Poppy file, with no extra merchant implementation. Sierra noted the automatic publication extends across Shopify businesses in more than 175 countries.

In a recent development, poppy handles the earlier interaction in which an agent identifies itself and learns what it may do, while Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) handles product discovery, carts and checkout. Every Shopify store supports UCP by default. The arrangement adds a common firm-discovery and permission layer in front of Shopify’s existing transaction flow.

It has been revealed that shopify also co-authored Poppy’s commerce extension, which links the two protocols. It supports guest and account-based shopping, requires customer approval before certain actions and connects to UCP Ask for direct conversations between shopper and store agents.

Recent findings suggest that mercury customers can use personal agents to check balances and transactions, categorize spending, maintain budgets and receipts, and initiate payments or transfers. Payment requests still pass through the account’s approval policy before anything is sent, preserving an authorization step around agent-initiated money movement.

It has been revealed that turkish Airlines supports agent checks of fares, flight status and stopovers, plus booking retrieval with a reference number and surname. Miles&Smiles members can have an agent find business-class upgrades, which customers approve before paying. It has been revealed that synchrony’s work is exploratory. Sierra said it is examining product discovery that considers affordability, relevant offers and financing products, with potential use across its network of more than 500,000 merchant locations.

The validator acts as a test personal agent and reports which protocol requirements a deployment meets. 📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (969 w)

Here’s how Google’s Android XR glasses are handling the camera & privacy

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle.
  • Industry observers note that to promptly summarize the problem at hand (and name names), Meta’s smart glasses developed a reputation of being abused by bad actors who would disable the visible privacy LED (which Meta only recently fixed) or use these glasses in tasteless ways.
  • Sources indicate that it’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle. The “perv glasses” stigma is very real because, frankly, early movers in this category didn’t respect privacy. Here’s how Android XR and Gemini are handling the camera and privacy on “Intelligent Eyewear,” and why I think Google has struck a near-perfect balance.

Industry observers note that to promptly summarize the problem at hand (and name names), Meta’s smart glasses developed a reputation of being abused by bad actors who would disable the visible privacy LED (which Meta only recently fixed) or use these glasses in tasteless ways. Combine that with improper handling of recordings on Meta’s part and it’s a recipe for distrust and an earned social stigma. It’s not like Google is a simple bystander here, either. The original Google Glass project was met with the “Glasshole” stigma, and it’s something that Google has clearly learned a lot of lessons from.

Sources indicate that it’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience. I recently talked about how the camera was my favorite part of smart glasses in an concern of our 9to5Google Weekender newsletter, but how it just feels a bit wrong now.

Anyway, with that context in mind, let’s look at how Google is handling this touchy subject.

It starts with the outward-facing light on every part of Android XR glasses, which works similarly to the privacy LED on Meta’s glasses. The key distinction here is this is a “recording light” on Android XR glasses. It turns on whenever the glasses are capturing content that can be viewed later in some form or fashion by the user. So if you’re taking a picture or recording a video, it lights up. If you’re just using Gemini for context, the light doesn’t activate. That’s because any camera captures being used for Gemini are deleted immediately after use. They won’t show up in your Gemini chat logs and that’s not a choice for the user – these images are purged immediately after they’ve been used so that you as the user nor Google can use them. That includes Google not using visuals from Gemini captures for AI training or advertising. Customers also have control over what apps on Android XR glasses can use the camera.

Importantly, the light on each pair of Android XR glasses is also designed to avoid any tampering. Android XR glasses automatically perform a system check to ensure the light is working on a regular basis – you might catch the light blinking in white and blue while charging which is a part of the system check ensuring the hardware is fully functional. If the light is found not to be working, the camera is disabled.

Recent findings suggest that one of the pieces of this package that really caught my attention is how Google is handling the privacy of those around you. When your Intelligent Eyewear glasses send a photo to Gemini, your phone automatically redacts faces from the image before it’s sent to Gemini. This happens locally on the phone, essentially as a part of the glasses app. Similarly, voice data sent to Gemini filters out other voices besides your own. The voice filtering bit is just one way in which Google is doing some impressive things with the microphones here, with another example being that the live translation feature works in a 60-degree “cone” in front of you, filtering out other voices in the space.

Industry observers note that continuing on with how the camera interacts with Gemini, Google explained in a conversation with 9to5Google that Gemini is tuned not to use the camera in cases where it’s not obvious that the user wants the camera to be active. An interaction such as “what painting is this” would very clearly imply that the user wants the glasses to view the scene in front of them and identify the art piece, where “how much money is on the table,” Google explained, would ask for a follow-up before using the camera seeing as it’s not obvious that the user expects the camera to be used in that sort of phrase.

Sources indicate that another way in which Android XR glasses will avoid the recording stigma is with their limits. Google is limiting Intelligent Eyewear video recording to 90-second sessions. While that does limit what the user can do, Google stated that most recordings fell within that window anyway. Meta, by comparison, offers recordings up to 5 minutes.

Beyond just the glasses app and Gemini, Google claims it is making other efforts across its ecosystem to protect against and deter misuse of the camera on Android XR glasses, including:.

For the most part, Google’s efforts around privacy on Android XR glasses aren’t groundbreaking. This is how it should work. But seeing as the bar is exceptionally low thanks to a rough start from competitors, I found myself reassured and even a bit impressed by the messaging here – a clear explanation of the indicator light and the automatic on-device face redaction and deletion of Gemini imagery both go a long way.

Google’s sentiment around privacy on glasses is pretty nearly summed up by a sentence in its privacy post today: “…when technology can see the world around you, it has a responsibility to the people around you, too.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Netflix Turns Operational Data Into a Knowledge Graph for AI-Driven Observability.
  • Nov 13, 2026 3 min read.
  • Netflix is developing an ontology-driven knowledge graph to accelerate production investigations and provide AI agents with a shared understanding of its operational environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Netflix Turns Operational Data Into a Knowledge Graph for AI-Driven Observability.

Nov 13, 2026 3 min read.

Netflix is developing an ontology-driven knowledge graph to accelerate production investigations and provide AI agents with a shared understanding of its operational environment. The platform connects information about applications, incidents, deployments, alerts, and infrastructure dependencies, addressing a problem that can leave engineers spending hours piecing together information scattered across different systems.

The company claims it handles more than 2 billion requests daily and upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. During the November 2024 Jake Paul-Mike Tyson fight, its infrastructure supported approximately 65 million concurrent streams. Yet investigating a typical application regression can take around four hours, with much of that time spent reconstructing relationships between systems rather than analysing the underlying data.

Netflix's solution is to make those relationships explicit through an operational ontology and knowledge graph, creating a foundation for automated root-cause analysis and, eventually, self-healing infrastructure.

Netflix already collects metrics, events, logs, and traces (MELT) across its applications and infrastructure. However, these signals are spread across systems such as alerting, incident management, deployment tooling, and engineering communication platforms.

Sources indicate that an application regression might originate from a client release, an experiment, infrastructure load shedding, or a service several dependencies downstream. Although each system contains useful information, engineers must often connect the evidence manually.

Netflix identified the missing capability as a consistent way to describe not just individual components, but how they relate to one another.

Its Observability Ontology provides that common model, defining operational entities, their properties, and the relationships between them. It uses established standards including RDF, OWL, SHACL, and SPARQL, while the resulting knowledge graph is stored in QuipuDB, Netflix's distributed RDF database built on Rust's redb storage engine.

The graph is populated through a pipeline of components Netflix calls enrichers. These consume information from operational systems and transform it into structured relationships, represented as subject-predicate-object triples.

Some enrichment is deterministic, while other stages use LLMs and probabilistic techniques to interpret less structured information. Netflix constrains these outputs through strict validation rules, including consistent entity types, URI naming conventions, and checks against its software catalogue.

Netflix also captures information from incident discussions, including hypotheses, rejected explanations, and mitigation decisions. This allows human reasoning to become part of the operational knowledge base rather than disappearing when an incident conversation ends.

Recent findings suggest that its correlation engine examines 13 types of signals, including log errors, metric anomalies, traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, configuration changes, experiments, and code changes. It searches for potential causal relationships, evaluating evidence such as temporal proximity and severity to produce ranked hypotheses.

Netflix describes the process as a knowledge flywheel: Observe, Enrich, Infer, and Adapt. As investigations produce upcoming insights, those relationships can inform future detection and analysis. The knowledge graph also underpins AutoRCA, Netflix's internal agentic AI system for root-cause analysis.

Industry observers note that rather than having specialist agents exchange loosely structured findings, they use the ontology as a common interface. Agents analysing traces, logs or deployments can contribute information about the same operational entities without needing to understand each other's internal implementations.

Netflix intends to use this foundation to produce ranked, evidence-backed explanations for incidents, with humans retaining approval authority over proposed changes and remediation.

Platforms such as Datadog, Dynatrace, and Splunk already correlate observability signals and increasingly incorporate AI into incident investigation. Netflix's approach emphasizes the semantic model behind those signals, making operational relationships persistent and directly accessible to both engineers and machines.

Sources indicate that the company ultimately wants to extend this capability from automated root-cause analysis into automated remediation and self-healing infrastructure. It also looks to explore integration with its Unified Data Architecture, connecting operational information to broader business and technology domains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wolters Kluwer Health unveiled on November 13, 2026, that it had signed an agreement to acquire AgileMD for up to $100 million, a transaction that would add interactive clinical pathways and AI-powered patient-deterioration surveillance to its clinical business.

Recent findings suggest that the consideration consists of a $40 million upfront payment and a deferred balance contingent on performance targets. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027 or sooner, subject to customary closing conditions and governmental approvals. It has not yet closed.

Recent findings suggest that agileMD was founded in 2011 and is based in San Francisco. Its co-founders are CEO Borna Safabakhsh and chief medical officer Dana Edelson, and all 23 employees are expected to join Wolters Kluwer Health.

Industry observers note that agileMD’s Pathways product brings a health system’s local guidelines into electronic health record (EHR) workflows. Clinicians can use the pathways to enter orders, align order sets and other decision support, generate documentation, and incorporate laboratory results and vital signs. The product also supports outcomes measurement, putting protocol delivery and subsequent review in the same working environment.

The second product, eCART, is a real-time AI surveillance engine that identifies and prioritizes patients at risk of all-cause clinical deterioration, meaning a worsening in their condition. Wolters Kluwer describes the FDA-cleared product as designed to help care teams escalate treatment and reduce mortality rates.

On AgileMD’s product page, the company notes eCART’s analytic was trained and tested on nearly 3 million patient encounters from 28 hospitals across six health systems. Retrospective and prospective validation covered sepsis, COPD, CHF and COVID populations.

Sources indicate that agileMD reports platform totals exceeding 400 hospitals, 150,000 clinical people and 4.425 million patient encounters. More than 4,800 pathways are live at partner institutions, covering adult, pediatric and neonatal topics across ambulatory, emergency, inpatient, intensive-care and women’s health settings. The figures describe both the software’s reach and the amount of protocol content already in clinical use.

Wolters Kluwer intends to combine AgileMD with UpToDate Expert AI and its partnerships, extending UpToDate into embedded workflows, local guidelines and upcoming digital health applications. Yaw Fellin, senior vice president of Wolters Kluwer Clinical Solutions, said the acquisition is also meant to help health systems improve patient care and obtain more value from their technology investments.

Safabakhsh noted UpToDate’s foundational capabilities would allow AgileMD to “accelerate and streamline the development and maintenance of more advanced clinical pathways for complex clinical decision-making support.”.

UpToDate Expert AI was introduced in September 2025. Wolters Kluwer reports that it has since been adopted by more than 2,700 U.S. hospitals and health systems, representing more than 95% of U.S.-based UpToDate Enterprise Edition customers. The acquisition would connect that customer footprint with AgileMD’s pathway and surveillance tools, while the expansion into additional workflows and applications remains a proposal ahead of closing.

Wolters Kluwer projects that AgileMD will reach $7 million in annual recurring revenue by the end of 2026 and that the acquisition will achieve a return on invested capital at or above its 8% after-tax weighted average cost of capital within three to five years, with an immaterial effect on adjusted earnings.

Sources indicate that for Wolters Kluwer, the strategic value lies in placing guidance and deterioration alerts directly inside clinical workflows. The deferred consideration and return target tie that blueprint to subsequent performance, while governmental approvals and other closing conditions still stand between the signed agreement and a completed acquisition.

It's hard to believe that Spotify Wrapped is about to give us all a brutal reality check on how we soundtracked 2026. Though the idea of it sends shivers through me, it's still one of the most anticipated and exciting events on the tech calendar.

If you thought it was too late to get in your final listening hours, fear not; Spotify hasn't stopped counting them yet. While we don't know when the exact cut-off is (Spotify's never disclosed it before, and the likelihood of it happening is slim), it's widely thought to be right up until the launch of Wrapped, which usually lands in late November or early December.

The good news is that we still have between two and three weeks left before that day arrives, so if there was ever a good time to crack down on the final Wrapped preparations, it's now!

It has been revealed that for years, your Spotify Taste Profile has been sitting behind the algorithm, using your listening behaviors to determine which new music it recommends to you. While you can exclude individual songs and playlists from infiltrating your Taste Profile, that's pretty much it as far as controlling how Spotify understands you.

Thankfully, the platform brought Taste Profile to the forefront of the experience earlier this year, allowing you to see exactly how Spotify understands your listening habits and how it uses this to shape your recommendations, and to flag any mistakes it makes. Not only that, but you can also speak directly to it and actively shape what it feeds you.

Industry observers note that using text prompts, you can ask your Taste Profile pretty much anything. If you want to explore a particular genre that's been on your list, you can prompt it to recommend more glam rock, experimental pop, or whatever you're feeling in the moment — and the same goes for artists.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

According to recent reports, if there's one thing that gets under my skin with music streaming apps is that, sometimes, you can run into artists you can't stand. No matter how much you try to ignore them, they're bound to crop up in your Discover Weekly or whenever you're listening to a Spotify-curated playlist — it's better to rid them completely, I say.

That's why I've gotten into the routine of blocking artists entirely from my feed. It's one of those features that, whenever I bring it up, others don't even know it exists. I'm here to tell you that it does, and it will change your life.

All you need to do is head to an artist's page in the Spotify app, tap the three dots next to the 'Follow' button, and then select 'Don't play this artist'. Once that's enabled, their page will go gray, and their discography will disappear from playlists. Their music also won't show up in features like your Discover Weekly or Daylist, so your blocked artists won't get in the way of newly introduced music discovery.

If you're on Spotify's Family blueprint and your young kids can't keep out of your profile, then I feel for you. There's nothing worse than waiting all year for Wrapped to arrive only to find that your top songs and artists are from your kids' favorite TV indicates — the Family plan has individual profiles for a reason!

It's been difficult to avoid this in Wrapped's past, but rest assured Spotify has put its foot down on this infiltration this time around, and you can amend your settings to ensure this music stays far away from your Wrapped summary.

In your settings, you'll find a toggle that, when enabled, excludes all kids and family music that's played on your profile. Not only does this help with steering your Wrapped in a more accurate direction, but it also ensures that your kids' favorite music doesn't affect your recommendations, Discover Weekly, and Daily Mix — so it's not just a benefit for Wrapped.

Google Open Sources Ambient Quality Agent (AQuA) to Diagnose Production AI Agent Failures

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Google Open Sources Ambient Quality Agent (AQuA) to Diagnose Production AI Agent Failures.
  • Nov 13, 2026 2 min read.
  • Google has open-sourced AQuA (Ambient Quality Agent), a reference implementation that analyzes production AI agent sessions, verifies recurring failure patterns, and investigates root causes against deployed source revisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Google Open Sources Ambient Quality Agent (AQuA) to Diagnose Production AI Agent Failures.

Nov 13, 2026 2 min read.

Google has open-sourced AQuA (Ambient Quality Agent), a reference implementation that analyzes production AI agent sessions, verifies recurring failure patterns, and investigates root causes against deployed source revisions. The tool targets silent quality regressions that conventional infrastructure monitoring can miss, such as agents ignoring user preferences or skipping required tool calls while returning successful responses.

AQuA runs alongside an agent in Google Cloud, outside its request path, reading telemetry from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging, or BigQuery. It samples up to 1,000 recent sessions per run and processes them through five stages: sampling, reviewing, clustering findings, verifying candidate clusters, and tracking issues. Developers can configure domain-specific quality criteria through a goal.md file and add deterministic custom metrics. AQuA can run on a schedule, after a deployment, or on demand.

In a recent development, for root cause analysis, AQuA compares failing sessions with an immutable source snapshot captured at deployment. Its diagnosis agent identifies relevant code or instructions, cites file and line ranges, and proposes changes when the cause lies in the repository. It can also attribute failures to external dependencies, tool handoffs, or retrieved data. AQuA does not apply fixes or open pull requests automatically.

AQuA sidecar architecture (Source: Google Developer Blog Post).

Google evaluated 32 sessions from a multi-agent travel application, identifying 42 findings grouped into nine candidate clusters. The verifier rejected three unsupported clusters after checking up to three full transcripts per candidate cluster, leaving six verified issues. Two involved bypassing seat availability checks and losing a traveler's vegan preference during delegation.

After developers modified prompts and replayed the sessions, seat-selection bypasses fell from 15 sessions to two, dietary-preference omissions dropped from seven to zero, and sessions passing all checks increased from five to 13. These results came from controlled replay, not production traffic.

An insight is its citations, not a self-reported confidence score.

Findings link to supporting traces, and proposed root causes must reference valid lines in the deployed snapshot. AQuA tracks findings as NEWLY INTRODUCED, RECURRING, or automatically RESOLVED after 14 days without being observed. Sampling can miss rare failures, and replay may not reproduce external state.

Reacting to the announcement on LinkedIn, Dmytro Aprelenko, engineering manager at Redcore, wrote,.

Agent orchestration definitely needs better continuous diagnosis to catch these loops early.

Recent findings suggest that AQuA validates source references and links findings to supporting traces. Cluster verification filters false positives, though it cannot confirm every session exhibits the same failure. Google's Agent Platform evaluation service supports regression testing and production quality monitoring, while Arize Phoenix provides open-source tracing and evaluation. AQuA focuses on grouping production failures and linking verified findings to deployed source code.

Google identifies sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state as constraints. Its open-source implementation helps teams integrate production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

#173. Industry News: Fady Saad, Founder and General Partner of Cybernetix Ventures – Interview Series

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3113 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite

Industry News: Fady Saad, Founder and General Partner of Cybernetix Ventures – Interview Series

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fady Saad is Founder and General Partner of Cybernetix Ventures, where he invests in early-stage robotics, automation, and industrial AI companies.
  • Sources indicate that cybernetix Ventures is a Boston-based venture capital firm investing in robotics, automation, and industrial AI startups in North America and Europe.
  • You co-founded MassRobotics in 2014, helping build one of the world’s leading robotics innovation ecosystems, before founding Cybernetix Ventures in 2021.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fady Saad is Founder and General Partner of Cybernetix Ventures, where he invests in early-stage robotics, automation, and industrial AI companies. He also co-founded MassRobotics, helping develop its corporate partnerships and support robotics startups as they moved toward commercialization. His experience connects engineering, business development, and the practical challenges of bringing machines into real operating environments, with an investment approach centered on customer needs and commercially viable deployment.

Sources indicate that cybernetix Ventures is a Boston-based venture capital firm investing in robotics, automation, and industrial AI startups in North America and Europe. Its focus includes manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, construction, and enabling technologies such as perception, autonomy, sensors, and cybersecurity for robotics. In this interview, Saad discusses the opportunities and limits of physical AI, the economics of specialized and humanoid robots, and the reliability, data, and infrastructure needed to turn promising technology into scalable businesses.

You co-founded MassRobotics in 2014, helping build one of the world’s leading robotics innovation ecosystems, before founding Cybernetix Ventures in 2021. What inspired your transition from supporting robotics startups to investing directly in them, and how did your experience at MassRobotics shape your investment philosophy?

I didn’t plan to become an investor. I came into robotics through Vecna, working on R&D and commercialization strategy, and I learned fast that robotics doesn’t follow the software playbook. You can push a software prototype out to users in six months. A robot needs manufacturing, a supply chain, testing, safety work, and a customer willing to let it onto their floor.

It has been revealed that that’s why we started MassRobotics in 2014. We called it a startup accelerator because the hard part isn’t building the prototype. It’s getting from a working prototype to a product someone can buy. I ran corporate partnerships, and for over six years I sat in more than 300 corporate meetings and helped build over 40 partnerships. I kept seeing the same picture: corporates with real problems, startups with real technology and almost no investors who understood both.

According to recent reports, by 2018 and 2019, it was obvious. VCs were clustered around SaaS or biotech, and robotics founders were the misfits. Too much hardware for software investors, and not enough biology for biotech investors. Good teams were stalling because the right capital didn’t exist. Mark Martin, who I met in 2017 when we brought Analog Devices into MassRobotics, saw the same gap from the corporate side. So we built Cybernetix, a fund that treats robotics as its own asset class, and debuted it in 2021.

MassRobotics shaped how we invest in a simple way. We start from the customer’s problem, not the technology. We like teams with at least one founder from the industry they sell into. And we bring our corporate network into every deal, because in this sector the right introduction to a buyer can be worth more than the check.

Physical AI is emerging as one of the most transformative areas of artificial intelligence, bringing intelligence into machines that interact with the real world. What technological breakthroughs are accelerating its adoption, and why do you believe the industry is reaching an important inflection point?

Two things moved at the same time. The brains got much better, and the bodies got much cheaper.

According to recent reports, on the software side, foundation models gave robots something they never really had: the ability to take an instruction and handle situations they weren’t explicitly programmed for. Simulation lets teams train and test thousands of scenarios before a robot ever touches a real factory. On the hardware side, sensors, edge compute, actuators, and batteries keep getting cheaper and better, so a startup can build a full-stack robot without being an industrial giant.

In a recent development, then there’s demand: labor shortages in manufacturing, logistics, agriculture and construction, an aging workforce, and a real push to bring production back home. I always say the labor shortage is an economic problem, not an engineering problem, and boards are treating it that way now.

So yes, it’s an inflection, but I’d be precise about where. Capability and capital have inflected; deployment at scale has not. ChatGPT runs on 20 or 30 years of digitized human knowledge and there’s no equivalent for the physical world. No dataset tells a robot that you need to hold an egg, a sheet of paper, or a piece of cloth differently. The companies that close that data gap, by deploying in real environments and learning every shift, will define the next phase.

It has been revealed that investment in robotics and physical AI has accelerated, driven by advances in AI, labor shortages, and growing demand for automation. What is fueling investor enthusiasm, and how much of this momentum reflects genuine commercial opportunities versus speculative excitement?

I think it’s both and investors don’t help anyone by pretending otherwise.

In a recent development, the demand is real. Deloitte and the Manufacturing Institute project U.S. manufacturers could need up to 3.8 million workers by 2033, with about 1.9 million of those jobs at risk of going unfilled. That’s not hype. That’s a hole in the economy.

Recent findings suggest that the capital is a different story. Crunchbase counted $18.8 billion invested in robotics startups in the first half of 2026, more than all of 2025. But PitchBook saw deal count drop in the second quarter while dollars hit a record, which tells you a handful of mega rounds are absorbing most of it. A lot of that money is buying a narrative: mostly humanoids and general-purpose robot models.

Recent findings suggest that my filter is boring on purpose. Does the customer buy again after the pilot? Does the robot hit the reliability the job needs, which on a production line is 99.99%, not 90%? Is there real revenue within a year or so? If the answers are yes, that’s a business. If the pitch is mainly about what the robot might do in 2030, that’s speculation priced like a certainty. Robotics has been through this cycle before, and the companies with paying customers come out of the shakeout stronger.

Cybernetix Ventures is raising its second fund to expand investments in early-stage robotics and AI companies. How has your investment thesis evolved since launching your first fund, and which emerging technologies or industries are attracting the greatest interest from institutional investors?

Recent findings suggest that the core belief hasn’t changed. Value in physical AI is captured where software meets real-world deployment, and the best robots are built backward from a specific problem. Fund II doubles down on that.

What’s changed is the map. Fund I focused on manufacturing, logistics, construction, and healthcare. Fund II keeps those and adds agriculture, energy and climate infrastructure, space, and defense as well as dual-use technology. The mix stays roughly two-thirds full-stack robotics companies and one-third enabling technology, things like AI models, perception and machine-to-machine cybersecurity. Our first Fund II checks went into a space robotics manufacturer and a perception model company, which tells you where the new generation is heading.

We also look hard at things that barely came up in 2021 – like where the components come from, how exposed the supply chain is to China, and how secure the robot is once it’s networked.

It has been revealed that from institutional and corporate investors, I hear two questions most. First, corporates ask how to get a window into a market they can’t build internally, which means scouting, market intelligence, and co-investment. Physical AI has become a CEO-level priority at a lot of these companies. But family offices and institutions ask something more direct: why not just get into one of the significant humanoid or robot model rounds through an SPV? My answer is that those are crowded, expensive, capital-hungry bets. The asymmetric returns are earlier… in companies the generalists haven’t found yet. That’s where a specialist earns its keep.

It has been revealed that humanoid robots have attracted enormous attention and investment, with companies such as Tesla and Figure AI pursuing increasingly ambitious capabilities. You’ve expressed skepticism about their commercial viability. Where do you believe investors are overestimating their near-term potential, and do specialized robots offer a more compelling investment opportunity?

Recent findings suggest that I’m skeptical of the timeline, not the technology. My rule is form follows function. If the job is moving parts or pick and place, ask whether you need a very complex, very expensive two-legged machine, or an arm, or two arms on a mobile base. On a flat warehouse or factory floor, legs don’t buy you much. They add cost, draw power, and rely on a robot that can fall.

Where investors overestimate humanoids is the near-term math. Valuations assume broad deployment soon, but the hard problems are still open – such as dexterous hands, touch and force feedback, batteries that last a few hours, and an AI stack that’s repeatable and traceable. A 10% error rate is fine in a chatbot. In a plant, one wrong move can hurt someone or cost a customer millions. I expect meaningful volume shipments in five to 10 years, not next year.

Humanoids make sense where the environment was built for people and can’t be redesigned. Space is my favorite example. NASA charges commercial consumers about $130,000 for one hour of astronaut time, so a robot that can work inside a station designed for humans pays for itself fast. Nuclear sites, disaster response and some defense work follow the same logic.

Recent findings suggest that so in the near term, yes, specialized robots are the better risk-adjusted bet. They’re shipping and getting paid today.

While humanoid robots dominate headlines, Cybernetix Ventures focuses on practical applications across manufacturing, healthcare, logistics, and construction. Which industries offer the greatest near-term economic impact from physical AI, and where are you already seeing measurable returns on automation investments?

The fastest impact indicates up where three things meet: an expensive problem, a labor gap, and a buyer who measures results in dollars.

Recent findings suggest that manufacturing comes first, especially existing plants. Most factories can’t be rebuilt around robots. A organization with hundreds of sites needs automation that fits the building it already has. That’s why AI vision that lets existing robot arms pick messy, shiny or transparent parts is so valuable. It upgrades what’s already on the floor.

Logistics is the most mature market, with clear ROI (return on investment) in picking, moving and loading. Even so, reliably picking any single item out of a mixed bin still isn’t fully solved.

Recent findings suggest that healthcare and life sciences are underrated. Automated labs turn slow, manual work into faster, reproducible results, and drug developers already know how to pay for faster answers.

Construction is at an earlier stage, but it has one of the worst labor shortages of all. Narrow jobs like layout and material hoisting are where robots are earning their keep.

Where I see measurable returns, it’s almost always the same pattern: one narrow job, done more reliably, with payback the customer can see in its own numbers, not in a five-year slide.

According to recent reports, advances in foundation models, computer vision, reinforcement learning, and simulation are transforming robotics capabilities. Which AI innovations do you consider most consequential over the next five years, and what technical limitations still prevent widespread deployment in unpredictable real-world environments?

Over the next five years, I’d watch four things.

Robot foundation models, especially those connecting vision, language, and action. But I expect them to win domain by domain, not as one model for everything. The path is a single purpose, then a scope of use cases, then maybe a whole domain — say, single-family home construction. I don’t believe one model will run construction, manufacturing and healthcare.

Industry observers note that simulation, because it makes training cheap. But simulation gets you to 80% or 90%. The last 10% is where robots drop things and hit things.

Touch. Vision is great for understanding the environment. But if you want to change the world, you have to feel it. Tactile sensing and better hands matter because manipulation is where most real work happens.

Sources indicate that data infrastructure. In autonomous vehicles, a generation of companies like Scale AI built substantial businesses collecting and labeling data, and Applied Intuition built one on simulation. Physical AI will produce its own version, and it’s one of the biggest opportunities in the space.

What still blocks deployment in messy, unpredictable environments is reliability and trust. Factories need 99.99%. Safety standards, certification and insurance haven’t caught up for mobile robots working around people. And every connected robot is a cybersecurity problem that very few people are pricing in yet.

Sources indicate that cybernetix Ventures has invested in companies such as Cambrian Robotics, Dash Bio, and Rugged Robotics. What attracted you to these companies, and what distinguishes a promising robotics technology from a commercially scalable business?

All three started from a customer’s problem, not from a cool demo.

Industry observers note that cambrian Robotics. Machine vision is crowded, but Cambrian reliably picks small, shiny and transparent parts that trip up most systems. It works with the major industrial robot brands, installs in about half a day, and was already being tested and deployed with manufacturers like Toyota, Audi and Electrolux when we co-led its seed round in 2024.

Dash Bio. Drug developers send a lot of their bioanalysis to outside labs that still run largely by hand. Dash built a highly automated lab, compliant with GLP (Good Laboratory Practice) standards, that combines robotics, AI and software to run key assays up to 10 times faster. They aren’t selling robots. They’re selling faster answers, which customers already know how to buy.

Rugged Robotics. On a construction site, someone still marks by hand where every wall, pipe and fixture goes. It’s slow, and mistakes get expensive once the walls go up. Rugged’s robot prints the drawings directly onto the floor. One narrow job, done faster and more accurately, on sites that can’t find enough skilled people.

What separates a promising technology from a scalable business? Ninety-nine percent of the time, starting with a shiny technical achievement and then hunting for a use case is a formula for a struggling manufacturer. The ones that scale start with the problem and work backward to the machine, the way Kiva, Locus and Universal Robots did. After that, I look for a customer who buys again after the pilot, deployment that doesn’t need a PhD on site, unit economics that hold at volume and a team that hits its milestones. Plenty of robots are impressive. Far fewer are businesses.

Industry observers note that as physical AI becomes more capable, concerns about workforce displacement, safety, and human oversight are growing. Do you see robotics primarily addressing labor shortages and augmenting human workers, or do you anticipate significant workforce disruption as adoption accelerates?

In the near term, it’s mostly filling gaps. In the factories, warehouses, labs and job sites we work with, the constraint is people, not demand. Jobs sit open for months.

According to recent reports, verve Motion, one of our portfolio companies, is the example I come back to. They make a soft exosuit that takes much of the strain off workers who lift heavy loads all day. A warehouse worker told the team that he finally had energy to play with his kids when he got home. That’s robotics doing good in the world, and it isn’t replacing anyone.

Sources indicate that I won’t pretend there’s no disruption. The most repetitive roles will shrink, and work will change faster than our training systems are built for. The honest answer is to invest in reskilling now, for technicians, operators and the people who maintain robot fleets. Every robot that ships creates work for someone who installs, programs and fixes it.

Recent findings suggest that on safety, robotics actually has a head start on software AI. Industrial robots have lived under safety standards and certification for decades. As robots get smarter, that culture has to carry over: clear accountability, secure machines and people in control of critical decisions.

In a recent development, looking ahead to 2030 and beyond, which developments in physical AI and robotics do you believe will have the greatest impact on the global economy? Are there any overlooked investment opportunities or emerging applications that deserve considerably more attention?

By 2030, I think three things will matter most for the global economy.

Recent findings suggest that robots that learn on the job will finally bring automation to small and midsize manufacturers who could never afford custom integration. That’s where most of the industrial base actually sits.

Automated labs will speed up science, with biology and drug discovery running around the clock.

Industry observers note that and the supply chain for robot components — actuators, motors, sensors and gears — will become strategic. Most humanoid makers don’t build those parts.   • Sources indicate that alpaca Engineering explains that every few months, a non-planar 3D printing demonstration goes viral, but is rarely adopted practically by most 3D printer owners.
  • Commercially available 3D printers are also not optimized for non-planar 3D printing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, alpaca Engineering posted a YouTube video yesterday showcasing his self-hostable non-planar slicer. He explains that most non-planar 3D printing — printing across all three axes, rather than in 2D horizontal layers — demonstrations are usually for research purposes, for demonstration and experimentation, with no easy way for most 3D printer owners to try out non-planar 3D printing. His project, named PancakeSlicer, aims to fix this by making his non-planar slicing algorithm as easy to implement as existing slicing workflows, even improving upon it with 3D printer management features.

Sources indicate that alpaca Engineering explains that every few months, a non-planar 3D printing demonstration goes viral, but is rarely adopted practically by most 3D printer owners. Most non-planar experiments are for research, with half-abandoned GitHub projects. He further explains that non-planar isn’t widely adopted not because there aren’t any general-purpose non-planar slicers, but because it’s not accessible and easily implemented in a familiar workflow, with 3D printer owners spoiled by modern workflows and not needing to manually run G-code directly from an SD card.

Commercially available 3D printers are also not optimized for non-planar 3D printing. The challenge with printing at various angles is the clearance angle needed to bring a print head up and down without crashing into its own print. The slicer uses 3D models of various print heads from different 3D printer models to know how to slice the object to avoid collisions, thus having limited support; but Alpaca Engineering has listed a large number of supported 3D printers from Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Voron, and many others. The varying shapes of the print heads also mean different printers will have different capabilities, with some managing less angle and curvature than others.

Alpaca Engineering also has great animations and practical demonstrations of the different slicing algorithms in the slicer, including how the algorithm slices the object for non-planar printing. We highly suggest you watch the video if you’re interested, as his animations explain non-planar slicing intuitively.

One of the best features of this slicer is its self-hosting features. Users can host the slicer from a desktop, NAS, or a home server and access it with a web UI, allowing multiple users to send print jobs from any device. It also has 3D printer management features, applying different profiles to different printer brands, unifying the experience without hopping from one slicer to another to operate multiple 3D printers — this is even available to Bambu Lab users, replacing Bambu Studio and Bambu Connect in LAN-only mode. The slicer can also manage two slice jobs at the same time in case other users happen to be slicing at the same time.

While PancakeSlicer isn’t the first to implement self-hosted 3D printer management features, it certainly levels up his initial goal of making non-planar slicing as easy to access as most modern workflows. We hope to see how more people can experiment with non-planar 3D printing, contribute their findings, and rapidly improve upon it as a genuinely practical slicing method.

According to recent reports, apple released the Siri AI Developer Preview in the 27.3 beta releases of its operating systems, enabling developers and apps to integrate with the assistant and hand off actions to it. During the Preview, access to Siri AI is restricted to developer builds and internal TestFlight testers.

Apple says that Siri AI is an entirely fresh version of its assistant which is "profoundly more capable, conversational, and personal".

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more.

It has been revealed that these new capabilities let owners make natural language requests and have Siri AI carry out any custom action supported by the app. The framework also supports complex requests through Skills, a new feature that lets developers "teach Siri AI how to combine several actions into a single experience".

According to recent reports, if a request does not specify an app name, it will automatically be routed to the app currently in the foreground, the app associated with an active Live Activity, or the app previously mentioned in the ongoing conversation. This allows consumers to continue conversations across an app and its Live Activity, or a different app altogether. While an app is running in the background, however, it will receive only requests that explicitly mention its name.

Requests can also include actions across apps, such as finding content in one app, sending it to another, and performing an action there.

Commenting on Apple's announcement, Reddit user sixtypercenttogether noted:.

In my limited testing so far it does what it indicates. If you include a good description on your intent and parameters, Siri can figure it out. THIS is what Siri should have been all along, all the way back in 26.0.
