📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic published recommendations for more reliable AI safety evaluations on November 13, 2026, reporting aggregate harmless-response rates of 94% to 98% for every recent model on its single-turn API tests.
  • In a recent development, A safety evaluation measures a model’s propensity to cause or contribute to harm, whether its response makes harm more or less likely and how severe that harm could be, rather than a specific capability.
  • It has been revealed that to construct these tests, a domain expert writes a specification for the simulated user’s objectives, tactics, persona, situation, tone and conversational style.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic published recommendations for more reliable AI safety evaluations on November 13, 2026, reporting aggregate harmless-response rates of 94% to 98% for every recent model on its single-turn API tests. Those saturated tests are useful mainly as regression checks on known failure modes; multi-turn evaluations offer more variation and can capture gradual changes across a conversation.

In a recent development, A safety evaluation measures a model’s propensity to cause or contribute to harm, whether its response makes harm more or less likely and how severe that harm could be, rather than a specific capability. A central concern is construct validity, or whether a test captures the concept it intends to measure. Refusal rate can be misleading for suicide and self-harm conversations because simply declining to engage may itself be a failure; the desired response offers support and directs the user toward human help. Anthropic’s multi-turn evaluations instead measure an appropriate-response rate across the entire conversation, using risk-specific rubrics in which one bad turn fails the whole exchange.

It has been revealed that to construct these tests, a domain expert writes a specification for the simulated user’s objectives, tactics, persona, situation, tone and conversational style. The first user turn remains fixed, while a separate Claude model generates subsequent turns in response to the tested model. Each scenario runs repeatedly with different combinations of characteristics, and a grader model scores the complete transcript against the relevant risk rubric.

Varying dimensions independently helps identify what drives behavior; if every severe case also uses an urgent tone, the effects of severity and tone cannot be separated. Anthropic also recommends building from observed behavior, public data, red-teaming transcripts, incident reports or expert interviews rather than invented situations alone. Its single-turn suites cover 16 policy areas in seven languages across multiple product surfaces, and the evaluation environment is matched to the deployment being tested.

Running the tests also requires containment. For cyber evaluations, the guidance calls for sandboxes without internet access and real-time monitoring so a run can be stopped if a model’s actions could cause real-world harm.

Automated graders create another measurement risk because broken systems can continue producing plausible scores. The recommended safeguards include atomic yes-or-no criteria, explicit treatment of disclaimers and borderline cases, loud failure alerts, and checks for response-length, position and self-preference biases. Human reviewers should independently label a sample of transcripts so grader-to-expert agreement can be compared with agreement among experts themselves.

According to recent reports, that human baseline determines the remedy. If experts agree with one another but not with the grader, the rubric or grader needs work; if experts disagree with each other, the evaluation may not have a stable answer to measure. The guidance also calls for preregistering metrics, comparisons and improvement thresholds before results are seen.

Sample sizes underpin those judgments. Anthropic uses floors of 100 items for complex multi-turn evaluations and 1,000 for simpler single-turn tests, alongside repeated runs to account for noisy, nondeterministic outputs. Anthropic reports that confidence intervals on multi-turn API evaluations can exceed ±10 percentage points: in a multi-turn romance-scam evaluation on claude.ai, Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 recorded appropriate-response rates of 98% and 94%, respectively, but the difference was not statistically significant. The example shows why a numerical gap alone cannot establish which model behaved more safely.

Sources indicate that deployment configuration is another documented variable. While reviewing Claude Fable 5.1, Anthropic found that some responses implicitly validated self-harm as a coping strategy even when they discouraged self-harm and pointed toward human support. The tech giant reports that re-running the evaluation with targeted system-prompt mitigations produced a 94% appropriate-response rate on claude.ai, compared with 60% on the API. The comparison shows why scores from different configurations cannot be treated as equivalent.

Recent findings suggest that the reporting recommendations extend to model versions, sampling settings, prompts, grader versions and dates, with continuous evaluation during fine-tuning rather than a single pre-release check. Severe flaws in deployed systems should be disclosed to the developer first so there is time to remediate before results are published.

Anthropic’s three highest priorities are to define the construct before collecting data, validate the grader against human judgment and report uncertainty. The broader implication is that a claim that one model is safer than another depends on the test’s design, deployment context and statistical power as much as the headline score.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Storage can be a constant issue if you're using a more budget-friendly or older device, but downloading the latest games doesn't mean you have to delete loads of pictures from your gallery or uninstall your favorite apps to create space.

That's because developer Level Infinite has just released a upcoming version of PUBG Mobile designed specifically to be the lightest version of the popular battle royale game yet. The initial download of PUBG Mobile Flash takes up just 0.96GB, with multiple tools available to ensure subsequent content downloads are limited to the maps and modes you want to play – keeping as much free space on your phone as possible.

PUBG Mobile Flash also supports a wider range of devices than the base game, including those with just 2GB of RAM, and promises better graphics optimization for smoother frame rates.

The file size may be small, but Level Infinite makes it clear that this is still a fully fledged version of what it calls "one of the world’s most popular mobile games.".

Recent findings suggest that PUBG Mobile Flash players will be able to squad up with their friends on regular PUBG Mobile. There is also seamless account cross-progression, so you'll be able to pick up where you left off if you already play the regular version of the game.

“Expanding access to PUBG Mobile has always been an important part of our long-term vision, and we’re continually looking for new ways to connect players around the world,” explained general manager and PUBG Mobile head Vincent Wang.

"With PUBG Mobile Flash, we’re taking another step towards that goal, making it easier for more players to enjoy the core PUBG Mobile experience, reconnect with friends, and remain part of our global community.".

Nothing has been teasing its first dedicated AI product and, as we expected, it really looks like an AI recorder.

Last week, Nothing CEO Carl Pei announced that the company would be launching its first “AI-native” product that doesn’t have a screen and “couldn’t have been an app.” Now, Pei is back with a brief teaser for the product, captioned “Context doesn’t live in a chat box.”.

Nothing is keeping the details of what this product is a secret for now, but it’s becoming painfully obvious that this is an AI recorder.

Recent findings suggest that the green and red lights paired with what looks like a record button paint a very clear picture. As we pointed out initially, Pei’s first post heavily implied this was some type of audio device. He said:.

Meanwhile, the context that matters most never reaches the model at all. Think about the last time someone said something worth keeping: an idea over coffee, a throwaway comment that unblocks your whole week. What did you do? “Hold on, let me write that down.” Out comes the phone, and by the time you look up, the moment has moved on without you. Or you don’t bother, and it’s gone by the end of the day.

There are many AI recorders already on the market, admittedly with varying levels of quality, so we’ll have to wait and see how Nothing’s differentiates itself.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Open Source DocumentDB 1.0 Reaches General Availability.
  • Nov 14, 2026 2 min read.
  • In a recent development, documentDB 1.0 is the first generally available release of the open source, MIT-licensed document database built on PostgreSQL, with compatibility for the MongoDB wire protocol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Open Source DocumentDB 1.0 Reaches General Availability.

Nov 14, 2026 2 min read.

In a recent development, documentDB 1.0 is the first generally available release of the open source, MIT-licensed document database built on PostgreSQL, with compatibility for the MongoDB wire protocol. Most MongoDB drivers, tools, and queries work without changes.

Industry observers note that documentDB consists of a PostgreSQL extension that provides MongoDB API-compatible functionality and a gateway that translates MongoDB protocol requests into PostgreSQL calls. Version 1.0 supports PostgreSQL 15–18 through container images, with Linux packages available for PostgreSQL 17 and 18, and includes a Kubernetes operator, with the GA focusing on security, stability, and fixes for indexing, aggregation, and geospatial queries.

Industry observers note that microsoft revealed the open source project early in 2025, aiming to provide the developer community with a NoSQL datastore built on PostgreSQL, and offering full visibility into the engine's architecture and implementation. The project joined the Linux Foundation a few months later, with support from other large database organizations including AWS, Cockroach Labs, Google, Snowflake, and Yugabyte. In the recent article "DocumentDB and the MIT License: What to Know Before You Build, Deploy, and Distribute," the team explains how DocumentDB’s permissive MIT license allows commercial use, modification, and hosting without requiring disclosure of proprietary code, contrasting it with MongoDB’s SSPL.

Even if the project provides a page discussing the DocumentDB name disambiguation, covering the open source project, Azure DocumentDB, and Azure Cosmos DB, the community remains perplexed about the choice. In a popular Hacker News thread, user marifjeren writes:.

According to recent reports, name it anything else for god's sake. DocumentDB is already what everybody calls Amazon DocumentDB.

In a recent development, with multiple open source options now on the market, Patty Chow, product manager at Microsoft, explains why open-source document databases need multiple implementations to give developers more choice in deployment and infrastructure while preserving compatibility with MongoDB drivers and queries. Chow writes:.

MongoDB has given developers a widely used way to work with document data. Familiar drivers and query patterns are worth preserving. Alternative implementations give developers a chance to keep using that knowledge while evaluating different approaches to storage and deployment.

In a recent development, in a Reddit thread, some practitioners raise concerns about current MongoDB compatibility and confusion with similarly named products. User 716green comments:.

Compatibility between MongoDB and FerretDB has been absolutely minimal compared to what you would probably expect. I've been a fan of DocumentDB for a long time and I love that Microsoft is supporting FerretDB.

DocumentDB provides the PostgreSQL extensions and its own MongoDB-compatible gateway, while FerretDB is a separate project that uses the DocumentDB extensions as its backend and provides its own MongoDB-compatible interface.

Layerbase recently ran an initial comparison of FerretDB and the PostgreSQL-based DocumentDB using YCSB benchmarks, finding that DocumentDB delivered 20–33% higher read throughput, while FerretDB had lower tail latency for updates in mixed workloads, but noting the results are not conclusive. An open GitHub problem reports higher query latency in DocumentDB 1.0 than MongoDB 9.0.4 across several workloads, but the results have not been independently verified.

Recent findings suggest that the DocumentDB release notes include upgrade paths and known concerns. The project aims separate long-term support and development tracks, with its versioning policy still under discussion.

  • According to recent reports, I've been passing mundane tasks to my Gemini through Gemini Notebook and Gems, but the newly introduced Task feature is a proper upgrade.
  • Here's everything you need to know about the Google Gemini Schedulefeature before getting started.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hot on the heels of Anthropic's MCP sniffing AI models, Google has decided to grace your Gemini Pro subscription with AI tools that actually go out and do things on your behalf.

According to recent reports, I've been passing mundane tasks to my Gemini through Gemini Notebook and Gems, but the newly introduced Task feature is a proper upgrade. I have been using it to track discounts, offers, and price drops for things I want to buy online, and it works.

Here's everything you need to know about the Google Gemini Schedulefeature before getting started.

Gemini is slowly evolving from a chatbot into an AI that can access your connected Google apps and execute tasks on your behalf. It comes as a 24/7 bot called Gemini Spark, and as alarming as that may sound, Google Gemini cannot do anything without your permission.

According to recent reports, there's now an extension of this skill called Schedule. It existed before the revision, but it was clunky. Google has updated it with a settings page to fine-tune the automation and made it reliable.

However, you will need a Gemini Pro subscription or higher to schedule tasks.

Sources indicate that here's how to enable a scheduled task in Google Gemini. Click the hamburger menu in the upper-left corner, and then click Scheduled. Here, you can define a scheduled task you want Gemini to run at set intervals.

You don't have to mess with the toggles; you can use the chat box and explain what you want the automation to do.

I told Gemini to track a smartphone price drop and notify me when the price drops below $200.

Recent findings suggest that I initially ran a sweeping check for a price drop on the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra at Best Buy, but that open-ended approach burned through my tokens. It's better to rein in the automation with time intervals and specific dates.

It has been revealed that if you set up the automation for a deal hunt on Best Buy across a category, you will burn through tokens in an instant. So it's better if you know what you want to buy during the Black Friday sale period.

While Google is happy to pocket more cash from your automated search queries, it's better to narrow your choices and set time limits for scheduled tasks.

I told Gemini to find reliable product links online, and then I cross-checked the website myself.

I wanted to buy these products during the sale, so I told it to set up an automation to run twice a day from the 19th to the 30th of November.

Now Gemini runs a scheduled task to check the websites for price drops during the Black Friday sale period. This way, Gemini doesn't burn through my token usage.

You can either set up scheduled tasks per product or set up a single task to run across multiple websites and product pages at a scheduled time and date.

If you don't want the AI to mess up an notable opportunity, set up a separate automation for the product with multiple websites listing the product.

Gemini's task feature uses a built-in browser similar to Claude's. However, this browser cannot access Amazon.

It's better to first check with Gemini whether it can access the website links you provided, or provide the product name and ask Gemini to search for sale listings on websites it can access.

Most brand websites allow access to AI bots and Google crawlers for indexing, and during my testing, Best Buy allows Gemini to search for products.

However, the biggest Black Friday sale is always on Amazon, but the website has blocked Gemini.

Sources indicate that amazon has upgraded its system. It combined Rufus with the Alexa model, and now the built-in AI system does price charting and auto-buys for you. You can set up Alexa to auto-buy anything if the price drops to a certain amount.

This is a great workaround for anyone who wants to use only Amazon for purchases, and it's simple to set up.

You can set up automation for the Amazon website through the Alexa for Shopping tab in the upper-left corner, next to the hamburger menu.

This is a free service for now, and it continues and remembers conversations across Echo devices, Alexa.com, the Alexa app, Fire tablets, and Fire TV.

#160. Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, finds evidence of DRAM collusion plausible after 500% price surge

Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, finds evidence of DRAM collusion plausible after 500% price surge

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed.
  • Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is.
  • The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed. According to the decision, the defendants’ argument that the legal action is just “a rerun” of the same antitrust case filed against the industry in 2018 was rejected as the plaintiffs have established that there’s some latest evidence suggesting that there was collusion between the significant three memory chip manufacturers.

Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is. Judge Wise disagreed with this characterization, though, saying that what they are accused of goes beyond that. “Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation — an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.”.

The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year. One of the events they cited included the “simultaneous DRAM production cuts” from October 2022 to April 2023, which was rapidly followed by a “coordinated pivot to HBM.” They also mentioned that the three companies revealed the winding down of DDR4 production in a span of three months and have failed to expand the production capacity “despite these extraordinary prices — the single most powerful supply signal the DRAM industry has ever produced.”.

Other factors that the suing parties brought to the table include the introduction of stringent customer vetting procedures in response to the shortage, the refusal to sign long-term contracts for DRAM customers, Micron’s decision to shut down Crucial (its consumer memory brand), multiple statements projecting the shortage, as well as their involvement in previous price-fixing scandals.

The big three memory chip makers argued that all of these are logical business moves so that they can maximize their revenue during a period of great demand and that they are “consistent with [their own] independent self-interest.” They also said that they appear to have similar behaviors because they’re in a highly concentrated market, and that they’re all “reacting to the same market pressures,” thus it would make sense for them to have a similar response.

It has been revealed that despite their rebuttals, the judge decided that the case is plausible enough to move forward. This isn’t a judgment, though — both sides would still have to show their evidence and speak their arguments before the court before getting a decision. Because of this, the three companies are given until December 7 to respond to the original complaint with the case management conference, which will determine the administrative matters on the case, set for January 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's fair to say that the headline-grabbing arrival of the iPhone Duo has made the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max feel a little less shiny than they otherwise might have.

Indeed, upon opening my new iPhone 18 Pro Max and restoring my data from its predecessor, the iPhone 17 Pro Max, it was hard not to feel a little disappointed by the lack of bells and whistles on Apple’s latest flagship.

That’s probably to be expected from a single-generation upgrade — and, to be fair, I don’t usually swap phones after just one year — but there is one feature that’s caught my eye during my time with my iPhone 18 Pro Max, and it’s been a game-changer for my everyday life: Apple’s fresh C2 modem.

I’ve been using iPhones for around two decades, but since moving to a more remote area in 2021, I have noticed that my mobile signal has been incredibly inconsistent (on some days, it's absolutely awful).

In truth, this spotty signal has been the bane of my digital life, both as a small business owner and a parent — I could be in the same spot on different days of the week and experience completely different levels of coverage. Worse yet, my recent iPhones have had a tendency to display a weak 5G signal when, in fact, there's been no signal at all.

With the iPhone 18 Pro Max, however, I’m seeing drastic improvements in signal strength just about everywhere I go.

Industry observers note that rather than awkwardly trying to fumble through phone tasks using train or café WiFi, I’ve actually been able to use my paid-for data strategy consistently, which has made my iPhone 18 Pro Max feel less like a very expensive iPod and more like a piece of cutting-edge computing. And that’s all thanks to the C2 modem.

Apple debuted its C1 chip in the iPhone 16e, and the C2 makes its debut in the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo.

The C2 features in every iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo model sold worldwide, but only in iPhone 18 Pro Max models sold outside of the US. If you’re in the US and have Apple's larger Pro model, you’ve got Qualcomm's Snapdragon X80 modem.

Apple hasn't yet disclosed why this is the case, but we suspect it's a result of contractual obligation (we know it's not a technical limitation, since the C2 modem features in all other iPhone 18 Pro Max models, and indeed even in iPhone 18 Pro models sold within the US).

It has been revealed that as you'd expect from a numbered hardware upgrade, the C2 modem improves on the C1 in several ways. It adds full mmWave support alongside the C1's existing sub-6GHz 5G capabilities, and consumes less energy than its predecessor.

There are other iPhone 18 Pro-specific advantages, too: “If an iPhone encounters congested data networks, the phone’s [A20 Pro] processor can signal to the modem which traffic is the most time-sensitive and put it ahead of other data transfers,” Apple told Reuters of its C2 modem.

Thankfully, I’m not alone in feeling the benefits of Apple’s C2 modem. Plenty of other iPhone 18 Pro users have found that the addition of this small feature is leading to much better 5G connectivity.

Recent findings suggest that of course, as this Reddit post mentions, a fresh modem will only help if you’re in an area covered by 5G in the first place. Luckily for me, my home isn't so remote as to rely on older-generation networks, but that's worth bearing in mind if you live out in the sticks (Apple's hardware wizardry can only work so much magic).

And don't get me wrong: a fresh 5G modem is hardly the most exciting upgrade on a phone that costs at least $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099, and perhaps it's the least we should expect from Apple when the year-on-year upgrades are so limited elsewhere.

Still, after years of awkwardly lifting my iPhone into the sky in the hope of securing stronger signal — or just simply not using my iPhone at all — this small improvement, combined with improved battery life and the ever-higher performance ceiling of this year’s chip upgrade, has made me appreciate the iPhone 18 Pro Max more than I originally anticipated.

2026 is still very much an ‘iPhone S-year’, though.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 pre-orders have broken records for the game development studio, as well as PlayStation and Xbox platforms, with sales already above $1 billion.

GTA 6 pre-orders have reportedly gone through the roof on both the PlayStation and Xbox platforms, surpassing $1 billion in sales, marking a huge milestone not only for Rockstar and its parent organization Take-Two Interactive, but for the PlaySation and Xbox platforms as well. According to data from Sensor Tower, GTA 6 has sold about 12.13 million copies, and made roughly $1.18 billion in revenue.

The split is pretty uneven, with about 75% of those sales being on PlayStation, and about 25% being on Xbox. That split has not stopped it from becoming the most pre-ordered game on either console though. GTA 6 is set to release on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, with some people having already obtained their copies of the game. Preloads for GTA 6 also started back on November 10.

According to recent reports, many suspected that GTA 6 pre-orders would be hitting large numbers, but both Sony and Microsoft have confirmed that not only did it do large numbers, it’s the most pre-ordered game in the history of either platform. In the pre-load post on the PlayStation Blog earlier this week, Sony Interactive Entertainment Content Communications Manager Tim Turi confirmed that GTA 6 was the most pre-ordered game in the history of the PlayStation Store. The store has been around since the PS3 days, so, that’s a good 20 years.

From a sales standpoint, GTA 6 is poised to break records of its own even beyond the pre-order phase, and this is without any availability on PC. The game is suspected to hit PC sometime towards the Summer of 2027, though Rockstar nor Take-Tow Interactive have announced a PC release or when it might hit the platform. The massive game is about 212GB in file size, so it’s big all-around.

  • Dyania Health describes Synapsis AI as a clinical reasoning engine that reads years of notes, operative reports, imaging reports and laboratory results, then answers clinical questions with evidence linked to the chart.
  • Recent findings suggest that the deployment uses NVIDIA AI Enterprise across the software stack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dyania Health and NVIDIA revealed on November 13, 2026 that Synapsis AI is running on hospital-owned NVIDIA accelerated computing, with an initial Cleveland Clinic study covering 7,812 aortic-valve replacement patients. The collaboration is designed to review records across patient populations without moving them outside health-system networks.

Dyania Health describes Synapsis AI as a clinical reasoning engine that reads years of notes, operative reports, imaging reports and laboratory results, then answers clinical questions with evidence linked to the chart. Its outputs are clinical signals intended to show care teams which patients need attention and why; clinicians review the evidence and make every decision.

Recent findings suggest that the deployment uses NVIDIA AI Enterprise across the software stack. Dyania trains its proprietary clinical models with NeMo, then uses TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize inference on hospital GPU servers. Inference therefore stays within the hospital’s private network instead of sending patient records to an external environment.

According to recent reports, NVIDIA stated the system remains assistive: it surfaces evidence from medical records that clinicians must confirm and act on. That distinction matters because the deployment automates chart review and signal detection, not the clinical decisions that follow.

The companies are targeting a manual bottleneck in hospital research and care management. Notable details often sit in narrative text rather than structured fields, limiting the charts staff can review for registries, outcomes studies and predictive models. Synapsis AI applies longitudinal review across a health system’s population, with potential uses including care-gap detection, observational research and clinical-trial matching.

The study examined patients who received aortic valve replacements between 2005 and 2021, reviewing up to 16 years of care per patient. Synapsis AI answered 88 clinical questions for each patient covering valve characteristics, co-existing conditions, laboratory trends, medications, follow-up ultrasound measurements and subsequent clinical events. Much of that history was contained in narrative notes and echocardiogram reports.

NVIDIA remarked the platform completed chart review across the full cohort, work that would have taken clinicians years to perform manually. The resulting dataset was used to train a predictive machine-learning model that estimates valve-failure and reintervention risk at three, five and 10 years and revises those estimates with each newly introduced ultrasound.

Recent findings suggest that dyania reported that implanted valve type was the strongest determinant of how rapidly a valve deteriorated, while age and other medical conditions influenced whether and when a second procedure occurred. The analysis also examined how follow-up information, such as post-surgery ultrasounds, can substantially raise predictive accuracy around future interventions.

In a recent development, “Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” stated Lars G. Svensson, chief of Cleveland Clinic’s Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute.

The study demonstrates dataset construction and risk prediction, not improved patient outcomes. Dyania states the tool is intended to inform care and requires external clinical validation before broader clinical reliance.

In a recent development, dyania’s collaboration announcement says the companies proposal to pursue health-system deployments in the United States and internationally, publish joint case studies and integrate Synapsis AI with NVIDIA’s healthcare software stack. Technologies under evaluation include NVIDIA Confidential Computing for training and inference, NVIDIA Dynamo for distributed inference serving and Multi-Instance GPU for partitioning GPUs across concurrent clinical workloads.

According to recent reports, the companies are also evaluating scaling to multiple Blackwell Ultra GPUs as processing moves from batch reviews toward near-real-time clinical insight at the point of care. These remain evaluation goals rather than completed deployments. For health systems, the practical question is whether externally validated models can turn population-scale record review into reliable clinical action while clinicians retain control of care decisions.

#156. Sustainable Web Design, An Excerpt

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 25m • 📚 Deep Dive (5092 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Alistapart

Sustainable Web Design, An Excerpt

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alistapart

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the 1950s, many in the elite running community had begun to believe it wasn’t possible to run a mile in less than four minutes.
  • In the 1950s, many in the elite running community had begun to believe it wasn’t possible to run a mile in less than four minutes.
  • But on May 6, 1956, Roger Bannister took everyone by surprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the 1950s, many in the elite running community had begun to believe it wasn’t possible to run a mile in less than four minutes. Runners had been attempting it since the late 19th century and were beginning to draw the conclusion that the human body simply wasn’t built for the task. But on May 6, 1956, Roger Bannister took everyone by surprise. It was a cold, wet day in Oxford, England—conditions no one expected to lend themselves to record-setting—and yet Bannister did just that, running a mile in 3:59.4 and becoming the first person in the record books to run a mile in under four minutes. This shift in the benchmark had profound effects; the world now knew that the four-minute mile was possible. Bannister’s record lasted only forty-six days, when it was snatched away by Australian runner John Landy. Then a year later, three runners all beat the four-minute barrier together in the same race. Since then, over 1,400 runners have officially run a mile in under four minutes; the current record is 3:43.13, held by Moroccan athlete Hicham El Guerrouj. We achieve far more when we believe that something is possible, and we will believe it’s possible only when we see someone else has already done it—and as with human running speed, so it is with what we believe are the hard limits for how a website needs to perform. Establishing standards for a sustainable web In most major industries, the key metrics of environmental performance are fairly well established, such as miles per gallon for cars or energy per square meter for homes. The tools and methods for calculating those metrics are standardized as well, which keeps everyone on the same page when doing environmental assessments. In the world of websites and apps, however, we aren’t held to any particular environmental standards, and only recently have gained the tools and methods we need to even make an environmental assessment. The primary goal in sustainable web design is to reduce carbon emissions. However, it’s almost impossible to actually measure the amount of CO2 produced by a web product. We can’t measure the fumes coming out of the exhaust pipes on our laptops. The emissions of our websites are far away, out of sight and out of mind, coming out of power stations burning coal and gas. We have no way to trace the electrons from a website or app back to the power station where the electricity is being generated and actually know the exact amount of greenhouse gas produced. So what do we do? If we can’t measure the actual carbon emissions, then we need to find what we can measure. The primary factors that could be used as indicators of carbon emissions are: Data transfer Carbon intensity of electricity Let’s take a look at how we can use these metrics to quantify the energy consumption, and in turn the carbon footprint, of the websites and web apps we create. Data transfer Most researchers use kilowatt-hours per gigabyte (kWh/GB) as a metric of energy efficiency when measuring the amount of data transferred over the internet when a website or application is used. This provides a great reference point for energy consumption and carbon emissions. As a rule of thumb, the more data transferred, the more energy used in the data center, telecoms networks, and end user devices. For web pages, data transfer for a single visit can be most easily estimated by measuring the page weight, meaning the transfer size of the page in kilobytes the first time someone visits the page. It’s fairly easy to measure using the developer tools in any modern web browser. Often your web hosting account will include statistics for the total data transfer of any web application (Fig 2.1). Fig 2.1: The Kinsta hosting dashboard displays data transfer alongside traffic volumes. If you divide data transfer by visits, you get the average data per visit, which can be used as a metric of efficiency. The nice thing about page weight as a metric is that it allows us to compare the efficiency of web pages on a level playing field without confusing the concern with constantly changing traffic volumes. Reducing page weight requires a large scope. By early 2020, the median page weight was 1.97 MB for setups the HTTP Archive classifies as “desktop” and 1.77 MB for “mobile,” with desktop increasing 36 percent since January 2016 and mobile page weights nearly doubling in the same period (Fig 2.2). Roughly half of this data transfer is image files, making images the single biggest source of carbon emissions on the average website. History clearly shows us that our web pages can be smaller, if only we set our minds to it. While most technologies become ever more energy efficient, including the underlying technology of the web such as data centers and transmission networks, websites themselves are a technology that becomes less efficient as time goes on. Fig 2.2: The historical page weight data from HTTP Archive can teach us a lot about what is possible in the future. You might be familiar with the concept of performance budgeting as a way of focusing a project team on creating faster user experiences. For example, we might specify that the website must load in a maximum of one second on a broadband connection and three seconds on a 3G connection. Much like speed limits while driving, performance budgets are upper limits rather than vague suggestions, so the goal should always be to come in under budget. Designing for fast performance does often lead to reduced data transfer and emissions, but it isn’t always the case. Web performance is often more about the subjective perception of load times than it is about the true efficiency of the underlying system, whereas page weight and transfer size are more objective measures and more reliable benchmarks for sustainable web design. We can set a page weight budget in reference to a benchmark of industry averages, using data from sources like HTTP Archive. We can also benchmark page weight against competitors or the old version of the website we’re replacing. For example, we might set a maximum page weight budget as equal to our most efficient competitor, or we could set the benchmark lower to guarantee we are best in class. If we want to take it to the next level, then we could also start looking at the transfer size of our web pages for repeat visitors. Although page weight for the first time someone visits is the easiest thing to measure, and easy to compare on a like-for-like basis, we can learn even more if we start looking at transfer size in other scenarios too. For example, visitors who load the same page multiple times will likely have a high percentage of the files cached in their browser, meaning they don’t need to transfer all of the files on subsequent visits. Likewise, a visitor who navigates to new pages on the same website will likely not need to load the full page each time, as some global assets from areas like the header and footer may already be cached in their browser. Measuring transfer size at this next level of detail can help us learn even more about how we can optimize efficiency for users who regularly visit our pages, and enable us to set page weight budgets for additional scenarios beyond the first visit. Page weight budgets are easy to track throughout a design and development process. Although they don’t actually tell us carbon emission and energy consumption analytics directly, they give us a clear indication of efficiency relative to other websites. And as transfer size is an effective analog for energy consumption, we can actually use it to estimate energy consumption too. In summary, reduced data transfer translates to energy efficiency, a key factor to reducing carbon emissions of web products. The more efficient our products, the less electricity they use, and the less fossil fuels need to be burned to produce the electricity to power them. But as we’ll see next, since all web products demand some power, it’s important to consider the source of that electricity, too. Carbon intensity of electricity Regardless of energy efficiency, the level of pollution caused by digital products depends on the carbon intensity of the energy being used to power them. Carbon intensity is a term used to define the grams of CO2 produced for every kilowatt-hour of electricity (gCO2/kWh). This varies widely, with renewable energy sources and nuclear having an extremely low carbon intensity of less than 10 gCO2/kWh (even when factoring in their construction); whereas fossil fuels have very high carbon intensity of approximately 200–400 gCO2/kWh. Most electricity comes from national or state grids, where energy from a variety of different sources is mixed together with varying levels of carbon intensity. The distributed nature of the internet means that a single user of a website or app might be using energy from multiple different grids simultaneously; a website user in Paris uses electricity from the French national grid to power their home internet and devices, but the website’s data center could be in Dallas, USA, pulling electricity from the Texas grid, while the telecoms networks use energy from everywhere between Dallas and Paris. We don’t have control over the full energy supply of web services, but we do have some control over where we host our projects. With a data center using a significant proportion of the energy of any website, locating the data center in an area with low carbon energy will tangibly reduce its carbon emissions. Danish startup Tomorrow reports and maps this user-contributed data, and a glance at their map shows how, for example, choosing a data center in France will have significantly lower carbon emissions than a data center in the Netherlands (Fig 2.3). Fig 2.3: Tomorrow’s electricityMap shows live data for the carbon intensity of electricity by country. That mentioned, we don’t want to locate our servers too far away from our users; it takes energy to transmit data through the telecom’s networks, and the further the data travels, the more energy is consumed. Just like food miles, we can think of the distance from the data center to the website’s core user base as “megabyte miles”—and we want it to be as small as possible. Using the distance itself as a benchmark, we can use website analytics to identify the country, state, or even city where our core user group is located and measure the distance from that location to the data center used by our hosting manufacturer. This will be a somewhat fuzzy metric as we don’t know the precise center of mass of our users or the exact location of a data center, but we can at least get a rough idea. For example, if a website is hosted in London but the primary user base is on the West Coast of the USA, then we could look up the distance from London to San Francisco, which is 5,300 miles. That’s a long way! We can see that hosting it somewhere in North America, ideally on the West Coast, would significantly reduce the distance and thus the energy used to transmit the data. In addition, locating our servers closer to our visitors helps reduce latency and delivers better user experience, so it’s a win-win. Converting it back to carbon emissions If we combine carbon intensity with a calculation for energy consumption, we can calculate the carbon emissions of our websites and apps. A tool my team created does this by measuring the data transfer over the wire when loading a web page, calculating the amount of electricity associated, and then converting that into a figure for CO2 (Fig 2.4). It also factors in whether or not the web hosting is powered by renewable energy. If you want to take it to the next level and tailor the data more accurately to the unique aspects of your project, the Energy and Emissions Worksheet accompanying this book shows you how. Fig 2.4: The Website Carbon Calculator shows how the Riverford Organic website embodies their commitment to sustainability, being both low carbon and hosted in a data center using renewable energy. With the ability to calculate carbon emissions for our projects, we could actually take a page weight budget one step further and set carbon budgets as well. CO2 is not a metric commonly used in web projects; we’re more familiar with kilobytes and megabytes, and can fairly easily look at design options and files to assess how big they are. Translating that into carbon adds a layer of abstraction that isn’t as intuitive—but carbon budgets do focus our minds on the primary thing we’re trying to reduce, and support the core objective of sustainable web design: reducing carbon emissions. Browser Energy Data transfer might be the simplest and most complete analog for energy consumption in our digital projects, but by giving us one number to represent the energy used in the data center, the telecoms networks, and the end user’s devices, it can’t offer us insights into the efficiency in any specific part of the system. One part of the system we can look at in more detail is the energy used by end users’ devices. As front-end web technologies become more advanced, the computational load is increasingly moving from the data center to users’ devices, whether they be phones, tablets, laptops, desktops, or even smart TVs. Modern web browsers allow us to implement more complex styling and animation on the fly using CSS and JavaScript. Furthermore, JavaScript libraries such as Angular and React allow us to create applications where the “thinking” work is done partly or entirely in the browser. All of these advances are exciting and open up new possibilities for what the web can do to serve society and create positive experiences. However, more computation in the user’s web browser means more energy used by their devices. This has implications not just environmentally, but also for user experience and inclusivity. Applications that put a heavy processing load on the user’s device can inadvertently exclude users with older, slower devices and cause batteries on phones and laptops to drain faster. Furthermore, if we build web applications that require the user to have up-to-date, powerful devices, people throw away old devices much more frequently. This isn’t just bad for the environment, but it puts a disproportionate financial burden on the poorest in society. In part because the tools are limited, and partly because there are so many different models of devices, it’s difficult to measure website energy consumption on end users’ devices. One tool we do currently have is the Energy Impact monitor inside the developer console of the Safari browser (Fig 2.5). Fig 2.5: The Energy Impact meter in Safari (on the right) shows how a website consumes CPU energy. You know when you load a website and your computer’s cooling fans start spinning so frantically you think it might actually take off? That’s essentially what this tool is measuring. It shows us the percentage of CPU used and the duration of CPU usage when loading the web page, and uses these figures to generate an energy impact rating. It doesn’t give us precise data for the amount of electricity used in kilowatts, but the information it does provide can be used to benchmark how efficiently your websites use energy and set targets for improvement.

In the 1950s, many in the elite running community had begun to believe it wasn’t possible to run a mile in less than four minutes. Runners had been attempting it since the late 19th century and were beginning to draw the conclusion that the human body simply wasn’t built for the task.

But on May 6, 1956, Roger Bannister took everyone by surprise. It was a cold, wet day in Oxford, England—conditions no one expected to lend themselves to record-setting—and yet Bannister did just that, running a mile in 3:59.4 and becoming the first person in the record books to run a mile in under four minutes.

Sources indicate that this shift in the benchmark had profound effects; the world now knew that the four-minute mile was possible. Bannister’s record lasted only forty-six days, when it was snatched away by Australian runner John Landy. Then a year later, three runners all beat the four-minute barrier together in the same race. Since then, over 1,400 runners have officially run a mile in under four minutes; the current record is 3:43.13, held by Moroccan athlete Hicham El Guerrouj.

We achieve far more when we believe that something is possible, and we will believe it’s possible only when we see someone else has already done it—and as with human running speed, so it is with what we believe are the hard limits for how a website needs to perform.

Recent findings suggest that in most major industries, the key metrics of environmental performance are fairly well established, such as miles per gallon for cars or energy per square meter for homes. The tools and methods for calculating those metrics are standardized as well, which keeps everyone on the same page when doing environmental assessments. In the world of websites and apps, however, we aren’t held to any particular environmental standards, and only recently have gained the tools and methods we need to even make an environmental assessment.

In a recent development, the primary goal in sustainable web design is to reduce carbon emissions. However, it’s almost impossible to actually measure the amount of CO2 produced by a web product. We can’t measure the fumes coming out of the exhaust pipes on our laptops. The emissions of our websites are far away, out of sight and out of mind, coming out of power stations burning coal and gas. We have no way to trace the electrons from a website or app back to the power station where the electricity is being generated and actually know the exact amount of greenhouse gas produced. So what do we do?

If we can’t measure the actual carbon emissions, then we need to find what we can measure. The primary factors that could be used as indicators of carbon emissions are:.

Let’s take a look at how we can use these metrics to quantify the energy consumption, and in turn the carbon footprint, of the websites and web apps we create.

Sources indicate that most researchers use kilowatt-hours per gigabyte (kWh/GB) as a metric of energy efficiency when measuring the amount of data transferred over the internet when a website or application is used. This provides a great reference point for energy consumption and carbon emissions. As a rule of thumb, the more data transferred, the more energy used in the data center, telecoms networks, and end user devices.

Sources indicate that for web pages, data transfer for a single visit can be most easily estimated by measuring the page weight, meaning the transfer size of the page in kilobytes the first time someone visits the page. It’s fairly easy to measure using the developer tools in any modern web browser. Often your web hosting account will include statistics for the total data transfer of any web application (Fig 2.1).

The nice thing about page weight as a metric is that it allows us to compare the efficiency of web pages on a level playing field without confusing the issue with constantly changing traffic volumes.

Sources indicate that reducing page weight requires a large scope. By early 2020, the median page weight was 1.97 MB for setups the HTTP Archive classifies as “desktop” and 1.77 MB for “mobile,” with desktop increasing 36 percent since January 2016 and mobile page weights nearly doubling in the same period (Fig 2.2). Roughly half of this data transfer is image files, making images the single biggest source of carbon emissions on the average website.

It has been revealed that history clearly indicates us that our web pages can be smaller, if only we set our minds to it. While most technologies become ever more energy efficient, including the underlying technology of the web such as data centers and transmission networks, websites themselves are a technology that becomes less efficient as time goes on.

It has been revealed that you might be familiar with the concept of performance budgeting as a way of focusing a project team on creating faster user experiences. For example, we might specify that the website must load in a maximum of one second on a broadband connection and three seconds on a 3G connection. Much like speed limits while driving, performance budgets are upper limits rather than vague suggestions, so the goal should always be to come in under budget.

Designing for fast performance does often lead to reduced data transfer and emissions, but it isn’t always the case. Web performance is often more about the subjective perception of load times than it is about the true efficiency of the underlying system, whereas page weight and transfer size are more objective measures and more reliable benchmarks for sustainable web design.

According to recent reports, we can set a page weight budget in reference to a benchmark of industry averages, using data from sources like HTTP Archive. We can also benchmark page weight against competitors or the old version of the website we’re replacing. For example, we might set a maximum page weight budget as equal to our most efficient competitor, or we could set the benchmark lower to guarantee we are best in class.

Sources indicate that if we want to take it to the next level, then we could also start looking at the transfer size of our web pages for repeat visitors. Although page weight for the first time someone visits is the easiest thing to measure, and easy to compare on a like-for-like basis, we can learn even more if we start looking at transfer size in other scenarios too. For example, visitors who load the same page multiple times will likely have a high percentage of the files cached in their browser, meaning they don’t need to transfer all of the files on subsequent visits. Likewise, a visitor who navigates to upcoming pages on the same website will likely not need to load the full page each time, as some global assets from areas like the header and footer may already be cached in their browser. Measuring transfer size at this next level of detail can help us learn even more about how we can optimize efficiency for users who regularly visit our pages, and enable us to set page weight budgets for additional scenarios beyond the first visit.

Industry observers note that page weight budgets are easy to track throughout a design and development process. Although they don’t actually tell us carbon emission and energy consumption analytics directly, they give us a clear indication of efficiency relative to other websites. And as transfer size is an effective analog for energy consumption, we can actually use it to estimate energy consumption too.

In summary, reduced data transfer translates to energy efficiency, a key factor to reducing carbon emissions of web products. The more efficient our products, the less electricity they use, and the less fossil fuels need to be burned to produce the electricity to power them. But as we’ll see next, since all web products demand some power, it’s key to consider the source of that electricity, too.

Sources indicate that regardless of energy efficiency, the level of pollution caused by digital products depends on the carbon intensity of the energy being used to power them. Carbon intensity is a term used to define the grams of CO2 produced for every kilowatt-hour of electricity (gCO2/kWh). This varies widely, with renewable energy sources and nuclear having an extremely low carbon intensity of less than 10 gCO2/kWh (even when factoring in their construction); whereas fossil fuels have very high carbon intensity of approximately 200–400 gCO2/kWh.

Most electricity comes from national or state grids, where energy from a variety of different sources is mixed together with varying levels of carbon intensity. The distributed nature of the internet means that a single user of a website or app might be using energy from multiple different grids simultaneously; a website user in Paris uses electricity from the French national grid to power their home internet and devices, but the website’s data center could be in Dallas, USA, pulling electricity from the Texas grid, while the telecoms networks use energy from everywhere between Dallas and Paris.

We don’t have control over the full energy supply of web services, but we do have some control over where we host our projects. With a data center using a significant proportion of the energy of any website, locating the data center in an area with low carbon energy will tangibly reduce its carbon emissions. Danish startup Tomorrow reports and maps this user-contributed data, and a glance at their map demonstrates how, for example, choosing a data center in France will have significantly lower carbon emissions than a data center in the Netherlands (Fig 2.3).

That remarked, we don’t want to locate our servers too far away from our customers; it takes energy to transmit data through the telecom’s networks, and the further the data travels, the more energy is consumed. Just like food miles, we can think of the distance from the data center to the website’s core user base as “megabyte miles”—and we want it to be as small as possible.

In a recent development, using the distance itself as a benchmark, we can use website analytics to identify the country, state, or even city where our core user group is located and measure the distance from that location to the data center used by our hosting company. This will be a somewhat fuzzy metric as we don’t know the precise center of mass of our people or the exact location of a data center, but we can at least get a rough idea.

For example, if a website is hosted in London but the primary user base is on the West Coast of the USA, then we could look up the distance from London to San Francisco, which is 5,300 miles. That’s a long way! We can see that hosting it somewhere in North America, ideally on the West Coast, would significantly reduce the distance and thus the energy used to transmit the data. In addition, locating our servers closer to our visitors helps reduce latency and delivers better user experience, so it’s a win-win.

Recent findings suggest that if we combine carbon intensity with a calculation for energy consumption, we can calculate the carbon emissions of our websites and apps. A tool my team created does this by measuring the data transfer over the wire when loading a web page, calculating the amount of electricity associated, and then converting that into a figure for CO2 (Fig 2.4). It also factors in whether or not the web hosting is powered by renewable energy.

If you want to take it to the next level and tailor the data more accurately to the unique aspects of your project, the Energy and Emissions Worksheet accompanying this book shows you how.

It has been revealed that with the ability to calculate carbon emissions for our projects, we could actually take a page weight budget one step further and set carbon budgets as well. CO2 is not a metric commonly used in web projects; we’re more familiar with kilobytes and megabytes, and can fairly easily look at design options and files to assess how substantial they are. Translating that into carbon adds a layer of abstraction that isn’t as intuitive—but carbon budgets do focus our minds on the primary thing we’re trying to reduce, and support the core objective of sustainable web design: reducing carbon emissions.

Data transfer might be the simplest and most complete analog for energy consumption in our digital projects, but by giving us one number to represent the energy used in the data center, the telecoms networks, and the end user’s devices, it can’t offer us insights into the efficiency in any specific part of the system.

One part of the system we can look at in more detail is the energy used by end users’ devices. As front-end web technologies become more advanced, the computational load is increasingly moving from the data center to users’ devices, whether they be phones, tablets, laptops, desktops, or even smart TVs. Modern web browsers allow us to implement more complex styling and animation on the fly using CSS and JavaScript. Furthermore, JavaScript libraries such as Angular and React allow us to create applications where the “thinking” work is done partly or entirely in the browser.

Recent findings suggest that all of these advances are exciting and open up new possibilities for what the web can do to serve society and create positive experiences. However, more computation in the user’s web browser means more energy used by their devices. This has implications not just environmentally, but also for user experience and inclusivity. Applications that put a heavy processing load on the user’s device can inadvertently exclude people with older, slower devices and cause batteries on phones and laptops to drain faster. Furthermore, if we build web applications that require the user to have up-to-date, powerful devices, people throw away old devices much more frequently. This isn’t just bad for the environment, but it puts a disproportionate financial burden on the poorest in society.

In a recent development, in part because the tools are limited, and partly because there are so many different models of devices, it’s difficult to measure website energy consumption on end users’ devices. One tool we do currently have is the Energy Impact monitor inside the developer console of the Safari browser (Fig 2.5).

According to recent reports, you know when you load a website and your computer’s cooling fans start spinning so frantically you think it might actually take off? That’s essentially what this tool is measuring.

In a recent development, it demonstrates us the percentage of CPU used and the duration of CPU usage when loading the web page, and uses these figures to generate an energy impact rating. It doesn’t give us precise data for the amount of electricity used in kilowatts, but the information it does provide can be used to benchmark how efficiently your websites use energy and set targets for improvement.

#154. Think the Google Fitbit Air is your only option? We've tested trending screenless fitness trackers to find the 6 best

Think the Google Fitbit Air is your only option? We've tested trending screenless fitness trackers to find the 6 best

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2395 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're experiencing always-on tech fatigue, which is in part why wearables like smart rings and now screenless fitness and health trackers are becoming popular.
  • Recent findings suggest that they can capture all the same data as a smartwatch or traditional fitness tracker, but do so passively, in the background, so you can go about your day without distractions.
  • Android Central has tested many of the latest screenless fitness bands extensively, often sporting more than one at a time to compare and contrast them and the data they collect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're experiencing always-on tech fatigue, which is in part why wearables like smart rings and now screenless fitness and health trackers are becoming popular.

Recent findings suggest that they can capture all the same data as a smartwatch or traditional fitness tracker, but do so passively, in the background, so you can go about your day without distractions. Screenless fitness trackers in particular are on the rise, graduating from a market once dominated only by Whoop to include huge brands like Google Fitbit and Garmin as well as smaller ones like Luna and Amazfit.

Android Central has tested many of the latest screenless fitness bands extensively, often sporting more than one at a time to compare and contrast them and the data they collect. At their core, they all do the same thing. But there are also notable differences in design, battery life, app experience, and subscription options (or membership requirements). You'll want to pick the right one to use alongside your Android device based on your needs, preferences, and budget.

The Google Fitbit Air is thin, comfortable, affordable, yet packs tons of power in a small band. Think Fitbit's history of accurate activity and sleep tracking combined with Google's knowledge in design, AI, and apps. With Google Health Premium, it's the best you can buy right now.

The Garmin CIRQA is thicker and chunkier than others, but it's a solid choice if fitness is your main priority. That's thanks to accurate automatic tracking and a side button for quickly triggering an activity, cute shareable post-workout cards, and decent battery life that keeps it going for more than a week per charge.

According to recent reports, the Luna Band combines some of the best aspects of apps like Google Health Premium in a subscription-free, AI-driven experience. I loved the LifeOS system with the Luna Ring 2, and with the consistent app updates, it continues to improve, making this a promising option.

You might need an executive-level salary to afford the Whoop MG's annual membership, but medical-grade ECG and blood pressure trends make it worthwhile for those with heart health concerns, especially. The app and system are among the most aggressive in terms of pushing you to get in shape, focus on your health, and slow the pace of aging. But for some, that's a good thing.

According to recent reports, with features like live heart rate broadcasting to compatible devices like gym equipment and an optional arm sleeve, the Amazfit Helio Strap is meant for gym-goers and runners. It's a simple design with accurate data capture, and best of all, no subscription.

It has been revealed that the Fitbit Air is one of the most accurate screenless fitness trackers, combining Fitbit's long history in the business with top-notch vitals and sleep tracking, along with Google's powerful processing and AI integration. While you can use the Fitbit Air with the free version of the app and get basic details, you will get a lot more out of it with a Google Health Premium subscription.

According to recent reports, AI Coach is one of the best I have used, answering questions about the data, like why you might not have slept well and what you can do to improve, what exercise would be good to work around a shoulder injury, and even logging specific dumbbell weights and reps to gather more details about a workout. I love how easy it is to log meals by either dictating what you just ate or snapping a photo. You'll see a detailed breakdown of calories consumed (versus burned), protein, fat, carbs, and more. It's a solid food diary if you want to use it for that, too.

According to recent reports, the companion app is easy to navigate with all the essentials at a glance, like heart rate, a detailed breakdown of sleep, blood oxygen, readiness score, and more. Most notably, the app guides you through how to tackle the day with commentary, analysis, motivation, suggestions, and advice. It really is like a virtual coach. A couple of substantial omissions, our reviewer notes, are the lack of ECG and built-in GPS. But considering how affordable the band is, we can live with that.

Along with what's captured from the band, the more information you provide with food logging, details about workouts, injuries, moments of stress, and more, the more intelligent it becomes in putting this all together. It's one of the few wearables where I'd say the subscription is worth the money.

Given the affordable price of the band, use the three-month trial to get an idea of what Premium adds and decide from there. It's a no-brainer option to keep on top of fitness and vitals.

The Garmin CIRQA is thicker and wider than other bands, but it's still incredibly comfortable to wear. Most importantly, it tracks all the essentials for free. You can opt for the Garmin Connect+ subscription for add-ons like Garmin Coach, AI-powered insights, and nutrition tracking. But it's not robust enough to be worth it, and that's pretty much all that's behind a paywall.

According to recent reports, the band accurately tracks activity, vitals, and sleep; the data provided is typically in line with other wearables I rely on. What I love is that it's the only screenless band I have seen to date with a physical side button you can press to manually start and stop an activity. You can later clarify in the app what it was, like a cardio class or baseball game. But it does a pretty good job of automatically picking up activities with distinct movements, like walks, runs, boxing, and strength training. I love the ability to add a post-workout selfie to a cute card with workout stats you can share on social media or with friends.

If you're looking for a band mainly to track fitness, the Garmin CIRQA is a good option. You don't get all the bells and whistles that come with Google Health Premium and Fitbit Air. It's also a higher upfront cost for the band. But you can keep track of everything that matters, including a detailed diary of your workouts and stats.

One of the lesser-known brands in this space, Luna is best known for its smart rings. But the firm launched its first screenless tracker at CES 2026 with the Luna Band, and it's a serious contender. It tracks all the same metrics as others and does so accurately, based on my month-plus of wearing it. This includes everything from activities to sleep, vitals like heart rate, HRV, stress, respiratory rate, and more.

Recent findings suggest that at the heart of the experience is the Life OS system, an AI-driven system that lets you ask questions, log things like stress and meals, get advice, dive deeper into data, and more. There's an "Ask Luna" hands-free voice option, though it's limited to iPhone support right now.

Seemingly inspired by Ultrahuman smart rings and the company's PowerPlugs, the Luna app also includes downloadable micro apps you can add to customize the experience. These include, at the time of this writing, sleep alarm, cycle tracker, calorie tracker, and circadian rhythm. The app indicates that new features are coming soon, like a Luna Age (cardio fitness score), supplement planner, and hydration analyzer.

Sources indicate that the app has been updated and redesigned several times since I started wearing the band. So, if you are looking to get in with a brand that's experimenting and continuously developing, this is a good option. Most importantly, you can be confident that the data is accurate.

Around since 2015, Whoop isn't technically the originator of this category, but it has a similar reputation to Oura as the brand that put the category on the map. But before you get excited about a Whoop tracker, they're expensive with a capital "E." And the Whoop MG is the top-line model.

It's a medical-grade tracker that, compared to its little sister, the Whoop 5.0, adds ECG and blood pressure insights. ECG is easy to measure any time by placing your thumb and index finger on the sensors on either side, and blood pressure requires an initial cuff measurement to then provide subsequent trend estimates.

The app is packed (and I really mean packed) with data that you might initially feel like you need a medical degree to interpret. Thankfully, however, it's thoughtfully laid out and explained to help you make sense of it all. It tracks all the expected metrics and has a Healthspan and Pace of Aging feature. After the 31-day logging period, it will report a Whoop Age that you can compare to your biological age and determine your pace of aging. It's a moving target, so if there's ever a stat that prompts you to work out, go for that walk, eat better, and head to bed early, it's that one.

In a recent development, if the Whoop MG is too rich for your blood and you are willing to forego ECG and blood pressure insights, consider the Whoop 5.0. Its membership options are slightly more affordable, but still more expensive than any other band over its lifetime.

If you love the concept behind the WHOOP MG but find the pricing too rich for your blood, even for the WHOOP 5.0, the Hume Band 2.0 is worth considering. While I haven't yet tested this model (stay tuned!), it is widely praised for offering some of the same benefits as WHOOP bands, including a focus on longevity and helping you reduce the speed of aging.

Industry observers note that while you get the core tracking features for free, including sleep, recovery, strain, HRV, skin temperature, and of course activity tracking as well as blood pressure trends, there is a Hume Premium subscription tier that unlocks more. But it's much cheaper at $8.99 per month, which works out to be almost half the price of the cheapest WHOOP One blueprint.

Sources indicate that the band and companion app capture useful data like metabolic capacity (similar to a readiness score), sleep apnea risk alerts, chronic illness detection (identifying early signs), and AI coaching with the subscription tier. You may have to take the data with a grain of salt. But the price of entry makes Hume Band 2.0 a good starting point if you're considering exploring the concept of a screenless tracker and value overall lifespan data more than daily metrics and workout stats.

Amazfit has a solid reputation in the smartwatch space, with many of its models ranking among the best affordable Android smartwatches. This reliability extends to the Amazfit Helio Strap, which is simple, affordable, and, based on customer feedback (we haven't reviewed this one yet), as reliable as its beloved smartwatches.

Industry observers note that one of the unique features is live heart rate broadcasting, which allows you to broadcast your heart rate to compatible devices, like a Garmin smartwatch, Apple Watch, or even gym equipment. The best part? There's no subscription required…for anything.

According to recent reports, there's a more premium option called the Amazfit Helio Strap Pro that boasts a dual-sensor system and is designed for hybrid athletes and HYROX training. But most people won't need that model. There are also useful accessories like an arm sleeve for wearing it around the bicep, something runners will appreciate so they can still wear a running watch on their wrist. This is a solid budget option for fitness enthusiasts who also want vital health tracking.

Choosing the right screenless fitness band comes down to two core things: recognizing your needs and budget.

Industry observers note that if you want something you only need to pay a single price for and that doesn't require recurring fees, choose one of those options. If you are serious about health, want guidance and granular data, and can afford it, you may find value in some subscription-based bands.

All these bands track both fitness and health, including vitals. But some focus more heavily on fitness, some on health, and some a mix of both. If you only want to monitor daily data, you can look for a simpler option. If you need guidance towards meeting goals, a more advanced one makes sense. For ECG readings, the Whoop MG is your only option in this category. If it's pricing doesn't meet your budget, however, you can consider a smartwatch with ECG instead.

Why you can trust Android Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

You'll be happy with any of these screenless fitness bands. For an AI-driven coaching experience, Fitbit Air can't be beat. But if you want to get something similar without a subscription, Luna Band is worth considering. If you exercise daily and want to track workouts as much as vitals, the Garmin CIRQA is a solid choice.

Industry observers note that the Whoop MG is a medical-grade device, ideal for serious athletes or someone who is especially concerned about heart health and/or blood pressure. But it comes in at executive-level pricing. It's worth noting that none of these trackers, even the Whoop MG, is a replacement for consultation from a medical professional, and they are not meant for diagnosis, only supplemental data.

The best overall budget option is the Fitbit Air. It doesn't cost much upfront, and you can gauge how the subscription works through the three-month trial. Once the trial lapses, see the difference without it and decide from there if it's worth paying the nominal monthly fee. Even with Google Health Premium, the cost is one less takeout lunch a month when all is remarked and done. And even after a year, the overall cost is still less than the upfront cost of most of these other bands.
