#127. Latest Update: I've been using the new Google Messages UI; one change is driving me crazy

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (793 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidpolice

Latest Update: I've been using the new Google Messages UI; one change is driving me crazy

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidpolice

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Messages is one of my most-used apps, and for the most part, I really like what Google has been doing with it lately.
  • I love that you can now copy a specific part of a message instead of the entire text, and I've also been using the swipe-to-reply gesture often, similar to how I use it on WhatsApp.
  • But every once in a while, Google introduces a change that makes me wonder why it needed to fix something that wasn't broken in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Messages is one of my most-used apps, and for the most part, I really like what Google has been doing with it lately.

I love that you can now copy a specific part of a message instead of the entire text, and I've also been using the swipe-to-reply gesture often, similar to how I use it on WhatsApp.

But every once in a while, Google introduces a change that makes me wonder why it needed to fix something that wasn't broken in the first place. And that's exactly how I feel about the fresh pinned conversations UI.

I've been using it for a while now, and while the upcoming search button is a welcome addition, I can't say the same about Google's redesign of pinned conversations.

It has been revealed that earlier this month, Google started rolling out a upcoming pinned chats UI for the Messages app. Previously, pinning a chat in Google Messages moved it to the top of the conversation list with a small pinned icon next to it.

But Google now seems to have taken inspiration from iMessage, introducing a newly introduced interface where pinned chats appear as large circular icons with the contact's photo and their name underneath.

I received the newly introduced pinned chats UI in Google Messages earlier this week, although I've seen several users on Reddit reporting that the redesigned interface still isn't available to everyone. Having used the new layout for the past few days, I have a couple of thoughts.

First, the new circular icons make it much clearer which conversations are pinned to the top. They're easier to distinguish from the rest of the messages in Google Messages, and you can also rearrange pinned conversations by holding and dragging them around.

When a newly introduced message arrives from a pinned conversation, the circular icon also highlights a preview of the latest message in place of the contact's profile photo, making it easier to see what's new.

Recent findings suggest that still, there are some clear downgrades compared to the previous interface. First, you can now pin only up to six conversations, whereas the previous layout allowed up to 20.

Industry observers note that the upcoming pinned chats also take up considerably more space at the top of the screen. If you have six conversations pinned, you're essentially losing half of your screen space.

Old Google Messages pinned chats UI.

What's even more annoying is that if you have just four pinned chats, there's a lot of wasted white space, with the pinned section still taking up a large portion of the screen.

Also, if a pinned conversation hasn't received a latest message recently, you can no longer see the last message you exchanged from the Google Messages home screen.

Sources indicate that sure, the newly introduced pinned chats UI looks sleek, and it's clearly designed to feel familiar to people coming from iMessage. But I feel Google could have improved it by letting owners swipe through pinned conversations when there are more than three, or at least offering that as an option.

The circular icons look nice, but you're also sacrificing quite a bit of useful screen space in the process.

Alongside the fresh pinned messages UI, Google has also rolled out a redesigned search button and a new Start Chat button in the app. Search, which used to sit at the top of the screen, is now placed next to the floating Start Chat button at the bottom, and I'm a huge fan of this change.

By default, the search icon is smaller, while the Start Chat button is larger. But as you start scrolling down, the Start Chat button collapses, making both options easier to access.

Old search icon in Google Messages.

So, if you're looking for a specific conversation, you can swiftly jump into search without scrolling all the way to the top. The animation and the way these buttons expand and collapse are really well done.

But what I particularly like is how accessible search has become. What used to be stuck at the top of the screen is now easily reachable with your thumb.

Recent findings suggest that thankfully, at least for me, the Gemini button has also disappeared from the bottom of the screen. I always found it annoying, especially since I never really used Gemini inside Google Messages.

I'm sure the latest UI is designed to appeal to iPhone people who have recently switched from iOS to Android, and while it looks clean, Google should at least give users the option to switch back to the previous layout.

That remarked, there are a couple of other Google Messages settings you can change to make the overall experience a little less annoying.

Humility: An Essential Value

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Humility, a designer’s essential value—that has a nice ring to it.
  • Industry observers note that humility, a designer’s essential value—that has a nice ring to it.
  • That said, this is a book for designers, and to that end, I’d like to start with a story—well, a journey, really.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Humility, a designer’s essential value—that has a nice ring to it. What about humility, an office manager’s essential value? Or a dentist’s? Or a librarian’s? They all sound great. When humility is our guiding light, the path is always open for fulfillment, evolution, connection, and engagement. In this chapter, we’re going to talk about why. That said, this is a book for designers, and to that end, I’d like to start with a story—well, a journey, really. It’s a personal one, and I’m going to make myself a bit vulnerable along the way. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've built a couple of React Native apps, the following probably feels familiar. You start with a colors.ts file and a simple Button component. Everything looks fine at first. Then the design changes a few times, and that small color file starts growing. Your Button also picks up another prop every time someone asks for a slightly different style.

The setup works at first, but after a few design changes, even a small update can mean checking several files across the project.

Here's what a typical color file looks like after a while:.

And here's what a typical Button looks like after a few redesigns:.

These are simplified examples, but you get the idea. The color object keeps growing, and the Button collects more props to handle every newly introduced design request.

In a recent development, each change seems reasonable when you make it. But the annoying part comes later, when changing one design decision means checking several files to see that nothing else has changed unexpectedly.

Part of the problem is how many component libraries are distributed. Their code lives in node_modules, so you usually customize them through the props and options they expose. When the library doesn't cover your exact use case, you add another prop or override. Keep doing that and the component can become harder to maintain than the original problem you were trying to solve.

It has been revealed that this is one reason I like shadcn/ui's approach. You don't install a traditional component package and treat its components as fixed. The CLI copies the source code into your project, where you can change it whenever you need to. For React Native, there's a project built around the same idea called React Native Reusables.

According to recent reports, to make this practical, I'll use React Native Reusables, Expo, and Uniwind to build a cart and checkout screen for a coffee shop's pickup orders. It includes order items with quantity controls, a pickup-time dropdown, a name field, an "own cup" toggle, a bill summary, a checkout bar that stays at the bottom, and an order-confirmation dialog. If you want to see how reusable sections come together in complete interfaces, you can also browse shadcn templates.

I'll also point out a few things that are easy to miss when working with these components, including:.

To follow along, you should have:.

You don't need any accounts or API keys, and nothing here costs money.

Before creating the app, let's look at the tools in this project. Each one has a specific job, and knowing that will make the setup easier to follow.

shadcn/ui is a collection of UI components for the web. It's not installed as a package. Instead, a command-line tool (CLI) copies the source code of each component into your project, and from then on the code is yours to edit.

In a recent development, react Native Reusables is the React Native version of shadcn/ui. It gives you components such as Button, Card, Select, and Dialog that are written for React Native and styled with Tailwind-style class names. It uses the same CLI idea as shadcn/ui.

Recent findings suggest that RN Primitives is a React Native port of Radix UI, which is the library that shadcn/ui uses for behavior on the web. A "primitive" is a component that handles the behavior but has no styling. For example, the select primitive knows how a dropdown opens and closes and how it's unveiled to screen readers, but it has no colors or borders. React Native Reusables adds the looks on top.

Recent findings suggest that uniwind is a tool that lets you style React Native components with Tailwind CSS class names, such as className="bg-primary p-4". It converts those classes into regular React Native styles while the app is being bundled, so there's no extra work at runtime. Nativewind does a similar job, and React Native Reusables supports both. This tutorial uses Uniwind.

In a recent development, expo and Expo Router provide the project setup, the development server, and file-based navigation. If you have used Next.js, Expo Router works in a similar way.

The React Native Reusables documentation opens with a quote from shadcn:.

Sources indicate that this is not a component library. It is how you build your component library.

You won't add shadcn/ui as a regular dependency in package.json. It uses a registry instead. A registry is a collection of JSON files hosted on a server. Each file describes a component and includes the information the CLI needs to add it to your project. When you run the CLI, it reads the relevant file and copies the component's source code into your project.

To see what this looks like, here's the registry entry for the Badge component. A Badge is a small label, such as the "Medium" tag next to a coffee in the cart you will build later. This is a shortened version of the real file:.

The file is public, so you can look at it yourself:.

Here's what the important fields mean:.

In a recent development, that's how a component gets from the registry into your app. The registry stores the component information, and the CLI uses it to create the files in your repository. React Native Reusables uses the shadcn CLI behind the scenes, so you can follow the same workflow when adding React Native components.

There are a few reasons this approach is useful when you're building an app:.

Industry observers note that there's one trade-off to keep in mind. Since the component code is copied into your project, updates from the registry aren't applied automatically. If a bug is fixed upstream, you'll need to run the CLI again with --overwrite. If you have customized that component, you may also need to reapply your changes. This is worth considering before you make large changes to several components.

According to recent reports, at the time of writing, React Native Reusables includes thirty components: accordion, alert, alert-dialog, aspect-ratio, avatar, badge, button, card, checkbox, collapsible, context-menu, dialog, dropdown-menu, hover-card, input, label, menubar, popover, progress, radio-group, select, separator, skeleton, switch, tabs, text, textarea, toggle, toggle-group, and tooltip. The available components cover many of the building blocks you need for a typical app interface.

Recent findings suggest that react Native is different from the web in several ways, so the components can't be an exact copy of the web version. The documentation lists the main differences, and you'll run into each of them in this tutorial. If you're also building web interfaces with shadcn/ui, shadcn components can be useful when you need more ready-made examples to work from.

We'll build a cart and checkout screen for a coffee shop where customers place an order and pick it up at the counter. The screen uses twelve components from the registry. While putting it together, I'll also explain a few React Native details that are easy to miss, including how dropdowns are rendered, how safe areas affect the layout, and how to keep the checkout bar visible while the rest of the page scrolls:.

The complete code is available in the GitHub repository if you want to compare your work with the final result.

We can let the React Native Reusables CLI create the initial project for us. It sets up Expo Router, the styling configuration, the theme file, and a few starter components. Run the following command to get started:.

What is the name of your project? The name you type becomes the folder name. It suggests my-app.

Select a template. There are three options, and the one you need isn't the one selected by default:.

According to recent reports, press the down arrow once and choose Minimal (Uniwind). This is the one choice that's tricky to change later. Nativewind and Uniwind are two different ways to use Tailwind in React Native, and the CLI keeps a separate registry for each one. The components it writes for Uniwind are different from the ones it writes for Nativewind, so the code in this tutorial won't match if you pick Nativewind.

Recent findings suggest that would you like to install dependencies? Choose yes, and select the package manager you use.

It has been revealed that would you like to initialize a Git repository? Choose yes. You're about to replace the starter screen, and having a commit to compare against is helpful.

The CLI creates the following files:.

Industry observers note that before moving on, let's take a look at a few files in this structure. You'll use them throughout the tutorial:.

Industry observers note that uniwind reads global.css while Metro bundles the app and turns your class strings into React Native style objects. This happens at build time, so a long className string doesn't slow down your app.

Press w to open it in the browser, i for the iOS simulator, or a for Android. The starter screen has a theme toggle in the header, which highlights that the theme setup is working.

You can also run a diagnostic command at any point if something seems wrong:.

It has been revealed that it checks your setup and reports which styling library it detects. For this project, the output should be:.

If it notes Nativewind, fix that before you add any components.

In a recent development, once the setup is working, you should see the starter screen. Try the theme toggle in the header to make sure light and dark mode both work, and check that the console is free of errors:.

Industry observers note that now that the app is running, let's look at its theme setup. The global.css file is where we'll define the colors used by the components. If you've previously kept these values in a colors.ts or theme.ts file, this is the setup that replaces it.

There are two conventions in this file that you need to know.

Industry observers note that first, the --color- prefix creates the class names. When you declare --color-primary, Tailwind automatically creates bg-primary, text-primary, and border-primary. If you declare --primary instead, you only get a CSS variable that nothing uses.

This is important because most shadcn theme generators produce the web format, where the variables are named --primary. If you paste that output without renaming the variables, nothing breaks, but nothing changes either. Step 12 shows you how to convert them.

Second, @variant light and @variant dark replace :root and .dark. On the web, dark mode works by adding a .dark class to the page. A phone has no page to add a class to, so Uniwind manages the switch. When you call Uniwind.setTheme, it swaps the active values. You'll use this in Step 11.

You may also notice that the file uses oklch() colors. Phones don't have a browser to read that format, but Uniwind converts the colors to a format React Native understands while bundling, so you can use modern color syntax anyway.

If you open lib/theme.ts, you'll find the same colors again as a JavaScript object. This duplication is needed because React Navigation, which draws the header and screen background, reads colors from a plain JavaScript object and can't read CSS variables. As a result, you have to keep two copies of your palette in sync. Step 12 indicates what happens when they differ.

In a recent development, let's change one of the tokens to see how the theme works. Enhancement the primary color in the light theme to a value that's easy to notice:.

Save the file and look at the starter screen. The Browse the Docs button is now red, even though you didn't edit button.tsx:.

According to recent reports, notice that every component using bg-primary picks up the latest color. You only changed one token, but the button updated without touching its component file. Change the value back before continuing.

Industry observers note that the starter project already gives us three components: Text, Button, and Icon. I'd take a few minutes to look through them before building the screen. They introduce patterns you'll see again in the other registry components.

In React Native, styles don't cascade the way they do in CSS. If you set a text color on a View, the text inside it doesn't inherit that color. This is a problem for a component such as , which needs its label to be white. The label is a Text component that the Button doesn't control, because it comes in through children. On the web, the Button would simply set a color and let it flow down to the label.

React Native Reusables solves this with React context. This is the code in components/ui/text.tsx:.

It has been revealed that A parent component, such as Button, puts a class string into the context. Every Text inside it reads that string and applies it. Your own className still wins because it comes last in the cn() call.

Sources indicate that the Text component also has a variant prop with options like h1 to h4, p, code, lead, large, small, and muted. For example, gives you the mobile version of text-muted-foreground text-sm. The variants also set the role and aria-level props, so screen readers announce headings correctly without any extra work.

According to recent reports, the Button in components/ui/button.tsx uses cva (class-variance-authority) the same way the web version does. Here's a shortened version:.

There are four differences from the web version:.

Icons from lucide-react-native take color and size as props, not as class names. The Icon component in components/ui/icon.tsx teaches Uniwind how to convert one into the other:.

This code reads the width from the class string and passes it as size, and it reads the color and passes it as color. That's why works the way you would expect. withUniwind is useful any time you use a third-party component that takes props where you want to use classes.

Sources indicate that you don't need to run anything for this step. The vital part is understanding what TextClassContext is doing. Once that clicks, the other components in the registry are much easier to follow.

Industry observers note that we already have three components from the template. For the checkout screen, we need a few more. The CLI can add all of them in one go:.

Recent findings suggest that the CLI detects that you're using Uniwind and writes the matching versions. It also installs any required @rn-primitives packages and adds a file called native-only-animated-view.tsx, which Select and AlertDialog use for their animations.

The CLI created ten files, which is more than the nine you asked for, because native-only-animated-view.tsx is a dependency of Select and AlertDialog. It skipped the three files that the template already gave you, so it does not overwrite your copies. This is the "you own the file" idea at work.

Recent findings suggest that run pnpm dev again to make sure the app still starts. The components/ui/ folder should now contain thirteen files.

Before we start building the UI, let's add the sample menu data and decide where the screen state will live. I'm going to store prices in cents rather than floating-point numbers. This avoids calculation results such as $4.7499999.

We'll also keep the state in the main screen component and pass the relevant values down as props. That way, changing an item quantity or selecting the own-cup option automatically updates the bill.

Recent findings suggest that the PICKUP_TIMES list is in this file instead of inside a component because two different components need it. You'll see why in Step 7.

This is basically how app/index.tsx looks. The parts that don't exist yet are left as comments, and you'll write the full file later in Step 10.

There are three details in this layout that you should examine more closely:.

At this stage, you should see only a header with the latest title and an empty page below it:.

In a recent development, the order row has quite a bit going on in a small space: an avatar, product name, size badge, price, and quantity controls. Long names make this especially tricky on a phone, so we'll handle the layout carefully.

Create components/cart/order-row.tsx:.

A few details in this component deserve a closer look.

Recent findings suggest that first, Avatar requires the alt prop. TypeScript won't compile without it. The value becomes the accessibility label, so a screen reader claims "Flat white" instead of just "image".

Industry observers note that the radius is repeated on the avatar fallback. Avatar and AvatarFallback are each rounded-full by default. If you only set rounded-2xl on Avatar, the emoji background stays a circle and pokes out of the rounded square.

Industry observers note that you should also use numberOfLines={1} instead of truncate. Tailwind's truncate relies on text-overflow: ellipsis, which React Native doesn't support, and Uniwind doesn't convert it. The class compiles to nothing, so a long product name pushes the price off the screen. The numberOfLines prop is the React Native way to do this, and it also works in the web build.

The name has shrink and its column has flex-1. Without shrink, a long name won't get smaller and will push the badge out of the row. This is regular Flexbox behavior, but it indicates up more on a phone because there's less width to work with.

According to recent reports, hitSlop={8} makes small buttons easier to tap. Apple recommends touch targets of at least 44 points and Android recommends 48dp, but a size-7 button is only 28 points wide. The hitSlop prop makes the touchable area larger without changing how the button looks. There's no CSS equivalent.

Finally, tabular-nums keeps digits the same width. In most fonts, the digit 1 is narrower than 8, so prices would shift sideways every time the quantity changes. Uniwind converts tabular-nums to React Native's fontVariant, so it works on iOS, Android, and the web.

After adding this component and rendering it inside a Card (which you'll do in Step 10), you should see three rows:.

In a recent development, tapping plus on the flat white should change its price from $9.50 to $14.25. Tapping the trash icon on an item with a quantity of one should remove the row. The minus button turns into a trash icon whenever the quantity is one.

Industry observers note that the pickup card brings together three controls: a Select, an Input, and a Switch. The input and switch are fairly straightforward. The Select needs a little more attention because it has three platform-related quirks, and two of them can fail silently.

Create components/cart/pickup-card.tsx:.

Sources indicate that when a dropdown opens, it needs to appear above the other content on the screen. For that reason, SelectContent isn't rendered in the same place where you declare it in the component tree. It uses @rn-primitives/portal to render the content in another part of the app. This technique is called a portal.

On the web, a portal renders into document.body, and every page has one. React Native has nothing like that. So the portal package keeps a list of portal contents in memory, and a component called PortalHost reads that list and displays it. This is a simplified version of that code from node_modules/@rn-primitives/portal/dist/index.js:.

Recent findings suggest that if no PortalHost is mounted, the content is saved but never displayed. The dropdown opens into nothing, and you get no error or warning.

The template already includes a PortalHost at the bottom of the root layout:.

There's another problem to consider when showing a dropdown on a phone. Parts of the screen are reserved for the operating system, such as the area around the notch and the home indicator. If a dropdown opens near the bottom of the screen, one of its options could appear underneath the home indicator. In that area, a tap may be handled by the operating system instead of your app.

To avoid this, pass the safe area insets to the content:.

The insets prop is part of PositionedContentProps in @rn-primitives/types, so every positioned component in the registry accepts it, including Popover, DropdownMenu, HoverCard, Tooltip, and Select. It's a good habit to pass it every time.

Recent findings suggest that one more thing to watch out for is the value returned by onValueChange. It may look like you're selecting a string, but the callback returns an Option object:.

According to recent reports, this causes a bug that only appears on one platform. If you store the whole Option in state and show option.label later, such as in a confirmation dialog, it displays correctly on a phone ("In 30 minutes") but incorrectly in the browser ("30").

The reason is in the primitive's source code. This is the native version, from select.js:.

Recent findings suggest that and this is the web version, from select.web.js. It uses Radix, which only returns a value:.

It has been revealed that so the label is correct on native, but on the web it's a copy of the value. If you only test in a simulator, you won't notice this problem.

The fix is to keep only the value in state and look up the label from your own list:.

Industry observers note that this is why PICKUP_TIMES is in lib/menu.ts. The pickup card needs it to build the options, and the main screen needs it to write the confirmation message.

The switch itself is quite small, so users may tap the label next to it instead. It makes sense to let that label toggle the switch as well. You can do that by adding an onPress handler to the Label:.

Giving both elements the same nativeID connects them for screen readers. The onPress on the Label is what makes the text toggle the switch, because React Native has no automatic behavior.

According to recent reports, while you're here, open components/ui/switch.tsx. On the web, shadcn colors a switch with data-[state=checked]:bg-primary, which reads an attribute set in the DOM. React Native has no data-* attributes, so the component checks the prop in JavaScript:.

The result is the same. Keep this in mind if you copy a data-[state=...] selector from a web example and it has no effect.

Input is a TextInput with your border and radius applied. You should set these four props on every text input:.

Together with automaticallyAdjustKeyboardInsets on the ScrollView from Step 5, this keeps the field visible while the keyboard is open. If you need more control, react-native-keyboard-controller is already a dependency of the template, and it provides KeyboardAwareScrollView and KeyboardProvider.

When you open the dropdown, it should appear right under the trigger at the same width, with a check mark next to the current value:.

Try picking a time and check that the trigger updates. Tap the words "Bringing my own cup" and confirm the switch flips. Type in the name field and confirm the keyboard doesn't cover it. If the dropdown opens and highlights nothing, check your PortalHost.

The bill component is pretty small, but there are two details you should pay particular attention to here, especially when the values change while someone is editing their order.

Create components/cart/bill.tsx:.

First, use tabular-nums on every number. Right-aligned prices in a proportional font don't line up at the decimal point, and using tabular-nums fixes that, as in the order rows.

Sources indicate that second, only show the discount row when it applies. The code uses {discount > 0 ? : null} instead of {discount && }. In JSX, if the left side of && is the number 0, React renders the 0. In React Native, a bare number outside a Text component throws the error Text strings must be rendered within a component. Using a boolean check and returning null avoids this whole category of bugs.

To test it, turn on the own cup switch and scroll down. An Own cup line should appear with -$0.25, and the tax should change from $1.54 to $1.52, because tax is calculated on the discounted subtotal:.

Sources indicate that the total changes from $20.19 to $19.92, which is 27 cents lower instead of 25. The extra two cents come from the lower tax.

Sources indicate that I want the total and checkout button to remain visible while the user scrolls through the cart. On the web, you might reach for position: sticky and bottom: 0. React Native doesn't work that way, but we can get the same result with a simple flex layout.

According to recent reports, you can get the same result with Flexbox. This is the layout from Step 5 again:.

The outer View is a column. The ScrollView has flex-1, so it takes all the leftover height. The checkout bar is a sibling placed after it, so it sits at the bottom and doesn't scroll. You don't need any positioning or z-index.

On phones without a home button, the bottom 34 points or so belong to the system. A button drawn there is hard or impossible to press. To avoid this, add the bottom safe area inset as padding.

Recent findings suggest that the bottom padding is an inline style instead of a class because its value depends on the device and is only known when the app runs. Using className and style on the same element is fine, and this is the case it's meant for.

On devices with no gesture bar, and in a browser tab, insets.bottom is 0, so the extra 12 keeps the bar from looking cramped.

Recent findings suggest that create the full component in components/cart/checkout-bar.tsx. It includes the confirmation dialog, which Step 10 explains.

border-t draws a line that's one logical point thick, which is two or three physical pixels on most modern screens. Next to a true one-pixel line, it looks heavy. React Native's StyleSheet.hairlineWidth gives you the thinnest line the screen can draw, and the template connects it to Tailwind with this line in global.css:.

Sources indicate that this adds hairline to Tailwind's spacing scale, so h-hairline gives you a divider that's one physical pixel tall. The Common Mistakes section later explains one catch when you try to use it as an override.

Recent findings suggest that that's the checkout bar in place. Scroll to the bottom of the screen and check that it stays below the bill:.

Scroll back to the top and the bar stays in the same place:.

It has been revealed that on a phone with a notch, the button should be above the gesture bar. If you remove all items with the trash buttons, the button should be disabled and the label should say "Nothing in the cart".

The checkout bar already contains the confirmation dialog. Before putting the full screen together, there are two differences between the React Native implementation and the web version that are worth looking at.

Recent findings suggest that on iOS, it also wraps itself in FullWindowOverlay from react-native-screens, so it draws above the native navigation header instead of under it. This is handled inside alert-dialog.tsx, which is why that file imports something that looks unrelated.

AlertDialogFooter uses flex-col-reverse and only becomes a row at the sm: breakpoint. On a phone, the button you write last is shown on top. Writing Cancel first and Action second puts the confirm button where the thumb is and the cancel button below it.

When the customer confirms the order, the confirm function calls Haptics.notificationAsync(Haptics.NotificationFeedbackType.Success). This gives a short success vibration on supported devices.

You might expect to wrap this call in a platform check because browsers don't have the same haptics support as native apps. In this case, expo-haptics already includes a web implementation that uses navigator.vibrate, with a fallback for iOS Safari. If the browser can't provide haptics, the call simply does nothing, so we don't need an extra platform check.

notificationAsync is meant for outcomes such as success or failure. impactAsync is for physical collisions, and selectionAsync is for moving through a list of options. Using the wrong one won't cause an error, but it feels slightly off.

Sources indicate that now we can bring everything together in the main screen. This is where we'll keep the state, calculate the bill using billFor, and pass the required values and callbacks to each component.

When an order is placed, it sets orderNumber, and the screen shows a confirmation instead. Inside that confirmation, changes the header title to "Order sent" without navigating anywhere, so the whole flow stays in one file and one route.

Notice that pickupLabel is the fix from Step 7 in use. The screen looks up the label from PICKUP_TIMES and passes a plain string to CheckoutBar, so CheckoutBar never touches an Option object or the incorrect web label.

To test it, place an order. The dialog should show your name and the pickup time you chose (such as "in 30 minutes"), not the raw value 30. Confirm the order, and you should see the confirmation screen:.

Tap "Start another order" and the cart returns to its original state.

In a recent development, the checkout screen is now working, and each part is kept in its own component. You can use the same approach when you build other screens: keep the component focused, pass the data it needs through props, and let the shared theme handle the styling.

Industry observers note that we already added the theme toggle in Step 10. Here's the component again so we can look at how it switches between light and dark mode:.

This code also uses the ios: and web: prefixes. Uniwind supports platform variants, so web:mx-4 only adds margin in the browser, and ios:size-9 only applies on iOS. It's similar to Platform.select, but it stays inside the class string.

Sources indicate that three things aren't handled by setTheme, and if you forget them, you end up with a screen that's only partly dark. The template already sets up the first two.

React Navigation takes its colors from a plain object, so the root layout needs to pass it the right one:.

The clock and battery icons are drawn by the operating system, so you need to tell it which style to use. Without this, you can get dark text on a dark bar.

Uniwind.setTheme only applies to the current session. The next time the app starts, it follows the system setting again. To keep the user's choice, save it with expo-secure-store or AsyncStorage and call setTheme when the app starts. You can call setTheme('system') to go back to following the operating system.

It has been revealed that when you tap the header icon, the cards, borders, inputs, switch, header, and status bar should all change together. You can explore more ready-made shadcn blocks if you want examples of how these components are used in larger interfaces:.

It has been revealed that look for anything that stays light while the rest goes dark. A light header usually means the ThemeProvider is not receiving the fresh NAV_THEME.

The screen is at the moment using the default gray theme. Let's change it to a coffee-inspired palette with warm cream backgrounds and brown accents. This will also help us see why the palette needs to be updated in both global.css and lib/theme.ts.

Replace the @layer theme block in global.css with this coffee palette:.

It has been revealed that if you don't want to choose thirty colors by hand, you can generate a theme with the shadcn theme generator or tweakcn. Both export CSS variables, but you need to make two changes before the output works in this project:.

Also remove --radius from what you paste, because the template already defines it along with the derived sizes. Remove any --shadow-* variables too, since nothing in the registry reads them.

After you save and reload, the result looks like this:.

The page is cream, the button is brown, and the badges have the right color, but the header is still white with a visible line under it. The reason is that React Navigation draws the header using lib/theme.ts, and that file still has the old palette. Nothing is broken and nothing warns you, so this mistake is easy to miss. If you're designing the same interface in Figma, the shadcn Figma resources can also help you keep the design and implementation aligned.

This isn't a direct copy of global.css, so three points need explanation:.

After this change, the header and page match in both light and dark mode, and you didn't edit any component files:.

Switch between light and dark a few times and watch the header. If it's a shade lighter or darker than the page, one of the values in lib/theme.ts is still from the old palette.

Sources indicate that if you're coming from web development, some of these differences may catch you off guard. I've collected the issues covered in the tutorial in the table below, along with the fix for each one. You can refer back to it when something doesn't behave as expected.

The last row needs more explanation, because it looks like a bug in cn(), but it's not.

cn() uses tailwind-merge, which resolves conflicts between classes. It knows the default Tailwind scale, but it doesn't know about custom values you declare in global.css. The value hairline comes from --spacing-hairline: hairlineWidth(), so tailwind-merge can't tell that h-hairline and h-[1px] set the same property, and it keeps both:.

According to recent reports, the second result is correct. In the first, which height wins depends on the order of the CSS. The other overrides in this tutorial, such as size-14 over size-8, work correctly because those are names tailwind-merge recognizes. If you want it to understand your custom scale, you can teach it with extendTailwindMerge in lib/utils.ts. Otherwise, use an arbitrary value, or edit the component file directly, since you own it.

Recent findings suggest that there's a related case in the stepper buttons. They pass size-7 to a Button whose icon size is h-10 w-10 sm:h-9 sm:w-9:.

Industry observers note that size-7 replaces the base h-10 w-10, but the two sm: classes stay, because tailwind-merge treats a responsive variant as a different class. On a phone this makes no difference, since sm: starts at 640px and phones are narrower than that. In a desktop browser, though, those buttons grow to 36 points.

In this tutorial, we built a coffee shop cart and checkout screen with React Native Reusables, Expo, and Uniwind. We added the order rows, pickup options, bill summary, fixed checkout bar, and confirmation dialog. We also looked at how the registry and CLI add component source code to the project and how the theme tokens control the app's colors.

One thing worth getting into the habit of is checking the component source when something doesn't behave the way you expect. Since the components live in your project, you can open them and see how they work. That's how we understood the difference in the Select label between web and native. It also makes customization easier because you can see which part of the component needs to change instead of adding more workarounds around it.

Recent findings suggest that you can find the complete project in the GitHub repository. If you run into an matter or want to compare your code with the finished screen, clone the repository and check the implementation. If you're looking for more complete starting points for your next project, take a look at shadcn templates.

In a recent development, I captured the screenshots using the React Native Web build at a phone-sized viewport. The same project also runs on iOS and Android. I've called out the platform differences in the relevant sections, including the Select label and portal host in Step 7, safe area handling in Step 9, and haptics in Step 10.

#124. I am a creative.

I am a creative.

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alistapart

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I do not so much do it, as let it be done through me.
  • According to recent reports, I am a creative.
  • Industry observers note that I am a creative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I am a creative. What I do is alchemy. It is a mystery. I do not so much do it, as let it be done through me. I am a creative. Not all creative people like this label. Not all see themselves this way. Some creative people see science in what they do. That is their truth, and I respect it. Maybe I even envy them, a little. But my process is different—my being is different. Apologizing and qualifying in advance is a distraction. That’s what my brain does to sabotage me. I set it aside for now. I can come back later to apologize and qualify. After I’ve said what I came to say. Which is hard enough. Except when it is easy and flows like a river of wine. Sometimes it does come that way. Sometimes what I need to create comes in an instant. I have learned not to say it at that moment, because if you admit that sometimes the idea just comes and it is the best idea and you know it is the best idea, they think you don’t work hard enough. Sometimes I work and work and work until the idea comes. Sometimes it comes instantly and I don’t tell anyone for three days. Sometimes I’m so excited by the idea that came instantly that I blurt it out, can’t help myself. Like a boy who found a prize in his Cracker Jacks. Sometimes I get away with this. Sometimes other people agree: yes, that is the best idea. Most times they don’t and I regret having  given way to enthusiasm. Enthusiasm is best saved for the meeting where it will make a difference. Not the casual get-together that precedes that meeting by two other meetings. Nobody knows why we have all these meetings. We keep saying we’re doing away with them, but then just finding other ways to have them. Sometimes they are even good. But other times they are a distraction from the actual work. The proportion between when meetings are useful, and when they are a pitiful distraction, varies, depending on what you do and where you do it. And who you are and how you do it. Again I digress. I am a creative. That is the theme. Sometimes many hours of hard and patient work produce something that is barely serviceable. Sometimes I have to accept that and move on to the next project. Don’t ask about process. I am a creative. I am a creative. I don’t control my dreams. And I don’t control my best ideas. I can hammer away, surround myself with facts or images, and sometimes that works. I can go for a walk, and sometimes that works. I can be making dinner and there’s a Eureka having nothing to do with sizzling oil and bubbling pots. Often I know what to do the instant I wake up. And then, almost as often, as I become conscious and part of the world again, the idea that would have saved me turns to vanishing dust in a mindless wind of oblivion. For creativity, I believe, comes from that other world. The one we enter in dreams, and perhaps, before birth and after death. But that’s for poets to wonder, and I am not a poet. I am a creative. And it’s for theologians to mass armies about in their creative world that they insist is real. But that is another digression. And a depressing one. Maybe on a much more notable topic than whether I am a creative or not. But still a digression from what I came here to say. Sometimes the process is avoidance. And agony. You know the cliché about the tortured artist? It’s true, even when the artist (and let’s put that noun in quotes) is trying to write a soft drink jingle, a callback in a tired sitcom, a budget request. Some people who hate being called creative may be closeted creatives, but that’s between them and their gods. No offense meant. Your truth is true, too. But mine is for me. #123. I’d rather use Android XR glasses over Meta Ray-Bans for the app alone

I’d rather use Android XR glasses over Meta Ray-Bans for the app alone

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.
  • It has been revealed that one of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration.
  • The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.

It has been revealed that one of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration. It’s something we see frequently, and perhaps most well-known on smartwatches.

The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple. While we can’t show you the full app just yet as the one we were able to try was not completely final, it’s a very simple experience.

Industry observers note that the app opens to an overview of your glasses to show their connection and battery status, with settings below for Gemini, apps, the camera, and more. You’ll also be able to see things such as what the various lights on the glasses mean, tutorials, and more. There’s no bloat and no messing around – it’s a utility to just make adjustments or control the glasses as needed.

Sources indicate that you’ll probably be using this app mostly to view the photos and videos captured on Android XR glasses. Google has this set up to auto-import photos in nearly real-time. It only takes about 4 seconds to import and the process starts immediately for photos. Videos, on the other hand, take longer and may need to be manually imported (for the sake of battery in part, Google mentioned).

According to recent reports, across the three main platforms, there are some differences. The iPhone app doesn’t import photos quite as fast, and Samsung has its own app to fit in with One UI’s design language for Galaxy users, but the core premise is the same across all three.

While we’ll have to see how this works in real life, I was blown away by how simple it all was, though that might be because the bar is below the floor.

Meta’s Ray-Bans (and newer Meta Glasses) dominate the smart glasses conversation, and I think that the app is one of the biggest problems. It’s certainly one of the biggest reasons I’ve barely touched my Wayfarers in recent months. That’s because, in early 2025, Meta replaced its dedicated “View” app for its glasses with a Meta AI app, which is just invasive and distasteful in my book. Meta is no stranger to shoving AI down the throat of its existing customers. Another well-known move was converting Facebook and Instagram search into AI search boxes with creepy levels of context and invasive actions – it makes Google’s AI Overviews look tame by comparison. But I’d argue the most aggressive was this move with its glasses. Something as simple as tweaking a setting or importing a photo now forces you to dodge an AI chatbot.

Truly, Meta’s app is the worst, and I applaud Google for building a very simple utility for Android XR glasses instead.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 15, 2026 2 min read.
  • Cloudflare recently made Application Services for Private Origins generally available, allowing public traffic to reach applications hosted on private networks without exposing their IP addresses or opening inbound firewall ports.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Cloudflare Introduces Private Origins for Application Services.

Nov 15, 2026 2 min read.

Cloudflare recently made Application Services for Private Origins generally available, allowing public traffic to reach applications hosted on private networks without exposing their IP addresses or opening inbound firewall ports. Private-to-private connectivity is not yet supported.

Unveiled in closed beta in June, the service is now generally available with a simplified configuration: private IP addresses are automatically detected in proxied DNS records, and private routing can be configured through the DNS API. Enrique Somoza, product development manager at Cloudflare, writes:.

We debuted this capability (...) to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet.

According to recent reports, existing Cloudflare connectivity can be used to apply WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, and Workers to private origins, just as with public-facing applications. The service also supports private TCP/UDP origins through Spectrum and private connectivity for Workers. Somoza adds:.

Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.

Industry observers note that using Private Origins requires a Private Origins entitlement, Cloudflare One connectivity, and Unified Routing (not required when using Cloudflare Tunnel). Cloudflare WAN and Mesh connections also require return routes for Cloudflare's IPv4 (100.64.0.0/12) and IPv6 (2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64) source ranges, as well as a proxied DNS record pointing to the private IP with private network routing enabled. Existing WAF, caching, and bot management policies apply automatically. Simon Painter, cloud network consultant, notes:.

It has been revealed that no extra connector software. WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching and Workers all sit in front of stuff that was never meant to be on the open internet. The interesting bit isn't the marketing wrapper — it's the DNS implication. For years the rule was: "if it answers a public DNS name, it's reachable from the public internet." That stops being true here.

Cloudflare is not the only cloud provider offering ways to connect public-facing services to private application backends. AWS, for example, offers CloudFront VPC Origins, while Microsoft provides similar capabilities through Azure Front Door Premium and Private Link. Giacomo Masseroni writes:.

In a recent development, finally. been punching holes in security groups just to let the edge in.

Sources indicate that with general availability, Cloudflare has updated the Private Origins developer documentation. The announcement does not clarify whether the feature carries an additional charge or is included in existing Enterprise contracts.

Industry observers note that cloudflare aims to extend the service to support private-to-private traffic, allowing customers, services, and AI agents on one private network to access applications on another. A closed beta is targeted for early 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming giants are always finding fresh ways to upgrade the user experience and adapt to evolving usage patterns, and Peacock is the latest platform to take its mobile app in a new direction with its biggest overhaul yet.

NBCUniversal declared a upcoming era of the Peacock mobile app this week (November 11), showcasing a roster of fresh upgrades it hopes will not only enhance the experience, but increase user engagement and get viewers to spend more time browsing its seemingly endless library of titles.

The streamer states it's already started testing the fresh tools and will continue into 2027.

"Our ambition is for Peacock to be more than a place to watch," remarked Jim Denney, Chief Product Officer, Global Streaming & NBCUniversal Media Group.

"With this latest mobile experience, we’re evolving Peacock into an entertainment platform that gives fans more ways to discover, participate, and strengthen their connection to their favorite stories, teams, and franchises, turning viewing into deeper engagement and lasting fandom and loyalty".

In a recent development, one of Peacock's most notable mobile upgrades is the addition of vertical video — which the platform claims is integral to creating an experience that's separate from the one you get on a TV. Netflix jumped on this a while back, so it was only a matter of time before Peacock followed suit.

The fresh Clips Feed exists as its own section, designed to give you a new means of discovering new titles across entertainment and sports that isn't just simply scrolling the homepage.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Recent findings suggest that peacock is also launching its new Franchise Hubs as a way to browse more content but with a community or fandom focus. This section of the app packs interactive games, live moments, and relevant episodes and podcasts centered on specific franchises, from Minions, Love Island USA, The Traitors, and more.

As well as short-form video, Peacock is jumping on the AI bandwagon, introducing conversational AI search to give you another way to find upcoming content. With this new function, you can browse titles by name or, if you can't decide what to watch but know what mood or theme you're looking for, it can pull up content based on that information, which you can refine as the conversation progresses.

Audience behavior evolves; there's no doubt, so in order for streaming platforms to adapt to these shifts, they have to make some changes.

Sources indicate that in the case of Spotify, for example, its Messages feature lifted a pain point with users by allowing them to share music and podcasts with their friends directly in the Spotify app, rather than having to screenshot everything and send it to group chats on other platforms. Those kinds of features are genuinely helpful, but even then, Spotify has also plagued its in-app hubs with short-form video, and I want to see the back end of it.

Sources indicate that when Netflix first unveiled its vertical video feeds, I wasn't surprised per se, but I certainly grimaced at the very thought of it. And now that more services are taking advantage of it, it's suddenly becoming the upcoming norm.

It has been revealed that but what gets under my skin most is how these vertical feeds are pitched to viewers. The streaming behemoths claim they're useful discovery tools, but at the crux of it, it's just another way to increase your screen time and how long you spend in apps. Doom-scrolling has taken over the social media landscape as it is; I don't need it to get in the way of how I browse movies and reveals.

#120. Opportunities for AI in Accessibility

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3520 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Alistapart

Opportunities for AI in Accessibility

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alistapart

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in reading Joe Dolson’s recent piece on the intersection of AI and accessibility, I absolutely appreciated the skepticism that he has for AI in general as well as for the ways that many have been using it.
  • In reading Joe Dolson’s recent piece on the intersection of AI and accessibility, I absolutely appreciated the skepticism that he has for AI in general as well as for the ways that many have been using it.
  • Sources indicate that I’d like you to consider this a “yes… and” piece to complement Joe’s post.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in reading Joe Dolson’s recent piece on the intersection of AI and accessibility, I absolutely appreciated the skepticism that he has for AI in general as well as for the ways that many have been using it. In fact, I’m very skeptical of AI myself, despite my role at Microsoft as an accessibility innovation strategist who helps run the AI for Accessibility grant program. As with any tool, AI can be used in very constructive, inclusive, and accessible ways; and it can also be used in destructive, exclusive, and harmful ones. And there are a ton of uses somewhere in the mediocre middle as well. I’d like you to consider this a “yes… and” piece to complement Joe’s post. I’m not trying to refute any of what he’s saying but rather provide some visibility to projects and opportunities where AI can make meaningful differences for people with disabilities. To be clear, I’m not saying that there aren’t real risks or pressing issues with AI that need to be addressed—there are, and we’ve needed to address them, like, yesterday—but I want to take a little time to talk about what’s possible in hopes that we’ll get there one day. Alternative text Joe’s piece spends a lot of time talking about computer-vision models generating alternative text. He highlights a ton of valid issues with the current state of things. And while computer-vision models continue to improve in the quality and richness of detail in their descriptions, their results aren’t great. As he rightly points out, the current state of image analysis is pretty poor—especially for certain image types—in large part because current AI systems examine images in isolation rather than within the contexts that they’re in (which is a consequence of having separate “foundation” models for text analysis and image analysis). Today’s models aren’t trained to distinguish between images that are contextually relevant (that should probably have descriptions) and those that are purely decorative (which might not need a description) either. Still, I still think there’s potential in this space. As Joe mentions, human-in-the-loop authoring of alt text should absolutely be a thing. And if AI can pop in to offer a starting point for alt text—even if that starting point might be a prompt saying What is this BS? That’s not right at all… Let me try to offer a starting point—I think that’s a win. Taking things a step further, if we can specifically train a model to analyze image usage in context, it could help us more rapidly identify which images are likely to be decorative and which ones likely require a description. That will help reinforce which contexts call for image descriptions and it’ll improve authors’ efficiency toward making their pages more accessible. While complex images—like graphs and charts—are challenging to describe in any sort of succinct way (even for humans), the image example shared in the GPT4 announcement points to an interesting opportunity as well. Let’s suppose that you came across a chart whose description was simply the title of the chart and the kind of visualization it was, such as: Pie chart comparing smartphone usage to feature phone usage among US households making under $30,000 a year. (That would be a pretty awful alt text for a chart since that would tend to leave many questions about the data unanswered, but then again, let’s suppose that that was the description that was in place.) If your browser knew that that image was a pie chart (because an onboard model concluded this), imagine a world where users could ask questions like these about the graphic: Do more people use smartphones or feature phones? How many more? Is there a group of people that don’t fall into either of these buckets? How many is that? Setting aside the realities of large language model (LLM) hallucinations—where a model just makes up plausible-sounding “facts”—for a moment, the opportunity to learn more about images and data in this way could be revolutionary for blind and low-vision folks as well as for people with various forms of color blindness, cognitive disabilities, and so on. It could also be useful in educational contexts to help people who can see these charts, as is, to understand the data in the charts. Taking things a step further: What if you could ask your browser to simplify a complex chart? What if you could ask it to isolate a single line on a line graph? What if you could ask your browser to transpose the colors of the different lines to work better for form of color blindness you have? What if you could ask it to swap colors for patterns? Given these tools’ chat-based interfaces and our existing ability to manipulate images in today’s AI tools, that seems like a possibility. Now imagine a purpose-built model that could extract the information from that chart and convert it to another format. For example, perhaps it could turn that pie chart (or better yet, a series of pie charts) into more accessible (and useful) formats, like spreadsheets. That would be amazing! Matching algorithms Safiya Umoja Noble absolutely hit the nail on the head when she titled her book Algorithms of Oppression. While her book was focused on the ways that search engines reinforce racism, I think that it’s equally true that all computer models have the potential to amplify conflict, bias, and intolerance. Whether it’s Twitter always showing you the latest tweet from a bored billionaire, YouTube sending us into a Q-hole, or Instagram warping our ideas of what natural bodies look like, we know that poorly authored and maintained algorithms are incredibly harmful. A lot of this stems from a lack of diversity among the people who shape and build them. When these platforms are built with inclusively baked in, however, there’s real potential for algorithm development to help people with disabilities. Take Mentra, for example. They are an employment network for neurodivergent people. They use an algorithm to match job seekers with potential employers based on over 75 data points. On the job-seeker side of things, it considers each candidate’s strengths, their necessary and preferred workplace accommodations, environmental sensitivities, and so on. On the employer side, it considers each work environment, communication factors related to each job, and the like. As a manufacturer run by neurodivergent folks, Mentra made the decision to flip the script when it came to typical employment sites. They use their algorithm to propose available candidates to companies, who can then connect with job seekers that they are interested in; reducing the emotional and physical labor on the job-seeker side of things. When more people with disabilities are involved in the creation of algorithms, that can reduce the chances that these algorithms will inflict harm on their communities. That’s why diverse teams are so crucial. Imagine that a social media company’s recommendation engine was tuned to analyze who you’re following and if it was tuned to prioritize follow recommendations for people who talked about similar things but who were different in some key ways from your existing sphere of influence. For example, if you were to follow a bunch of nondisabled white male academics who talk about AI, it could suggest that you follow academics who are disabled or aren’t white or aren’t male who also talk about AI. If you took its recommendations, perhaps you’d get a more holistic and nuanced understanding of what’s happening in the AI field. These same systems should also use their understanding of biases about particular communities—including, for instance, the disability community—to make sure that they aren’t recommending any of their users follow accounts that perpetuate biases against (or, worse, spewing hate toward) those groups. Other ways that AI can helps people with disabilities If I weren’t trying to put this together between other tasks, I’m sure that I could go on and on, providing all kinds of examples of how AI could be used to help people with disabilities, but I’m going to make this last section into a bit of a lightning round. In no particular order: Voice preservation. You may have seen the VALL-E paper or Apple’s Global Accessibility Awareness Day announcement or you may be familiar with the voice-preservation offerings from Microsoft, Acapela, or others. It’s possible to train an AI model to replicate your voice, which can be a tremendous boon for people who have ALS (Lou Gehrig’s disease) or motor-neuron disease or other medical conditions that can lead to an inability to talk. This is, of course, the same tech that can also be used to create audio deepfakes, so it’s something that we need to approach responsibly, but the tech has truly transformative potential. Voice recognition. Researchers like those in the Speech Accessibility Project are paying people with disabilities for their help in collecting recordings of people with atypical speech. As I type, they are actively recruiting people with Parkinson’s and related conditions, and they have intends to expand this to other conditions as the project progresses. This research will result in more inclusive data sets that will let more people with disabilities use voice assistants, dictation software, and voice-response services as well as control their computers and other devices more easily, using only their voice. Text transformation. The current generation of LLMs is quite capable of adjusting existing text content without injecting hallucinations. This is hugely empowering for people with cognitive disabilities who may benefit from text summaries or simplified versions of text or even text that’s prepped for Bionic Reading. The importance of diverse teams and data We need to recognize that our differences matter. Our lived experiences are influenced by the intersections of the identities that we exist in. These lived experiences—with all their complexities (and joys and pain)—are valuable inputs to the software, services, and societies that we shape. Our differences need to be represented in the data that we use to train upcoming models, and the folks who contribute that valuable information need to be compensated for sharing it with us. Inclusive data sets yield more robust models that foster more equitable outcomes. Want a model that doesn’t demean or patronize or objectify people with disabilities? Make sure that you have content about disabilities that’s authored by people with a range of disabilities, and make sure that that’s well represented in the training data. Want a model that doesn’t use ableist language? You may be able to use existing data sets to build a filter that can intercept and remediate ableist language before it reaches readers. That being said, when it comes to sensitivity reading, AI models won’t be replacing human copy editors anytime soon. Want a coding copilot that gives you accessible recommendations from the jump? Train it on code that you know to be accessible. I have no doubt that AI can and will harm people… today, tomorrow, and well into the future. But I also believe that we can acknowledge that and, with an eye towards accessibility (and, more broadly, inclusion), make thoughtful, considerate, and intentional changes in our approaches to AI that will reduce harm over time as well. Today, tomorrow, and well into the future. Many thanks to Kartik Sawhney for helping me with the development of this piece, Ashley Bischoff for her invaluable editorial assistance, and, of course, Joe Dolson for the prompt.

In reading Joe Dolson’s recent piece on the intersection of AI and accessibility, I absolutely appreciated the skepticism that he has for AI in general as well as for the ways that many have been using it. In fact, I’m very skeptical of AI myself, despite my role at Microsoft as an accessibility innovation strategist who helps run the AI for Accessibility grant program. As with any tool, AI can be used in very constructive, inclusive, and accessible ways; and it can also be used in destructive, exclusive, and harmful ones. And there are a ton of uses somewhere in the mediocre middle as well.

Sources indicate that I’d like you to consider this a “yes… and” piece to complement Joe’s post. I’m not trying to refute any of what he’s saying but rather provide some visibility to projects and opportunities where AI can make meaningful differences for people with disabilities. To be clear, I’m not saying that there aren’t real risks or pressing issues with AI that need to be addressed—there are, and we’ve needed to address them, like, yesterday—but I want to take a little time to talk about what’s possible in hopes that we’ll get there one day.

Joe’s piece spends a lot of time talking about computer-vision models generating alternative text. He highlights a ton of valid challenges with the current state of things. And while computer-vision models continue to improve in the quality and richness of detail in their descriptions, their results aren’t great. As he rightly points out, the current state of image analysis is pretty poor—especially for certain image types—in large part because current AI systems examine images in isolation rather than within the contexts that they’re in (which is a consequence of having separate “foundation” models for text analysis and image analysis). Today’s models aren’t trained to distinguish between images that are contextually relevant (that should probably have descriptions) and those that are purely decorative (which might not need a description) either. Still, I still think there’s potential in this space.

As Joe mentions, human-in-the-loop authoring of alt text should absolutely be a thing. And if AI can pop in to offer a starting point for alt text—even if that starting point might be a prompt saying What is this BS? That’s not right at all… Let me try to offer a starting point—I think that’s a win.

Taking things a step further, if we can specifically train a model to analyze image usage in context, it could help us more quickly identify which images are likely to be decorative and which ones likely require a description. That will help reinforce which contexts call for image descriptions and it’ll improve authors’ efficiency toward making their pages more accessible.

While complex images—like graphs and charts—are challenging to describe in any sort of succinct way (even for humans), the image example shared in the GPT4 announcement points to an interesting opportunity as well. Let’s suppose that you came across a chart whose description was simply the title of the chart and the kind of visualization it was, such as: Pie chart comparing smartphone usage to feature phone usage among US households making under $30,000 a year. (That would be a pretty awful alt text for a chart since that would tend to leave many questions about the data unanswered, but then again, let’s suppose that that was the description that was in place.) If your browser knew that that image was a pie chart (because an onboard model concluded this), imagine a world where users could ask questions like these about the graphic:.

Setting aside the realities of large language model (LLM) hallucinations—where a model just makes up plausible-sounding “facts”—for a moment, the opportunity to learn more about images and data in this way could be revolutionary for blind and low-vision folks as well as for people with various forms of color blindness, cognitive disabilities, and so on. It could also be useful in educational contexts to help people who can see these charts, as is, to understand the data in the charts.

Taking things a step further: What if you could ask your browser to simplify a complex chart? What if you could ask it to isolate a single line on a line graph? What if you could ask your browser to transpose the colors of the different lines to work better for form of color blindness you have? What if you could ask it to swap colors for patterns? Given these tools’ chat-based interfaces and our existing ability to manipulate images in today’s AI tools, that seems like a possibility.

Now imagine a purpose-built model that could extract the information from that chart and convert it to another format. For example, perhaps it could turn that pie chart (or better yet, a series of pie charts) into more accessible (and useful) formats, like spreadsheets. That would be amazing!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • HP has introduced an expensive workstation that brings computing hardware previously associated with large-scale AI infrastructure into an office-sized machine.
  • The ZGX Fury G1n combines Nvidia's GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra processor with an enormous memory allocation designed for demanding artificial intelligence workloads.
  • Its starting price of $132,000 makes it considerably more expensive than conventional professional computers, even before customers consider optional upgrades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HP has introduced an expensive workstation that brings computing hardware previously associated with large-scale AI infrastructure into an office-sized machine.

The ZGX Fury G1n combines Nvidia's GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra processor with an enormous memory allocation designed for demanding artificial intelligence workloads.

Its starting price of $132,000 makes it considerably more expensive than conventional professional computers, even before customers consider optional upgrades.

The mobile workstation combines two different memory technologies, LPDDR5X and HBM3e, with 496GB allocated to system memory and another 252GB dedicated to graphics processing.

The LPDDR5X allocation runs at 6,400 MT/s and connects to a 72-core Arm Neoverse V2 Grace CPU, supporting demanding processing workloads.

Meanwhile, the HBM3e memory is integrated into Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra GPU, providing dedicated high-bandwidth capacity for graphics and AI operations.

Customers opting for additional graphics hardware can increase the available video memory to 276GB through selected configurations.

Together, these components provide the advertised 748GB capacity, although customers purchasing additional graphics hardware can increase available video memory to 276GB.

HP also offers configurations featuring discrete Nvidia RTX PRO workstation graphics cards, including the RTX PRO 2000 and RTX PRO 4000.

The memory capacity serves a particular purpose beyond running conventional office applications or demanding professional software.

Developers and researchers working with large language models can use the machine to process substantial workloads without depending entirely on remote computing infrastructure.

HP indicates the available memory can accommodate local adjustment of language models containing up to 100 billion parameters.

The system can also perform inference using models reaching one trillion parameters through FP4 quantization, although actual performance depends on workload requirements.

Running powerful computing components inside a relatively compact enclosure introduces thermal management requirements that ordinary desktop cooling systems cannot necessarily accommodate.

HP therefore equips the workstation with liquid cooling alongside a 1,600W Titanium-certified power supply.

The device ships with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, making Linux its supplied operating system rather than Microsoft's Windows environment.

This configuration caters to developers and technical professionals who need software environments suitable for demanding computing and AI development.

Networking is another crucial component, with an Nvidia ConnectX-8 SuperNIC providing two QSFP112 connections rated at 400Gbps.

These connections allow multiple machines to communicate through high-speed networking when organizations need additional computing resources.

The enclosure also supports installation inside a 5U equipment rack, giving organizations another deployment option beyond placing it beneath an office desk.

This flexibility allows organizations to deploy the workstation individually or install multiple units inside equipment racks for larger computing operations.

Getting all these specifications will cost $132,000 for the standard configuration, enough to buy a brand-latest 2026 Cadillac Escalade IQL, although not quite a Ferrari.

Customers opting for the RTX PRO 2000 configuration will pay $133,000, while the more powerful RTX PRO 4000 option raises the price to $136,000.

At these prices, the ZGX Fury is unlikely to attract ordinary desktop buyers looking for additional memory or improved everyday computing performance.

Instead, its potential customers are organizations that require substantial local computing resources and can justify spending considerably more than conventional workstation prices.
