InfoQ Homepage News Uber's Secure AI Framework Governs Autonomous AI Agents Across Their Lifecycle.

Nov 15, 2026 3 min read.

Industry observers note that in a recent article, Uber Engineering highlights the limitations of traditional identity and API controls in securing AI agents that dynamically reason over external content and take real-world actions. To address this challenge, Uber developed a framework to determine whether an agent's action is appropriate given the user's request, the agent's intended purpose, its permissions, and the context of the interaction.

Identity and authorization systems can determine whether a user or service has permission to access a resource, but they can't determine whether an agent's proposed action is appropriate in context.

This creates multiple risks, including prompt injection, tool and memory poisoning, goal hijacking, behavioral drift, and hallucination-driven actions, which Uber's framework addresses through three layers spanning the entire agent lifecycle, from pre-deployment to runtime enforcement to post-deployment continuous assurance.

At provisioning time, agents must be registered in the Uber AI Registry, establishing identity, ownership, persona, permitted intents, constraints, dependencies, and risk classification. This process is automated using Argus, which analyzes the agent's source code, prompts, configurations, dependencies, exposed endpoints, and tool-invocation paths to identify security weaknesses. The same approach is enforced for MCP servers and tools used by the agents.

At runtime, the framework extends the traditional security model based on policy administration, policy decision, and policy enforcement to incorporate behavioral authorization, which evaluates whether an agent's actions are appropriate in a given context.

Behavioral authorization is implemented through three components: the AI Registry, AI guards, and Agent Guard runtime hooks. The AI Registry defines and manages agent policies, personas, intents, and constraints, while AI Guards evaluate interactions and proposed actions against established policies. Agent Guard runtime hooks invoke AI Guard "at critical checkpoints and applying its verdict before an interaction or action is allowed to proceed".

After deployment, the focus shifts to Continuous Assurance, which relies on end-to-end observability, auditing, explainability, and replay. This layer comprises two main main components: a unified execution trace that connects agent actions, tool calls, and security decisions; and recorded interactions that can be replayed whenever policies and guardrails are updated to assess their effectiveness in the latest context.

Uber also identified several challenges in implementing security controls in production, including balancing policy restrictiveness to avoid both excessive false positives and insufficient protection, minimizing runtime latency, reducing developer friction during framework setup, and moving beyond generic controls towards agent-specific policies, which "made enforcement more contextual and precise".

Sources indicate that commenting on Uber's approach on LinkedIn, UN senior information technology officer Tristan G. raised several concerns, noting that while "per-agent personas, intents, constraints and calibration" is what adds the most value, they also come at a significant cost, as "the effort scales with the number of workflows". Additionally,.

Sources indicate that by its own account, the strongest control was restricting agents to explicit constraints, which is least privilege rather than a upcoming idea. For me, the open question is how this works for agents you don't build, such as vendor or SaaS agents where you can't insert your own enforcement hooks.

On similar lines, AI architect Pratik Dhanave also observes that:.

In a recent development, the lesson they call least glamorous is the one they rate most effective: explicit intents and constraints per agent. Not generic thresholds, which failed because every agent has a different purpose and risk profile. The cost is flexibility, and they say it is worth paying.

Recent findings suggest that uber's Secure AI framework is still in evolving, with plans to expand its capabilities across all the areas outlined above. 📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon took down more than 70,000 phishing websites and 14,000 scam phone numbers in 2025.
  • With Black Friday deals everywhere, scam emails will likely become even more rampant.
  • I gave the free tiers of Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude 20 emails and texts: 15 modeled on scams the FTC and Amazon have warned about, and five written like real Amazon messages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon took down more than 70,000 phishing websites and 14,000 scam phone numbers in 2025.

With Black Friday deals everywhere, scam emails will likely become even more rampant. So, I decided to test whether your AI chatbot can catch these scam emails for you.

I gave the free tiers of Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude 20 emails and texts: 15 modeled on scams the FTC and Amazon have warned about, and five written like real Amazon messages.

According to recent reports, all three models performed well at the start, but only one could reliably tell real from fake. Let me explain.

I started the test with 15 scam messages mixed with five written like actual Amazon messages.

The scams included fake order confirmations, Prime renewal threats, refund phishing, a WhatsApp "Amazon recruiter" message, a gift card demand, and an Instagram DM asking for my password.

The three tools got all 20 correct. They flagged the scams and identified the legitimate messages without raising false alarms.

It has been revealed that I also tried a pattern scammers love: a text with the link amazon.com.order-review[.]net. The amazon.com at the beginning makes it look legit.

Recent findings suggest that but the real domain is order-review[.]net. All the tools flagged it and correctly explained why.

Claude gave the most practical next steps. It mentioned reporting scam texts to 7726, the US carrier spam number.

Meanwhile, ChatGPT cited Amazon's help pages, while Gemini leaned on forum posts.

In my first test, I sent all 20 messages together in one prompt.

For this one, I used single messages in new private chats: an Amazon sign-in alert from account-update@amazon.com with no links, and a refund email that linked to amazon.com.

Gemini first said it was impossible to tell for certain. In a second run, it said the same email was almost certainly a phishing scam and called the Houston sign-in location a fear tactic.

Then I tried the refund email. Gemini gave no verdict and just sent general safety tips.

Like Gemini, Claude initially remarked it couldn't verify the sign-in email from the text alone.

But the second time, it said to treat it as suspicious, whereas Gemini outright called it a scam. It also doubted the refund email, saying the sender's address looked less typical.

Recent findings suggest that in all my runs, ChatGPT correctly called the sign-in email legitimate. It also cleared the refund email.

It still told me to verify by checking the email's headers, Amazon's Message Center, or forwarding the email to verify@amazon.com, which is Amazon's service for confirming messages.

It was the only chatbot to mention that service.

I told all three tools I'd clicked a link in a scam email and entered my password and card details to see which would give me the most helpful tips.

Gemini covered everything you'd want to check in that situation:.

But it also opened with a big "WARNING: Immediate Financial Risk" label, which is the last thing you want to see when you're panicking.

Unlike Gemini's panic-inducing opening statement, ChatGPT started with "Act immediately, but don't panic.".

It was the only one to tell me to secure my email account and check it for forwarding rules a scammer might have added. It also asked follow-up questions to figure out how exposed I was.

It pretty much covered Gemini's advice but skipped the FTC report; still, it's the answer I'd want at that moment.

Claude gave some reasonable tips, like calling the bank first and changing any reused passwords, starting with your email.

According to recent reports, but it skipped signing out of all devices and reporting to the FTC. It also told me to forward the email to reportphishing@amazon.com, an email I couldn't find on Amazon's pages.

Amazon lists reportascam@amazon.com for reporting suspicious messages.

All three AI tools can spot scams, but ChatGPT was the only one that consistently recognized real messages.

Sources indicate that false alarms might not seem like a significant deal, but they can be harmful. You could skip a genuine Amazon warning or ignore a request to secure your account.

If you're still unsure, the safest option is to check with Amazon: check the Message Center in your account or forward the message to verify@amazon.com.

#96. An Holistic Framework for Shared Design Leadership

An Holistic Framework for Shared Design Leadership

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alistapart

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture this: You’re in a meeting room at your tech tech giant, and two people are having what looks like the same conversation about the same design problem.
  • Recent findings suggest that picture this: You’re in a meeting room at your tech company, and two people are having what looks like the same conversation about the same design problem.
  • In a recent development, this is the beautiful, sometimes messy reality of having both a Design Manager and a Lead Designer on the same team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture this: You’re in a meeting room at your tech tech giant, and two people are having what looks like the same conversation about the same design problem. One is talking about whether the team has the right skills to tackle it. The other is diving deep into whether the solution actually solves the user’s problem. Same room, same problem, completely different lenses. This is the beautiful, sometimes messy reality of having both a Design Manager and a Lead Designer on the same team. And if you’re wondering how to make this work without creating confusion, overlap, or the dreaded “too many cooks” scenario, you’re asking the right question. The traditional answer has been to draw clean lines on an org chart. The Design Manager handles people, the Lead Designer handles craft. Problem solved, right? Except clean org charts are fantasy. In reality, both roles care deeply about team health, design quality, and shipping great work. The magic happens when you embrace the overlap instead of fighting it—when you start thinking of your design org as a design organism. The Anatomy of a Healthy Design Team Here's what I’ve learned from years of being on both sides of this equation: think of your design team as a living organism. The Design Manager tends to the mind (the psychological safety, the career growth, the team dynamics). The Lead Designer tends to the body (the craft skills, the design standards, the hands-on work that ships to users). But just like mind and body aren’t completely separate systems, so, too, do these roles overlap in vital ways. You can’t have a healthy person without both working in harmony. The trick is knowing where those overlaps are and how to navigate them gracefully. When we look at how healthy teams actually function, three critical systems emerge. Each requires both roles to work together, but with one taking primary responsibility for keeping that system strong. The Nervous System: People & Psychology Primary caretaker: Design ManagerSupporting role: Lead Designer The nervous system is all about signals, feedback, and psychological safety. When this system is healthy, information flows freely, people feel safe to take risks, and the team can adapt quickly to upcoming challenges. The Design Manager is the primary caretaker here. They’re monitoring the team’s psychological pulse, ensuring feedback loops are healthy, and creating the conditions for people to grow. They’re hosting career conversations, managing workload, and making sure no one burns out. But the Lead Designer plays a crucial supporting role. They’re providing sensory input about craft development needs, spotting when someone’s design skills are stagnating, and helping identify growth opportunities that the Design Manager might miss. Design Manager tends to: Career conversations and growth planning Team psychological safety and dynamics Workload management and resource allocation Performance reviews and feedback systems Creating learning opportunities Lead Designer supports by: Providing craft-specific feedback on team member development Identifying design skill gaps and growth opportunities Offering design mentorship and guidance Signaling when team members are ready for more complex challenges The Muscular System: Craft & Execution Primary caretaker: Lead DesignerSupporting role: Design Manager The muscular system is about strength, coordination, and skill development. When this system is healthy, the team can execute complex design work with precision, maintain consistent quality, and adapt their craft to new challenges. The Lead Designer is the primary caretaker here. They’re setting design standards, providing craft coaching, and ensuring that shipping work meets the quality bar. They’re the ones who can tell you if a design decision is sound or if we’re solving the right problem. But the Design Manager plays a crucial supporting role. They’re ensuring the team has the resources and support to do their best craft work, like proper nutrition and recovery time for an athlete. Lead Designer tends to: Definition of design standards and system usage Feedback on what design work meets the standard Experience direction for the product Design decisions and product-wide alignment Innovation and craft advancement Design Manager supports by: Ensuring design standards are understood and adopted across the team Confirming experience direction is being followed Supporting practices and systems that scale without bottlenecking Facilitating design alignment across teams Providing resources and removing obstacles to great craft work The Circulatory System: Strategy & Flow Shared caretakers: Both Design Manager and Lead Designer The circulatory system is about how information, decisions, and energy flow through the team. When this system is healthy, strategic direction is clear, priorities are aligned, and the team can respond quickly to new opportunities or challenges. This is where true partnership happens. Both roles are responsible for keeping the circulation strong, but they’re bringing different perspectives to the table. Lead Designer contributes: User needs are met by the product Overall product quality and experience Strategic design initiatives Research-based user needs for each initiative Design Manager contributes: Communication to team and stakeholders Stakeholder management and alignment Cross-functional team accountability Strategic business initiatives Both collaborate on: Co-creation of strategy with leadership Team goals and prioritization approach Organizational structure decisions Success measures and frameworks Keeping the Organism Healthy The key to making this partnership sing is understanding that all three systems need to work together. A team with great craft skills but poor psychological safety will burn out. A team with great culture but weak craft execution will ship mediocre work. A team with both but poor strategic circulation will work hard on the wrong things. Be Explicit About Which System You’re Tending When you’re in a meeting about a design problem, it helps to acknowledge which system you’re primarily focused on. “I’m thinking about this from a team capacity perspective” (nervous system) or “I’m looking at this through the lens of user needs” (muscular system) gives everyone context for your input. This isn’t about staying in your lane. It’s about being transparent as to which lens you’re using, so the other person knows how to best add their perspective. Create Healthy Feedback Loops The most successful partnerships I’ve seen establish clear feedback loops between the systems: Nervous system signals to muscular system: “The team is struggling with confidence in their design skills” → Lead Designer provides more craft coaching and clearer standards. Muscular system signals to nervous system: “The team’s craft skills are advancing faster than their project complexity” → Design Manager finds more challenging growth opportunities. Both systems signal to circulatory system: “We’re seeing patterns in team health and craft development that suggest we need to adjust our strategic priorities.” Handle Handoffs Gracefully The most critical moments in this partnership are when something moves from one system to another. This might be when a design standard (muscular system) needs to be rolled out across the team (nervous system), or when a strategic initiative (circulatory system) needs specific craft execution (muscular system). Make these transitions explicit. “I’ve defined the new component standards. Can you help me think through how to get the team up to speed?” or “We’ve agreed on this strategic direction. I'm going to focus on the specific user experience approach from here.” Stay Curious, Not Territorial The Design Manager who never thinks about craft, or the Lead Designer who never considers team dynamics, is like a doctor who only looks at one body system. Great design leadership requires both people to care about the whole organism, even when they’re not the primary caretaker. This means asking questions rather than making assumptions. “What do you think about the team’s craft development in this area?” or “How do you see this impacting team morale and workload?” keeps both perspectives active in every decision. When the Organism Gets Sick Even with clear roles, this partnership can go sideways. Here are the most common failure modes I’ve seen: System Isolation The Design Manager focuses only on the nervous system and ignores craft development. The Lead Designer focuses only on the muscular system and ignores team dynamics. Both people retreat to their comfort zones and stop collaborating. The symptoms: Team members get mixed messages, work quality suffers, morale drops. The treatment: Reconnect around shared outcomes. What are you both trying to achieve? Usually it’s great design work that ships on time from a healthy team. Figure out how both systems serve that goal. Poor Circulation Strategic direction is unclear, priorities keep shifting, and neither role is taking responsibility for keeping information flowing. The symptoms: Team members are confused about priorities, work gets duplicated or dropped, deadlines are missed. The treatment: Explicitly assign responsibility for circulation. Who’s communicating what to whom? How often? What’s the feedback loop? Autoimmune Response One person feels threatened by the other’s expertise. The Design Manager thinks the Lead Designer is undermining their authority. The Lead Designer thinks the Design Manager doesn’t understand craft. The symptoms: Defensive behavior, territorial disputes, team members caught in the middle. The treatment: Remember that you’re both caretakers of the same organism. When one system fails, the whole team suffers. When both systems are healthy, the team thrives. The Payoff Yes, this model requires more communication. Yes, it requires both people to be secure enough to share responsibility for team health. But the payoff is worth it: better decisions, stronger teams, and design work that’s both excellent and sustainable. When both roles are healthy and working well together, you get the best of both worlds: deep craft expertise and strong people leadership. When one person is out sick, on vacation, or overwhelmed, the other can help maintain the team’s health. When a decision requires both the people perspective and the craft perspective, you’ve got both right there in the room. Most importantly, the framework scales. As your team grows, you can apply the same system thinking to new challenges. Need to launch a design system? Lead Designer tends to the muscular system (standards and implementation), Design Manager tends to the nervous system (team adoption and change management), and both tend to circulation (communication and stakeholder alignment). The Bottom Line The relationship between a Design Manager and Lead Designer isn’t about dividing territories. It’s about multiplying impact. When both roles understand they’re tending to different aspects of the same healthy organism, magic happens. The mind and body work together. The team gets both the strategic thinking and the craft excellence they need. And most importantly, the work that ships to users benefits from both perspectives. So the next time you’re in that meeting room, wondering why two people are talking about the same problem from different angles, remember: you’re watching shared leadership in action. And if it’s working well, both the mind and body of your design team are getting stronger.

What Happens When You Upload a Large File & Generate a Temporary Download Link

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sending a 5 GB video file might seem simple.
  • The file has to travel across a network, reach a server, and be stored somewhere before another person can download it.
  • According to recent reports, file transfer services use HTTP requests, storage systems, databases, encryption, and background processes to manage these tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sending a 5 GB video file might seem simple. You select the file, click Upload, wait for the progress bar to finish, and share a link with someone. But there are several things happening in the background while the file is being uploaded.

The file has to travel across a network, reach a server, and be stored somewhere before another person can download it. The service also needs to make sure that the recipient can access the file without accessing the sender's account. If the internet connection drops halfway through the upload, it needs a way to continue without sending the entire file again.

According to recent reports, file transfer services use HTTP requests, storage systems, databases, encryption, and background processes to manage these tasks. But how does a website actually handle a file that's several gigabytes in size? Does it upload everything in one request? Where does the file go after the upload finishes? And what happens when its download link expires?

In this article, we'll look at how file transfer services handle large uploads, store files, generate download links, and manage interrupted connections and expired transfers. Then, once you understand the theory behind how it all works, we'll also build a basic chunked file uploader using Node.js to see some of these processes in action.

In a recent development, before looking at dedicated file transfer services, it helps to understand why we can't just attach massive files to an email. Sending large files through email is fundamentally flawed because the underlying architecture was built for text, not high-resolution media.

Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) handles the transmission of email messages across the internet. Because servers have limited bandwidth and storage, email providers impose strict attachment size limits, usually capping out around 25 MB. However, these limits apply to the encoded message size, not just the original file sitting on your hard drive.

It has been revealed that email attachments are commonly encoded using MIME and Base64 formats. Base64 is necessary because it converts binary data into text-compatible characters that email servers can safely route. While this solves the transmission problem, it creates a massive efficiency issue: this encoding increases the data size by approximately 33%.

It has been revealed that you can read the foundational specifications for this in RFC 2045, which defines MIME's Base64 transfer encoding. In practice, this means a 30 MB video file will require roughly 40 MB of space before additional message overhead is even calculated, guaranteeing it will bounce back from most email servers.

To bypass the limitations of email, file transfer services use a specialized, decoupled architecture. Having built a few of these systems myself, I believe establishing a clear mental model of the five major components is crucial for understanding the flow of data.

It has been revealed that the journey begins in the client, which is usually a web browser or a desktop application where the sender selects a file. Modern browsers use JavaScript's File API to access file metadata, read the raw contents and intelligently divide the file into smaller, manageable parts before any data hits the network.

Once the client starts sending data, the upload server steps in. This server receives the upload requests, authenticates the user, validates incoming data and coordinates the entire upload process. It acts as the traffic cop, ensuring that chunks of data are arriving in the correct format.

Recent findings suggest that traditional application servers are terrible at holding massive files, so the storage layer handles the actual heavy lifting. Uploaded files are typically routed directly to object storage solutions. This allows the system to scale infinitely without crashing the primary upload servers.

While the physical file goes to object storage, the application needs a way to remember what that file is. The metadata database stores critical information, including the original filename, file size, content type, the specific object storage key, a unique transfer identifier and the exact expiration timestamp.

Recent findings suggest that when someone opens a shared link, the download server takes over. It checks the database to verify permissions and expiration dates, and if everything is valid, it retrieves the stored object from the storage layer for delivery.

According to recent reports, transferring a 5 GB file in one continuous network request is a disaster waiting to happen. If a connection drops at 99%, a single-request architecture forces the user to start all over again.

It has been revealed that to solve this, modern clients divide large files into smaller parts, such as 10 MB chunks. Each chunk is uploaded to the server as an independent HTTP request. The server meticulously tracks which chunks have arrived. Some advanced systems even allow multiple chunks to upload simultaneously in parallel, drastically reducing the overall waiting time.

It's key to note that chunked uploads are an architectural pattern, which is entirely different from HTTP chunked transfer encoding (a mechanism for framing an HTTP message body).

Suppose 80% of a massive file has successfully uploaded when your Wi-Fi randomly disconnects. Without resumable uploads, that progress is lost. With resumable architecture, the client reconnects and asks the server for the upload offset, the exact number of bytes successfully received and stored. The client then seamlessly continues uploading from that exact position.

Network transfers can sometimes flip bits, resulting in corrupted files. To prevent this, clients generate a cryptographic hash (checksum) for an individual chunk before sending it. The server receives the chunk, calculates its own hash, and compares the two. If the checksums don't match, the server rejects the chunk and asks the client to try again.

It has been revealed that if you're looking to implement this, the TUS Resumable Upload Protocol is a fantastic, standardized reference for managing upload offsets and checksum verification. Also, the Amazon S3 Multipart Upload Documentation provides an industry-standard blueprint for handling parallel transfers and retrying failed parts.

Once every chunk is verified and reassembled, the service needs a secure place to keep the file until the recipient is ready to download it.

In my opinion, attempting to store gigabytes of user uploads on a traditional local server directory is architectural malpractice. Instead, services rely on object storage. Files are stored as flat objects and each object is assigned a unique key. Object storage is highly durable and scales quite easily to accommodate millions of massive files simultaneously.

The relationship between the stored file and its shareable link relies on the metadata database. When the upload finishes, the application saves the file's storage key in the database and generates a unique access token. The recipient receives a URL containing that specific token. When they click the link, the server reads the token, locates the relevant file in the database and checks the download permissions.

A secure file transfer link relies heavily on high entropy, which is randomness that makes tokens mathematically near-impossible to predict. Also, secure systems use signed URLs. These are URLs containing cryptographic signatures that authorize access for a limited, strictly-enforced period.

As outlined in the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet, a random link isn't automatically secure without appropriate access controls, expiration policies, and protection against token leakage.

File transfer services process petabytes of data, meaning they can't store uploaded files forever without going bankrupt. They rely on aggressive lifecycle management.

Every transfer is assigned a Time to Live (TTL) or expiration timestamp. Once that time passes, the database instantly invalidates the transfer identifier, ensuring that the download link no longer authorizes access.

Because link expiration and physical deletion aren't necessarily simultaneous, background workers or scheduled cron jobs handle the actual cleanup. These workers periodically scan the database to find expired transfers, mark them as permanently unavailable, delete the associated multi-gigabyte objects from the storage layer, and finally remove the outdated metadata.

Some services also allow senders to limit how many times a file can be downloaded. Once the download count reaches the threshold, the link behaves exactly as if the TTL had expired, offering an excellent way to control unauthorized distribution.

Security in file transfers is never about a single magic feature. It requires multiple layers of defense to keep data safe from interception or theft.

Sources indicate that when data travels between the sender, the transfer service, and the recipient, it's heavily encrypted. Modern platforms use HTTPS backed by strict TLS protocols to ensure no one can snoop on the data packets mid-route.

Industry observers note that for a deep dive into how this is configured at an enterprise level, NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 offers exhaustive guidelines for TLS implementations.

Sources indicate that once the file arrives at the storage layer, encryption at rest ensures that even if a bad actor physically accessed the server hardware, they would only find scrambled, unreadable data. It's important to note that encryption at rest isn't the same as end to end encryption. The service provider still manages the encryption keys in a standard setup.

To prevent unauthorized customers from accessing a valid URL, senders can add a password. This creates a secondary access-control layer that must be cleared before the server will even attempt to fetch the file from object storage. Additional safeguards, like rate-limiting against automated password guessing, ensure this layer remains effective.

Seeing how established companies implement these concepts helps bridge the gap between theory and practice.

In a recent development, weTransfer is built entirely around temporary shareable links. Transfers have strict expiration timelines and premium users can enforce password protection. According to their security documentation, they utilize standard TLS encryption during transit and AES-256 encryption at rest to secure files on their servers.

It has been revealed that unlike a standard shared folder, Dropbox Transfer creates standalone downloadable links. Recipients don't need a Dropbox account to download the payload. They utilize configurable expiration dates, passwords, and automated download notifications, with maximum file size limits dictated by the sender's specific subscription proposal.

Send Anywhere takes a fascinating hybrid approach. Its six-digit key transfer mechanism operates in real-time for one-time use within a 10-minute window, often leveraging peer to peer connections. Conversely, its standard Share Link option falls back to a server-based architecture, uploading files and keeping the link valid for up to 48 hours.

Offering robust email and shareable-link delivery options, Filemail handles massive payloads easily. They provide highly configurable expiration controls and rigorous password protection. Their free service tier currently allows a 5 GB transfer limit, holding the data securely for a maximum seven-day storage period before automated cleanup takes over.

Understanding the theory is great, but building it yourself proves how it actually works. Let's create a simple application that divides a file into smaller chunks in the browser, uploads them to a Node.js server and stitches them back together.

You'll need Node.js, the Express framework, and multer for handling incoming file chunks. The built-in fs module will handle our file operations. First, create a Node project and install the required dependencies:.

Recent findings suggest that first, create a public directory inside your project folder if it doesn't already exist. Then, create a file named upload.js inside that directory. We'll use the browser's JavaScript File API and its slice() method to read smaller portions of a file without loading the entire 5 GB payload into your computer's RAM.

Here, crypto.randomUUID() generates a unique ID for the upload. The browser sends each chunk separately and uses the same ID to associate all the chunks with the original file.

On the server side (server.js), we need an endpoint to receive and temporarily store each chunk. The server uses the upload ID and chunk index to determine where each part belongs, while the total number of chunks helps validate the upload. We use multer to parse the incoming multipart form data.

The server stores each chunk using its upload ID and index, making it possible to identify and retrieve the individual parts when the upload is complete.

Sources indicate that once the client confirms all chunks have been transmitted, it triggers a final reassembly route. The server first checks whether every expected chunk exists in the chunks/ directory. It then reads the chunks sequentially using fs.createReadStream() and writes them to the same output file using fs.createWriteStream(). The first chunk creates the file, while subsequent chunks are appended to it. Once the original file has been reassembled, the server deletes the temporary chunks to free up space.

Open your browser's Network tab to observe how the file is divided into chunks and sent sequentially. Finally, check your server's uploads/ directory. The assembled file should have the same byte size as the original and should open correctly.

Recent findings suggest that note: This implementation demonstrates the basic mechanics of chunked uploads and file reassembly. It doesn't implement resumable uploads, checksum verification, authentication, object storage, or temporary download links.

A production-grade file transfer service would also require persistent upload states, access controls, retry handling, integrity checks, and automated cleanup.

Sources indicate that sending a large file involves several processes working together. From upload handling and chunk management in the browser to object storage, metadata tracking, encryption, and automated cleanup, each component has a specific role in making file transfers work.

These processes also explain how services handle interrupted uploads, control access to shared files, and remove data when a transfer expires. Understanding how these components work together makes it easier to see what happens behind the scenes whenever someone uploads a large file and shares a download link.

After rumors of Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards being withdrawn from the consumer retail channel, it is pleasing to see major U.S. e-tailers like Newegg stuffed with stock today. Checking out this popular online electronics retailer, we note that there are 21 RTX 5090 SKUs available, and 11 are sold by and shipped by Newegg. Sadly, pricing remains in 3x MSRP+ territory at the time of writing. Remember, you can sift through pricing trends in our comprehensive GPU price tracking 2026 feature to see that Nvidia's Blackwell flagship was once available at its fabled sub-$2,000 price.

According to recent reports, despite what looks on the surface like an ample supply (but there are order limits of one per customer), prices for RTX 5090s remain extremely high. The best prices we can see at Newegg are $6,599, but this price applies only to a water-cooled Aorus model and another sold inside a Gigabyte AI BOX eGPU. They might still appeal to you, depending on your setup, though.

For a ‘standard’ air-cooled graphics card, albeit a very nice Aorus RTX 5090 Master, you’ll need to squeeze at least $6,659 out of your savings. A bonus with this card, alongside several others from the Gigabyte stables now purchasable from Newegg, is that it comes with a free motherboard. Many of these Gigabyte Aorus designs are being bundled with a full-ATX-sized X870 Aorus Elite WIFI7 AM5 motherboard, purportedly worth $319. Please note that the same motherboard is available to purchase outside this bundle for a more reasonable $249.

If you have money to burn, there are plenty of even more expensive SKUs to pick from. There are no opulent Golden Dhabab models on Newegg, sadly, but you’ll still be asked to part with $11,896 for the Asus ROG Astral GeForce RTX 5090 Edition 20 (sold by a Newegg marketplace partner). Perhaps surprisingly, given recent trending pricing news, that’s the only model above $10K, but there are still many models that are almost $10,000 from Asus, MSI, and Zotac. Even an Nvidia Founders Edition RTX 5090 refurb is priced at $8,899.

In context, these RTX 5090s are still at astronomical prices for consumer gaming PC add-in hardware. But they are now purchasable from a major retailer with fast delivery, rather than off a random scalper. It was only a month ago that rumors swirled about the RTX 5090 and the RTX 5080 being withdrawn from retail. That seemed to trigger crazy levels of price inflation, and reports of $10,000+ prices for the flagship card seemed to become the norm.

One can only hope that stock continues to flow to Newegg and other outlets, and RTX 5090 / RTX 5080 prices will settle lower as a result.

If you have a large family as well as a hefty circle of friends, remembering everyone's birthdays is a challenge in itself. Luckily for Samsung users, the tech organization could be working on a management feature that helps take the stress out of this.

As spotted in one of Android Authority's APK teardowns, it appears that Samsung is at the moment developing a tool that makes tracking your friends' and family members' birthdays easier. According to the outlet's findings, this will be native to the Contacts app on Samsung phones in One UI 9.5, and splits birthdays into three categories: Past, Today, and Upcoming.

Recent findings suggest that as it stands, you can manually add birthdays to the details of individual contacts, but it doesn't notify you when you have an upcoming celebration, meaning you'll have to dig through your Calendar or browse your contacts. The tool would help fill this gap and, more importantly, spare you the backlash from friends and family.

Alongside the feature itself, Android Authority also spotted lines of code that state 'Set a birthday that can be shared with others', which points to an additional function.

When your contacts add their birthdays to their profile on their device, they'll have the option to enable a toggle that allows them to share their birthday with others. Once enabled, you'll be able to see their date of birth when viewing their contact information, and it works the other way around.

Remembering birthdays is one thing, but then gift-giving is a completely different ordeal. Don't worry, Samsung has your back there, too.

Recent findings suggest that as well as birthday nods, additional lines of code reveal Samsung's plans to develop a shortcut tool for sending cards and gifts. The One UI 8 update introduced Now Brief, where you can send AI-generated birthday cards to others, so it makes sense that the gift-giving function also sends them digitally.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

It's a small, yet functional trick that makes juggling important dates much smoother. That being stated, it also gives you no more excuses if you miss another birthday again...

Design Dialects: Breaking the Rules, Not the System

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Language is not merely a set of unrelated sounds, clauses, rules, and meanings; it is a totally coherent system bound to context and behavior." — Kenneth L.
  • It has been revealed that "Language is not merely a set of unrelated sounds, clauses, rules, and meanings; it is a totally coherent system bound to context and behavior." — Kenneth L.
  • Sources indicate that the web has accents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Language is not merely a set of unrelated sounds, clauses, rules, and meanings; it is a totally coherent system bound to context and behavior." — Kenneth L. Pike The web has accents. So should our design systems. Design Systems as Living Languages Design systems aren't component libraries—they’re living languages. Tokens are phonemes, components are words, patterns are phrases, layouts are sentences. The conversations we build with users become the stories our products tell. But here’s what we've forgotten: the more fluently a language is spoken, the more accents it can support without losing meaning. English in Scotland differs from English in Sydney, yet both are unmistakably English. The language adapts to context while preserving core meaning. This couldn’t be more obvious to me, a Brazilian Portuguese speaker, who learned English with an American accent, and lives in Sydney. Our design systems must work the same way. Rigid adherence to visual rules creates brittle systems that break under contextual pressure. Fluent systems bend without breaking. Consistency becomes a prison The promise of design systems was simple: consistent components would accelerate development and unify experiences. But as systems matured and products grew more complex, that promise has become a prison. Teams file “exception” requests by the hundreds. Products launch with workarounds instead of system components. Designers spend more time defending consistency than solving user problems. Our design systems must learn to speak dialects. A design dialect is a systematic adaptation of a design system that maintains core principles while developing fresh patterns for specific contexts. Unlike one-off customizations or brand themes, dialects preserve the system’s essential grammar while expanding its vocabulary to serve different users, environments, or constraints. When Perfect Consistency Fails At Booking.com, I learned this lesson the hard way. We A/B-tested everything—color, copy, button shapes, even logo colors. As a professional with a graphic design education and experience building brand style guides, I found this shocking. While everyone fell in love with Airbnb’s pristine design system, Booking grew into a giant without ever considering visual consistency. The chaos taught me something profound: consistency isn’t ROI; solved problems are. At Shopify. Polaris (https://polaris-react.shopify.com/) was our crown jewel—a mature design language perfect for merchants on laptops. As a product team, we were expected to adopt Polaris as-is. Then my fulfillment team hit an “Oh, Ship!” moment, as we faced the challenge of building an app for warehouse pickers using our interface on shared, battered Android scanners in dim aisles, wearing thick gloves, scanning dozens of items per minute, many with limited levels of English understanding. Task completion with standard Polaris: 0%. Every component that worked beautifully for merchants failed completely for pickers. White backgrounds created glare. 44px tap targets were invisible to gloved fingers. Sentence-case labels took too long to parse. Multi-step flows confused non-native speakers. We faced a choice: abandon Polaris entirely, or teach it to speak warehouse. The Birth of a Dialect We chose evolution over revolution. Working within Polaris’s core principles—clarity, efficiency, consistency—we developed what we now call a design dialect: ConstraintFluent MoveRationaleGlare & low lightDark surfaces + light textReduce glare on low-DPI screensGloves & haste90px tap targets (~2cm)Accommodate thick glovesMultilingualSingle-task screens, plain languageReduce cognitive load Result: Task completion jumped from 0% to 100%. Onboarding time dropped from three weeks to one shift. This wasn’t customization or theming—this was a dialect: a systematic adaptation that maintained Polaris’s core grammar while developing new vocabulary for a specific context. Polaris hadn’t failed; it had learned to speak warehouse. The Flexibility Framework At Atlassian, working on the Jira platform—itself a system within the larger Atlassian system—I pushed for formalizing this insight. With dozens of products sharing a design language across different codebases, we needed systematic flexibility so we built directly into our ways of working. The old model—exception requests and special approvals—was failing at scale. We developed the Flexibility Framework to help designers define how flexible they wanted their components to be: TierActionOwnershipConsistentAdopt unchangedPlatform locks design + codeOpinionatedAdapt within boundsPlatform provides smart defaults, products customizeFlexibleExtend freelyPlatform defines behavior, products own presentation During a navigation redesign, we tiered every element. Logo and global search stayed Consistent. Breadcrumbs and contextual actions became Flexible. Product teams could immediately see where innovation was welcome and where consistency mattered. The Decision Ladder Flexibility needs boundaries. We created a simple ladder for evaluating when rules should bend: Good: Ship with existing system components. Fast, consistent, proven. Better: Stretch a component slightly. Document the change. Contribute improvements back to the system for all to use. Best: Prototype the ideal experience first. If user testing validates the benefit, patch the system to support it. The key question: “Which option lets users succeed fastest?” Rules are tools, not relics. Unity Beats Uniformity Gmail, Drive, and Maps are unmistakably Google—yet each speaks with its own accent. They achieve unity through shared principles, not cloned components. One extra week of debate over button color costs roughly $30K in engineer time. Unity is a brand outcome; fluency is a user outcome. When the two clash, side with the user. Governance Without Gates How do you maintain coherence while enabling dialects? Treat your system like a living vocabulary: Document every deviation – e.g., dialects/warehouse.md with before/after screenshots and rationale. Promote shared patterns – when three teams adopt a dialect independently, review it for core inclusion. Deprecate with context – retire old idioms via flags and migration notes, never a massive-bang purge. A living dictionary scales better than a frozen rulebook. Start Small: Your First Dialect Ready to introduce dialects? Start with one broken experience: This week: Find one user flow where perfect consistency blocks task completion. Could be mobile users struggling with desktop-sized components, or accessibility needs your standard patterns don’t address. Document the context: What makes standard patterns fail here? Environmental constraints? User capabilities? Task urgency? Design one systematic change: Focus on behavior over aesthetics. If gloves are the problem, bigger targets aren’t “"breaking the system”"—they’re serving the user. Earn the variations and make them intentional. Test and measure: Does the change improve task completion? Time to productivity? User satisfaction? Show the savings: If that dialect frees even half a sprint, fluency has paid for itself. Beyond the Component Library We’re not managing design systems anymore—we’re cultivating design languages. Languages that grow with their speakers. Languages that develop accents without losing meaning. Languages that serve human needs over aesthetic ideals. The warehouse workers who went from 0% to 100% task completion didn’t care that our buttons broke the style guide. They cared that the buttons finally worked. Your users feel the same way. Give your system permission to speak their language.

Industry observers note that all available through Amazon, Nothing has essentially every product it sells on sale today – and no, it’s not Black Friday yet! The “Early Black Friday Deal” is stuffed with major discounts, but there are some clear standouts here.

In a recent development, good smartphone deals are becoming increasingly rare in RAMageddon. Most discounts we’re seeing just bring the price back down to what it was at launch, as so many products have gotten price hikes in recent months.

2025’s flagship-ish Nothing Phone (3) drops to $499 for the 12/256GB model and $599 for 16/512GB. Slightly out of date, sure, but a great deal nonetheless on a phone that’s still got plenty of life left to give.

#90. Tech Report: Design for Amiability: Lessons from Vienna

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3986 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Alistapart

Tech Report: Design for Amiability: Lessons from Vienna

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alistapart

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, today’s web is not always an amiable place.
  • It has been revealed that today’s web is not always an amiable place.
  • According to recent reports, these tensions are often at odds with a site’s goals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, today’s web is not always an amiable place. Sites greet you with a popover that demands assent to their cookie policy, and leave you with Taboola ads promising “One Weird Trick!” to cure your ailments. Social media sites are tuned for engagement, and few things are more engaging than a fight. Today it seems that people want to quarrel; I have seen flame wars among birders. These tensions are often at odds with a site’s goals. If we are providing support and advice to customers, we don’t want those customers to wrangle with each other. If we offer news about the latest research, we want readers to feel at ease; if we promote upcoming marches, we want our core supporters to feel comfortable and we want curious newcomers to feel welcome. In a study for a conference on the History of the Web, I looked to the origins of Computer Science in Vienna (1928-1934)  for a case study of the importance of amiability in a research community and the disastrous consequences of its loss. That story has interesting implications for web environments that promote amiable interaction among disparate, difficult (and sometimes disagreeable) people. The Vienna Circle Though people had been thinking about calculating engines and thinking machines from antiquity, Computing really got going in Depression-era Vienna. The people who worked out the theory had no interest in building machines; they wanted to puzzle out the limits of reason in the absence of divine authority. If we could not rely on God or Aristotle to tell us how to think, could we instead build arguments that were self-contained and demonstrably correct? Can we be sure that mathematics is consistent? Are there things that are true but that cannot be expressed in language? The core ideas were worked out in the weekly meetings (Thursdays at 6) of a group remembered as the Vienna Circle. They got together in the office of Professor Moritz Schlick at the University of Vienna to discuss problems in philosophy, math, and language. The intersection of physics and philosophy had long been a specialty of this Vienna department, and this work had placed them among the world leaders. Schlick’s colleague Hans Hahn was a central participant, and by 1928 Hahn brought along his graduate students Karl Menger and Kurt Gödel. Other frequent participants included philosopher Rudolf Carnap, psychologist Karl Popper, economist Ludwig von Mises (brought by his brother Frederick, a physicist),  graphic designer Otto Neurath (inventor of infographics), and architect Josef Frank (brought by his physicist brother, Phillip). Out-of-town visitors often joined, including the young Johnny von Neumann, Alfred Tarski, and the irascible Ludwig Wittgenstein. When Schlick’s office grew too dim, participants adjourned to a nearby café for additional discussion with an even larger circle of participants. This convivial circle was far from unique. An intersecting circle–Neurath, von Mises, Oskar Morgenstern–established the Austrian School of free-market economics. There were theatrical circles (Peter Lorre, Hedy Lamarr, Max Reinhardt), and literary circles. The café was where things happened. The interdisciplinarity of the group posed real challenges of temperament and understanding. Personalities were often a challenge. Gödel was convinced people were trying to poison him. Architect Josef Frank depended on contracts for public housing, which Mises opposed as wasteful. Wittgenstein’s temper had lost him his job as a secondary school teacher, and for some of these years he maintained a detailed list of whom he was willing to meet. Neurath was eager to detect muddled thinking and would interrupt a speaker with a shouted “Metaphysics!” The continuing amity of these meetings was facilitated by the personality of their leader, Moritz Schlick, who would be remembered as notably adept in keeping disagreements from becoming quarrels. In the Café The Viennese café of this era was long remembered as a particularly good place to argue with your friends, to read, and to write. Built to serve an imperial capital, the cafés found themselves with too much space and too few customers now that the Empire was gone. There was no need to turn tables: a café could only survive by coaxing customers to linger. Perhaps they would order another coffee, or one of their friends might drop by. One could play chess, or billiards, or read newspapers from abroad. Coffee was invariably served with a glass of purified spring water, still a novelty in an era in which most water was still unsafe to drink. That water glass would be refilled indefinitely. In the basement of one café, the poet Jura Soyfer staged “The End Of The World,” a musical comedy in which Professor Peep has discovered a comet heading for earth. Prof. Peep: The comet is going to destroy everybody! Hitler:  Destroying everybody is my business. Of course, coffee can be prepared in many ways, and the Viennese café developed a broad vocabulary to represent precisely how one preferred to drink it: melange, Einspänner, Brauner, Schwarzer, Kapuziner. This extensive customization, with correspondingly esoteric conventions of service, established the café as a comfortable and personal third space, a neutral ground in which anyone who could afford a coffee would be welcome. Viennese of this era were fastidious in their use of personal titles, of which an abundance were in common use. Café waiters greeted regular customers with titles too, but were careful to address their patrons with titles a notch or two greater than they deserved. A graduate student would be Doktor, an unpaid postdoc Professor. This assurance mattered all the more because so many members of the Circle (and so many other Viennese) came from elsewhere: Carnap from Wuppertal, Gödel from Brno, von Neumann from Budapest. No one was going to make fun of your clothes, mannerisms, or accent. Your friends wouldn’t be bothered by the pram in the hall. Everyone shared a Germanic Austrian literary and philosophical culture, not least those whose ancestors had been Eastern European Jews who knew that culture well, having read all about it in books. The amiability of the café circle was enhanced by its openness. Because the circle sometimes extended to architects and actors, people could feel less constrained to admit shortfalls in their understanding. It was soon discovered that marble tabletops made a useful surface for pencil sketches, serving all as an improvised and accessible blackboard. Comedies like “The End Of The World” and fictional newspaper sketches or feuilletons of writers like Joseph Roth and Stefan Zweig served as a second defense against disagreeable or churlish behavior. The knowledge that, if one got carried away, a parody of one’s remarks might shortly appear in Neue Freie Presse surely helped Professor Schlick keep matters in hand. The End Of Red Vienna Though Austria’s government drifted to the right after the War, Vienna’s city council had been Socialist, dedicated to public housing based on user-centered design, and embracing  ambitious programs of public outreach and adult education. In 1934 the Socialists lost a local election, and this era soon came to its end as the new administration focused on the imagined threat of the International Jewish Conspiracy. Most members of the Circle fled within months: von Neumann to Princeton, Neurath to Holland and Oxford, Popper to New Zealand, Carnap to Chicago. Prof. Schlick was murdered on the steps of the University by a student outraged by his former association with Jews. Jura Soyfer, who wrote “The End Of The World,” died in Buchenwald. In 1939, von Neumann finally convinced Gödel to accept a job in Princeton. Gödel was required to pay large fines to emigrate. The officer in charge of these fees would look back on this as the best posting of his career; his name was Eichmann. Design for Amiability An impressive literature recounts those discussions and the environment that facilitated the development of computing. How can we design for amiability? This is not just a matter of choosing rounded typefaces and a cheerful pastel palette. I believe we may identify eight distinct concerns that exert design forces in usefully amiable directions. Seriousness: The Vienna Circle was wrestling with a notoriously difficult book—Wittgenstein’s Tractus Logico-Philosophicus—and a catalog of outstanding open questions in mathematics. They were concerned with consequential problems, not merely scoring points for debating. Constant reminders that the questions you are considering matter—not only that they are consequential or that those opposing you are scoundrels—help promote amity. Empiricism: The characteristic approach of the Vienna Circle demanded that knowledge be grounded either in direct observation or in rigorous reasoning. Disagreement, when it arose, could be settled by observation or by proof. If neither seemed ready to hand, the matter could not be settled. On these terms, one can seldom if ever demolish an opposing argument, and trolling is pointless. Abstraction: Disputes grow worse when losing the argument entails lost face or lost jobs. The Vienna Circle’s focus on theory—the limits of mathematics, the capability of language—promoted amity. Without seriousness, abstraction could have been merely academic, but the limits of reason and the consistency of mathematics were clearly serious. Formality: The punctilious demeanor of waiters and the elaborated rituals of coffee service helped to establish orderly attitudes amongst the argumentative participants. This stands in contrast to the contemptuous sneer that now dominates social media. Schlamperei: Members of the Vienna Circle maintained a global correspondence, and they knew their work was at the frontier of research. Still, this was Vienna, at the margins of Europe: old-fashioned, frumpy, and dingy. Many participants came from even more obscure backwaters. Most or all harbored the suspicion that they were really schleppers, and a tinge of the ridiculous helped to moderate tempers. The director of “The End Of The World” had to pass the hat for money to purchase a moon for the set, and thought it was funny enough to write up for publication. Openness: All sorts of people were involved in discussion, anyone might join in. Each week would bring different participants. Fluid borders reduce tension, and provide opportunities to broaden the range of discussion and the terms of engagement. Low entrance friction was characteristic of the café: anyone could come, and if you came twice you were virtually a regular. Permeable boundaries and café culture made it easier for moderating influences to draw in raconteurs and storytellers to defuse awkward moments, and Vienna’s cafés had no shortage of humorists. Openness counteracts the suspicion that promoters of amiability are exerting censorship. Parody: The environs of the Circle—the university office and the café—were unmistakably public. There were writers about, some of them renowned humorists. The prospect that one’s bad taste or bad behavior might be ridiculed in print kept discussion within bounds. The sanction of public humiliation, however, was itself made mild by the veneer of fiction; even if you got a little carried away and a character based on you made a splash in some newspaper fiction, it wasn’t the end of the world. Engagement: The subject matter was notable to the participants, but it was esoteric: it did not matter very much to their mothers or their siblings. A small stumble or a minor humiliation could be shrugged off in ways that major media confrontations cannot. I believe it is notable that this environment was designed to promote amiability through several different voices. The café waiter flattered each newcomer and served everyone, and also kept out local pickpockets and drunks who would be mere disruptions. Schlick and other regulars kept discussion moving and on track. The fiction writers and raconteurs—perhaps the most peripheral of the participants—kept people in a good mood and reminded them that bad behavior could make anyone ridiculous. Crucially, each of these voices were human: you could reason with them. Algorithmic or AI moderators, however clever, are seldom perceived as reasonable. The café circles had no central authority or Moderator against whom everyone’s resentments might be focused. Even after the disaster of 1934, what people remembered were those cheerful arguments.

According to recent reports, these tensions are often at odds with a site’s goals. If we are providing support and advice to customers, we don’t want those customers to wrangle with each other. If we offer news about the latest research, we want readers to feel at ease; if we promote upcoming marches, we want our core supporters to feel comfortable and we want curious newcomers to feel welcome.

In a study for a conference on the History of the Web, I looked to the origins of Computer Science in Vienna (1928-1934)  for a case study of the importance of amiability in a research community and the disastrous consequences of its loss. That story has interesting implications for web environments that promote amiable interaction among disparate, difficult (and sometimes disagreeable) people.

In a recent development, though people had been thinking about calculating engines and thinking machines from antiquity, Computing really got going in Depression-era Vienna. The people who worked out the theory had no interest in building machines; they wanted to puzzle out the limits of reason in the absence of divine authority. If we could not rely on God or Aristotle to tell us how to think, could we instead build arguments that were self-contained and demonstrably correct? Can we be sure that mathematics is consistent? Are there things that are true but that cannot be expressed in language?

The core ideas were worked out in the weekly meetings (Thursdays at 6) of a group remembered as the Vienna Circle. They got together in the office of Professor Moritz Schlick at the University of Vienna to discuss problems in philosophy, math, and language. The intersection of physics and philosophy had long been a specialty of this Vienna department, and this work had placed them among the world leaders. Schlick’s colleague Hans Hahn was a central participant, and by 1928 Hahn brought along his graduate students Karl Menger and Kurt Gödel. Other frequent participants included philosopher Rudolf Carnap, psychologist Karl Popper, economist Ludwig von Mises (brought by his brother Frederick, a physicist),  graphic designer Otto Neurath (inventor of infographics), and architect Josef Frank (brought by his physicist brother, Phillip). Out-of-town visitors often joined, including the young Johnny von Neumann, Alfred Tarski, and the irascible Ludwig Wittgenstein.

It has been revealed that when Schlick’s office grew too dim, participants adjourned to a nearby café for additional discussion with an even larger circle of participants. This convivial circle was far from unique. An intersecting circle–Neurath, von Mises, Oskar Morgenstern–established the Austrian School of free-market economics. There were theatrical circles (Peter Lorre, Hedy Lamarr, Max Reinhardt), and literary circles. The café was where things happened.

Recent findings suggest that the interdisciplinarity of the group posed real challenges of temperament and understanding. Personalities were often a challenge. Gödel was convinced people were trying to poison him. Architect Josef Frank depended on contracts for public housing, which Mises opposed as wasteful. Wittgenstein’s temper had lost him his job as a secondary school teacher, and for some of these years he maintained a detailed list of whom he was willing to meet. Neurath was eager to detect muddled thinking and would interrupt a speaker with a shouted “Metaphysics!” The continuing amity of these meetings was facilitated by the personality of their leader, Moritz Schlick, who would be remembered as notably adept in keeping disagreements from becoming quarrels.

Recent findings suggest that the Viennese café of this era was long remembered as a particularly good place to argue with your friends, to read, and to write. Built to serve an imperial capital, the cafés found themselves with too much space and too few customers now that the Empire was gone. There was no need to turn tables: a café could only survive by coaxing customers to linger. Perhaps they would order another coffee, or one of their friends might drop by. One could play chess, or billiards, or read newspapers from abroad. Coffee was invariably served with a glass of purified spring water, still a novelty in an era in which most water was still unsafe to drink. That water glass would be refilled indefinitely.

In the basement of one café, the poet Jura Soyfer staged “The End Of The World,” a musical comedy in which Professor Peep has discovered a comet heading for earth.

Prof. Peep: The comet is going to destroy everybody!

Hitler:  Destroying everybody is my business.

Of course, coffee can be prepared in many ways, and the Viennese café developed a broad vocabulary to represent precisely how one preferred to drink it: melange, Einspänner, Brauner, Schwarzer, Kapuziner. This extensive customization, with correspondingly esoteric conventions of service, established the café as a comfortable and personal third space, a neutral ground in which anyone who could afford a coffee would be welcome. Viennese of this era were fastidious in their use of personal titles, of which an abundance were in common use. Café waiters greeted regular customers with titles too, but were careful to address their patrons with titles a notch or two greater than they deserved. A graduate student would be Doktor, an unpaid postdoc Professor. This assurance mattered all the more because so many members of the Circle (and so many other Viennese) came from elsewhere: Carnap from Wuppertal, Gödel from Brno, von Neumann from Budapest. No one was going to make fun of your clothes, mannerisms, or accent. Your friends wouldn’t be bothered by the pram in the hall. Everyone shared a Germanic Austrian literary and philosophical culture, not least those whose ancestors had been Eastern European Jews who knew that culture well, having read all about it in books.

The amiability of the café circle was enhanced by its openness. Because the circle sometimes extended to architects and actors, people could feel less constrained to admit shortfalls in their understanding. It was soon discovered that marble tabletops made a useful surface for pencil sketches, serving all as an improvised and accessible blackboard.

Comedies like “The End Of The World” and fictional newspaper sketches or feuilletons of writers like Joseph Roth and Stefan Zweig served as a second defense against disagreeable or churlish behavior. The knowledge that, if one got carried away, a parody of one’s remarks might shortly appear in Neue Freie Presse surely helped Professor Schlick keep matters in hand.

It has been revealed that though Austria’s government drifted to the right after the War, Vienna’s city council had been Socialist, dedicated to public housing based on user-centered design, and embracing  ambitious programs of public outreach and adult education. In 1934 the Socialists lost a local election, and this era soon came to its end as the newly introduced administration focused on the imagined threat of the International Jewish Conspiracy. Most members of the Circle fled within months: von Neumann to Princeton, Neurath to Holland and Oxford, Popper to New Zealand, Carnap to Chicago. Prof. Schlick was murdered on the steps of the University by a student outraged by his former association with Jews. Jura Soyfer, who wrote “The End Of The World,” died in Buchenwald.

According to recent reports, in 1939, von Neumann finally convinced Gödel to accept a job in Princeton. Gödel was required to pay large fines to emigrate. The officer in charge of these fees would look back on this as the best posting of his career; his name was Eichmann.

An impressive literature recounts those discussions and the environment that facilitated the development of computing. How can we design for amiability? This is not just a matter of choosing rounded typefaces and a cheerful pastel palette. I believe we may identify eight distinct complications that exert design forces in usefully amiable directions.

According to recent reports, seriousness: The Vienna Circle was wrestling with a notoriously difficult book—Wittgenstein’s Tractus Logico-Philosophicus—and a catalog of outstanding open questions in mathematics. They were concerned with consequential problems, not merely scoring points for debating. Constant reminders that the questions you are considering matter—not only that they are consequential or that those opposing you are scoundrels—help promote amity.

Empiricism: The characteristic approach of the Vienna Circle demanded that knowledge be grounded either in direct observation or in rigorous reasoning. Disagreement, when it arose, could be settled by observation or by proof. If neither seemed ready to hand, the matter could not be settled. On these terms, one can seldom if ever demolish an opposing argument, and trolling is pointless.

Recent findings suggest that abstraction: Disputes grow worse when losing the argument entails lost face or lost jobs. The Vienna Circle’s focus on theory—the limits of mathematics, the capability of language—promoted amity. Without seriousness, abstraction could have been merely academic, but the limits of reason and the consistency of mathematics were clearly serious.

Formality: The punctilious demeanor of waiters and the elaborated rituals of coffee service helped to establish orderly attitudes amongst the argumentative participants. This stands in contrast to the contemptuous sneer that now dominates social media.

Schlamperei: Members of the Vienna Circle maintained a global correspondence, and they knew their work was at the frontier of research. Still, this was Vienna, at the margins of Europe: old-fashioned, frumpy, and dingy. Many participants came from even more obscure backwaters. Most or all harbored the suspicion that they were really schleppers, and a tinge of the ridiculous helped to moderate tempers. The director of “The End Of The World” had to pass the hat for money to purchase a moon for the set, and thought it was funny enough to write up for publication.

Openness: All sorts of people were involved in discussion, anyone might join in. Each week would bring different participants. Fluid borders reduce tension, and provide opportunities to broaden the range of discussion and the terms of engagement. Low entrance friction was characteristic of the café: anyone could come, and if you came twice you were virtually a regular. Permeable boundaries and café culture made it easier for moderating influences to draw in raconteurs and storytellers to defuse awkward moments, and Vienna’s cafés had no shortage of humorists. Openness counteracts the suspicion that promoters of amiability are exerting censorship.

Parody: The environs of the Circle—the university office and the café—were unmistakably public. There were writers about, some of them renowned humorists. The prospect that one’s bad taste or bad behavior might be ridiculed in print kept discussion within bounds. The sanction of public humiliation, however, was itself made mild by the veneer of fiction; even if you got a little carried away and a character based on you made a splash in some newspaper fiction, it wasn’t the end of the world.

Engagement: The subject matter was notable to the participants, but it was esoteric: it did not matter very much to their mothers or their siblings. A small stumble or a minor humiliation could be shrugged off in ways that major media confrontations cannot.

I believe it is notable that this environment was designed to promote amiability through several different voices. The café waiter flattered each newcomer and served everyone, and also kept out local pickpockets and drunks who would be mere disruptions. Schlick and other regulars kept discussion moving and on track. The fiction writers and raconteurs—perhaps the most peripheral of the participants—kept people in a good mood and reminded them that bad behavior could make anyone ridiculous. Crucially, each of these voices were human: you could reason with them. Algorithmic or AI moderators, however clever, are seldom perceived as reasonable. The café circles had no central authority or Moderator against whom everyone’s resentments might be focused. Even after the disaster of 1934, what people remembered were those cheerful arguments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

KTC is preparing to challenge the expensive end of the high-resolution monitor market with a fresh display scheduled for CES 2027.

The upcoming M32P2 combines a 31.5-inch IPS panel with 6K resolution and Mini-LED backlighting, giving professionals another option.

Although pricing remains undisclosed, KTC's history of selling advanced displays at relatively accessible prices makes this announcement particularly interesting.

The KTC M32P2 6K monitor sports a 6K panel delivering 6,016 x 3,384 pixels at 60Hz, offering substantially more workspace than conventional 4K displays.

The Mini-LED backlight also incorporates 2,304 individually controlled dimming zones, allowing different screen areas to receive different levels of illumination.

KTC specifies peak brightness of 1,000 nits when displaying HDR content, while standard viewing conditions get a maximum rating of 400 nits.

The panel has a typical contrast ratio of 1,000:1 and supports approximately 1.07 billion colors through its 8-bit plus FRC implementation.

Its advertised color reproduction figures include 98% Adobe RGB coverage, 99% DCI-P3 coverage, and complete 100% sRGB coverage.

These specifications could make the display relevant to professional image editing and content production, although independent testing will determine actual color accuracy.

The manufacturer has also included connectivity options covering two HDMI 2.1 inputs and one DisplayPort 1.4 connection, along with a USB-C port supporting the full display resolution while delivering up to 90W of power to connected devices.

Additional connections include three USB 3.0 ports, divided between one upstream and two downstream connections, alongside a headphone output.

The adjustable stand provides between -5 and 20 degrees of tilt, alongside 110mm of height adjustment for different working arrangements.

Buyers can also use its 100 x 100mm VESA mounting points when installing the display on compatible arms or wall mounts.

KTC acknowledged that the high-resolution category remains relatively limited, describing its upcoming exhibition units as unfinished products.

“We don’t have many 5K or 6K monitors available at the moment. We have these two units at the show, but they are only samples and not launched yet,” a marketing specialist from KTC told TechRadar Pro.

The biggest unanswered question surrounding the M32P2 concerns its eventual retail price, particularly considering KTC's established reputation for affordable display hardware.

Its H27P3 27-inch 5K monitor has previously sold for approximately $530, considerably less than several competing professional displays.

The manufacturer has also attracted attention with affordable Mini-LED gaming monitors, including its M27T6S, which has appeared at around $300.

Those products provide some indication of KTC's pricing approach when introducing display technologies normally associated with more expensive products.

However, neither example establishes what the manufacturer will charge for its upcoming 31.5-inch model.

#88. What Does A 'No Thru Trucks' Road Sign Mean?
