What Does A 'No Thru Trucks' Road Sign Mean?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (438 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, most vehicles travel anywhere between 25 and 80 mph, so drivers should ideally be able to understand a road sign's meaning within two seconds.
  • As the first and final words imply, "No Thru Trucks" signs are meant to restrict road access for trucks.
  • Let's construct an example to help you understand how these signs function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, most vehicles travel anywhere between 25 and 80 mph, so drivers should ideally be able to understand a road sign's meaning within two seconds. However, some traffic signs are confusing. Usually, these signs provide instructions for the road in the immediate vicinity, but one sign acts as a "do not enter" notification that only applies to specific drivers.

As the first and final words imply, "No Thru Trucks" signs are meant to restrict road access for trucks. But what is a "Thru Truck" anyway? It isn't some obscure electric truck; it just means that trucks can't use the roads with this sign unless their destination is somewhere along the path. In other words, "No Thru Trucks" signs are just "Local Traffic Only" road signs designed specifically for commercial and construction trucks. You can usually find these signs in residential areas and near (but not necessarily on) highways.

Let's construct an example to help you understand how these signs function. Say you are an Amazon delivery driver. You start your route in the warehouse with all your packages and while driving, you come across a street with a "No Thru Trucks" sign. Check what deliveries you need to make that day. If you don't have a package to deliver on that street or a street connected to it, you should find another route, no matter how much more time and gas it will require. If you are supposed to deliver a package there, you are allowed to enter the road.

Depending on where you drive, you could spend your entire life without seeing a "No Thru Trucks" sign. Instead, places might use alternatives, such as "No Trucks Except Local Deliveries" or "Commercial Vehicles Prohibited." Different song, same tune.

Industry observers note that as a general rule of thumb, if you drive a commercial truck and ignore a "No Thru Trucks" sign without having a delivery in the area, you might face a fine and court time. The restrictions that dictate truck traffic are from local government, which sets up the signs and catches violators. And that's assuming the sign is installed in the correct location, because while it is rare, sometimes road workers make mistakes.

Even if a "No Thru Trucks" sign is placed seemingly in the middle of nowhere, many drivers follow its instructions anyway. Residents who are sick and tired of hearing trucks speed by their homes might request the sign's installation, so its presence is a regulation meant as a way to give people who live nearby some peace and quiet. Is that really so much to ask?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that I want to discuss accessibility because it is the most important thing for making websites.
  • I want to start off with a couple of statements, and you will agree:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I want to discuss accessibility because it is the most crucial thing for making websites. Other A List Apart articles give you innovation and insight. This article will give you homework. These are just my personal views, but they’re pretty good. I want to start off with a couple of statements, and you will agree: Designers are good people. I have never heard a designer say, “I don’t care if somebody can’t read this text”, “Not my fault if somebody can’t use this device”, or “Who cares if this is confusing?” Some designs exclude people. You have seen people unable to read the text on a website or app that somebody designed. You’ve seen people unable to use a physical device that somebody has designed. You’ve seen people utterly bamboozled while trying to use a service that somebody designed. So what? The first question is, “Is this life-or-death stuff?” The answer is, “Yes.” In my favorite essay, This Is All There Is, Aral Balkan makes the point that pretty much everything that we design can affect life events and death events. Aral gives the example of how even a straightforward bus timetable app can affect life and death events, if we design it badly: somebody might miss a life event, such as their daughter’s fifth birthday party; or somebody might miss a death event, such as the chance to say goodbye to a dying grandmother. The next—and frustrating—question is, “Why do some designs still exclude people?” After all, we know that: not everybody can see perfectly; not everybody can hear perfectly; not everybody thinks the same way; and not everybody moves the same way. I think the answer is that there’s too much to recall. Consider, if you will, the wide variety of topics that A List Apart articles cover. Designers are expected to remember all of that guidance, plus all of the accessibility guidance, plus so much more. It is too much. Recognizing accessibility challenges while designing I’d like to point toward one possible solution, starting from Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design. These are from the mid-1990s, and—although there’s a good chance that you, gentle reader, are a lot younger than that—please bear with me. Seeing as the problem is that there’s too much to recall, I want to look at heuristic № 6, “Recognition rather than Recall.” Jakob Nielsen said that for users, information required to use the design should be visible or easily retrievable when needed. I suggest we tweak that to make life easier for designers. Let’s say that the information required to produce the design should be visible or easily retrievable when needed. In other words, let’s make it easier to recognise accessibility issues while we’re designing. How are we going to do that? I really like the book A Web for Everyone—Designing Accessible User Experiences by Sarah Horton and Whitney Quesenbery. I really like this book not only because it includes a quote from me—actually two quotes, but I don’t like to boast—but because it includes personas that are perfect for helping us to recognise accessibility issues. That’s the good news. The even better news is that these personas are available now for free on the companion website to the book What Every Engineer Should Know About Digital Accessibility, again by Sarah Horton, with David Sloan this time. Meet your users I’m going to introduce you to these personas now: Vishnu, an engineer and global citizen with low vision says, “I want to be on the same level as everyone else”, “If I can adjust my screen, I can read comfortably”, and, “Translating in my head is easier with simpler sentences.” Trevor, a high school student with autism, says, “I like consistent, familiar places on the web”, “When I can learn the pattern, I can find my way”, and, “Reading is hard for me”. Steven, a deaf graphic artist and American Sign Language speaker, says, “My only disability is that everyone doesn’t sign”, and, “Without captions, it’s meaningless to me”. Maria, a bilingual community health worker, says, “I love this. It’s all here … when I can find it”, “When a site is confusing, I just leave”—fair enough, Maria!—and, “When I hear and see it, health information makes more sense”. Lea, an editor living with fatigue and pain, says, “No one gets that this really is a disability”, “Don’t make me work so hard”—please do not bombard this lady with drop-down lists—and, “Links at the top of the page make navigation easier for me”. Jacob, a blind paralegal and a bit of a geek, says, “The right technology lets me do anything”, and “This makes it possible to do my job”. Emily, who has cerebral palsy and is living independently, says, “I want to do everything for myself”, “Simpler screens are easier screens”—hell yeah, Emily!—and, “Tell me what I need in advance”. Carol, a grandmother with macular degeneration which affects her sight, says, “My grandkids are dragging me into the world of technology”, “I don’t understand what the screen is saying”, and, “Why can’t the text be just a little bit larger?” I want to throw one more persona at you now, because, well, A List Apart readers are overachievers. One of my favorite authors, Cennydd Bowles—who literally wrote the book on Future Ethics—says to create Personas Non Grata. In other words, every time we design something, we have to think about what a bad guy could do with that thing, and whom that might affect. To actually use these personas while designing, I like what Eric Meyer and Sara Wachter-Boettcher in Design for Real Life call the Designated Dissenter: for each project that you work on, one of your teams should be responsible for asking, “Will this work for Vishnu?”, “How’s Trevor going to get on with this?”, and so on. Then, once you’ve used the personas to recognise the accessibility issues, you can look up the guidelines for whichever platforms you’re designing for:  Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 Accessibility designing — Material Design 3 Accessibility — Windows apps Accessibility | Apple Developer Documentation Check your interface for accessibility (Ubuntu) Your mission, should you choose to accept it I told you in the introduction of this article that I would give you homework. You thought I was joking. So, here’s your homework: I want you to grab the personas from the Know About Accessibility website, and use them throughout every design project to help you recognise accessibility issues while you work—and reclaim design for everyone. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite Jensen Huang’s resignation from NVIDIA as the manufacturer’s CEO, a number of employees are reportedly calling for Huang to be reinstated as the company’s leader.

Some NVIDIA employees are calling for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as the manufacturer’s CEO not even 24 hours after Huang had stepped down, which was shortly before the board was to begin investigations following Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang, who has been President and CEO of NVIDIA since it’s founding way back in 1993, was discovered this week to have had an affair with an individual named Alice Huang, who reportedly works for one of NVIDIA’s main Chinese rivals, Megaspeed, and who was reportedly an alleged Chinese spy, prompting the organization to confirm they would be investigating the situation.

The following day after his affair had been made public, it was discovered that Huang had had another affair with NVIDIA’s VP of healthcare, who reported directly to him. On November 12, it was then reported that Huang had allegedly had a third affair, this time with another NVIDIA employee who is currently unnamed. Despite these actions, which are being viewed as damaging to the company’s reputation and potential for future expansion, a large number of NVIDIA’s employees want Jensen Huang to remain the company’s leader.

According to a latest report, An “internal suggestion box” has been posted within the company that is urging the board to reconsider Huang’s exit. The post has gained over 1,600 comments from employees calling for his return, with some noting that “NVIDIA is NVIDIA because of Jensen.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports on November 13, 2026, after communication problems affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, according to its preliminary statement.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy remarked in a public statement that the matter affected all Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the facilities that handle high-altitude traffic, and that FAA technicians were investigating. The initial statements did not identify a root cause or connect the ground stop to a particular technology system.

It has been revealed that the disruption followed the FAA’s November 10, 2026 announcement that the AI-assisted Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system would expand nationwide. ASI remarked in a statement that the ground stop was not based on or caused by SMART, any ASI product or the manufacturer’s integration with the FAA and air traffic control.

The expansion takes SMART beyond an initial National Capital Region rollout to the airspace of all 22 centers. The cloud-based platform centralizes 200 data streams, including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics, giving the FAA a consolidated planning picture.

Recent findings suggest that an FAA fact sheet says the system uses AI to analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur. Its shared view is intended to help the FAA, airlines and other operators agree on efficient routes and departure times.

In a recent development, the platform serves as a planning layer alongside existing FAA systems, while controllers remain responsible for keeping aircraft safely separated. Recommendations also move through a human review chain: FAA specialists at the SMART center in Washington, D.C., analyze and validate the data before sending scheduling recommendations to the Air Traffic Control System Command Center in Warrenton, Virginia. The Command Center routes those recommendations to air traffic control facilities for local leadership to consider.

The FAA dates SMART’s start to September 21, 2026. By the expansion announcement, the agency reported that the system had helped reroute 180 flights, with average savings of 10 minutes and almost 80 gallons of fuel per rerouted flight. Those figures cover the initial deployment and do not measure performance after the nationwide expansion.

It has been revealed that the FAA presents earlier identification of constraints and conflicts as a way to adjust routes and timing before a problem spreads. Its stated goals are better efficiency, predictability and systemwide performance while maximizing existing airspace capacity as airlines, cargo operations and advanced air mobility compete for the same airspace.

Sources indicate that SMART’s documented role is distinct from the function at the center of the ground stop. The platform produces pre-departure analysis and scheduling recommendations, while the FAA attributed the stop to communications problems at centers handling high-altitude traffic. Determining what caused those problems, and whether any connected FAA system contributed, remains the central unanswered question. SMART’s expansion explains the attention on the platform, but timing alone is not evidence that AI caused the disruption.

#82. Breaking: Designed for a Dead Language

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2991 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Alistapart

Breaking: Designed for a Dead Language

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alistapart

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, every language app in your pocket inherited a teaching method built for Latin.
  • Every language app in your pocket inherited a teaching method built for Latin.
  • In 1788, Prussia introduced the Abitur, a standardized national examination required for entry into universities and the civil service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every language app in your pocket inherited a teaching method built for Latin. Understanding why that happened is a more useful design lesson than anything the apps themselves will teach you. In 1788, Prussia introduced the Abitur, a standardized national examination required for entry into universities and the civil service. To pass it, students needed to demonstrate measurable, gradable knowledge. The system needed to teach language to large classrooms, produce consistent outcomes, and do it with one teacher and thirty students. The educators responsible for designing this system reached for the only teaching template they had, one that had been used in European schools for two centuries: the method developed to teach Latin. Latin, by 1788, was a dead language. Nobody needed to speak it. The scholars who studied it were reading Cicero and Virgil, not conducting conversations. The method built around it, memorizing grammar rules, constructing translations, analyzing written texts, reflected that reality exactly. Oral skills were irrelevant. Comprehension of written form was everything. The method was not designed to produce speakers. It was designed to produce readers of texts in a language nobody spoke. When Prussia applied this template to French and German, living languages spoken by living people, the premise did not change. Johann Valentin Meidinger's textbook Praktische Französische Grammatik, published in 1804, ran to 37 editions across Europe by 1857. Karl Plotz formalized the approach into what became the dominant model for teaching modern languages across Europe and eventually the United States, where it became known simply as the Prussian Method [1]. Each institution that adopted it trained teachers in it, who trained students who became teachers. The constraint that created the method, how do you grade language at scale with limited resources, became invisible inside the method itself. What remained was the assumption: language is a body of rules to be learned consciously and measured. It was a design decision dressed up, over time, as a pedagogical truth. The observation that should have ended it There are people in the world who cannot read or write a language and speak it fluently. There are children who hold full conversations years before they can read a single word. There are immigrants who arrive in a country knowing nothing of its language and come out, years later, speaking it naturally, not because they studied it, but because they lived inside it. Literacy and fluency are separate things produced by entirely separate mechanisms. The Grammar-Translation method, as it became known, assumed they were the same thing. That assumption was inherited from a method designed for a language nobody needed to speak, and it was wrong the moment it was applied to a language people actually used. The evidence against it accumulated slowly. In the mid to late nineteenth century, reformers including François Gouin in France and Maximilian Berlitz in the United States argued independently that language should be taught the way it is actually acquired, through immersive exposure to real communication in the target language, not through analysis of its rules. Berlitz built an entire school network around this principle. The reformers were correct. They were also largely ignored by mainstream education systems, because the Grammar-Translation method had one decisive advantage that direct immersion did not: it could be graded. In 1982, the linguist Stephen Krashen gave the argument its most formal articulation in what he called the Monitor Model of second language acquisition. His distinction was precise: language acquisition, the unconscious process through which children absorb their native language and through which adults succeed in immersive environments, is categorically different from language learning, the conscious study of grammar rules and vocabulary that classrooms deliver [2]. Acquisition produces fluency. Learning, at best, produces the ability to pass a test. The evidence supporting this distinction, and the observation that immersive exposure to real native-speaker communication is the mechanism that produces genuine fluency, has only grown since. I went to Brazil without a word of Portuguese and came out speaking it. I studied French in a classroom for years and cannot hold a conversation in French today. This is not an unusual experience. It is the expected outcome, and it has been the expected outcome for as long as we have had formal language education. The same decision, made again in a different medium Prussian educators faced the question: How do you deliver language learning at scale, measure progress, and retain consumers over time? The answer it arrived at was structurally identical to the one arrived at in 1788. Duolingo gamified the grammar drill into a streak. Anki formalized the translation exercise into a spaced-repetition flashcard. Babbel organized grammar lessons into structured modules. The interfaces were upcoming. The underlying assumption, that language is a thing you study rather than an environment you inhabit, was not. This was not a failure of design skill. The products that emerged from these decisions are, in many respects, genuinely well-crafted. Duolingo's retention mechanics are sophisticated. Anki's spaced repetition is grounded in real cognitive science. They are excellent at what they actually do. The problem is what they actually do: produce measurable engagement with a proxy for language rather than the conditions that produce language itself. A streak is measurable. A vocabulary score is measurable. The moment a user walks out of an app and holds a real conversation in another language, that happens in the world, outside the product, and cannot be instrumented. When the outcome a user needs is difficult to measure directly, the design process tends to reach for something that can be measured. The proxy becomes the goal. The interface optimizes for it. The gap between what the product delivers and what the user actually needed grows. This is not a pattern unique to language learning. It is a pattern that repeats across product categories whenever a design constraint—the need to measure, the need to scale, the need to produce a grade—gets built into a system so deeply that it stops being visible as a constraint and starts being mistaken for a truth about the problem itself. What happens when the constraint changes The constraint that made the Grammar-Translation method necessary in 1788 was real and rational. One teacher. Thirty students. A standardized exam. You cannot grade a conversation at scale. You can grade a translation exercise. The method was not chosen because it produced fluency. It was chosen because it produced a score. That constraint no longer exists in the same form. Technology has made it possible to deliver immersive, real-time conversation practice to anyone with a smartphone, at a cost that continues to fall. The design problem is no longer how to make language learning gradable at scale. It is how to make the conditions of genuine language acquisition accessible to people who cannot move to another country or afford a native-speaker tutor. The products that are now closest to solving the actual problem are not the ones that invented a new pedagogy. They are the ones that removed the access barrier to an old one. Praktika builds AI conversation partners with distinct personalities, regional dialects, and cultural context, replicating the specificity of a real native speaker rather than a generic language-learning voice. Langua clones native speaker voices so that the interaction feels like a real conversation rather than a lesson. Rosetta Stone's foundational methodology, image association in the target language with no translation, was built on the same insight Berlitz arrived at in the nineteenth century: language is acquired through immersive exposure, not through analysis of its rules [3]. A 2025 meta-analysis of 31 studies found that AI conversation tools produced a statistically significant improvement in language learning outcomes, a result that no amount of flashcard optimization has consistently matched [4]. None of these products invented a new theory of language acquisition. They translated an existing one into something more people could reach. The design question this leaves The Grammar-Translation method persisted not because educators were wrong about design, but because a design decision made under a specific constraint became, over two centuries, indistinguishable from the thing itself. The constraint, how do you grade language at scale, was forgotten. The method it produced was inherited as if it were a description of how language works, passed from Prussia to Europe to America to the App Store, from the grammar drill to the streak. Every time a design team optimizes for a metric because the actual outcome is hard to measure, they are making a version of the same decision. It is often the right decision given real constraints. The question worth asking is whether the constraint that made it necessary still exists, or whether it has simply become invisible inside the system it originally produced. Before reaching for what can be measured, it is worth asking what the user actually needs to do, and what stopped them from doing it before. Sometimes the answer is a new solution. More often it is an old one that was always out of reach.

Before reaching for what can be measured, it is worth asking what the user actually needs to do, and what stopped them from doing it before. Sometimes the answer is a upcoming solution. More often it is an old one that was always out of reach.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tech writer who enjoys exploring upcoming gadgets, trying out apps, and capturing moments through photography.
  • According to recent reports, texting used to be simple: someone sent a message, I answered, and that was it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tech writer who enjoys exploring upcoming gadgets, trying out apps, and capturing moments through photography. He likes getting hands-on with technology and sharing what he learns with readers.

According to recent reports, texting used to be simple: someone sent a message, I answered, and that was it. Emojis and stickers were there, but conversations didn't have all the extra effects and suggestions Google Messages offers now.

According to recent reports, google Messages now does a lot more than handle everyday conversations. Some additions help, while others make the app feel busier than I want it to.

I wanted to know whether I was better off without a few of them, so I turned off a handful of features and kept using the app the way I normally do.

For each one, I asked myself something simple: does it help me understand or answer a message, or is it just one more thing on the screen?

In a recent development, there's a Gemini icon on the main screen of Google Messages. One tap opens a dedicated Gemini conversation, where you can ask questions, brainstorm ideas, or get help with other everyday tasks.

I use the standalone Gemini app, so a second way in didn't do much for me. I rarely tapped it.

I turned off the option under Messages settings > Gemini in Messages. This removed the icon and archived my existing Gemini conversation, both of which returned when I switched the setting back on.

Google Messages suggests things in a few different ways. Smart Reply offers possible responses when someone messages you, and even a plain greeting brings up suggested replies and emojis. Suggested stickers watch what you type: write congratulations or thanks, and related GIFs show up.

Recent findings suggest that nudges does something else. It brings birthdays and unanswered conversations back to your attention. Once it reminded me about a contact's birthday, and another time, it prompted me to follow up on a message that never got an answer.

Those reminders were useful, so I kept Nudges enabled. You can manage these reminders through Nudges settings.

I see why people use Smart Reply and sticker suggestions. A suggested reply saves a few seconds when you're in a hurry, and a sticker suggestion helps when nothing comes to mind.

According to recent reports, I don't use them, though. I'd rather type my own replies and pick a GIF or emoji myself. So I turned both off, and sending messages worked exactly as before.

In a recent development, link previews were harder to give up. I noticed the difference as soon as I turned them off. A shared link appeared without the preview card, so I had to open it to find out where it led. That's not always helpful, particularly when someone sends a link without explaining what it contains.

I tried restricting previews to web links, but that didn't make much difference in my conversations. Turning previews off only affected new links, since the ones already in my conversations stayed in place. I switched them back on because a preview gives me an idea of where a link leads before I open it.

I wasn't particularly attached to Expressive animations. When the feature is on, certain emojis, phrases, and reactions move on screen. With it off, I can still send the same emojis and react to messages, but they appear without the animation, and phrases are no longer animated. I didn't miss the extra movement.

Voice message transcription was one thing I definitely wanted to keep. I can read an incoming voice message without playing the audio, and the transcripts were clear and accurate when I used the feature. This is useful when playing audio is awkward or when I want to skim a long message.

It has been revealed that bubbles solve a different problem. A bubble lets me reply while I'm in another app, without going back to the full Messages screen. I can keep my place in whatever I was doing. That helps most when I'm busy with something else and want to reply right away.

Sources indicate that I kept two other settings enabled. Pinch to zoom lets me enlarge text in conversations, though how much it helps depends on how you use your phone.

Actions come in handy. It picks out dates, phone numbers, and addresses in a message, and when someone texts me a phone number, Messages offers to call it, message it, copy it, or share it.

Google Messages feels simpler now, though I use it the same as before. I still send and receive messages as usual. The Gemini shortcut, the automatic reply and sticker suggestions, and extra animations are gone from my conversations.

Link previews, Nudges, voice message transcription, Bubbles, Pinch to zoom, and Actions stayed because each one gives me information or makes a conversation easier to reach.

It has been revealed that I didn't go back to a bare-bones texting app. I just stopped leaving every option on because it was there, and now I choose additions that fit how I communicate.

In a recent development, your list will probably look different from mine. If you open Gemini from Messages often, keep the shortcut. If suggested replies save you time, keep the shortcut. If suggested replies save you time, keep those too.

Industry observers note that google Messages will keep adding features, so it's worth asking the same question of each fresh one: Does it help me understand or answer a message? That's what made texting feel simpler for me.

Before anyone films a video, shoots an ad or draws the final pages of a comic, someone usually sketches the blueprint as a storyboard: one picture per shot, in order, with a short note about what happens and how long it lasts.

Most people already have those pictures. They are phone photos, screenshots, rough sketches or AI-generated frames sitting in a folder. What they don't have is a quick way to turn that folder into clean, numbered sheets they can print or send to a client.

In this tutorial, you'll build a browser-based tool that does exactly that. You'll add a set of images, give each one a title, a description and a duration, choose a layout, preview the sheets, and download a print-ready PDF.

Everything runs in the browser. The images are never uploaded to a server, which matters when the frames are unreleased product shots or client work.

Along the way, you'll learn how to fix sideways phone photos, sort files the way people expect, lay out a page in PDF points, wrap text on a canvas, save a draft with IndexedDB, and build a PDF that keeps photos sharp without making the file huge.

It has been revealed that I built this tool for AllInOneTools, where it runs as the Image Storyboard to PDF tool. This article walks through a simplified version that you can build in three files.

Sources indicate that PDF-lib can write real text into a PDF, but only with a font file you embed. The standard PDF fonts only cover basic Latin characters, so a description in Hindi, Gujarati, Arabic or Japanese would fail.

According to recent reports, A canvas, on the other hand, can draw any text the device can show, using the fonts the device already has. So this tool draws all the text on a canvas at 300 dpi and puts that canvas into the PDF as an image.

It has been revealed that the trade-off is that the text in the PDF isn't selectable or searchable. For a storyboard, which is mostly printed and looked at, that's usually fine. If you need searchable text, you'd embed a font with PDF-lib's fontkit support instead.

Open index.html through a local server (for example, the Live Server extension in VS Code) rather than as a file:// page, so that IndexedDB and downloads behave the same way they will on a real site.

Pinning the version means a future release of the library can't break your tool without you knowing.

In a recent development, the settings panel is a list of select and number inputs. Each one has an id that matches a key in the settings object you'll create in JavaScript:.

The preview panel has the canvas, the sheet navigation and the download controls:.

It has been revealed that the workspace uses display: grid and the draft bar uses display: flex. Those rules are more specific than the browser's default style for the hidden attribute, so without this line, hidden elements would still show.

At the top of script.js, set up the constants, the state and the element references:.

The paper sizes are in PDF points. One point is 1/72 of an inch, so an A4 page is 595.28 × 841.89 points. You'll do all layout math in points and only convert to pixels when drawing.

The "Select images" button opens the hidden file input, and dropping files anywhere on the page adds them too:.

Industry observers note that resetting fileInput.value after each pick lets the user choose the same file again later. The dataTransfer.types.includes('Files') check makes sure the drop highlight only appears for files, not for frames being dragged inside the list.

Phones don't rotate the pixels when you hold them sideways. They save the image in the sensor's orientation and add an EXIF tag that states "rotate this 90° when you show it.".

If you draw such a photo on a canvas with an img element in some browsers, or read its width and height before the rotation is applied, the frame comes out sideways or with the wrong shape.

createImageBitmap with imageOrientation: 'from-image' asks the browser to apply the EXIF rotation while decoding:.

According to recent reports, if createImageBitmap isn't available or fails, the code falls back to a normal img element. Modern browsers apply EXIF rotation to img elements by default too.

canvasToBlob wraps the callback-based canvas.toBlob() in a Promise, so you can use it with await.

The white fill before drawing matters for PNG images with transparency. JPEG has no transparency, so transparent areas would otherwise turn black.

It has been revealed that people name their files shot-1.jpg, shot-2.jpg … shot-10.jpg. A normal string sort puts shot-10 before shot-2, because it compares the character 1 with 2.

localeCompare with the numeric option compares the numbers inside the names as numbers:.

addFiles filters out unsupported files, sorts the rest, turns each into a frame and reports anything it skipped:.

splice(from, 1) removes the frame, and splice(to, 0, frame) puts it back at its new position.

This is the same idea as object-fit: contain in CSS. The smaller of the two scale factors wins, so the whole picture always fits.

Industry observers note that localStorage won't do here. It only stores strings, and most browsers limit it to about 5 MB, which is less than two phone photos. IndexedDB can store Blob objects directly and allows far more space.

Recent findings suggest that finally, "Start over" clears the state, the draft and the object URLs. The last two lines of the file read the default settings and check for a saved draft when the page loads:.

Here's the whole workflow in the finished tool.

Drop a folder's worth of images on the page or click Select images. They're sorted by file name, so shot-1, shot-2 … shot-10 land in the right order.

Drag a thumbnail onto another card, or use the Up and Down buttons.

Give each frame a title, a description and a duration. The total running time updates as you type.

Pick one frame per page, a grid, panels with notes or a film strip, then set the paper size and orientation.

Use Previous and Next to look at every sheet before you download.

Type a file name, choose the image quality and click Download PDF.

Use thumbnails for everything on screen. The preview redraws often, while the user types and changes settings. Drawing 1000-pixel thumbnails instead of full photos keeps it fast. Only the PDF export touches the original files.

Decode thumbnails once. In drawSheet, each frame keeps its decoded thumbnail in frame.thumbPic, so switching sheets doesn't decode the same image again.

In a recent development, process images one at a time. Reading or exporting dozens of large photos with Promise.all can use more memory than a phone has. A simple for loop with await keeps only one large image in memory at a time.

Size pictures for the page, not the camera. A picture's pixel size in the PDF should depend on how massive it is on the page and the chosen dpi. That one line in buildPdf is often the difference between a 3 MB file and a 60 MB file.

Release memory as you go. Call close() on an ImageBitmap when you're done with it, set used canvases to width = 1, and revoke object URLs you no longer need.

Sideways phone photos. If you read an image's size or draw it without applying EXIF orientation, portrait photos come out landscape. Use createImageBitmap(blob, { imageOrientation: 'from-image' }).

Stretched pictures. Drawing an image straight into a cell with drawImage(img, x, y, cellW, cellH) stretches it. Always fit it with a "contain" calculation like fitContain first.

In a recent development, wrong order of files. The order files arrive from a file picker or a drop isn't guaranteed. Sort them yourself, and use a numeric sort so shot-10 comes after shot-9.

Forgetting to flip the y axis. Canvas y goes down from the top, PDF y goes up from the bottom. Convert with pageHeight - y - height when placing anything with PDF-lib.

In a recent development, black backgrounds on transparent PNGs. JPEG has no transparency. Fill the canvas with white before drawing a PNG you'll save as JPEG.

It has been revealed that rebuilding the list while the user types. Re-rendering inputs on every key press moves the cursor and loses focus. Update the state from the input event and only rebuild the list when the order changes.

Canvases that are too large. Browsers limit canvas size, and phones have tight limits. An A3 page at 300 dpi is about 4960 × 3508 pixels, which is fine, but don't multiply that by the device pixel ratio as well.

In this tutorial, you built a browser-based tool that turns a set of images into storyboard sheets and a print-ready PDF.

You learned how to apply phone photo rotation with createImageBitmap, sort file names numerically, keep layout math in PDF points so the preview and the PDF always match, wrap text on a canvas, save a draft of images and text in IndexedDB, and build a two-layer PDF with sharp text and compact photos using PDF-lib.

All of it runs locally in the browser, so the images stay on the user's device.

You can try the full version of this tool, with more options such as sheet colors, a handwritten font, one PDF per frame and PNG export, at Image Storyboard to PDF.

Less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed.

Fireworks’ exposure of the key allowed data to be copied from a read-only bucket used for Cursor’s data sharing with the vendor. Other accessed material included limited support data and email conversations, product-usage metrics and contact details, summaries of some coding-agent conversations, and credentials consumers had sent to Cursor’s support team.

Among users not using Privacy Mode, coding-agent traces were exposed for fewer than 0.05%, and Cursor stated it identified and notified each affected user directly. The exposed traces were limited to storage used for historical offline analysis. Current customer data and live traffic, active inference requests, and Privacy Mode prompts and code were not affected.

In a recent development, cursor also reported no impact to the production systems and infrastructure that run its service, or to customer code repositories. Official app updates and code shipped to clients and cloud services were unaffected: release code sits in a separate hosting system the attacker never accessed, and no release-signing keys were exposed. The company validated all other extensions in its VS Code marketplace and reviewed and rebuilt that store.

In a recent development, the enhancement connects the intrusion to Cursor’s earlier malicious Claude Code extension disclosure. On October 29, 2026, the attacker used a credential stolen from the exposed internal data to put unauthorized builds directly on the cache serving Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. Anthropic did not publish them, its product was not vulnerable, and Open VSX, the marketplace source, never carried the malware. Cursor estimates that at most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions potentially received a malicious build during approximately 11 hours of availability.

According to recent reports, cursor published indicators of compromise and remediation material on October 30, 2026, and began notifying affected owners and team administrators through in-app messages and email. Administrators received lists of specific keys to rotate where credentials were exposed, and Cursor asked the issuing third-party services to revoke them. Customers whose support or business data may have been involved were notified directly.

In a recent development, cursor’s monitoring systems identified the unauthorized activity. The organization temporarily disabled more internal and product services than the evidence required as a precaution, disrupting certain features, and restored each after review. Cursor believes the incident is contained: the last attacker activity it observed occurred on November 1, 2026, and was blocked. Monitoring for anomalous activity continues.

Cursor moved all inference traffic off Fireworks, deactivated the vendor key and cut off Fireworks’ access to all datasets shared with it. Every exposed Cursor credential identified was rotated, followed by all credentials in use across internal systems as a precaution, even where there was no evidence of exposure. Cursor also expanded network restrictions across service providers where possible, added secret scanning to code repositories and other internal data sources, redeployed production infrastructure and engaged external forensics experts.

Separately, Fireworks AI’s own security bulletin reports that a third-party cloud provider hosting its research-and-development machines experienced an incident on October 23, 2026. An unauthorized party reached Fireworks development machines on October 24, 2026, and ran an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer-data impact; Fireworks detected the activity that day. It has not detected further successful unauthorized access on the customer platform since October 25, 2026. Those findings remain subject to an ongoing investigation.

Sources indicate that fireworks revoked and replaced credentials and service accounts, removed unnecessary elevated privileges, restricted network pathways, tightened storage and analytics access controls, and enhanced logging and monitoring with assistance from Palo Alto Networks Unit 42. It disabled self-serve dataset uploads and downloads used by Batch Inference and dataset-based training during the investigation. Training SDK remains available with zero data retention, meaning no training data is stored at rest, while Lab-based training operates in an isolated environment.

The latest account places the marketplace compromise at the end of a chain that began with a vendor key and continued through credentials left in historical traces. That makes vendor-access revocation and broad credential rotation central to Cursor’s containment assessment, while Fireworks’ ongoing investigation leaves the vendor-side findings open to revision.

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Thanks to the popularity of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, followed by Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, a growing number of companies have entered the flight simulation peripheral market — offering everything from budget-friendly products to high-end equipment designed for professional and home cockpits.

Cockpit-Master and Cockpit-Simulator were jointly founded in 2018 to develop and manufacture flight simulation equipment. In 2024, the company was split into two divisions, with Cockpit-Simulator focusing on more premium, professional-grade equipment.

Sources indicate that today, we are looking at the CS 737X CDU v2, a 1:1 replica of the Boeing 737 Control Display Unit (CDU). We will examine its build quality, how closely it replicates the real 737 CDU, and how well it integrates with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

Before taking a look at the product itself, let’s first look at the real 737 Control Display Unit (CDU) and explain its functionality.

In a recent development, the CDU is the primary interface pilots use to interact with the aircraft’s Flight Management System (FMS). The FMS can be thought of as the aircraft’s “brain,” handling a wide range of navigation and performance-related tasks. Pilots use the CDU to enter and modify the flight strategy, while the FMS calculates the lateral route and vertical profile of the flight. It also manages performance calculations, monitors fuel and flight progress, and provides guidance to the autopilot.

Industry observers note that the CDU features a display screen with six line select keys on either side. These keys allow pilots to select and enter information into specific fields on the display, including data entered into the scratchpad. The CDU also includes dedicated function keys for tasks such as accessing performance information and entering instrument departures and approaches. Below the display is an alphanumeric keypad, which pilots use to enter text and other data before transferring it to the selected field using the line select keys.

Unlike other consumer grade CDUs on the market, the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a full-metal, CNC-machined aluminum shell.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The buttons are made of silicone rubber, which also closely replicates what we felt in our time on a 737 simulator.

The display is where we noticed the biggest departure from the real 737 CDU. The real unit uses a thick, chemically strengthened, anti-glare optical glass cover, whereas the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a standard commercial display. As a result, there is some glare, although the display itself is excellent and offers very wide viewing angles. Despite this difference, the visual presentation is remarkably close to that of the real 737 CDU. The font styling, image sharpness, and color reproduction all closely match what you would see on the real flight deck.

Sources indicate that the CS 737X CDU v2 also features a handle, which on the real aircraft is used for the maintenance crew to remove the CDU. This isn’t entirely necessary in a home setup, but it is a nice touch.

The unit can be easily placed on a desk using the included desktop stand, or integrated directly into a larger cockpit setup.

The weight, rigidity, and metallic construction closely replicate the feel of the CDU we experienced in a 737 simulator. The silicone buttons also require a firm, deliberate press to actuate, helping prevent accidental double-inputs during turbulence. This tactile resistance closely matches the experience of using the real unit. Manually entering a long route, rather than importing it from SimBrief, will give your fingers a workout – and will give you a newfound appreciation for the import button.

In a recent development, for our testing inside of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, we used the PMDG 737-800. We flew the following routes:.

This allowed us to examine how the CS 737X CDU v2 handles routes of various duration.

For hardware, the device only requires a USB connection. It also requires the CockpitSimulator Bridge, which needs to be left open throughout the flight. This can be downloaded from the official Cockpit-Simulator site.

Our flow was similar in each case:.

According to recent reports, the overall feel of the unit, combined with the firm, deliberate key presses, adds another layer of immersion. More importantly, having a physical CDU means we can operate it directly — rather than panning the camera toward the virtual CDU, zooming in, and navigating it with a mouse. This makes interacting with the FMS considerably faster and more intuitive.

Industry observers note that this is particularly useful when ATC gives you a direct-to instruction shortly after takeoff, while you are still hand-flying the aircraft. Performing the direct-to operation on a physical CDU is much easier than interacting with the virtual CDU, as it allows you to make the necessary inputs without taking your eyes away from the Primary Flight Display.

One of the first things that stood out was the extremely low input latency. Our key presses were reflected almost instantly on both the unit’s physical display and the virtual CDU inside Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, making the two feel effectively synchronized.

Recent findings suggest that we were also able to switch seamlessly between the various CDU pages, even with longer flight aims loaded into the unit. Everything shown on the virtual CDU was accurately reproduced on the hardware, including aircraft-specific options for the PMDG 737-800 we were flying. The information was presented with accurate fonts, colors, and formatting, making the physical CDU feel like a natural extension of the one inside the simulator.

According to recent reports, the CS 737X CDU v2 is the most premium and immersive Boeing 737 CDU we have tested. From the weight and feel of its metallic construction to the tactile resistance of the silicone keys and the accurate rendering of fonts and colors on the display, nearly every aspect of the unit contributes to an authentic experience. It's a fitting addition to any high-end home cockpit setup.

This level of construction and attention to detail comes at a price: the CS 737X CDU v2 retails for $799, which means it will likely be out of reach for many flight simmers. But if you're building a dedicated, high-end cockpit and looking for a CDU that closely replicates the experience of the real aircraft, it's an excellent addition.

#71. What Are The Disadvantages Of Pontoon Boats?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1085 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

What Are The Disadvantages Of Pontoon Boats?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the pontoon boat has been a staple of recreational boating for decades now.
  • Pontoon boats are particularly popular for parties.
  • In a recent development, these boats can make for a really fun day on the water, but they aren't great for everything.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the pontoon boat has been a staple of recreational boating for decades now. Though its origins aren't definitive, it's believed the first pontoon boat was invented back in 1952 by a man named Ambrose Weeres. He took a flat piece of wooden deck and tied two hollow aluminum tubes to each side to keep it afloat. Though it's been refined over the years, that's still the basic idea of the pontoon boat. Nowadays, they're no longer made out of wood, and you'll typically have a motor and modern driving controls as well.

Pontoon boats are particularly popular for parties. Because they are generally these wide, flat surfaces, there's a lot of room for many people to be milling about on the deck, and the hollow metal tubes keeping it afloat also offer a good deal of balance as well. Because the design is so simple, there are many different ways you can use the boat's substantial, open space. Of course, you could also want a pontoon boat for other reasons, be it some relaxing fishing or taking the family out to the middle of a lake for a swim.

In a recent development, these boats can make for a really fun day on the water, but they aren't great for everything. The design of pontoon boats can make it difficult to do certain things other boats can do on the water or actually hinder the more casual experience they're designed for. Here, we're going to look at several of the possible downsides to using a pontoon boat that may make you want to choose a different design when you want to go out on the water.

Few people can resist the thrill of driving a boat really fast on the water. When all you have is open water surrounding you, you want to push the capabilities of that boat and feel the wind in your face. Beyond that, many people enjoy water sports like water skiing or wakeboarding. If you're going out to engage in these activities with a large group of people, the natural instinct may be to get a pontoon boat because it will comfortably hold everyone. However, these boats put somewhat of a limit on how fast you're actually able to go.

Industry observers note that pontoon boats typically cruise somewhere between 20 and 30 mph. You certainly can water ski, wakeboard, or tube at these speeds, and for families, kids, or inexperienced people, these speeds are perfectly adequate for a fun time. However, if you're going out on the water looking for some serious thrills, a conventional pontoon boat might not deliver.

Industry observers note that for these people, a V-hull speedboat is the preferable option. With a high-quality engine, you can reach speeds up to 50 or 60 mph with these boats. Plus, their design gives them more maneuverability, making it easier to take sharp turns for even more excitement. Speedboats designed for water sports are also better equipped for towing activities, allowing for a better experience when you're being pulled behind the boat. The speed of pontoon boats may be plenty exciting for some, but others may want a lot more from their thrill-seeking.

One of the major benefits of a pontoon boat is its steadiness. Since its buoyancy is at the opposite sides of the boat rather than at one point in the center, you won't experience as much rocking on the water as you would with a more traditional V-hull design. Some pontoon boats even have a third metal tube along their center, called a tritoon, for even better stability. That's why pontoon boats make for such great boats for parties or entertaining, as deck-focused activities won't be disrupted all that much by the constant back-and-forth swaying of the boat.

However, a pontoon boat's steadiness is really only achievable in calm or minimally choppy waters. Once the waters really start rocking, whether from inclement weather or even the wake of a larger boat passing by, you could be in a world of trouble. These boats are designed to be flat surfaces that float on top of the water. If water starts flying up onto the boat, you could find yourself with a lot of very wet passengers. If the boat takes on too much water, it could become swamped, potentially causing it to capsize or sink.

A V-hull design is much better equipped to handle rough waters. That centralized buoyancy that is actually beneath the surface allows it to cut through waves far easier. So, if you're planning on going out on the water with a pontoon boat, make sure you double-check the weather conditions and stay away from other boats as best you can. If that's not possible, choose a different kind of boat.

Sources indicate that it's a little tricky to figure out where exactly you should put the motor on a pontoon boat. Most designs opt for an outboard motor. This means that the motor is externally attached to the stern of the boat, fully exposed to the air. Some of the coolest pontoon boats have inboard motors inside the hull, but that's rarer. In terms of driving the boat, there's no issue with an outboard motor in the slightest. Where the issue can come in is with how much noise it produces.

With an inboard motor, you're naturally going to have some muffling of the sound, as the parts of the motor are either underwater or concealed within the hull. An outboard motor being exposed means that there's less of a barrier to block the sound, which can result in a louder experience on the water. Because you likely want to use a pontoon boat for entertaining purposes, a loud outboard motor could make it difficult for people to comfortably talk to one another, drown out music playing onboard, or just be a general irritant to passengers.

Industry observers note that some modern motors have been able to decrease the amount of sound they produce. However, if you're renting a pontoon boat, you have no control over what motor is affixed to the stern, and if you own a boat, that means purchasing an expensive new motor just for sound control. If your pontoon boat party is okay with dealing with the noise until you get out to a certain part of the water to turn the engine off, great. If not, you could have a lot of people yelling at one another to be heard.
