#70. Breaking: Schema Drift vs. Semantic Drift in Data Pipelines

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3566 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Freecodecamp

Breaking: Schema Drift vs. Semantic Drift in Data Pipelines

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Freecodecamp

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When a column is removed from a source database or dataset, the next pipeline run usually fails, making the problem easy to detect.
  • In a recent development, this happens because a schema describes the structure of data, not what the values actually represent.
  • As a result, most pipeline checks are designed to catch obvious errors, such as missing columns or incorrect data types, but often fail to detect less obvious problems where the data looks correct but its meaning or values have changed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When a column is removed from a source database or dataset, the next pipeline run usually fails, making the problem easy to detect. But when a field keeps the same name and data type but its meaning changes (known as semantic drift), the pipeline can continue running normally, allowing the problem to go unnoticed.

In a recent development, this happens because a schema describes the structure of data, not what the values actually represent. It tells us which fields exist, their data types, and whether they can contain null values, but not whether a timestamp uses UTC, a durability score should range from 10 to 100, or an empty string means something different from null.

As a result, most pipeline checks are designed to catch obvious errors, such as missing columns or incorrect data types, but often fail to detect less obvious problems where the data looks correct but its meaning or values have changed.

I wanted to see how far this limitation reaches in practice, so I built a small lab where I introduced nine types of pipeline failures and tested four detectors against each one. This article looks at what each detector caught and what happened when changes went unnoticed and corrupted the data.

You can find the code here and reproduce the experiment with a few commands.

To follow along and run the lab yourself, you’ll need:.

I intentionally kept the pipeline simple. It reads 1,000 game-inventory records from a JSONL file, flattens the nested stats and attributes objects, loads the data into SQLite, and calculates six metrics: total number of records, unequipped items, item counts by rarity, average attack per category, items acquired per day, and average durability. I also left out defensive checks so that each change could affect the pipeline in the same way it might affect a real pipeline when someone assumes the source data is reliable.

Each drift applies a deterministic function that takes one record and returns a changed one, so every result is repeatable. For instance, the timezone drift shifts each UTC timestamp to UTC+4 wall time and drops the offset:.

Sources indicate that after applying each drift, I ran the pipeline and saved its output in a separate SQLite database. I then compared it with the database generated from the original data, checking each row and column for differences. This step helped identify whether the pipeline had produced correct results, rather than simply checking whether it ran successfully.

The comparison placed each change into one of four categories:.

Sources indicate that I tested each drifted file with four detectors. Each detector follows the same structure: it takes the baseline file and the incoming file as input, checks for changes, and returns whether it found a problem along with a message. This shared interface keeps the setup simple and makes it easy to add more detectors.

Industry observers note that the rest of this article uses two terms: data shape and data meaning. Data shape refers to the fields in a dataset, their paths, and the types of values they contain. The schema detector captures this information by checking each field and the types found in it.

According to recent reports, for the baseline, this returns entries like acquired_at: {'str'}, equipped_slot: {'NoneType', 'str'}, and attributes.durability: {'int'}.Data meaning, however, includes everything the dictionary leaves out including the unit and time zone of a value, its expected range, the set of valid strings, and what a null value represents. This reveals a limitation of any detector that only looks at data shape. Since the schema detector bases its results on the dictionary of field paths and data types, it can't distinguish between datasets that produce the same dictionary but contain values with different meanings.

According to recent reports, three of the nine drifts left this dictionary unchanged: the timezone shift, the fresh enum value, and the durability scaling. As a result, the schema detector didn't flag any of them.

Detectors can check data at different levels:.

The four detectors cover the first three levels. The fourth level goes beyond what these detectors can establish because a dataset can pass checks on its structure, individual values, and statistical distributions while its meaning has changed. To know what the data means, we need context that can't be gotten from its values alone.

The results matrix summarizes how each of the four detectors responded to the nine drift scenarios.

It demonstrates which changes they caught, which they missed, and whether the pipeline failed or continued with incorrect data.

Sources indicate that "Yes (only)” means that detector was the only one to catch the change. “n/a” means the pipeline crashed, so no rows were loaded.

The strict model detected the most changes (7 out of 9), followed by the schema diff (6), the loose model (4), and the statistical profile (2).

It has been revealed that but each detector missed some changes. Three drifts were detected by only one detector: the strict model caught the timezone shift, the schema diff caught the level change, and the statistical profile caught the durability scaling.

Five of the nine drifts changed the data structure. These included renaming rarity, removing equipped_slot, adding a guild field, replacing the stats object with an array, and changing level from an integer to a string.

Recent findings suggest that the schema diff detected all five changes. The strict model detected four, and the loose model detected three. This shows that the schema diff was the most effective at detecting structural changes.

The pipeline failed on three of the drifts, but some error messages were more useful than others. Renaming rarity caused a KeyError: 'rarity', which tells us exactly which field is missing. Replacing stats with [attack, defense, speed] caused a TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str. This message explains the type of error but doesn't identify the field involved. To find the cause, the reader has to trace the error back through the transformation code.

The classifier labels the first error loud and the second confusing.It makes this distinction by checking whether the error message mentions a field affected by the drift.

The Pydantic detectors ran on the same file and reported stats: Input should be a valid dictionary, directly identifying the field with the problem.

The level change reveals another way a structural change can go undetected. Both Pydantic models accepted it because Pydantic's default lax mode converts the string "42" into the integer 42. The pipeline also accepted it because SQLite's INTEGER affinity converts text that looks like a number when inserting it into an INTEGER column. As a result, the database matched the baseline, and the classifier labeled the run passed_clean.

Only the schema diff detected the change because it checks the type of the raw value before any conversion takes place. This indicates the limitation of checking data after coercion: once a value has been converted, the original type change is no longer visible. In this case, the simplest detector caught a change that both Pydantic models accepted.

The experiment also revealed that not every detected change causes a problem. Adding guild and changing level from an integer to a string both triggered alerts. The schema diff detected both changes, while the strict model detected only the addition of guild. But neither change corrupted any rows because the load step reads only the fields it expects.

According to recent reports, this highlights the need to distinguish between changes that should stop a pipeline and those that only need to be logged. If detectors flag too many harmless changes, users may start to ignore their warnings.

The remaining drifts didn't change the fields or data types. They changed what the values represented. These changes were harder to detect but had real effects on the results. The table below shows the impact of each drift and whether it was visible in the pipeline's output.

In a recent development, A major thing I noticed is that most of the numbers still look normal. For example, moving timestamps forward by four hours shifts some items onto the next calendar day. Since four hours is one-sixth of a day, roughly one in six items moves to a different day. Each day loses some items to the next day but also gains items from the previous day.

The total number of items remains 1,000, and the daily counts change very little overall. With an average of about 5.5 items per day, the counts already vary by two or three items. So a drop from 9 items to 6 can easily look like typical variation rather than a data problem.

In a recent development, the pipeline's total-row-count check still passed because no items were lost. Any check that only compares totals would also miss the problem. The total is correct, but some items are now counted under the wrong day.

I also looked at why the pipeline didn't report a problem. The original timestamp, 2026-01-02T22:30:00+00:00, changed to 2026-01-03T02:30:00 after the drift. The upcoming timestamp has no timezone offset, so datetime.fromisoformat reads it as a naïve datetime. The isoformat() method then writes it back without an offset. SQLite's DATE() treats this offset-free timestamp as UTC, placing the item on January 3 instead of January 2.

According to recent reports, the pipeline processed the timestamp without errors but assigned the item to the wrong day. If the producer had written 2026-01-03T02:30:00+04:00 instead, the timestamp would have represented the same instant as the original. SQLite would have converted it to UTC, and the item would still have been counted on January 2.

Recent findings suggest that the problem was the missing timezone offset. Without it, the pipeline had no way to know which timezone the timestamp represented, so it treated the time as UTC.

It has been revealed that the empty-string drift caused a different problem. Replacing null with "" kept the field as a string, so checks that only verify the data type still passed.

The schema diff caught the change because the type set for equipped_slot changed from {'NoneType', 'str'} to {'str'}. The pipeline raised no errors, but the query WHERE equipped_slot IS NULL returned no rows. The dashboard would show 0 unequipped items instead of 205, making it look as though every player had equipped their gear.

The statistical profile revealed what had happened: equipped_slot: null rate 20% -> 0%; equipped_slot='': share 0% -> 20%. The null values had been replaced with empty strings, not real values.

The new mythic rarity went through the pipeline without an error for a similar reason. The drift changed 20 records to mythic: 10 from common (619 to 609), 9 from uncommon (236 to 227), and 1 from rare (98 to 97). The query GROUP BY rarity accepted the new value without any error. It simply created a new row for mythic and reduced the counts for the other rarities. A dashboard that only knows the five original rarities might hide mythic or group it under "other", depending on how it handles unknown values.

The durability change reveals most clearly how data can keep the same structure but mean something different. In the original data, durability ranges from 10 to 100, so an average of 547.85 is clearly wrong. But the field kept the same name and integer type, so the schema diff didn't detect the change.

According to recent reports, the pipeline also accepted the values because nothing checked them against the expected range. Only a check that knows durability should be between 10 and 100 can catch this problem. To test this, I added a range constraint to the strict Pydantic model:.

This caught 985 of the 1,000 drifted records. The remaining 15 had an original durability value of 10, which became 100 after scaling by 10. Since 100 still falls within the allowed range, those records passed validation.

The four drifts corrupted 1,000, 205, 20, and 1,000 rows, but each one changed only one of the six metrics the pipeline calculates. The other five metrics stayed the same. Anyone monitoring the pipeline could miss the damage unless they checked the affected metric and knew its expected value.

The main finding is that data can change across many rows without changing most of the results people monitor. People only notice the problem if they check the metric that the drift affects.

To catch changes beyond the data structure, we need checks that examine the values themselves.

It has been revealed that the strict model checks whether values follow specific rules. It caught the timezone drift because AwareDatetime rejects timestamps without a timezone offset (acquired_at: Input should have timezone info). It also caught the empty-string slot because its Literal rule only accepts five known slot names and rejects "".

Sources indicate that the loose model has fewer restrictions. It accepts any string for acquired_at, any string or None for equipped_slot, and unknown fields. As a result, it missed the timezone shift, the empty-string slot, and the upcoming column.

The strict model also missed the durability change because I hadn't defined an allowed range for that field. In a separate run, I added Field(ge=10, le=100) to a copy of the model. This caught 985 of the 1,000 changed rows. It missed the remaining 15 because their original durability was 10, which became exactly 100 after scaling and still passed the check.

The statistical profile compares data distributions with the baseline. It was the only detector to catch the durability scaling because it doesn't need a predefined range. It simply detected that the average durability rose from 54.8 to 547.9.

It has been revealed that but it may also flag normal changes in the data. To test this, I scaled durability by factors from 1.02 to 1.3 and tried four mean-change thresholds. I also tested the detector on 200 clean files generated with different seeds to see how often it raised false alarms. I excluded the baseline seed because it would produce identical data.

It has been revealed that the 2% threshold shows how easily the detector can flag normal variation. Durability is roughly uniform from 10 to 100, so a 1,000-row sample has a standard deviation of about 26. That means the sample mean typically lands within about 0.8 of the true mean, which is roughly 1.5% of its value. A 2% threshold is only a little bigger than that, so it should fire on roughly 18% of clean files. It fired on 37 of 200 (18.5%). This shows a tradeoff that lowering the threshold helps catch small changes but also increases false alarms.

Industry observers note that the results also show why one threshold doesn't work for every numeric field. stats.attack, level, and player_id vary more than durability relative to their averages. At a 2% threshold, at least one of these fields triggered an alarm in 188 of 200 clean files. At 5%, they caused all 23 false alarms, while durability caused none. stats.attack caused 15 of those alarms. Even player_id triggered alarms, although its average has no useful meaning.

Using a single threshold treats every numeric field the same, even though some vary more than others and some shouldn't be checked by their average at all.

The category-share check uses a fixed 5-percentage-point threshold, so changing the mean threshold doesn't affect its results. It raised 26 alarms across 22 of the 200 clean files (11%). Seventeen alarms involved equipped_slot, and 16 of those involved chest or off_hand.

Sources indicate that there are two reasons for these alarms. First, the check calculates each slot's share using only the 795 non-null rows, not all 1,000. This gives each share a standard error of about 1.4 percentage points.

Second, my baseline doesn't match the intended shares exactly. chest makes up 17.2% of the baseline instead of the intended 20%. As a result, a clean file only needs to reach 22.2% to trigger an alarm. This happens in roughly 6% of files. off_hand has the opposite problem: its baseline share is higher than intended, at 22.3%. This indicates that a baseline can contain its own sampling errors, which then affect every comparison.

Industry observers note that one more limitation comes from the detector design, not from a measured result. I didn't test this case, but the code shows why it would go undetected. The strict model caught the timezone drift because the timestamp lost its offset. But a producer could shift the clock and keep the Z suffix. Every detector would then accept the data. The strict model checks only whether a timestamp has an offset, not whether the time is correct. The statistical profile skips timestamp strings because they have too many distinct values to treat as categories and aren't numeric.

This is a limitation of the fourth layer: the timestamp still looks valid, but it represents the wrong time. None of the detectors checks whether the timestamp matches the actual time it is supposed to represent.

The results suggest that combining all four detectors provides better coverage because each one catches changes the others miss.

The schema diff is simple and cheap to run on every load. It caught six of the nine drifts, including the level change that both Pydantic models missed because they converted the value before checking it. It also identified the field that caused an error when the pipeline's own error message did not. But it caught only one of the four drifts that corrupted data.

The strict model and statistical profile caught all four harmful drifts between them. I'd use the strict model for fields with known rules, such as timezone-aware timestamps, allowed values, and numeric ranges. I'd use statistical checks for notable metrics that have no clear validation rules, setting a separate threshold for each field based on past data.

The lab indicated why one threshold doesn't work for every field. A global 5% mean threshold raised 23 false alarms across 200 clean files, all from fields other than durability. I'd only apply statistical checks to fields where the average is meaningful and set thresholds based on how much each field normally varies.

Recent findings suggest that the fourth layer requires the producer and consumers to agree on what the data means. If the producer changes a field's unit, time zone, or allowed values without telling anyone, consumers can't interpret it correctly. Both sides should agree on clear rules, such as the unit of measurement, the time zone, and the allowed values.

In a recent development, this is a recommendation based on what my detectors couldn't catch. I haven't tested this approach in the lab yet.

The data is synthetic and independent, so it's much simpler than real data, which often has seasonal patterns and natural growth. Real-world false-alarm rates may therefore be higher than the ones I measured. I also used one fixed baseline, so any sampling error in that sample affects every comparison. A production system would likely use a rolling baseline instead.

According to recent reports, I used the same thresholds across fields. Setting a separate threshold based on how much each field normally varies might work better, but I didn't test this. I also tested only four detectors from a much larger set of available tools. These results show where the detectors have blind spots, not which tools are best.

Finally, I chose to group changes into "shape" and "meaning," but some changes, such as replacing null with an empty string, could fit into either group.

In a recent development, my first threshold test also contained a bug. I used the wrong variable name (SEED instead of seed) in the data generator, which caused all 20 clean files to match the baseline exactly. This produced zero false alarms. A result that good at a 2% threshold seemed unlikely, so I checked the code and found the mistake. I corrected the bug and excluded seed 42, the baseline's own seed, because it would generate identical data and could never trigger an alarm. All results in this article use the corrected run.

It has been revealed that the experiment revealed that schema changes are not the only source of pipeline failures. The schema diff caught all five structural changes but missed semantic changes that left field names and types untouched. For example, timestamps shifted to the wrong day, null values became empty strings, and durability values increased tenfold. In each case, the pipeline ran successfully but produced incorrect results.

According to recent reports, the four detectors caught different types of changes, and using them together improved detection coverage. However, detecting changes is only part of the problem. Pipeline checks also need to validate whether values fall within expected ranges and whether they still represent what downstream calculations assume.

Sources indicate that A pipeline completing successfully doesn't necessarily mean the data is correct. It’s just as important to check that the data retains its intended meaning and that downstream calculations still produce reliable results.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we drive in cars and trucks every day, but many of us have a limited understanding of how the mechanisms that power them actually work. Some people go their whole lives without considering what controls their car beyond the gas, brake, and steering wheel. Learning about how engines work can often seem intimidating, as the terminology can sometimes be a bit confusing to the mechanically uninitiated. Of course, you don't need to know all the ins and outs of automotive engineering in order to drive a car, but you may wish to have a better understanding of what exactly these motor specifications are saying when it comes time to choose your next vehicle.

It has been revealed that there are several different types of combustion engines out there, and they all work a little differently. For instance, you might hear the terms "four-cylinder engine" and "four-stroke engine," and understandably wonder if these two descriptions mean the same thing. They sound similar, and they're closely related in terms of the parts of the engine that they're referring to. A lot of modern car brands have 2.0L 4-cylinder engines, and virtually all modern passenger vehicles use four-stroke engines.

Sources indicate that these are actually completely different specifications, however. One refers to the physical design of the engine itself, while the other refers to the way that the piston and crankshaft move during each individual power cycle. Understanding the difference between these two can help you gain a better understanding of how combustion engines work and what manufacturers are referring to when they use these terms.

To understand what a four-cylinder engine is, we first need to take a look inside the engine block. At its core, a gas engine is essentially a metal housing containing mechanical components that turn the concussive force of combusting fuel into rotational motion. Every gas engine has a certain number of cylinders. These are cylindrical holes bored into the solid metal block (or blocks). Inside each cylinder, you'll find a piston, intake and exhaust valves, a spark plug, and a fuel injector (or intake port in carbureted engines). A piston is essentially a heavy metal plug that fits snugly inside the cylinder. The combustion cycle taking place in the section of the cylinder that is above the piston is what generates the energy to move the piston downward toward the crankshaft, creating the force required to rotate the crankshaft, which all of the pistons are connected to.

Recent findings suggest that some engines, such as those found in most push mowers and some motorcycles, might only have a single cylinder while others may have over a dozen. As you might have guessed from the name, a four-cylinder engine is an engine with four cylinders. There are many different kinds of four-cylinder engines, including inline-fours, flat-fours, and V4s. These terms refer to the way the four cylinders are oriented. Different engines will also offer different cylinder sizes. Engines with larger cylinders will offer more fuel displacement, which has a direct correlation to the amount of power and torque that the vehicle is able to produce. There are several pros and cons to four-cylinder engines. They typically don't generate as much power as engines that contain six or eight cylinders, but they're also usually lighter, more fuel-efficient, and cheaper to maintain.

Now that we've established that the number of cylinders refers to the physical hardware inside of the engine, let's take a look at what the term "stroke" means on an engine. There is a physical design aspect to this as well, but the term generally refers less to the layout of the engine and has a lot more to do with the way the pistons and crankshaft move during the combustion cycle.

Recent findings suggest that A combustion cycle consists of four phases: intake, compression, combustion, and exhaust. The intake is when the fuel mixture is sent into the combustion chamber; compression is when the piston pushes up on the fuel in the chamber; combustion is when this fuel is ignited, pushing the piston back down; and exhaust is when the spent fuel is ventilated from the chamber. The components in the engine react differently depending on whether the engine is a two-stroke or four-stroke engine.

Two-stroke engines complete this cycle in just two strokes of the piston: once during intake and compression, and once during the combustion and exhaust phases. In simpler machines, like dirt bikes, boats, and power tools, these require oil to be mixed into the fuel and are typically used. Four-stroke engines are designed to make the piston move on each of the four phases, requiring twice as many strokes of the piston per combustion cycle. They're generally more fuel efficient, cleaner burning, run cooler, and last longer. Four-stroke engines are used in the vast majority of modern passenger vehicles, regardless of the number of cylinders the engine has.

  • Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to owners across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired.

In a recent development, fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.

Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business.

Some key findings from the report include the following:.

Sources indicate that agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses.

In a recent development, better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights.

Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context.

According to recent reports, insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive.

Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Diesel engines have a number of pros and cons, but they can be a powerful source of extra vehicular oomph, particularly for industrial applications. A diesel engine in a trailer may sound like a bizarre fit, but in Upcoming Zealand's Kaingaroa State Forest back in the '90s, it was the defining feature of the Pacific P510 logging truck.

It has been revealed that commissioned by the Magee family and driven almost exclusively by Lance Magee, it operated out of Murupara under its Marathon Truck and Trailer banner. Caterpillar, a storied truck engine manufacturer, supplied the diesel in the rig, a 3406B ATAAC engine. Its lead trailer, meanwhile, added another Caterpillar, specifically a 3406A. Together, the two engines produced a massive 900 horsepower, with the trailer's engine packing muscle farther back in the logging train.

Both engines were turbocharged, 14.6-liter inline-sixes, each connected to its own Allison automatic transmission. The additional engine sat between the lead trailer's axles, giving it its own, independent propulsion.

It has been revealed that the combo was built to haul logs from remote skids, the areas in a forest where timber is gathered and staged before transport. Getting a fully laden logging train away from skids was a tall order that required a tremendous amount of horsepower. While 900 HP may sound like a wild, unnecessary flex, the Pacific P510 operated as a double, a triple, and occasionally even a quad, meaning it was sometimes required to haul four lumber trailers simultaneously. A pair of diesel engines, which often provide more torque than their gas counterparts, were the only logical answer to get the sheer hauling power necessary.

Murupara had a history of operating trucks in the rugged Kaingaroa wilderness, a plantation forest planted mainly with radiata pine for commercial logging. Former driver Pat Cox recalled Canadian Pacific trucks assembled locally by Kaingaroa Logging Company, with trailers manufactured in its workshops. According to Cox, the front axles of these trucks were so heavy they couldn't be used on highways. Off-highway roads had to be carved out to give those heavy beasts access to the timber and the skids where it was staged. Specialized trucks pulling multiple trailers were a common feature in Kaingaroa, and this P510 pushed the idea to its logical extreme by slapping a second diesel where another truck would haul cargo.

  • Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal fresh institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).
  • The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.

Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal fresh institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).

The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.

It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).

Sources indicate that but most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.

So one month in, who’s on board?

Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a fresh request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period.

It has been revealed that there have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon confirmed an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.

The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order indicates it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents).

According to recent reports, as for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.

According to recent reports, but Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too.

In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a latest rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.

But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.

According to recent reports, are Massive Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.

But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.

Recent findings suggest that in an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.

Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too.

One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his organization to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order, leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month.

Industry observers note that but I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.

People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change.

If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. It’s easy to imagine that two people chatting about, say, whether chatbots are good or bad for our mental health will stop once they realize one of them is saying “super intelligence” and the other “AI.” That would be a shame for us all.

Midterm elections are tomorrow. Americans say AI is more important to them in this election than environmental and climate policy (and Democrats even rank it above abortion and gun policy). We’re only just beginning to have a national conversation about what AI will mean for our lives. Whether or not “Super Intelligence” catches on, turning the terminology itself into a loyalty test will do nothing to advance a national conversation about AI that’s only just getting started.

How to Speed Up CI in the Age of AI-Written Code

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Freecodecamp

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that coding agents now write code faster than most CI pipelines can check it.
  • That second figure shows where all those commits end up: in CI.
  • In a recent development, most of that delay comes from a few causes, and each has a known fix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that coding agents now write code faster than most CI pipelines can check it. In April 2026, GitHub COO Kyle Daigle remarked that his platform was handling 275 million commits a week, on pace for 14 billion in the year, up from about 1 billion in 2025. In the same post, he put GitHub Actions at 2.1 billion minutes in a single week, up from 500 million a week in 2023.

That second figure shows where all those commits end up: in CI. A 15-minute pipeline is tolerable if a dev pushes a few times a day. When an agent opens ten PRs in an afternoon, that pipeline turns into a queue. You wait for results, agents wait to retry, and the time saved writing code is lost checking it.

In a recent development, most of that delay comes from a few causes, and each has a known fix. You can speed up CI in five ways:.

It has been revealed that in this article, we'll walk through each fix in order. You’ll learn how to find the slowest steps in your GitHub Actions workflows, cache dependencies and Docker layers with stable keys, and move heavy jobs to faster runners. You’ll also see how to shard tests across a matrix of parallel jobs, and how to skip unneeded work with path filters, affected-only tests, and concurrency groups.

Industry observers note that most teams try to guess which step is slowing things down, and they're often wrong. A job that feels like a test problem may be 90 seconds of installs and 30 seconds of tests.

Recent findings suggest that start with data you already have. GitHub shows job execution time for every run, with a timing for each step. Open the last ten runs of your slowest workflow and note the three longest steps. Use the median, not the worst case, since one slow run can be a network blip.

Also separate waiting from working. Queue time, setup time, and run time need different fixes. If jobs sit in a queue for a minute, no test tuning will help.

Recent findings suggest that the fastest work is work you never repeat. Every run starts on a fresh machine, so without a cache you download the same packages again and again.

According to recent reports, the dependency caching reference explains how actions/cache works. You give it a path and a key. If the key matches a saved cache, the files are restored. If not, the step runs, and the files are saved when the job ends.

According to recent reports, everything depends on that key. The usual pattern hashes your lockfile, so the key changes only when your dependencies change.

The restore-keys line is the part that tends to get skipped. When the exact key misses, it restores the closest older cache. You still install a few upcoming packages, but not all of them. Be careful with keys that include a timestamp or a commit SHA. Those never match twice, so you save a new cache on every run and never reuse one.

Docker builds need the same thinking. Docker images are built in layers, and a layer is reused only if everything above it is unchanged. Copy your lockfile and install dependencies first, then copy your source code. That way a code change doesn't rebuild the install layer. To keep layers between runs, point BuildKit at the GitHub Actions cache backend with cache-from and cache-to set to type=gha.

One catch is that these caches live in remote storage. Each restore is a network download, which on a big cache can rival the install it replaces.

It has been revealed that caching avoids repeating work. This improvement is different. It runs the work itself on faster machines.

Standard GitHub-hosted runners for private repositories have 2 vCPUs and 7 GB of RAM. Avrea is a drop-in replacement for GitHub Actions runners. You change one line, from runs-on: ubuntu-latest to an Avrea label such as runs-on: avrea-ubuntu-latest, and the rest of your workflow stays the same. By Avrea's own numbers, jobs run about 2x faster on hardware alone, and up to 10x faster with cache hits.

Independent numbers point the same way. RunsOn maintains a public runner benchmark that builds three open-source projects on nine runner services with build caches turned off: a Rust test suite, TypeScript typechecks, and a production Docker build of PostHog. In the 4-vCPU x64 category, as of November 2026, Avrea finished all three in about 7 minutes of build time, compared with about 18.5 minutes on GitHub's 4-core runner, not counting runner start-up.

Industry observers note that built-in caching is the other half, and it connects to the section above. Avrea keeps its caches in the same datacenter as its runners, so a restore doesn't cross a slow network. Most of it is pre-configured.

It has been revealed that the GitHub Actions cache and package downloads for npm, pip, Go modules, and Cargo work with no workflow changes. Build caches for tools such as Go, Bazel, Gradle, Turborepo, Nx, and sccache are set up on the runner, and some need a small workflow addition. So a team gets cache hits without writing key logic for each tool.

According to recent reports, other providers take other routes. Depot offers faster GitHub Actions runners and remote Docker builds, and now runs its own CI engine that accepts GitHub Actions workflows. RunsOn is self-hosted: it starts EC2 instances inside your own AWS account, so you pay AWS for compute plus a flat yearly license, instead of a per-minute fee to RunsOn. GitHub's own larger runners, available on Team and Enterprise Cloud looks, add more CPU, RAM, and disk, plus options like static IPs and GPUs, billed by the minute. Check each provider's site for current details, since all of them change often.

Sources indicate that once each job is fast, make sure jobs don't wait in a line. A long test suite on one runner is the classic bottleneck.

According to recent reports, start with independent jobs. Lint, type checks, unit tests, and build rarely need each other. GitHub runs jobs in parallel unless you add needs, so remove any needs line that's only there for habit.

Next, use a matrix. A matrix strategy creates one job per combination of values, and they all run at once. Teams often use it for Node versions, but it's also the simplest way to shard tests.

It has been revealed that jest's --shard flag splits the suite across jobs by test file. Four shards can turn a twelve-minute suite into about three, plus setup time, if the files take similar time. If a few files are much heavier, one shard will run long, so split those files up. Setting fail-fast: false lets every shard finish, so you see all failures at once.

Playwright works the same way. Run npx playwright test --shard=1/4 in each matrix job, then merge the reports at the end.

It has been revealed that sharding has a limit. Each shard pays its own setup cost, so past a point more shards add cost without saving time. Inside a single job, tools like pytest-xdist spread tests across the CPUs on the machine.

The last one is the cheapest: don't run what you don't need to run.

Path filters are the easiest start. In the workflow syntax, the paths and paths-ignore keys let a workflow run only when certain files change. A change to the docs folder shouldn't trigger a full backend build.

Recent findings suggest that one warning: if a required status check never runs because of a path filter, the pull request stays stuck on a pending check. For required checks, let the workflow run and skip the job with an if: condition instead, since GitHub counts a skipped job as passed.

In a monorepo, go further and run only affected tests. Tools such as Nx, Turborepo, and Bazel work out which packages a change touches and skip the rest. In Nx that's nx affected -t test, and in Turborepo it's turbo run test --affected. Both compare your branch against main, so check out enough Git history for that comparison, since actions/checkout fetches a single commit by default.

Recent findings suggest that most commits touch a small part of a large codebase, so the savings add up. This matters more when agents open many small pull requests, each touching a package or two.

Sources indicate that finally, stop paying for runs that no one needs. When you push twice in a row, the first run is already out of date. A concurrency group cancels it.

Industry observers note that this matters more as AI tools push more commits. Agents may enhancement a branch many times an hour, and each push starts a full run. Don't use it on deploy workflows, though. Cancelling a deploy halfway can leave a bad state, so queue those instead.

Measure first, because that shows which of the other four fixes is worth your time. Cache with stable keys and order your Dockerfile so slow layers stay put. Move heavy jobs to faster runners, and compare providers on your own workflow. Shard tests until setup time dominates. Then cut needless work with path filters, affected-only tests, and cancelled stale runs.

Make one change at a time and re-check your timings after each. Saving two minutes on a job that runs fifty times a day beats a clever fix on a job that runs once.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It used to be a big deal for cars to have built-in navigation systems, especially in the days of printed turn-by-turn directions.
  • In a recent development, your car's computer systems build a detailed profile of your daily driving habits, including the time of day you drive the most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that your car doesn't have to be a "smart car" to know a thing or two about you. These days, modern cars are basically computers on wheels, and they keep track of more than just your gas mileage. Many mechanical components have now been replaced by computerized ones, which allow your car to track more data about how the car operates and, ultimately, learn about your driving habits.

It used to be a big deal for cars to have built-in navigation systems, especially in the days of printed turn-by-turn directions. These days, having something like Apple CarPlay or Android Auto is pretty much a given. You might not expect your car to remember everywhere you travel, but this is the case for many newer cars. For example, Ford mentions that its vehicles track location data if your car uses connected services or has factory-installed connectivity technology. Honda also says it collects trip start and end locations. Many cars have GPS technology that can pinpoint a location via satellite, even if you're not using those same systems to plan a route.

In a recent development, your car's computer systems build a detailed profile of your daily driving habits, including the time of day you drive the most. This profile comes from a combination of GPS technology, built-in telematics, and other onboard systems that track various parts of your driving. If you're driving your normal morning and evening commute, running errands at lunch, or making an occasional late-night trip, your car will create a timestamp every time you're behind the wheel. Eventually, these records can create recurring driving patterns.

Some cars may track how quickly you accelerate and how hard you brake, often to make sure your vehicle is working properly. Computers and sensors control many parts of your car, and those parts can eventually fail or stop working properly, just like mechanical parts. Tracking this sort of data gives automakers feedback about how your vehicle is working and whether it's doing its job correctly. For example, when you press the brake, you're activating systems like anti-locking brakes and traction control. These systems directly affect how your vehicle handles on the road. This data can help your vehicle to avoid skidding or locking the wheels.

In a recent development, years ago, when something went wrong with your car, you had to wish and hope it would make the same sound for the mechanic as it did for you. It could take a lot of trial and error (and sometimes hundreds of dollars) to figure out what was wrong. In modern cars, diagnosing challenges is a bit easier. Auto techs can look at a car's error codes on its computerized parts and have an informed idea of what to do next. That diagnostic data has to come from somewhere, though.

Industry observers note that naturally, your car keeps tabs on data collected from many sensors (including temperature readings, oxygen sensors, emissions, tire pressure monitoring, fuel injection timing). A few other pieces might surprise you, like odometer readings, maintenance history (and whether you skipped recommended services), and crash detection. These data pieces might not mean much right now, but if you were to ever sell or trade your car, they could be telling about how you cared for the vehicle and its history, provided the buyer can access them.

Industry observers note that between things like remote car start and driving cameras and infotainment systems, cars have more features than ever. And your car is probably tracking how you use some of them. For example, Tesla Model 3 has been known to save short video snippets from the car's many cameras. Toyota mentions using data like the vehicle's location and other driving data in relation to its voice commands feature ("Hey Toyota"), which is part of its connected driver services. The automaker cites that this data allows the firm to provide its customers with personalized convenience.

Industry observers note that tracking battery performance doesn't offer much beyond the battery, but tracking the charging stations you're using also reveals information about where you've been traveling, how much you drive, and how long you go in between charges. Tesla doesn't specify whether this type of data is among the pieces that are not associated with specific VINs or accounts. Each car manufacturer might handle this type of data differently.

Sources indicate that in some cases, you can limit the data your car collects about you. Some car-connected services require you to opt in. Take some time to review the privacy policies for these features and see what types of data they collect and who might have access to it. If you're not comfortable with certain features tracking you, you might be able to opt out.

In a recent development, you won't be able to eliminate all types of data collection, because some are baked into how a car functions. For example, braking data affects how the braking system works. In some cases, you might be able to opt out of whether your automaker shares certain data with third parties, however.

According to recent reports, california passed a law in 2020 that allows consumers to opt out of having their data shared or sold. Other states have followed suit. And if opting out entirely isn't an option, you may be able to limit how your automaker uses the data. Since data collection can vary so much between car manufacturers and privacy laws can vary by state, your best option is to explore what's applicable to you based on what you drive and where you live. The worst case scenario is that you're in the same situation as you are now. And the best case: you regain control over some of your privacy while on the road, whether you want to live more privately or just want to make a statement.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary, use-case-agnostic framework for incorporating trustworthiness and risk management across the AI lifecycle.

In a recent development, NIST AI Risk Management Framework deserves a precise explanation because its name identifies a particular information flow, training choice, runtime mechanism, or governance boundary. Treating it as a synonym for “advanced AI” makes claims impossible to test. This guide follows the concept from its input and assumptions through its observable result, then tests the shortcut most likely to be confused with it.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary, use-case-agnostic framework for incorporating trustworthiness and risk management across the AI lifecycle. The definition contains three practical commitments: there is an identifiable input, a transformation or decision that is characteristic of NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and an outcome that can be evaluated against a stated objective. If one of those elements is missing, the label may describe an aspiration rather than an implemented mechanism.

Capability, safety, security, and governance interact but answer different questions. A capable system can be insecure; a compliant process can still have weak measurements; a strong benchmark can be irrelevant to a particular deployment. For NIST AI Risk Management Framework, this system view matters because performance can be determined by the surrounding data, interfaces, hardware, permissions, and people even when the underlying model is unchanged. A useful explanation therefore separates the model’s learned behavior from the product that decides when, where, and with what authority that behavior is used.

It has been revealed that the nearest misleading shortcut is a certification that declares an AI system safe after one audit. It may share a visible feature with NIST AI Risk Management Framework, yet it changes the causal story: different evidence would establish success, different resources would dominate cost, and different controls would prevent harm. The boundary is therefore operational rather than terminological.

Recent findings suggest that the diagram is a compact causal map for NIST AI Risk Management Framework, not a claim that every implementation uses five software components. Some systems combine stages and others repeat them in a loop. The map remains useful because it forces each change in information or authority to have an owner, an input, an output, and a test.

Sources indicate that at this stage of NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the system must govern roles, policies, and accountability. The useful question is not merely whether that operation occurs, but which information it consumes, which state it changes, and what evidence proves that the change was valid. A reviewer should be able to distinguish the operation from a certification that declares an AI system safe after one audit and reproduce its result under the same stated conditions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apps like Google Messages have evolved into rich messengers. There are so many features and options to tweak now, from Gemini integration to chat themes.

The abundance of features has made Google Messages too heavy on my eyes. Conversations are loaded with too many functions, and certain settings are buried in menus.

Industry observers note that I have five tricks that have made my Google Messages experience a lot more seamless. See if any of these tips help you, too.

First, pin your most notable conversations to the top of the list. These make them instantly accessible the moment you fire up Google Messages.

Industry observers note that aside from the usual family and friends, I also pin threads from banks and online services. This helps me separate legitimate texts from scam messages.

It has been revealed that to do this, press and hold a conversation, then tap the pin icon at the top. However, you can't manually sort pinned chats. Everything is sorted in descending order based on the last received message.

In a recent development, you can also add a star to individual messages by long-pressing a message and selecting Star in the submenu. This doesn't pin messages to the inbox; instead, they enter their own category in Search.

To remove a starred message, tap the star icon beside the message.

Since we're on the topic of Search, you can find message categories hidden inside the search icon. Tapping the icon reveals the search bar and at least eight categories.

You can go straight to the specific contact or message you're looking for by typing in the search bar, or you can explore any of the categories.

The categories include unread messages, texts from known or unknown contacts, and media files, among others. The most key one is Starred, which contains the messages you've starred earlier.

If you have two SIM cards like I do, you'll find your network operators listed here. These categories display the specific chats each mobile operator is involved in.

Here's something that is often overlooked, but makes inbox decluttering easier: You can choose two different swipe actions for chats.

To customize these gestures, open your profile icon in the upper-right corner of the main page, head to the Messages settings, then select Swipe actions.

It has been revealed that you can pick between Archive, Trash, and Mark as read or unread. You can choose one gesture for the right swipe and another for the left swipe.

In a recent development, I set Trash for the right swipe and Mark as read/unread for the left swipe. In the rare instance I need to archive a conversation, I long-press the chat and tap the archive icon at the top.

Archived conversations are found inside Profile > Archived.

Sources indicate that I often go through my unread messages late at night before going to bed. When I have to reply to someone but don't want to disturb their sleep, I schedule my text for the next morning.

I start by drafting the message, then long-pressing the Send button. This gives me four scheduling options.

According to recent reports, the first three are pre-made. Examples include: Tomorrow, 8:00; Tomorrow, 13:00; and Tomorrow, 18:00. If none of these suit your needs, select Pick date and time.

Industry observers note that from here, you can schedule a message days or weeks in advance. Just make sure you're connected to a mobile network or Wi-Fi during that scheduled sending time.

Sources indicate that when group chats become overbearing, it's natural to ignore incoming messages. To stop Google Messages from pushing notifications for a period of time, you can snooze entire chats.

Industry observers note that all you do is tap and hold a conversation, then select the snooze icon at the top. You can choose 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or Always.

To ensure you receive notifications for the messages you're mentioned in, check the appropriate option at the bottom of the submenu. This sends push notifications only when you're tagged.

It has been revealed that if you're the type who sets latest messages aside, only to forget to reply later, you can ask Google Messages to remind you automatically. Turn this setting on via Settings > Suggestions & Actions > Nudges > Suggest message reminders.

If you notice vital messages going to spam, lower the spam protection. Go to Settings > Protection & Safety and pick Standard protection instead of Enhanced protection.

Much of the texting friction comes from a buildup of annoyances, not a single interface-breaking patch. These tricks aim to reduce hassle and boost productivity in Google's primary messaging app.

It has been revealed that google Messages is no longer a basic SMS app. It's now loaded with features that could make or break the flow. By investing a few minutes into configuring pins, swipes, and reminders, you can regain control over your daily messaging.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past couple of decades, Ryobi has positioned itself as one of the biggest players in the cordless power tool market. It's done so by building out an extensive list of budget-friendly, lithium-ion-powered tools and devices that can cover virtually any need a DIYer might face at home, in the yard, and beyond. That tool lineup features devices that run on different levels of lithium-ion power, including 4V, 18V, and 40V, among others.

You may not realize it, but some of those batteries can provide additional functionality apart from just powering your tools. In fact, those USB lithium packs can serve as chargers for your mobile device in a pinch. As for the 40V battery packs, they can provide a similar function; only they might be able to power much larger devices, even some major appliances.

Recent findings suggest that there is a catch, of course, which is that, unlike the USB lithium batteries, those 40V rechargeables are not equipped with a USB port that allows you to directly connect a device to draw power. Rather, they require the use of an inverter device. Ryobi refers to these as "power sources" or "power stations" on its site, with the devices essentially taking the DC (direct current) power supplied by the batteries and turning it into the sort of AC (alternating current) power required for devices plugged into traditional two- and three-pronged outlets. Yes, if you buy the right one, you may be able to power your refrigerator.

Industry observers note that such a device could prove invaluable in an emergency situation or during a power outage. It could even prove handy in a home garage or workshop setup. If you're curious, Ryobi's power sources and stations are not limited to its 40V lineup either, with the Techtronic Industries-owned brand also featuring a couple of 18V devices in its lineup, and even a USB lithium charger that features multiple ports.

Industry observers note that the USB Lithium device is the cheapest available, of course, with Ryobi selling it for $59.97. An 18V Power Source with a single built-in 120V outlet, on the other hand, will set you back $69.97. Sticker prices go up pretty sharply from there, as does the max power output, with Ryobi topping out with 1,800-watt power stations for both its 18V and 40V battery families. Those devices each boast standard USB and USB-C ports, as well as multiple 120V outlets, and are at the moment selling for $649 each. While they can run on a single battery pack, using multiple batteries can drive the price considerably higher if you don't have them on hand already.

Sources indicate that there are things to consider before you make that investment, as power inverters can be finicky and potentially dangerous if not used correctly. And yes, there is a right way and a wrong way to use and care for portable power stations. You should also remove the batteries when storing the station and avoid blocking its vents or overloading it, as overheating and battery damage could result.

How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.
  • As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.
  • Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.

Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.

The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.

Recent findings suggest that now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.

Recent findings suggest that an example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.

In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.

A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).

Industry observers note that instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.

The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.

A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”.

Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he indicates.

Sources indicate that during training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.

According to recent reports, there is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.

Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he noted. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.

In a recent development, alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he claims. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”.

Sources indicate that one potential concern with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.

It has been revealed that it’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.

It has been revealed that “Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris states. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.

Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.).

According to recent reports, whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?

“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he notes of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.
