💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's almost baffling that the fastest Atlantic crossing by an ocean liner was achieved nearly 75 years ago and hasn't been beaten since.
  • Industry observers note that today, ocean liners are largely a thing of the past.
  • The Queen Mary 2 is the only liner still running a scheduled liner crossing like the express liners of the 1950s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's almost baffling that the fastest Atlantic crossing by an ocean liner was achieved nearly 75 years ago and hasn't been beaten since. The SS United States, set to be sunk off the coast of Florida soon, set the record by crossing from New York to England in just 3 days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes. It did so in July 1952, as part of its maiden voyage. During that era, the typical express liner voyage took around five days.

Industry observers note that today, ocean liners are largely a thing of the past. In fact, there's only one that still runs through roughly the same route — the Queen Mary 2, operated by Cunard Line. However, it usually takes seven days to complete it. Cunard's itinerary for a December 2027 westbound sailing says the ship starts in Southampton, takes six days at sea, and concludes in Fresh York on Day 8.

It's a fair comparison, too. The Queen Mary 2 is the only liner still running a scheduled liner crossing like the express liners of the 1950s. Even so, it takes two days longer than the average trip of decades ago and nearly twice as long as the super-speedy SS United States.

And it's not just ocean liners that are taking longer, since regular cruise ships are slower, too. Royal Caribbean, a cruise firm, says that its ships average 18 to 20 knots. At that speed, covering the same 2,949-nautical-mile route non-stop would take roughly six to seven days. However, the actual voyages are slower since these ships tend to spend time at port stops such as the Azores and Bermuda. As an example, Celebrity Cruises says its ships take 11 to 16 nights to cross the Atlantic.

The main reason is that people don't book ocean liners or even cruise ships for the speed anymore. In fact, not long after that record was set, liners were already starting to lose travelers to jets. In 1957, more people crossed the Atlantic by air than by sea for the first time, enabled by propeller planes like the Lockheed Constellation. Then came the Boeing 707, a wholly different beast: It could cruise at nearly 600 mph and complete a transatlantic trip in just over six hours. So obviously, anyone who traveled by ship to cross the ocean in the shortest possible time simply gave up on them.

By 1968, Cunard, a major passenger line at the time, lost more than $40 million on its passenger ships over six years. It then repositioned itself to avoid competing with jets and decided it would focus on the leisure business instead. Naturally, speed stopped being a priority: People on vacation don't normally wish their trips to end in the shortest possible time.

It has been revealed that today, Queen Mary 2 crosses at about 21.5 knots, according to a 2012 Business Travel News report. This is slower than the original Queen Mary, which sailed from 1936 to 1967, at 28.5 knots. Besides the lack of need for speed, some of it has to do with cost. The thing with the Queen Mary 2 is that it runs on two kinds of engines: a pair of gas turbines and four diesel engines, and diesel engines are cheaper to run.

The thing with ships like the Queen Mary 2 is that they rarely go all out. The ship's own chief designer, according to an Ingenia report, indicates that it was contracted for a top speed of 29.35 knots, though it could go even faster in sea trials, hitting 29.65 knots. This specific speed, the report adds, was picked after studying the logs of Cunard's previous liner, then tested against five years of real Atlantic weather. It lets the ship make up any lost time if it ever gets delayed by weather.

In a recent development, beyond operating costs, building faster ships is also pretty expensive. Speed and rough seas are a formula that doesn't mix together — you need a deeper hull and extra strength, especially to push through stormy weather, and that promptly raises costs. In fact, according to the Ingenia report, building a true ocean liner with its specific strength requirements incurs a 40% increase in the cost of construction versus a cruise ship of the same size.

Supersized ships also need much more power to move fast, which we observe with the Queen Mary 2. The Mary 2 measures about 150,000 gross tons and is the largest liner ever. It's nearly three times bigger than the SS United States, which measured 53,329 tons, and nearly twice as massive as the largest liners from the 1950s. It also helps that the SS United States had roughly twice Queen Mary 2's propulsion power. In other words, more power for a significantly smaller overall package.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Joe Henson and Alexis Smith, the composers for 007 First Light's soundtrack, joined the project very early by industry standards and could write the score based on advanced footage.
  • "If I remember correctly, we came on board about 18 months before release," Smith said in an interview with TechRadar Gaming.
  • Smith revealed that with First Light, IO Interactive had a "vertical slice" of the game "already at an advanced level, so he and Henson "could see what the vision for the project really was.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joe Henson and Alexis Smith, the composers for 007 First Light's soundtrack, joined the project very early by industry standards and could write the score based on advanced footage.

"If I remember correctly, we came on board about 18 months before release," Smith said in an interview with TechRadar Gaming. "In the film and TV world, that would be very early, but with games that’s relatively late on.".

Smith revealed that with First Light, IO Interactive had a "vertical slice" of the game "already at an advanced level, so he and Henson "could see what the vision for the project really was.".

Industry observers note that "We still had enough time to feel fully integrated into the audio team at IO Interactive, and to be able to influence gameplay from a music point of view," Henson added. "They are a very welcoming group of people, very open to new ideas and suggestions, and we feel we have made some firm friends.".

The composers explained that for a score like 007 First Light, their primary goal was to give the Bond franchise "a gentle nudge into the modern day, without completely reinventing it," and the cinematic nature of the game allowed them to compose a score that not only served the narrative, but the player.

"There are a lot of 'cinematic' style sections in this game where the music can work more like a traditional non-interactive score, but there are also a lot of parts where the music must guide and inform the player," Smith remarked.

Henson explained that video game projects are always a "mixture" of composing for the game and for the player who can enjoy the game through the music, and it's "one of the reasons we love working on them.".

"Sometimes we are simply scene setting, other times we are helping shape the emotional moments, or enforcing the action," he continued.

"Although for most of the time we hope the player barely notices we are there, the worst thing for an interactive sequence is for the music to jar in some way, to be too intrusive, destroying the immersion and pulling the player out of the game.".

The Flight’s soundtrack for 007 First Light is nominated in the Best Original Video Game Score category at the Ivors Composer Awards, which are taking place at Grosvenor House in London on November 17, 2026.

The 2021 Discovery Sport is five years old as of 2026, and if you're interested in selling yours, you're probably interested in knowing how much your model can fetch in the secondhand market, considering luxury cars typically lose value faster.

In a recent development, similarly, if you're planning to buy a used 2021 Discovery Sport, you'll want to know what to expect to pay in today's used-car market. According to estimates from CarEdge, a Land Rover Discovery Sport depreciates by 59.1% after five years, which translates to a resale value of 40.9%. The site says the average resale value for a five-year-old Discovery Sport is $21,611, having lost around $31,189 of its original value. The site's estimates assume the car is in average condition and has clocked about 67,500 miles. iSeeCars' Land Rover Discovery Sport depreciation values differ slightly from CarEdge's.

Industry observers note that the site estimates the model loses 54.9% of its value over the same period, with an estimated average resale value of $22,515. Kelley Blue Book's (KBB) data also show that the 2021 Discovery Sport has lost a considerable chunk of its original value, depreciating by 58.27%. The site shows the model has retained just 41.73% of its original value, based on the combined original MSRP of $182,000 and the total current Fair Purchase Price of $75,950.

In a recent development, overall, based on data from the three reference sites, the Land Rover Discovery Sport doesn't have the best resale value. It loses more than 50% of its original value after five years, which is more than the average car. According to iSeeCars, the average car will depreciate by 41.7% over the same period, which is roughly 13 percentage points less than the Land Rover Discovery Sport. KBB notes that the average car retains 44.7% of its value, which is higher than the Discovery Sport.

Industry observers note that iSeeCars also has data on the depreciation rate of different car segments as a whole, and the Disco Sport doesn't fare any better. The average SUV only loses about 44.8% of its value, 10.1 percentage points less than Land Rover's model. Even worse, the overall luxury compact SUV segment, which the Disco Sport belongs to, fares a bit better with 49.6% depreciation after five years, per iSeeCars. If that wasn't enough, CarEdge ranks the Discovery Sport among luxury cars with the worst resale value after five years.

So if you're considering buying a Land Rover Discovery, be warned that it isn't the best option available if you care about resale value. If resale value is vital, then you'd better look elsewhere. In fact, with Land Rover considered one of the worst depreciating car brands, you'll have to consider models outside the manufacturer's portfolio.

Industry observers note that buying a used Land Rover Discovery Sport is appealing due to its affordable price in the secondhand market. For example, a used 2021 Disco Sport is at the moment fetching an average national price of $18,988, down from its average original MSRP of $45,500, according to KBB's Fair Purchase Price data. Thanks to its high depreciation rate, buying a used Disco Sport presents an opportunity to get your hands on a premium compact SUV without paying the high price of a brand-latest model. However, the lower price doesn't necessarily mean you should get the vehicle.

Sources indicate that another key factor you should consider is the model's reliability. Even if you're given a Disco Sport for free, it'll cost you much more if it has recurring problems. According to What Car?, the common issues reported by customers were related to electrical faults, warning lights, and the infotainment system.

According to recent reports, additionally, there have been several recalls affecting various model years of the Discovery Sport. That said, if you can find a clean model with a complete service history, a clean inspection report, and preferably a warranty, it can be a worthwhile purchase. Organizers of the independent Stand with Jensen campaign revealed in a November 14, 2026 post that their open letter urging NVIDIA’s board to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang had surpassed 100,000 signatures in less than 24 hours.

The campaign reported that the total included more than 5,000 self-identified current NVIDIA employees, nearly 1,000 former employees and more than 54,000 shareholders. Its website’s live press summary subsequently displayed 107,918 signatures, while the public signer list demonstrated 72,021 matching entries. Signers can keep their names private, so the public list represents only part of the total.

Among the displayed entries dated November 13, 2026 are the names Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney, Garry Tan, Amjad Masad and Gavin Baker. The campaign cautions that it does not verify identities, affiliations or titles and describes itself as independent of, and not endorsed by, NVIDIA and Huang. The entries therefore document what the site displays, not authenticated endorsements from the named executives.

The letter’s first request is to restore Huang as CEO while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless directors can provide compelling evidence that his removal serves NVIDIA’s best interests. If the board considers his continued absence necessary, the letter requests a specific, evidence-based explanation.

The remaining requests seek disclosure of the inquiry’s scope, independence and expected timeline, a meaningful opportunity for Huang to respond before a final decision, and a timely public explanation. That explanation would cover the concerns, supporting evidence and how employee and shareholder interests were weighed, while respecting legitimate confidentiality.

Organizers acknowledge that they lack access to the board’s private deliberations and frame their due-process objections as concerns rather than established findings. The letter’s position is that Huang’s leadership record does not place him above accountability, but that accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing and a reasoned decision.

Signing requires no account. Email addresses are not published, signers receive a private code that lets them withdraw, and affiliation categories are optional and self-reported. New signatures may be held for organizer review, in which case they are neither published nor counted unless approved.

Sources indicate that the site says every new signer’s name, including names kept private, is sent to OpenAI for a language-aware format check that does not verify identity. Malformed or uncertain names, or unavailable checks, can be held for organizer approval rather than automatically rejected.

Messages chosen for publication receive a separate OpenAI review using only the message text. Mockery or negative sentiment toward Huang can cause the entire signature to be rejected, while uncertain or unsafe messages can remain pending, uncounted and unpublished until organizers approve them.

It has been revealed that NVIDIA confirmed on November 12, 2026 that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and director, effective immediately, after 33 years leading the firm he co-founded. Colette Kress agreed to serve as interim CEO while remaining executive vice president and CFO until a permanent successor is named. The board initiated a search considering internal and external candidates and appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first chair.

According to recent reports, the campaign has built a substantial public response around a leadership change already being executed. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes.
  • This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically.
  • Sources indicate that consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient.

Sources indicate that A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in fresh forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.

Sources indicate that consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

#41. Tech Report: The World's Fastest Torpedo Is Basically An Underwater Rocket

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (534 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Tech Report: The World's Fastest Torpedo Is Basically An Underwater Rocket

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, torpedoes have existed in various forms since the 19th century, and in 1864, the CSS Hunley became the first successful submarine to destroy an enemy ship.
  • 48 Heavyweight torpedo is the deadliest in the world, but compared to the fastest torpedo ever made, it's incredibly slow.
  • Recent findings suggest that dodging an incoming torpedo moving more than four times as fast as the fastest sub is difficult.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, torpedoes have existed in various forms since the 19th century, and in 1864, the CSS Hunley became the first successful submarine to destroy an enemy ship. The Hunley was destroyed in the process while using a spar torpedo, but thankfully, the technology has improved since that time. Modern torpedoes are incredibly complex vehicles that combine speed, maneuverability, targeting, and warhead lethality into a single package that often costs millions of dollars to produce.

The United States' Mk. 48 Heavyweight torpedo is the deadliest in the world, but compared to the fastest torpedo ever made, it's incredibly slow. Speed is one of the most crucial factors in torpedo operation, and the Soviet Union managed to perfect that particular aspect of torpedo design in the 1970s. The VA-111 Shkval entered into service with the Russian Navy in 1978, and it can travel at speeds in excess of 200 knots, which amounts to around 230 mph. Making something move that quickly underwater is an engineering challenge, to say the least.

Recent findings suggest that dodging an incoming torpedo moving more than four times as fast as the fastest sub is difficult. The Shkval is particularly effective at quickly reaching its target. To reach 200+ knots, the torpedo employs a process known as supercavitation, which is accomplished by continuously vaporizing water as it travels. This creates a thin bubble of gas surrounding the torpedo, significantly reducing friction from hydrodynamic drag. Of course, it doesn't hurt that the Shkval isn't powered by a propeller, and instead employs a rocket engine for thrust.

Recent findings suggest that torpedoes typically have domed or somewhat pointed forward sections, but the Shkval's nose doesn't follow this trend. Instead, its design was purposefully made as a means of diverting rocket exhaust out via several openings in front of the torpedo as it travels. This is what creates the gas bubble surrounding the weapon system as it moves, achieving its incredible speed.

Recent findings suggest that with great speed comes a significant tradeoff in maneuverability, and the Shkval is neither highly maneuverable nor guided like most torpedoes. Instead, it relies on speed to close the distance between the launcher and the target, so it has an advantage there, since it's difficult for a submarine to outrun a normal torpedo, much less a supercavitating one. If the torpedo changes course or direction even slightly, it disrupts the gas bubble, canceling out supercavitation until it reforms around the torpedo's body. Because of this, once it reaches a target area, it slows down and switches on its targeting system to locate its target.

Sources indicate that interestingly, the earliest versions of the Shkval had no guidance system due to the incredible noise the rocket engine made, disrupting its ability to locate a target. When the Soviets designed the Shkval, it was likely meant to carry a nuclear warhead, so maneuverability wouldn't have been paramount in their design process. In terms of its size and specs, the Shkval has a maximum range of a little over 4.26 miles. It carries a 460-lb warhead, and the Shkval torpedo is used by the Russian and Iranian navies; the latter likely reverse-engineered the technology.

If your geek is an Apple user, then they can't go wrong with the Apple USB-C to 3.5mm jack adapter — Apple's tacit admission that people still like and want to use wired headphones.

The most annoying part of using one of these adapters (aside from the burning rage at having your headphone jack stolen) is that you can't charge your phone at the same time. In that case, consider this USB-C to 3.5-millimeter headphone and charger adapter. The extra USB-C dongle supports PD 3.0 and up to 60-watt fast charging. It also supports hi-fi 24 bits/96 kHz audio. In a recent development, A USB-C to 3.5 mm dongle can emit great wired audio, but the next level up is a dedicated DAC and amp combo that can drive a pair of high-impedance headphones. The FiiO/Snowsky Tiny is a perfect example. It claims to support PCM 384 kHz/32 bit and DSD256 on Android phones and PC — no iPhones supported, unfortunately. Headphones that have their own mic and controls will still work. For geeks that want to go deeper, the adapter supports PEQ EQ tuning. It's a lot of technobabble, we admit, but the point is this is a high-performance adapter for discerning listeners.

In a recent development, note there are two versions of this product, the Tiny A and the Tiny B. The former includes a USB-C port for simultaneous charging; the latter has a second headphone jack for less-common 4.4-millimeter headphones and allows two people to listen at the same time. We'd recommend the Tiny A, however, unless you know for a fact your recipient has headphones with a 4.4-millimeter plug. People who know headphones recommend the FiiO. Most importantly, this "professional-grade" hardware only sets you back $20.

According to recent reports, have you ever plugged a device into one of those free charging stations at airports? That may have been one of the riskiest things you've ever done, digitally speaking. Hackers use these as honeypots to get a direct, physical connection to your device so they can hit you with a malware payload. It's not something the average person usually knows, but it's certainly something the geek in your life does. They'll appreciate a PortaPow Data Blocker.

PortaPow makes two varieties of data blocker. One, a USB-A to USB-C adapter for a charging cable; helpful if the only available plug at a charging station is USB-A. Or if USB-C is available, a USB-C-only data blocker adapter. Both types have gotten strong reviews over the years and confirm it is impossible to transmit data when using one of these. They work through a very simple principle: they do not have data-transmission hardware whatsoever, entirely eliminating the possibility that a bad actor could gain access. Each set of two costs $9.99.

Sources indicate that geeks are not like the common man. The common man is satisfied with the same charging brick they've been using for the past decade, while a geek can comfortably own two or ten. Reviewers who have had their hands on this thing can all agree it's an excellent choice for a small, single-port charger. It fits right into a stocking, too.

It is a bit on the pricey side at $39.99, but at the time of writing, it's on sale for $25.99 for Prime Members and it has dipped down to $25.99 for everyone else on multiple occasions already.

It has been revealed that believe it or not, geeks like to go outside. No, really. The USB-C standard is in a weird place right now. It's more common than ever, having become the default port on phones, some laptops, and even now starting to creep into 2.4Ghz dongles that were once exclusively USB-A. Yet, we still have a ton of USB-A devices that are not going away anytime soon. This can get really annoying for geeks, who want a USB thumb drive that they can use on their modern laptop and that old one they probably put Linux on. A great USB thumb drive for this frustrating transitional period is the SanDisk 128 GB Ultra Dual Drive.

Recent findings suggest that spec-wise, this is just a typical USB 3.1 Gen 1 flash drive, but with a twist: it has a USB-A and USB-C plug on each side, so you can add files to it from an older USB-A-only device and transfer them seamlessly to a USB-C device, without any intermediaries. We'd also say it's pretty fairly priced in the midst of this memory crisis at $29.99, and reviews for it are strong.

A major matter with USB-C is that cables may look identical on the outside, but they can support wildly different charging and transfer speeds and protocols. Unless you know where you bought it, it's effectively a mystery cable that you'll have to hope does what you want it to. Enter: the Treedix USB cable tester.

Like other cable testers, you insert both ends of a cable into the provided slots, and the readout will tell you everything about it. It tells you which USB generation it is (USB 2.0, 3.2, 4.0, etc.), its power transmission capabilities (like Power Delivery), what sort of transfer speeds it supports (including if it's a Thunderbolt cable, and what generation), and a lot of other geeky stuff only people who test cables in the first place would know.

It's an indispensable tool for finding the right cable for the job, including testing cables that you've just purchased against advertised specs, and going through older cables to see if they're worth keeping. Reviewers love it, and geeks will too.

However, reviewers quite like the new profile, and the inclusion of modern conveniences (aside from the USB-C connector) like a microphone for calls. It has been revealed that one of the downsides to buying a PS5 is that you're heavily limited in what Bluetooth accessories you can connect to it. In particular, Bluetooth audio. A PS5 will just flat-out refuse to connect to headphones and speakers not strictly endorsed by Sony — so not even Sony's noise-canceling headphones will connect. Trust me, I've tried. Unless, of course, you use a USB adapter. If the person you're gifting to has a PS5, they might like this Ugreen USB-C Bluetooth adapter that supports Bluetooth audio for the PS5 as well as computers that might not have functioning Bluetooth — though not TVs.

It actually works, too, with modern hi-fi codecs like aptX (read: really high-quality wireless audio). It claims to have sub-100ms latency, which is pretty good when it comes to Bluetooth audio. Any Bluetooth audio device should work, whether it's headphones, earbuds, or a speaker. Just make sure to double-check that the gift recipient isn't using a PS4 or PS Portal, as it doesn't work on that hardware. In my experience, the USB-C port matters because it lets you connect to the front of the PS5, rather than the back, where the signal might be interrupted.

It has been revealed that we've already discussed the USB cable tester, but another useful tool in a geek's arsenal is a USB-C power meter. Plug it into a device — like a phone, laptop, or gaming handheld — then plug in your charging cable to the back end, and the meter tells you exactly how much current is flowing through. This can be helpful for identifying charging problems, when the device isn't taking as much as it can support, or the brick it's connected to isn't putting out as much as it supports, and so on.

Sources indicate that in addition to this, it can identify protocols like Power Delivery. Everything is displayed in real time on an ISP display. Experts who have tested it find it to be reliable and useful. Also, it earns the vaunted "customers usually keep this item" status, the highest praise Amazon can bestow — and it's only $13.97.

Most people these days just use the flashlight on their phone when they need one. Not geeks, though. They buy rechargeable flashlights such as this one that produce a disproportionately large and powerful beam. It's a 1200-lumen LED flashlight, which in practical terms means it can reach 155 meters and runs for 500 hours on its lower settings. Digging into the specs, it boasts a whole bunch of geeky features like an eye-strain-free non-PWM beam and 4000K and 5000K color temperatures. The flashlight sells for a pretty reasonable $35.99, too.

It's durable, waterproof (IPX8, which means 30 meters underwater for 30 minutes), pocketable, and has a magnetic bottom to attach to things. And importantly for our purposes, it supports USB-C charging, not replaceable batteries. People who review flashlights love it. I don't know about you, but when a geek in a highly niche category gives something the thumbs up, that's all I need.

Recent findings suggest that one too many USB-A devices still exist for the transition to USB-C to be complete, but luckily some of them can be "retrofitted," particularly USB storage devices like sticks and external drives. Take this Anker USB-C adapter. Unlike a lot of USB-C adapters I've used that only support glacial USB 2.0 transfer speeds, this one has USB 3.0, which means 5 Gbps (or 5,120 Mbps), so drives with USB-A plugs are able to move files at not-snail speeds.

Industry observers note that plus, these plugs are high quality, so I've been able to leave them on the devices that they retrofit basically permanently, only taking them off if I needed them somewhere else. Anker states that aside from USB storage, it can support other things like peripherals, printers, cameras, and data transfer from mobile devices. It's only $12.99 for a two-pack, and it's one of those things you can buy blindly for basically any geek in your life, knowing they will, in all likelihood, have a use for it.

According to recent reports, some people use ointments to treat bug bites, but geeks? They want technical solutions. So if they're prone to bug bites, grab them the heat it USB-C Bug Bite Healer. Heat it found a highly unconventional solution to alleviating bug-bite itch that's backed by science: heating the site rapidly to 124 degrees Fahrenheit without burning you. No, really. It's a USB-C dongle you connect to your phone and activate with an app before applying to the site. Done. No more itching, no more pain.

In a recent development, it sounds like one of those sketchy products you'd see in a Walgreens aisle on a shelf labeled "as seen on TV," a shelf you probably avoid. Except this time, the product actually works. People who have used heat it on real bug bites can attest to relief lasting hours, with only really bad bites needing repeat treatments. Since it plugs into your phone, you can bring it with you anywhere, and it uses only an infinitesimally small fraction of your battery per bite. Geeks who go out into Mother Nature — yes, they do exist, raising my hand here — will love it. And for $29.95, it's the cheapest lifelong treatment option money can buy.

In a recent development, as geeks ourselves who know what geeks want, we carefully selected items on this list so they aren't stocking stuffers that will eventually end up in an e-waste bin. Most importantly, we focused on small, relatively cheap gadgets that fit into a stocking and a tight-ish budget; after all, stocking stuffers usually aren't expensive presents. Voile, a rock-solid list of recommendations we're confident includes at least one perfect gift for any tech geek this holiday season.

It utilizes a real-time fresh-water roller cleaning system. It has a four-stage process that combines water spraying, active scrubbing, dirt scraping, and wastewater recovery. Lefant notes that the cycle is designed to refresh the cleaning surface during operation rather than simply dragging the same damp pad across the floor.

Sources indicate that this system uses a 20cm roller operating at up to 240 RPM, with a stated contact pressure of 15N. According to Lefant, the roller is designed to tackle common household stains such as coffee, soy sauce, fruit juice, milk, and ketchup.

It also has an 800ml dustbin positioned in the upper section of the robot. When the robot returns to the station, it automatically replenishes fresh water, drains wastewater, rinses the roller, and dries it with airflow.

It has been revealed that the station has a 2.4L clean-water tank and a separate 1.5L wastewater tank. Keeping the water supplies separate supports the fresh-water cleaning cycle and allows dirty water collected during operation to be stored independently.

The all-in-one station automates roller washing, fresh-water replenishment, wastewater collection, and air drying.

  • It has been revealed that democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton.
  • According to recent reports, even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Major Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

It has been revealed that democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail.

According to recent reports, even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry's DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That's when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities, began changing course himself.

Developers noted the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and latest ones could be halted altogether.

In a recent development, the governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.

That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Significant Tech, which have ambitious intends for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center at the moment operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.

Recent findings suggest that the potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on upcoming ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.

Recent findings suggest that voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on latest data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Substantial Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.

A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.

It has been revealed that it’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.

According to recent reports, this is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.

Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While many tools advertise their uses on the box, sometimes companies pick odd names. Just look at the catalog of Leatherman camping multitools. You'd assume the Signal includes a flare gun or something similar. Yet the multitool has a ferro rod to start fires, but no flares. By that same token, some people might shop for Leatherman tools wondering what an "EOD" is. It's just a not-so-fancy way of saying army personnel use them to make battlefields safer.

The term "EOD" is little more than an acronym that stands for "Explosives Ordinance Disposal," sort of like how "IED" stands for "Improvised Explosive Device." However, an "EOD" label only means that the multitool was designed with bomb squads in mind. Even though you can easily purchase one through the Leatherman website — such as the MUT EOD, which costs $229.95 — owning one doesn't immediately make you a bomb disposal expert.

In a recent development, so what sets a Leatherman EOD multitool apart from the rest of the firm's catalog? Well, they aren't more expensive, and while EOD tools are certainly heavy and seemingly built to withstand a ton of abuse, they aren't heavier than similar Leatherman products. Instead, it comes down to loadouts.

The MUT EOD, for instance, shares many tools with the standard MUT multitool, including needlenose pliers, a saw, a combo knife (a knife with an edge divided into straight and serrated sections), and a hammer. However, the MUT EOD includes unique attachments such as fuse wire cutters (which cut wires without producing sparks) and a C4 Punch (which punches holes into plastic explosives). This specialization comes at a cost, however: the MUT EOD only includes 15 tools, whereas the vanilla MUT boasts 16 attachments.

While Leatherman's MUT EOD is a variant of the standard MUT (which is currently sold out), the MUT EOD isn't Leatherman's only EOD offering. Aside from the MUT EOD, the Super Tool 300 EOD is Leatherman's only other dedicated EOD multitool.

Sources indicate that as its name suggests, this product is a variant of the Super Tool 300 — one of the best Leatherman multitools for gardening, we might add. Like the MUT EOD, the Super Tool 300 EOD trades out certain attachments for instruments you might find in a bomb disposal unit's toolbox, such as a specialized t-shank metal saw. Don't worry, the Super Tool 300 EOD still has the awl tool you can find on the regular Leatherman Super Tool 300.

Recent findings suggest that even though Leatherman's catalog of EOD multitools only consists of two products, the company also offers EOD attachments, such as a wire cutter kit and that C4 punch. These aren't standalone tools, however; they are primarily designed to replace the specialized instruments that come with EOD multitools, as they wear out with regular use.

It has been revealed that then there's the MUT EOD Accessory Kit, which can either serve as an inventory of replacement tools or retrofit a standard MUT into a MUT EOD. And yes, Leatherman sells a MUT Accessory Kit that can replace broken MUT tools or turn a MUT EOD into a regular MUT.

#27. I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1336 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview

I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner.
  • It has been revealed that I was also motivated by journalistic interest.
  • Recent findings suggest that because this data is so valuable to Tau, the firm charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.

It has been revealed that I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.

Recent findings suggest that because this data is so valuable to Tau, the firm charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.

Industry observers note that but the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.

Industry observers note that with all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.

The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.

It has been revealed that when I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.

Sources indicate that inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she indicates that’s no longer necessary.).

In a recent development, you can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl promptly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.

In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.

According to recent reports, the robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.

But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she noted when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.

According to recent reports, tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.

Industry News: I'm ditching Google Keep for good; Claude and ChatGPT are why

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are many note-taking apps that are more powerful than Google Keep.
  • It has been perfect for these tasks because it works across all my devices and is simple and fast to use.
  • But as I have started integrating more AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude into my daily workflow, Keep's biggest limitation has become impossible to ignore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are many note-taking apps that are more powerful than Google Keep. Yet I keep coming back to it when I need to promptly take a note, save links, or capture ideas before they slip my mind.

It has been perfect for these tasks because it works across all my devices and is simple and fast to use.

But as I have started integrating more AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude into my daily workflow, Keep's biggest limitation has become impossible to ignore.

It keeps my notes locked away from the other AI assistants I use every day, and that's pushing me to switch.

In a recent development, the sole reason I have stuck with Google Keep for so long is its simplicity. I don't need a complicated note-taking system with nested folders or elaborate formatting options.

In a recent development, while those features are nice to have, they aren't what I want when I need to jot something down swiftly. That's where Keep excels, and that's why, despite its flaws and shortcomings, it has remained an integral part of my workflow.

But most of the time, the information I capture ends up sitting in Keep until I remember to search for it.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes I forget I saved something useful. Even when I remember, I need to manually find that note and copy its content into whichever app I am using.

This workflow made sense until last year. However, the more I integrate Claude and ChatGPT into my workflow, the more I realize how big a bottleneck Keep is becoming.

Recent findings suggest that I use both ChatGPT and Claude to brainstorm ideas, research topics, organize information, and work through tasks. For that, these assistants need access to the relevant information I stored in Keep. But they can't see those notes, and that's a problem.

Until a few months ago, my biggest complaint with Google Keep was its limited formatting options and basic organization features. Now, it's the lack of an official Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration.

In a recent development, MCP allows AI assistants to talk to external apps and services. Instead of making you copy information between apps and an AI assistant, it lets the assistant access that data and take relevant actions.

It is an open standard, so nothing stops Google from bringing it to Google Keep.

For example, if Google Keep supported MCP, I could ask Claude or ChatGPT to search my notes about useful Android apps I have come across this year, summarize the information, and turn it into something useful.

Or I could ask ChatGPT to go through my saved ideas, tell me their pros and cons, and suggest how I could implement them.

Since Keep doesn't integrate with ChatGPT or Claude through MCP, I have to do all this manually: search for the notes, copy their content, and paste it into the AI assistant I'm using. All of this slows down my workflow.

It has been revealed that the frustrating part is that Google has started embracing MCP across its Workspace products. It offers developer preview MCP integrations for Google Drive, Docs, Gmail, and Calendar. But for some reason, Keep is missing. And while there are some unofficial Google Keep MCP servers, I am not comfortable using them.

There's also a Keep API; however, it's primarily meant for enterprise and security use cases.

Keep only talks to Gemini, Google's own AI assistant. However, it's not my preferred assistant for several reasons.

I would love to end this article by saying that I have found a perfect Google Keep replacement with MCP integration. However, that's not the case.

It has been revealed that many note-taking apps offer MCP integration, so finding one isn't difficult when you look outside Google's ecosystem. The problem is that they are not as simple or quick to use as Google Keep. Plus, some excellent note-taking apps are still only available on iPhones and Macs.

For me, a replacement needs to get the basics right first. I should be able to rapidly open the app and capture a thought in a few seconds. I don't want to select a folder, pick from a template, or deal with an overly complicated interface.

It has been revealed that google Keep gets a lot right, which makes moving away from it harder than expected. But my workflow has changed, and I need my note-taking app to change with it.

Recent findings suggest that quickly capturing an idea or note is now only one part of the equation. I also want my AI agent to take action on it automatically, even when I am away from my PC.

Until Google opens up Keep to those assistants, I'll have to look for an alternative that fits how I work.

Why Your Air Conditioner Might Sound Like Running Water

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, after installing any type of newly introduced air conditioner, you might hear a variety of sounds.
  • Sources indicate that the sound of water flowing is usually caused by the refrigerant flowing around the system.
  • You might also hear a similar flowing sound when the system is first switched on, as the refrigerant flows more swiftly in order to promptly start cooling your home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after installing any type of newly introduced air conditioner, you might hear a variety of sounds. Some of them are nothing to worry about, and others are a potential cause for concern. One sound that's common to hear is the sound of water flowing or running. In most cases, this sound is simply a result of the system's normal operation, so you don't have to concern yourself with trying to fix it.

Sources indicate that the sound of water flowing is usually caused by the refrigerant flowing around the system. If your system has both an indoor coil and an outdoor coil, you're likely to notice it more during the winter months, when the system is going through a defrost cycle. This is because colder temperatures can eventually lead to condensation collecting and freezing on the outdoor coil, even if the ambient temperature outside isn't below freezing. The defrost cycle switches the direction of the refrigerant to temporarily heat up the outdoor coil, melting any condensation and therefore ensuring that the system can keep working efficiently.

You might also hear a similar flowing sound when the system is first switched on, as the refrigerant flows more swiftly in order to promptly start cooling your home. In any case, a running water sound on its own isn't a reason to worry. Other similar watery noises can also be part of a system's normal operation, like dripping or occasional sloshing sounds. However, there are some other air conditioner sounds and smells that could be an indication that something is amiss.

Recent findings suggest that if you've already had your air conditioner installed for some time and it suddenly starts making louder sounds than it did before, it's worth investigating further. An unusually loud sound when the system starts or stops can indicate that there's an glitch with the system's compressor or capacitor. Unusually loud humming or clicking sounds while the system is running can also indicate a fault, with various components potentially being the cause.

It has been revealed that A sudden hissing sound might be the result of a leak in the system, and this isn't definitely something that should be ignored. It's best to shut off the system and call in a professional to diagnose the glitch. Aside from that, an unexpected sound on its own isn't an immediate sign that you'll need to replace your HVAC system. But if it's paired with other red flags — like a sudden loss of heating and cooling performance or a strange, unpleasant smell — the system may need repairs. Make sure you're on top of routine maintenance to keep an air conditioner system in good working order and minimize the chance of encountering the most common problems. That includes cleaning out the air filters and servicing the air conditioner itself regularly to prevent concerns.

Sources indicate that google is giving Gemini another way to make itself useful by connecting the AI assistant to Google Wallet. The integration opens up possibilities for spending summaries and budgeting suggestions, making Gemini more like a personal financial assistant.

Starting today, customers in the US on Android, iOS and the web can link Google Wallet to the Gemini app via Plaid, a third party service that connects bank and credit card accounts. The integration is done through Gemini’s Connected Apps feature, which gives the assistant access to information from supported Google services.

Then, you can pull up @Google Wallet in Gemini to roast — or more respectfully, analyze — your purchase history. Gemini can then visualize cash flow, track asset allocation and help you build budgets based on actual spending rather than rough estimates.

Google has some real-world examples. You can ask Gemini to look at your spending last quarter and find a way to save $1,000 over the next three months. It can also identify recurring subscriptions, flag services that increased their prices, and use last year’s holiday spending to suggest a more realistic budget for the next shopping season.

In a recent development, of course, there are some reasonable privacy questions about giving an AI access to your financial activity. According to Google, Gemini can view your information, but it can't transfer money, manage accounts, make investments or complete transactions. You can also control the connection and turn it on or off anytime you want.

The feature is part of Google’s broader Personal Intelligence push, which already ties Gemini to services like Gmail, Google Photos, YouTube, and Search.

Recent findings suggest that to try it, open Gemini, go to Settings, tap Personal Intelligence>Connected Apps, and add Google Wallet. You can also prompt @Google Wallet to start with a tag.

Industry observers note that it's not hard to guess whether customers will trust Gemini enough to incorporate it into their financial routine. But at least, for now, Google is keeping the assistant on the advisory side of the equation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting latest technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance.

Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, states the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test upcoming hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it's not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.”.

Industry observers note that scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust.

"Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they're about to create," Rao notes, "things go a lot better." Cloud infrastructure also gives the manufacturer flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers.

These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product's life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI's ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands.

Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It's not just a single technology. I think it's the combination of all of these, and it'll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.".

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that so long as you maintain it properly, a chainsaw chain can last a reasonably long time.
  • Recent findings suggest that the reasoning behind this comes down to how wood reacts to colder temperatures.
  • Industry observers note that additionally, this angle lowering will put less strain on your guide bar, since you won't find yourself pushing it through the wood with prematurely dulled blades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that so long as you maintain it properly, a chainsaw chain can last a reasonably long time. This entails not pushing it beyond its physical limits, remembering to clean it, and, naturally, sharpening it once the blade edges begin to dull. Adding further nuance to that third task, you should be mindful of the angle you're sharpening the chain blades. As it turns out, when temperatures drop and winter is in full swing, you want to slightly lower the blade angle more than you normally would. This is done to make wood-cutting easier, and put less stress on your tool in the process.

Recent findings suggest that the reasoning behind this comes down to how wood reacts to colder temperatures. Temperatures drop and lead to freezing, which makes trees and branches notable harder than they would be during warmer weather. Thus, you don't want an especially sharp, high-angled series of blades on your chain, as their cutting edge will struggle and break faster on the hardened wood. Instead, you should bring your sharpening angle down by about five degrees, finding a nice balance between your chain's ability to bite through the wood and remain durable enough to avoid breaking down promptly.

Industry observers note that additionally, this angle lowering will put less strain on your guide bar, since you won't find yourself pushing it through the wood with prematurely dulled blades. That stated, as important as lowering your chainsaw blade's angle is, it's just one part of winter chainsaw use to keep in mind. There are other precautions and chainsaw additions to consider before trimming branches or felling trees in the cold.

By keeping your blade angle low during the freezing winter months, you've taken care of just one key element of chainsaw use and maintenance during this time of year. There are a few other elements worth highlighting to further ready your chainsaw for winter, such as changing out the chain and bar oil for a winter-specific blend. For the latter, this oil type not only prevents rust and keeps essential parts moving smoothly, but its lower viscosity nature prevents gelling when temperatures get especially low. Therefore, you don't have to worry about performance struggles in this regard during wintertime.

Another great way to prepare for winter chainsaw use is to invest in winter-specific parts for your chainsaw, like starter housing and a winter air filter. This housing piece is excellent for keeping snow from entering the engine area and inhibiting performance, while a winter filter prevents ice formation that could bring similar negative impacts.

According to recent reports, additionally, like in any season, you want to keep your chainsaw clean during winter. That means wiping away debris, and not leaving it covered in snow and water, which could soon become ice. Snow can enter the fuel tank and impair performance, sawdust can trap moisture, and ice can expand and crack sensitive plastic and rubber components. When the work is done, don't forget to store your chainsaw properly, too.

Chainsaws, especially great ones, can accomplish a lot, even in the worst of conditions. Still, there's no need to make winter especially hard for your tool, hence why something as simple as adjusting your blade sharpening angle and other minor winter preparation tasks are paramount for making the season's labor just a bit easier.

Pixel Tag is a brilliant Band-Aid on a Find Hub network Google can’t easily fix

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Google Pixel Tag is here and, at least so far, it’s really good.
  • Industry observers note that the good news on Pixel Tag: this is a well-built tracker that, unlike others, is the clear product of the hardware having direct access to the software.
  • Google’s Find Hub network has improved dramatically over the two years since its launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Google Pixel Tag is here and, at least so far, it’s really good. But fresh hardware and some latest features can’t fix the core problem. Google’s Find Hub network has been restricted from the very start, and it’s not something Google can easily fix.

Industry observers note that the good news on Pixel Tag: this is a well-built tracker that, unlike others, is the clear product of the hardware having direct access to the software. Little touches like being able to adjust ringer volume on the fly combine nicely with UWB – the latter something we rarely see on third-party devices largely due to Apple – all things that elevate the Find Hub tracker to what we called the new “gold standard.”.

The bad news: this is still a Find Hub tracker.

Google’s Find Hub network has improved dramatically over the two years since its launch. Where Google originally had to admit that tracking performance was lacking (a nice way of putting it, frankly), improvements started arriving in 2025. We noticed that the network seemed to be working much better a few months after its wide rollout, and Google later confirmed speed improvements.

But, ultimately, the Find Hub network is still reeling from how it debuted.

Google had a privacy focus when launching what was originally called the “Find My Device” network, defaulting the network to only be active on Android phones in “high-traffic areas” only. Users could switch this to “all areas,” but the initial rollout defaulted to effectively cutting off anywhere that wasn’t a major metro, airport/travel hub, etc. It left the network useless to many. Google defended this as a “first-of-its-kind safety protection,” but I’d argue it hindered the network into a state of inefficacy.

It has been revealed that again, it’s gotten better since then, but it’s still not as good as it should be. Samsung’s network, limited solely to Galaxy phones, shouldn’t outperform Google’s. Find Hub trackers should be just as good as AirTags and the third-party trackers that work with Apple’s network. They’re just not, and I truly do believe it all boils down to this initial choice. One of the reasons this is getting better is that Google has been pushing owners to the “all areas” setting during the setup of a new device – I’ve noticed this on some recent devices I set up, but it’s not been completely consistent just yet. That’s a good step forward but, even if it is the new default, that still requires millions of users to upgrade their devices, and we’ve never been in a better time to not upgrade your phone.

All of that is to say, the Pixel Tag isn’t fixing this problem. Surely, it’ll give Google some needed fire to fix the problem, but fresh hardware isn’t the solution. That’s something I was discussing with 9to5Google readers on our review. UWB is a tentpole feature of the Pixel Tag, but it doesn’t change the network problems, it just improves precision finding. We needed a first-party tracker like this regardless of the state of the network, something that really takes advantage of the platform and pushes it forward, but it’s just a quick fix, a Band-Aid.

What do you think? Have you found the Find Hub network reliable enough, or is there still room for improvement? Sound off in the comments below!

Industry News: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI.
  • It has been revealed that I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are swiftly running out of time to regulate AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

It has been revealed that I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are swiftly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”.

Recent findings suggest that wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very promptly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”.

Sources indicate that wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.

In a recent development, wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener claims that couldn’t be further from the truth.

It has been revealed that “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Major Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”.

Wiener claims that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really vital to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.

Industry observers note that he also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what's going on,” he notes.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”.

Industry observers note that above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically notable that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”.

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener claims he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

Industry observers note that “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”.

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

Industry observers note that but he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”.
