If you're planning a trip in the Asia-Pacific region, this receiver can also read data from the QZSS and IRNSS satellite systems. This means mapping is fast, and a GPS fix is quick enough that you won't get lost as long as the device has charge. With Garmin claiming 16 hours of battery life in GPS mode, you shouldn't run into complications during your travels as long as you charge it at least once a day. One thing to note: it doesn't support USB-C and uses a mini USB port instead.

As useful as the GPSMAP 65s may be, they lack satellite communication. Finding a route is great, but you also need a way to contact friends and loved ones if you end up stranded on the trail. In that situation, the Garmin inReach Mini 2 lets you use sat comms to keep people updated and request an SOS if needed. It's one of the most useful mini gadgets for any camping trip. Keep in mind this device can't make voice calls — you'll have to use texts only, and those can take a while on the inReach Mini 2. Thankfully, the SOS button lets you contact Garmin's 24x7 emergency response center when you can't send a text message. You can also connect this device to your phone with the Garmin Messenger app to make things easier if this small device is a pain to type on.

Its compact size makes it a great mini gadget to take on the go, and its 3.5-ounce weight further underscores its portability. Garmin indicates this device can stay active for up to a full month on a single charge, which is great for a sat comm device that may need to stay on for a long time when you're stuck and need help. Unfortunately, to ensure your safety and maintain communication at all times, you'll have to pay a hefty amount. $349.99 is already eye-watering, but you'll also need to pay at least $7.99 per month to activate the device and use a few of its features. If you want to expand this suite of options, subscription costs can reach as high as $49.99 per month.

Industry observers note that who says that the Flip 7 is the only portable Bluetooth speaker worth buying from JBL? If you want to stick with this brand but pay less, the JBL Grip is an affordable alternative to the JBL Flip 7. For outdoorsy people, the slightly smaller design and IP68 rating make the Grip a solid Bluetooth speaker for taking into the wild. JBL says this speaker can last 14 hours at 50% volume, another reason this mini gadget is such a cost-effective purchase. This portable speaker weighs just 13.6 ounces, and the LED can also serve as a nightlight, not just add flair when the music is blaring.

Recent findings suggest that sound-wise, the JBL Grip does just enough to impress critics. However, a few caveats remain. TechRadar noted that the sound was too compressed at higher volumes, and Trusted Reviews felt the speaker walked a fine line: energetic at its best, but awfully thin otherwise. Finally, PCMag felt the audio lacked bass and high-end detail. Other issues with the JBL Grip are pretty minor, in comparison. Because the speaker lacks a mic, you can't make hands-free calls. It also lacks a USB-C cable in the box, which is a bit inconvenient but not a dealbreaker.

Industry observers note that for people who don't want to spare any expense to keep an eye on their dog at all times, the $429.99 Dogtra Pathfinder2 is an advanced collar that might be up to the task. Keep in mind this isn't a standalone device — you will need the companion app on your phone to access all its advertised features. Beyond GPS location tracking, you can set up a geofence to get alerts if your dog goes beyond these digital boundaries. This dog collar has an IPX9K waterproof rating, so your dog can jump into pools and mud puddles without worrying about the collar malfunctioning.

According to recent reports, the 9-mile range is excellent and should cover any distance your dog might head off to. However, critics didn't give the battery life the same plaudits, finding its 8- to 10-hour lifespan somewhat lacking. Critics also noted that the smartphone app can be a bit of a pain to set up for non-tech-savvy people, given the sheer number of features to mess around with. On top of that, Lion Country Supply noted that the app can start hanging after updates, which only adds to the frustration.

#8. Breaking: Who Makes NASA's Rockets, And Where Are They Built?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (417 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Breaking: Who Makes NASA's Rockets, And Where Are They Built?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for most of the history of humanity's operations in space, government agencies have taken on the brunt of operations.
  • In a recent development, for example, several hardware components of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS), one of the most powerful rockets ever made that is scheduled to take people to the moon as part of the Artemis program, were built by Northrop Grumman in Utah before being transported to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
  • It has been revealed that once completed, it's then transported to Kennedy Space Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for most of the history of humanity's operations in space, government agencies have taken on the brunt of operations. However, NASA gets help from outside manufacturers to build its rockets, working with partners such as Lockheed Martin, L3Harris, Boeing, and Airbus Defense.

In a recent development, for example, several hardware components of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS), one of the most powerful rockets ever made that is scheduled to take people to the moon as part of the Artemis program, were built by Northrop Grumman in Utah before being transported to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Meanwhile, NASA's Michoud Facility in Newly introduced Orleans — which has operated as "America's Rocket Factory" for over 50 years and seen its work launched from NASA sites in Florida and California — produces the main core stage, which was designed and led by The Boeing Firm.

It has been revealed that once completed, it's then transported to Kennedy Space Center. After all of the components arrive at their destination in Florida, they're assembled vertically in NASA's humongous Vehicle Assembly Building. When everything is put together, it's ready for the launchpad.

It has been revealed that while you might think it would be best to produce everything needed at Kennedy Space Center, that's not how NASA functions. NASA operates 10 field centers, with Kennedy Space Center being its premier multi-user spaceport. It works with around 100 private-sector partners at the site, employing nearly 250 partnership agreements.

NASA's Booster Fabrication Facility near the spaceport's Launch Complex 39 at the Kennedy Space Center is where the aft skirt and forward assembly for the twin solid rocket boosters used in the SLS are manufactured, assembled, and refurbished. It's primarily operated by Northrop Grumman alongside NASA personnel. The site also upgrades boosters, and has worked on various systems dating back to the Space Shuttle Program.

Outside of the rockets and engines needed to send humanity back to the moon, the Artemis program features the Orion spacecraft, which will take astronauts to lunar orbit and return them to Earth. Various components are produced in a variety of locations by several firms. Lockheed Martin performs the primary welding for the Crew Module at the Michoud Assembly Facility, while Airbus Defense and Space produces the European Service Module at its facility in Bremen, Germany. The design work was conducted by Lockheed out of Littleton, Colorado, while various parts and subsystems were produced in California, Latest Jersey, and Washington State.

#5. The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1151 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview

The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub.
  • It has been revealed that driving through it is surreal.
  • It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.

It has been revealed that driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Substantial Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Sources indicate that here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).

The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.

According to recent reports, elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she states—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

Recent findings suggest that the overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.

Recent findings suggest that but the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

In a recent development, the notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

Sources indicate that so what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, revealed the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Massive Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”.

#4. Should You Soak A Latest Chainsaw Chain In Oil Before Using It?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (437 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Should You Soak A Latest Chainsaw Chain In Oil Before Using It?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (437 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finally gave your trusty saw a latest chain?
  • Your first order of business should be to get out your bar and chain oil and pour an amount that will cover the entire chain in a single container.
  • In a recent development, quick pop quiz: What happens to metal once it gets warm?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finally gave your trusty saw a latest chain? The good news is that this set of teeth will make the saw nearly as good as new. The not-so-good news is that you can't just slap it on, tension it, and go chopping some trees, as you need to do some preventative care first. Generally speaking, maintaining your chainsaw chain proactively can keep rust away. The same applies to one fresh out of the box, but does that include oiling too?

In a recent development, yes. Your first order of business should be to get out your bar and chain oil and pour an amount that will cover the entire chain in a single container. Let the chain soak for a few hours, which will see to it that all the pivot points on the chain are evenly lubricated. After a generous amount of time has passed, take out the chain and hang it up, allowing the excess oil to drip off before putting it on the bar. To help avoid an oily mess, consider hanging the chain above the oil container until the droplets stop, and then install the upcoming chain.

In a recent development, quick pop quiz: What happens to metal once it gets warm? It expands. A chainsaw chain has a bunch of pivot points, so the first time you fire up the chainsaw, even if you tension the chain correctly, the heat generated will make it slack again. Thus, you'll need to break in the new chain first. Fortunately, that's relatively easy, albeit a little annoying.

Tension the chain once and then run the tool until it's warm enough. Power off the chainsaw, allow the chain to cool, and readjust the tension to eliminate the slack. Underwhelming as it may be, the upcoming chain still won't be ready for heavier work, which is why it's best to then use the chainsaw for about half an hour just cutting smaller branches. Once the saw finally starts working the way you remember, the whole world (or at least a tree or two) will be your oyster, and you can cut to your heart's content.

Sources indicate that in the future, try to incorporate chainsaw maintenance tips and tricks into your routine. Everything matters with this tool. Despite the chain being relatively cheap to purchase, the costs will add up swiftly if you start ignoring regular TLC, and you'll burn through chains as if they owe you money. So, clean your tools before and after use, store them correctly, lubricate them frequently, and they will work more reliably and cost less to own.

#2. Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (726 w)
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview

Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”.
  • Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China.
  • When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”.

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “upcoming, untested, and potentially infeasible.”.

But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the tech giant could implement them.

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster states, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.

It has been revealed that other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it declared a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

It has been revealed that in early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”.

Sources indicate that the recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

In a recent development, the Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.

Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the fresh tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster states, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”.
